name: Pathological Physiology
description: Complete study manual · 27 practical class topics

topics.title: The effect of etiologic factors on the organism. Pathophysiology: subject, methods and tasks. General nosology, etiology and pathogenesis

goals.text: To introduce the student to the subject, methods and history of pathological physiology; to master the basic concepts of the general doctrine of disease (nosology), etiology and pathogenesis; to understand the role of causes and conditions in the origin of disease; and to teach the student to analyze any disease according to the scheme “cause — conditions — pathogenesis — outcome”.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the subject of pathophysiology, its components, methods and links with other disciplines;
the main stages in the history of the discipline and its founders;
the concepts of health, disease, the “predisease” state, pathological reaction, pathological process and pathological state;
the periods and outcomes of disease and the mechanisms of recovery;
the doctrines of etiology and the difference between causes and conditions;
the concept of pathogenesis, its main link and the “vicious circle”;
the principles of the nomenclature and classification of diseases (ICD-10, ICD-11).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish the etiologic factor and the conditions in any disease;
identify the cause-and-effect chain in pathogenesis, the main link and the vicious circle;
distinguish a pathological reaction, process and state with examples;
justify the principles of etiotropic, pathogenetic and symptomatic treatment.

summary.text: The main tasks of pathophysiology: to identify the causes and conditions of diseases and pathological processes; to reveal the mechanisms of their development (pathogenesis); to study the protective, adaptive and compensatory reactions of the organism; to study the outcomes of diseases and the mechanisms of recovery; and to develop the scientific (experimental) basis of treatment and prevention.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Animals and humans differ in structure, metabolism and reactivity (interspecies differences). Therefore the result of an experiment is not transferred to humans **directly** — it must be confirmed by clinical observations. For example, rats synthesize vitamin C, whereas humans do not; for this reason a model of scurvy cannot be created in rats.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“R-P-S-D”** — Reaction → Process → State → Disease: complexity and duration increase. A reaction is “a moment”, a process is “a movement”, a state is “a trace”, a disease is “the whole organism”.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A protective-adaptive reaction can also become harmful when excessive. For example, fever is a protective reaction against infection, but above 41 °C the brain is injured; edema in inflammation delimits the focus, but laryngeal edema leads to asphyxia. This is **the dialectical unity of protection and injury**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Conventional durations by course of disease: **hyperacute** — up to 4 days, **acute** — 5–14 days, **subacute** — 15–40 days, **chronic** — months and years. These durations are defined separately for each disease and are only approximate.

summary.label: Caution

summary.label: Remember

Thus, **the cause is necessary, but not always sufficient** — disease arises from the interaction of the cause and the conditions.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The main link** is the link of the pathogenetic chain whose elimination breaks the whole chain and leads to recovery. The goal of pathogenetic treatment is precisely to find the main link and act on it. In blood loss the main link is the decrease in circulating blood volume, which is why the main treatment is transfusion of blood and blood substitutes.

summary.label: Memory aid

summary.label: Caution

A common exam mistake is to answer a question on pathogenesis with a list of causes.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Symptomatic treatment alone can be dangerous: removing the signs makes diagnosis harder, while the disease continues. For example, if an analgesic is given for “acute abdomen” pain before a diagnosis is made, the signs of acute appendicitis may be masked and peritonitis may be missed.

blocks.text: **Pathological physiology (pathophysiology)** is the science that studies the vital activity of the diseased organism and the general laws of the origin, development, course and outcomes of diseases and pathological processes. The term comes from the Greek words pathos — suffering, disease; physis — nature; logos — study.

The object of study of the discipline is the diseased organism. Pathophysiology studies disease at different levels of integration — molecular, subcellular, cellular, tissue, organ, system and whole-organism level. That is why it is considered an integrative science: on the one hand it relies on biology, physiology, biochemistry, histology and pathological anatomy, and on the other hand on the clinical disciplines.

parts.text: The main tasks of pathophysiology:

items: to identify the causes and conditions of diseases and pathological processes;
to reveal the mechanisms of their development (pathogenesis);
to study the protective, adaptive and compensatory reactions of the organism;
to study the outcomes of diseases and the mechanisms of recovery;
to develop the scientific (experimental) basis of treatment and prevention.

blocks.text: Pathophysiology and pathological anatomy are closely interrelated: pathological anatomy studies the changes in **structure** in disease, and pathophysiology studies the changes in **function**. Structure and function form an inseparable unity — there is no functional disorder without a change in structure, and vice versa.

The main method of pathophysiology is **experiment**, that is, modeling of diseases and pathological processes in animals. Experiment makes it possible to study the cause of a disease, its mechanism of development and methods of treatment without risk to humans, in dynamics and at any level of integration.

blocks.title: Table 1.2. Research methods of pathophysiology
head: Method
Essence
Advantage and limitation
rows: Artificial induction and observation of a pathological process in an animal
Studies cause and effect directly; the result cannot be fully transferred to humans
Examination of patients by functional, biochemical and immunological methods
Gives information directly about humans; the possibility of intervention is limited
Study of processes through computational models
Predicts situations in which an experiment cannot be performed
Generalization of accumulated data, creation of theories
Gives a comprehensive picture of the disease

blocks.text: The following methods are used in experiments: **removal of an organ** (extirpation — for example, modeling diabetes mellitus by removing the pancreas), **stimulation**, the **isolated organ** method, **parabiosis** (joining the circulations of two animals), **recording** (ECG, EEG, biochemical parameters), cell and tissue cultures, and genetic modeling (transgenic and “knockout” animals).

parts.text: Animals and humans differ in structure, metabolism and reactivity (interspecies differences). Therefore the result of an experiment is not transferred to humans **directly** — it must be confirmed by clinical observations. For example, rats synthesize vitamin C, whereas humans do not; for this reason a model of scurvy cannot be created in rats.

blocks.text: Bioethical rules are followed when performing experiments: reducing the animal's suffering (analgesia, anesthesia), minimizing the number of animals and, where possible, replacing them with alternative models (cell culture, computer model) (the “3R” principle: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement).

Views on the nature of disease developed together with medicine. Hippocrates (5th–4th centuries BC) regarded disease as an imbalance of four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile) (the humoral theory). In “The Canon of Medicine”, Avicenna (Ibn Sina) divided the causes of diseases into external and internal factors, suggested that infectious diseases are spread by invisible creatures, and divided medicine into theoretical and practical parts.

parts.text: The three main methodological principles of pathophysiology: **experiment** (modeling), **the systems approach** (disease is the response of the whole organism) and **cause-and-effect analysis** (determinism).

blocks.text: **Nosology** (Greek nosos — disease, logos — study) is the doctrine of disease. **General nosology** studies the general laws of the nature, causes, development and classification of disease, whereas **special nosology** studies individual diseases (nosological entities).
**Health**, according to the definition of the World Health Organization (WHO, 1948), is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

**The norm** is the state of the organism that is optimally adapted to the conditions of the external environment. The concept of the norm is relative: an increased heart rate during physical work is normal, but at rest it may be a sign of disease. The reference ranges of laboratory parameters cover 95% of the healthy population, that is, in 5% of healthy people a parameter may fall “outside the norm”.

**Disease** is a complex systemic response of the organism to the action of a harmful factor, in which injury (alteration) and protective-adaptive reactions appear at the same time; as a result, the adaptation of the organism to the external environment and its working capacity decrease.

parts.text: The main features of disease:

items: it has a cause (there is no disease without a cause);
it has two opposite sides: injury and protection-adaptation;
it is a disease of the whole organism (even with local signs, the response is systemic);
the adaptive capacity and working capacity of the organism decrease;
it is a new qualitative state: the diseased organism is not a “reduced” copy of the healthy one.

blocks.text: **The predisease (prenosological) state** is an intermediate state between health and disease: the adaptive capacity of the organism is reduced, but there are no definite signs of disease yet. Examples are intermittent rises in arterial pressure, impaired glucose tolerance (prediabetes) and chronic fatigue. Preventive measures are most effective during this period.
Pathological reaction, pathological process, pathological state

blocks.title: Table 1.4. Main forms of pathology
head: Concept
Definition
Examples
rows: A disproportionate, short-term, unusual response to a stimulus
A brief rise in arterial pressure, pathological reflexes, allergic itching
A regular combination of injury and protective-adaptive reactions
A slowly developing or stable, long-lasting change
A scar, the state after amputation, congenital defects, contracture
A combination of one or several pathological processes, with reduced working capacity

blocks.text: There is no sharp boundary between a pathological process and a pathological state: under a new influence a pathological state can again turn into a process (for example, a pigmented spot (nevus) can turn into melanoma under mechanical or ultraviolet influence).

**Typical pathological processes** are processes formed during evolution that develop according to the same laws in different diseases, different organs and different animal species: inflammation, fever, hypoxia, edema, tumor growth, degeneration, local circulatory disorders and allergy.

parts.text: **“R-P-S-D”** — Reaction → Process → State → Disease: complexity and duration increase. A reaction is “a moment”, a process is “a movement”, a state is “a trace”, a disease is “the whole organism”.

blocks.text: Protective-adaptive reactions in disease
In disease, the organism activates a number of reactions in response to injury:

items: **protective reactions** — removal and neutralization of the pathogenic factor: barriers (skin, mucous membranes, the blood-brain barrier), protective reflexes (cough, sneezing, vomiting, lacrimation), phagocytosis, the immune response;
**adaptive reactions** — adjustment of the organism's activity to changed conditions (for example, an increase in the number of red blood cells at high altitude);
**compensatory reactions** — replacement of an impaired function by other mechanisms (hypertrophy of one kidney after removal of the other, tachycardia in anemia);
**restorative (reparative) reactions** — restoration of the injured structure (regeneration).

parts.text: A protective-adaptive reaction can also become harmful when excessive. For example, fever is a protective reaction against infection, but above 41 °C the brain is injured; edema in inflammation delimits the focus, but laryngeal edema leads to asphyxia. This is **the dialectical unity of protection and injury**.

blocks.text: Outcomes of disease:

items: **Complete recovery** — the impaired structures and functions are fully restored. However, the recovered organism does not return exactly to its state before the disease: it acquires new properties (for example, immunity).
**Incomplete recovery** — some traces of the disease (residual phenomena) remain: a scar, partial reduction of organ function.
**Relapse** (recurrence) — reappearance of the signs of disease after they have disappeared. The period of improvement between relapses is called **remission**.
**Transition to a chronic form** — the disease has a long, undulating course.
**Death** — transition through terminal states (preagony, agony, clinical death) to biological death.

blocks.text: Mechanisms of recovery

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Mechanisms of recovery by speed
head: Type
Time
Examples
rows: Protective reflexes (cough, vomiting), the stress reaction (epinephrine, glucocorticoids), reflexes maintaining arterial pressure, glucose and osmotic pressure
Mobilization of the reserve capacities of organs, reactive leukocytosis, detoxification of poisons (liver), reaction of connective tissue and macrophages
Compensatory hypertrophy, reparative regeneration, immunity, plastic reactions of the central nervous system

parts.text: The reserve capacity of organs is very large: 20–25% of the respiratory surface of the lungs, 20–25% of the renal glomeruli and 12–15% of the liver parenchyma are sufficient for life. That is why chronic diseases run a “silent” course for a long time, and clinical signs appear when the organ reserve is exhausted (for example, in kidney failure when 70–80% of the glomeruli have been lost).

blocks.text: **Nomenclature** is the list of names of diseases; **classification** is the grouping of diseases according to certain features. In medical practice the international classification is used — the **International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)**. At present **ICD-11** is gradually replacing ICD-10 (it was brought into force by the WHO on 1 January 2022).

Groups

Diseases of the heart, lungs, liver, kidneys
Allergic, neoplastic, inflammatory, degenerative, metabolic diseases
Diseases of children, of the elderly (geriatrics), of women
Diseases specific to a certain geographic region (endemic), for example endemic goiter

parts.text: Conventional durations by course of disease: **hyperacute** — up to 4 days, **acute** — 5–14 days, **subacute** — 15–40 days, **chronic** — months and years. These durations are defined separately for each disease and are only approximate.

Textbooks give different durations of the course (the textbooks of N.H. Abdullaev and V.V. Novitsky differ slightly). In practice the durations for each disease are defined by the relevant clinical protocol.

blocks.text: **Etiology** (Greek aitia — cause, logos — study) is the doctrine of the causes and conditions of the origin of diseases.

**The cause of disease (etiologic factor)** is the factor that produces the disease and gives it its specific features. There is no disease without a cause, and without the action of the cause the disease does not develop.
**Conditions** are factors that do not themselves produce the disease but promote or hinder the realization of the action of the cause.

parts.text: A large part of the population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (according to the WHO, about one quarter of the world's population), but only 5–10% of them develop active tuberculosis during their lifetime. Thus, **the cause is necessary, but not always sufficient** — disease arises from the interaction of the cause and the conditions.

blocks.text: Classification of etiologic factors

blocks.title: Table 1.9. Types of etiologic factors
head: Group
Factors
rows: Mechanical injury, high and low temperature, ionizing radiation, electric current, changes in barometric pressure, acceleration, noise, vibration
Acids, alkalis, heavy metals, poisons, drugs (in overdose), alcohol

Starvation, deficiency or excess of protein, vitamins and trace elements

blocks.text: By origin, factors are **exogenous** (from the external environment) or **endogenous** (formed in the organism itself: for example, autoantibodies, tumor cells, mutated genes).
Main schools of thought in etiology

Disease results from the interaction of the cause, the conditions and the reactivity of the organism

blocks.text: **Risk factors** are factors that statistically increase the probability of developing a disease. They are mostly used for polyetiologic (multicausal) chronic diseases. For example, the risk factors for ischemic heart disease are smoking, arterial hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity, physical inactivity, hereditary predisposition, male sex and age.

parts.text: Knowing the etiologic factor makes **etiotropic treatment** (treatment directed against the cause) possible: an antibiotic in bacterial infection, an anthelmintic in helminthiasis, an antidote in poisoning. Knowing the risk factors is the basis of **prevention**: stopping smoking and controlling arterial pressure significantly reduce the risk of cardiovascular diseases.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis** (Greek pathos — disease, genesis — origin) is the doctrine of the mechanisms of development, course and resolution of diseases and pathological processes. Etiology answers the question “why?”, whereas pathogenesis answers the question “how?”.
The role of the etiologic factor in pathogenesis
The etiologic factor takes part in pathogenesis in different ways:

items: **it acts only at the onset of the disease** and then disappears (burns, mechanical trauma, ionizing radiation) — the disease continues on its own according to the laws of pathogenesis;
**it acts throughout the disease** (most infectious diseases, helminthic infestations) — in this case removing the cause leads to recovery.

blocks.text: Basic concepts of pathogenesis

Each effect becomes the cause of the next change

Cell injury by a toxin, followed by edema and ischemia
The change that determines the development of the disease and on which all other links depend
Insulin deficiency in diabetes mellitus; decreased circulating blood volume in blood loss

A local process produces systemic reactions, and vice versa

parts.text: **The main link** is the link of the pathogenetic chain whose elimination breaks the whole chain and leads to recovery. The goal of pathogenetic treatment is precisely to find the main link and act on it. In blood loss the main link is the decrease in circulating blood volume, which is why the main treatment is transfusion of blood and blood substitutes.

**Vicious circle = “the snake bites its own tail”**: the consequence comes back and amplifies the cause. To break it, any link of the circle can be targeted, but the most effective is to act on the main link.

blocks.text: The unity of structure and function in pathogenesis

Any functional change is based on a certain structural change — it may be at the molecular or subcellular level and may not be detectable by ordinary methods. The concept of “functional” diseases (for example, neuroses) only means that no structural change has been found with current research methods.
The role of the nervous and endocrine systems in pathogenesis

The nervous system plays a dual role in pathogenesis: it regulates protective reactions (reflexes, stress), and at the same time it can itself be the source of a pathological process (neuroses, pathological reflexes, degenerative processes). The endocrine system regulates the stress reaction (the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system), metabolism and reactivity.

parts.text: Do not confuse “etiology” and “pathogenesis”. “The etiology of pneumonia is the pneumococcus” (cause); “the pathogenesis of pneumonia is inflammation in the alveoli, accumulation of exudate, impaired gas exchange, hypoxemia” (mechanism). A common exam mistake is to answer a question on pathogenesis with a list of causes.

head: Type of treatment
Goal
Examples
rows: To remove or weaken the cause of the disease
Antibiotics, antidotes, anthelmintics, removal of a foreign body
To break the links of pathogenesis, especially the main link
Insulin in diabetes; infusion in blood loss; diuretics in edema

To supply a lost function from outside
Hemodialysis, hormone replacement therapy, enzyme preparations
To restore function and working capacity

parts.text: Symptomatic treatment alone can be dangerous: removing the signs makes diagnosis harder, while the disease continues. For example, if an analgesic is given for “acute abdomen” pain before a diagnosis is made, the signs of acute appendicitis may be masked and peritonitis may be missed.

sections.title: 10. Practical part: pathophysiological analysis of a disease

blocks.text: No experiment is performed in this session; the main practical task is to learn to analyze a clinical situation from the standpoint of etiology and pathogenesis. The analysis is carried out according to the following plan.
Plan for analyzing a disease

items: Identify the etiologic factor (cause) and state its type (physical, chemical, biological, etc.).
Distinguish the conditions (external and internal) that promoted and those that hindered the development of the disease.
Identify the initial injury (at which level and in which structure).
Write down the cause-and-effect chain of pathogenesis in sequence.
Mark the main link and, if present, the vicious circle.
Distinguish local and systemic, specific and nonspecific changes.
State the protective-adaptive and compensatory reactions.
Determine the period of the disease and its probable outcome.
Justify the directions of etiotropic, pathogenetic and symptomatic treatment.

blocks.text: Example: pathophysiological analysis of lobar pneumonia

blocks.title: Table 1.13. Analysis of lobar pneumonia
head: Stage
Content
rows: Chilling, fatigue, alcoholism, old age, recent influenza, smoking (impaired bronchial clearance)
Injury of the alveolar epithelium and capillaries by toxins and inflammatory mediators
Inflammation → fibrinous exudate in the alveoli → consolidation of the lung lobe → ventilation-perfusion mismatch → hypoxemia → tachypnea, tachycardia
Inflammation and exudation in the alveoli
Hypoxemia → myocardial hypoxia → decreased cardiac output → worsening hypoxia
Local: consolidation of the lobe, crepitation, pleuritic pain; systemic: fever, leukocytosis, intoxication
Etiotropic — antibiotic; pathogenetic — oxygen therapy, detoxification; symptomatic — antipyretics, expectorants

parts.text: A student who has mastered this plan can independently analyze any disease in the clinical departments. The structure of the clinical diagnosis is based on the same logic: the underlying disease (with its etiology), complications (consequences of pathogenesis) and concomitant diseases.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing cause and conditions

items: Find the factor that gives the disease its specific features — this is the cause.
Ask whether the disease could develop without it: if not, this factor is the cause.
Determine whether other factors increase or decrease the probability of the disease; these are conditions.
Divide the conditions into external (environment) and internal (organism) groups.
Write a conclusion: “Cause — ...; promoting conditions — ...; hindering conditions — ...”.

skills.title: Skill: drawing a scheme of pathogenesis

items: Write the etiologic factor at the top of the scheme.
Indicate the initial injury.
Connect each subsequent change with an arrow to build the cause-and-effect chain.
Check which link, if removed, makes the others disappear as well — this is the main link.
Find the place where the effect amplifies its own cause and mark it with a reverse arrow — this is the vicious circle.
Add the protective-compensatory reactions to the scheme in a different color.
Mark the points targeted by pathogenetic treatment.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Four members of one family fell ill with influenza at the same time. The 25-year-old son recovered in 5 days. The 70-year-old grandmother, who has diabetes mellitus, was hospitalized with secondary bacterial pneumonia against the background of influenza. The father (45 years old, smokes 20 cigarettes a day) was treated for a long time for the complication of bronchitis. The mother had previously been vaccinated against influenza and had a mild form of the disease.
cases.ask: What is the cause of the disease? What factors can explain the different courses of the disease? Which rule of etiology does this example confirm?
cases.answer: The cause is the influenza virus (a biological etiologic factor); it is the same in all family members. The different courses of the disease depend on the conditions and the reactivity of the organism: in the grandmother, old age and diabetes mellitus (reduced immunity and regeneration) are promoting internal conditions; in the father, smoking has impaired the mucociliary clearance of the bronchi; in the mother, the immunity produced by vaccination is a hindering condition. The example confirms the modern view that “the cause is necessary, but the course and outcome of the disease depend on the interaction of the cause, the conditions and the reactivity of the organism” and shows the limitations of monocausalism.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 40-year-old patient lost 1.5 liters of blood as a result of bleeding from a gastric ulcer. Arterial pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min, the skin is pale and covered with cold sweat. The ECG shows signs of myocardial ischemia.
cases.ask: Indicate the main link of pathogenesis. What vicious circle has formed in the patient? What should pathogenetic treatment be aimed at?
cases.answer: The main link is a sharp decrease in circulating blood volume (hypovolemia). Vicious circle: hypovolemia → decreased venous return to the heart → decreased cardiac output and arterial pressure → decreased coronary blood flow → myocardial hypoxia → decreased contractility → further decrease in cardiac output. Tachycardia and spasm of the skin vessels are compensatory reactions. Pathogenetic treatment is aimed at the main link: restoration of circulating blood volume by transfusion of blood and blood substitutes; this also breaks the vicious circle. Etiotropic treatment is stopping the bleeding (endoscopic or surgical hemostasis).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: At an exam, a student answered: “The pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes mellitus is hereditary predisposition, viral infections and stress.” The teacher marked the answer as wrong.
cases.ask: What mistake did the student make? Briefly state the correct pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes mellitus and indicate the main link.
cases.answer: The student confused etiology (causes and conditions) with pathogenesis (the mechanism of development): hereditary predisposition, viruses and stress are etiologic factors and conditions. Pathogenesis: autoimmune injury of the pancreatic beta cells → insulin deficiency → decreased entry of glucose into tissues, increased gluconeogenesis and lipolysis → hyperglycemia, glucosuria, polyuria, ketoacidosis. The main link is insulin deficiency; therefore the pathogenetic treatment is insulin replacement therapy.

topics.title: The importance of external conditions in the development of pathological processes. The pathogenic action of physical, chemical and biological factors

goals.text: To explain to the student the role of external environmental conditions in the origin and development of diseases and pathological processes; to teach the mechanisms of the pathogenic action of physical (temperature, barometric pressure, electric current, ionizing radiation, mechanical action), chemical, biological and social factors; and to teach the student to observe and analyze in an experiment the effect of ambient temperature on the development of hypoxic hypoxia.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of external conditions and their role in the development of disease;
the stages, pathogenesis and outcomes of hyperthermia and hypothermia;
the mechanisms of the changes caused by decreased and increased atmospheric pressure (mountain sickness, decompression sickness);
the mechanisms of the pathogenic action of electric current and ionizing radiation, and the forms of acute radiation sickness;
the features of the action of chemical, biological and socio-ecological factors;
how ambient temperature changes resistance to hypoxia.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to create a model of hypoxic hypoxia in a pressure chamber and record its stages;
to compare the resistance to hypoxia of animals kept at different temperatures and explain the result;
to analyze a pathological state caused by an external factor according to the scheme “cause — conditions — pathogenesis”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: External conditions act in two ways: **promoting** — they amplify the action of the cause (chilling, starvation, fatigue, stress, air pollution); **hindering** — they weaken the action of the cause or prevent the development of disease (proper nutrition, hardening, physical activity, vaccination, hygiene).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Do not confuse **hyperthermia** and **fever**! In fever, the thermoregulatory center is “reset” by pyrogens to maintain the temperature at a higher level (an active process). In hyperthermia, the thermoregulatory center tries to maintain the normal level, but heat loss is insufficient (passive heat accumulation). That is why antipyretics (paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen) are ineffective in hyperthermia — the body must be cooled physically.

summary.text: Prevention of decompression sickness: slow, stepwise ascent from high pressure (according to decompression tables) and use of a helium mixture for breathing instead of nitrogen. Treatment: immediate placement of the patient in a pressure chamber, raising the pressure again (recompression) and then lowering it slowly.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The law of Bergonié and Tribondeau:** the radiosensitivity of a tissue is directly proportional to the mitotic activity of its cells and inversely proportional to their degree of differentiation. The most sensitive tissues are hematopoietic tissue (bone marrow), lymphoid tissue, intestinal epithelium and germ cells. The most resistant are nervous tissue, muscle and bone.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The time of onset of the primary reaction (vomiting) gives an approximate idea of the dose: the earlier vomiting begins, the higher the dose. The patient's feeling of well-being in the latent period is deceptive — it is precisely during this period that the reserve of bone marrow cells is being depleted.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The pathogenicity of an external factor depends on three things: **the factor itself** (its nature, strength and duration), **the conditions of action** (in what environment and by what route it acts) and **the reactivity of the organism**. The same factor can be harmless under one condition and fatal under another.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The effect of cold has two stages: with brief chilling (while body temperature has not yet fallen), thermogenesis in the mouse — shivering and metabolism — increases, oxygen demand **rises**, and resistance to hypoxia may decrease. Resistance increases only **after body temperature has fallen** (hypothermia). That is why in the experiment it is important to check by body temperature that the mouse has been cooled sufficiently.

blocks.text: As discussed in the previous topic, disease develops from the interaction of the cause and the conditions. Conditions are **external** (related to the environment) or **internal** (related to the organism itself). The same factor may be a cause in one case and a condition in another: for example, low temperature is the **cause** of frostbite but a **condition** of pneumonia (chilling lowers the organism's resistance to infection).

parts.text: External conditions act in two ways:

items: **promoting** — they amplify the action of the cause (chilling, starvation, fatigue, stress, air pollution);
**hindering** — they weaken the action of the cause or prevent the development of disease (proper nutrition, hardening, physical activity, vaccination, hygiene).

blocks.text: Humans are homeothermic (warm-blooded) organisms: their body temperature is kept at about 36–37 °C by the balance between heat production (thermogenesis) and heat loss (thermolysis). The thermoregulatory center is located in the hypothalamus. When the external temperature is very high or very low, this balance is disturbed and **hyperthermia** or **hypothermia** develops.
The action of high temperature. Hyperthermia

**Hyperthermia** is a rise in body temperature resulting from insufficient heat loss relative to heat production. It occurs with high external temperature, high air humidity (sweat does not evaporate), heat-insulating clothing and heavy physical work.

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Stages of hyperthermia
head: Stage
Mechanism
Signs
rows: Thermolysis increases: skin vessels dilate, sweating increases, breathing becomes rapid; thermogenesis decreases
Body temperature almost normal, flushed skin, profuse sweating, tachycardia
Thermoregulatory mechanisms are insufficient, heat accumulates
Body temperature rises above 40–41 °C, weakness, headache, nausea, dehydration
Injury of the thermoregulatory center, cerebral edema, collapse
Sweating stops, the skin is dry and hot, loss of consciousness, convulsions, disturbed breathing and cardiac activity

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of heatstroke (based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009, Fig. 2.2)

parts.text: Do not confuse **hyperthermia** and **fever**! In fever, the thermoregulatory center is “reset” by pyrogens to maintain the temperature at a higher level (an active process). In hyperthermia, the thermoregulatory center tries to maintain the normal level, but heat loss is insufficient (passive heat accumulation). That is why antipyretics (paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen) are ineffective in hyperthermia — the body must be cooled physically.

blocks.text: **Sunstroke** is overheating, hyperemia and edema of the brain and its membranes resulting from the direct action of the sun's rays on the head. Its main signs are severe headache, vomiting and impaired consciousness.

**A burn** is the local action of high temperature. By depth, degrees I–IV are distinguished. With extensive burns (more than 15–20% of the body surface, and even less in children and the elderly), **burn disease** develops: it runs through the periods of burn shock, toxemia, septicotoxemia and recovery.

parts.text: The **“rule of nines”** for estimating the burned area: head and neck — 9%, each arm — 9%, front of the trunk — 18%, back of the trunk — 18%, each leg — 18%, perineum — 1%. The patient's palm (with the fingers) equals about 1% of the body surface.

blocks.text: The action of low temperature. Hypothermia

**Hypothermia** is a fall in body temperature below normal (below 35 °C) resulting from heat loss exceeding heat production. In cold water the body cools much faster than in air, because the thermal conductivity of water is about 25 times higher than that of air.

blocks.title: Table 2.3. Stages of hypothermia
head: Stage
Mechanism
Signs
rows: Thermogenesis increases (shivering, increased metabolism), thermolysis decreases (skin vessels constrict)
Pale skin, “goose bumps”, shivering, tachycardia, raised arterial pressure
Thermoregulatory mechanisms are exhausted, the central nervous system is inhibited
Body temperature falls, shivering stops, drowsiness, bradycardia, slow breathing, hypoxia
The activity of the vital centers ceases
Below 24–25 °C — ventricular fibrillation or respiratory arrest

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Degrees of clinical hypothermia
head: Degree
Body temperature
Main signs
rows: Shivering, tachycardia, apathy, impaired coordination of movements
Coma, loss of reflexes, risk of ventricular fibrillation

parts.text: **Artificial hypothermia** is used in medicine: in heart and brain operations, cooling the body to 28–32 °C reduces the oxygen demand of tissues and increases their resistance to hypoxia. In resuscitation after cardiac arrest, targeted temperature management protects the brain. This rule is also confirmed in the experimental part of the session.

blocks.text: **Frostbite** is the local action of low temperature. Its main mechanism is vascular spasm, slowing of blood flow, stasis and thrombosis, tissue ischemia and necrosis. The fingers, ears, nose and feet are most often affected.
Decreased atmospheric pressure. Mountain sickness and altitude sickness

When ascending to altitude, two factors act on the organism: **decreased atmospheric pressure (decompression)** and **decreased partial pressure of oxygen (pO~2~) in the air**. As P. Bert and I.M. Sechenov showed, the main pathogenic factor of altitude is the fall in pO2 and the resulting **hypoxic (exogenous) hypoxia**.

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Atmospheric pressure and partial pressure of oxygen by altitude (approximate)
head: Altitude
Atmospheric pressure
pO2 in the air

blocks.title: Table 2.6. Zones of the effect of altitude on the human organism (N.H. Abdullaev, 2008)
head: Zone
Altitude
State of the organism
rows: No significant changes, working capacity fully preserved
Pulmonary ventilation and cardiac output increase; heavy physical work becomes difficult
General condition deteriorates, headache, euphoria, reduced working capacity
Working capacity is profoundly impaired; an unacclimatized person quickly loses consciousness at 7000 m
Without oxygen a person remains conscious for 2–3 minutes, followed by profound inhibition and death

blocks.text: **Mountain sickness** develops gradually, several hours or days after ascent; **altitude sickness**, in contrast, arises rapidly (within minutes and seconds) when the sealing of an aircraft is suddenly lost.

Pathogenesis of mountain sickness: fall in pO2 → hypoxemia → stimulation of chemoreceptors → hyperventilation → hypocapnia and respiratory (gas) alkalosis → constriction of cerebral vessels → worsening of cerebral hypoxia. In severe cases **pulmonary edema** and **cerebral edema** develop.

**Changes related to decompression:** intestinal gases expand (at 6000 m the volume of gas roughly doubles) — flatulence, abdominal pain; pain in closed cavities (middle ear, maxillary sinus); above 7000–8000 m, nitrogen dissolved in the blood forms bubbles (gas embolism); at an altitude of about 19 km, water begins to boil at body temperature (“altitude emphysema”).

parts.text: Mechanisms of adaptation (acclimatization): hyperventilation, tachycardia, release of red blood cells from blood depots (urgent); increased production of erythropoietin in the kidneys, increased red blood cell count and hemoglobin, increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in red blood cells, and an increased number of capillaries and mitochondria in tissues (long-term). Stepwise ascent into the mountains (N.N. Sirotinin's method) prevents mountain sickness.

blocks.text: Increased atmospheric pressure. Decompression sickness

Under water, pressure increases by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 m of depth. Under high pressure (divers, caisson workers), more gas dissolves in the blood and tissues — **saturation**. Nitrogen accumulates especially in lipid-rich tissues (nervous tissue, adipose tissue) and causes **nitrogen narcosis** (euphoria, then impaired coordination of movements and clouding of consciousness). A high partial pressure of oxygen leads to **oxygen toxicity** (formation of free radicals, injury of the lungs and central nervous system).

**Decompression (caisson) sickness** is gas embolism, tissue ischemia and compression of nerve endings resulting from the release of nitrogen dissolved in the blood and tissues in the form of bubbles (**desaturation**) during rapid transition from high to normal pressure. Signs: pain in joints and muscles, itching of the skin, shortness of breath, paralysis.

parts.text: Prevention of decompression sickness: slow, stepwise ascent from high pressure (according to decompression tables) and use of a helium mixture for breathing instead of nitrogen. Treatment: immediate placement of the patient in a pressure chamber, raising the pressure again (recompression) and then lowering it slowly.

blocks.text: Electric current acts on the organism in two ways: **specifically** (electrochemical, electrothermal, electromechanical action) and **nonspecifically** (injury by light, sound and mechanical force). The harmful effect of current depends on the following:

items: **current strength** (the main factor) — a current of more than 0.1 A passing through the heart can cause ventricular fibrillation;
**voltage** — a voltage above 40 V is considered dangerous;
**type and frequency of current** — alternating current with a frequency of 40–60 Hz is the most dangerous; high-frequency (UHF) current acts mainly as heat and is used in physiotherapy;
**skin resistance** — dry skin has a high resistance, while the resistance of wet skin falls sharply;
**the path of the current (“current loop”)** — paths through the heart and brain (hand — hand, left hand — legs) are the most dangerous;
**duration of exposure** and **state of the organism** (resistance changes with fatigue, alcohol and sleep).

blocks.text: Local changes: at the points of entry and exit of the current, **“current marks”** (electrical marks) — gray-yellowish, hard, painless spots; burns, tissue necrosis. Systemic changes: loss of consciousness, convulsions, respiratory arrest (paralysis of the respiratory center or tetanic contraction of the respiratory muscles), disturbance and arrest of the heart rhythm.

parts.text: First aid for electrical injury: first separate the victim from the source of current without endangering the rescuer (switch off the current, push away with dry wood), then check breathing and circulation and, if necessary, start cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Even with an apparently mild injury, the patient must remain under observation because of the risk of delayed arrhythmias.

blocks.text: Ionizing radiation (X-rays and gamma rays, alpha and beta particles, neutrons) passes through tissues and ionizes atoms and molecules. The absorbed dose is measured in **grays (Gy)** (1 Gy = 1 J/kg).
Mechanism of action:

items: **direct action** — direct injury of DNA, protein and enzyme molecules;

**indirect action** — radiolysis of water produces active free radicals (OH•, H•, hydrogen peroxide), which injure biomolecules. Because about 70% of the organism consists of water, the indirect action is the main one.

parts.text: **The law of Bergonié and Tribondeau:** the radiosensitivity of a tissue is directly proportional to the mitotic activity of its cells and inversely proportional to their degree of differentiation. The most sensitive tissues are hematopoietic tissue (bone marrow), lymphoid tissue, intestinal epithelium and germ cells. The most resistant are nervous tissue, muscle and bone.

blocks.title: Table 2.7. Forms of acute radiation sickness (after a single whole-body exposure)
head: Form
Dose
Main injury
rows: Pancytopenia, infections, bleeding; degrees of severity: mild (1–2 Gy), moderate (2–4 Gy), severe (4–6 Gy), extremely severe (6–10 Gy)
Death of the intestinal epithelium, diarrhea, dehydration, sepsis
Injury of the central nervous system, death within several hours or days

blocks.text: In the bone marrow form of acute radiation sickness, four periods are distinguished: **the primary reaction** (nausea, vomiting, weakness — a few hours after exposure), **the latent period** (“false well-being”), **the full-blown period** (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, infectious complications, bleeding) and **the recovery period**.

parts.text: The time of onset of the primary reaction (vomiting) gives an approximate idea of the dose: the earlier vomiting begins, the higher the dose. The patient's feeling of well-being in the latent period is deceptive — it is precisely during this period that the reserve of bone marrow cells is being depleted.

blocks.text: Mechanical factors (impact, compression, stretching, acceleration, vibration) disrupt the integrity of tissues: wounds, contusions, bone fractures. In severe mechanical injury, systemic reactions develop together with local changes — **traumatic shock** (discussed in detail in Topic 27).

**Crush syndrome (prolonged compression syndrome)** develops as a result of prolonged (several hours) compression of soft tissues (most often of the limbs). Pathogenesis: ischemia and muscle necrosis in the compressed tissues → when the pressure is removed, blood flow is restored and myoglobin, potassium and toxic products pass from the tissues into the blood → hyperkalemia (risk of arrhythmia and cardiac arrest), myoglobinuria and obstruction of the renal tubules → **acute kidney injury**; marked edema of the injured limb → plasma loss and hypovolemia.

parts.text: In crush syndrome, it is recommended to apply a tourniquet to the limb and start intravenous infusion **before** the pressure is removed — this prevents a sudden release of potassium and toxins into the blood. In victims of earthquakes and accidents, this syndrome is one of the main causes of death.

blocks.text: **Acceleration** (aviation, space flight, transport) leads to redistribution of blood: with acceleration directed toward the head, blood pools in the legs, and cerebral ischemia and blackout are observed. With prolonged exposure, **noise** and **vibration** cause occupational diseases (deafness, vibration disease).
Chemical factors

The effect of chemical substances depends on their nature, dose, route of entry into the organism and the state of the organism. The action may be **local** (burns by acids and alkalis) or **systemic** (after absorption — resorptive). Most poisons act selectively on certain organs (organotropism):

carbon monoxide blocks hemoglobin, cyanides block the enzymes of tissue respiration (cytochrome oxidase), organophosphorus compounds inhibit cholinesterase, mercuric chloride injures the kidneys, and carbon tetrachloride injures the liver.

The organism detoxifies poisons mainly in the liver (oxidation, reduction, conjugation with glucuronic and sulfuric acids) and excretes them through the kidneys, intestine and lungs. In liver and kidney diseases the effect of poisons is enhanced.
Biological factors

Biological factors include viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, helminths and prions. Their pathogenicity is determined by **virulence** (the degree of ability to cause disease), **invasiveness** (the ability to penetrate and spread in tissues) and **toxigenicity** (production of exotoxins and endotoxins). The development of disease depends on the number of microorganisms (infectious dose), the route of entry and the resistance of the macroorganism.
Psychogenic and social factors

Prolonged mental strain (distress) activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system and the sympathetic nervous system. This promotes the development of psychosomatic diseases such as arterial hypertension, ischemic heart disease and peptic ulcer. Social factors (standard of living, nutrition, education, availability of medical care) largely determine the morbidity and mortality of the population.

parts.text: The pathogenicity of an external factor depends on three things: **the factor itself** (its nature, strength and duration), **the conditions of action** (in what environment and by what route it acts) and **the reactivity of the organism**. The same factor can be harmless under one condition and fatal under another.

sections.title: 8. Experimental part: the effect of ambient temperature on the development of hypoxic hypoxia

blocks.text: **Aim:** to observe how an external condition — ambient temperature — changes the development and outcome of a pathological process (hypoxic hypoxia).

**Equipment:** white mice (3, of the same weight), a Komovsky pressure chamber (or a sealed chamber with a pump) and a manometer, a vessel with ice (+5 °C), a thermostat (+40 °C), an electric thermometer, a stopwatch.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Scheme of the experiment

blocks.text: Procedure

items: Assess the initial state of the mice: motor activity, respiratory rate (per minute), color of the skin, ears and tail, rectal temperature.
Leave mouse 1 at room temperature (+20 °C) — control.
Place mouse 2 in the vessel at +5 °C and keep it there until its body temperature falls noticeably (until signs of chilling appear).
Place mouse 3 in the thermostat at +40 °C and keep it there until signs of hyperthermia (increased motor activity and rapid breathing) appear.
Place each mouse in turn in the pressure chamber and lower the pressure at the same rate (corresponding to an “ascent” of about 1000 m per minute).

Using the manometer reading, record the “altitude” and the time at which each stage appears: motor excitation, rapid breathing, cyanosis of the ears and tail, lying on the side, convulsions, agonal (slow, deep) breathing.
As soon as agonal breathing appears, immediately return the pressure to normal and observe the animal's recovery time.
Enter the results in the table and compare them.

blocks.title: Table 2.8. Sample table for recording the results of the experiment
head: Parameter
Control (+20 °C)
Cooled (+5 °C)
Heated (+40 °C)

blocks.text: Expected results and their analysis

items: **The heated mouse** is the least resistant to hypoxia: convulsions and agonal breathing appear at a lower “altitude” and sooner. The reason is that in hyperthermia metabolism and the oxygen demand of tissues rise sharply, while oxygen delivery is reduced.

**The cooled mouse** (with reduced body temperature) is the most resistant to hypoxia: the signs appear at a higher “altitude” and later. The reason is that in hypothermia metabolism slows, the central nervous system is inhibited and oxygen demand decreases.
**The control mouse** shows an intermediate result.

parts.text: The effect of cold has two stages: with brief chilling (while body temperature has not yet fallen), thermogenesis in the mouse — shivering and metabolism — increases, oxygen demand **rises**, and resistance to hypoxia may decrease. Resistance increases only **after body temperature has fallen** (hypothermia). That is why in the experiment it is important to check by body temperature that the mouse has been cooled sufficiently.

blocks.text: **Conclusion:** the same cause (a decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the air) under different external conditions (ambient temperature) leads to different development and outcomes of hypoxia. This confirms the important role of external conditions in the development of a pathological process.

skills.title: Skill: creating a model of hypoxic hypoxia in a pressure chamber

items: Check the sealing of the pressure chamber and the functioning of the manometer.
Record the animal's initial parameters (respiratory rate, movement, color, temperature).
Place the animal in the pressure chamber and close the lid tightly.
Lower the pressure evenly with the pump; convert the manometer reading into meters using the altitude table.
Record the “altitude” and the time whenever a new sign appears.
As soon as agonal breathing appears, immediately restore the pressure.
Observe the animal's recovery and record the result in the protocol.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing the results of the experiment

items: Enter in the table the “altitude” and the time at which the signs appeared for each group.
Compare with the control group and determine whether resistance increased or decreased.
Explain the difference by the level of metabolism and oxygen demand.
Distinguish the cause (hypoxia) and the condition (temperature) and write a conclusion.
State the clinical significance of the result (artificial hypothermia, the sensitivity of a febrile patient to hypoxia).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In July, at an air temperature of +42 °C, a 35-year-old construction worker did heavy physical work outdoors all day and drank little water. In the evening he complained of severe headache and nausea, and then lost consciousness. On examination: the skin is dry and hot, there is no sweating, body temperature is 41.5 °C, pulse 140 beats/min, arterial pressure 85/50 mm Hg, convulsions.
cases.ask: What condition has developed in the patient? Explain its pathogenesis. Why are antipyretics ineffective in this condition?
cases.answer: The patient has developed the decompensation stage of hyperthermia — heatstroke. High external temperature and heavy physical work increased heat production, while heat loss was insufficient. Profuse sweating led to dehydration, loss of sodium and chloride, hemoconcentration and a decrease in circulating blood volume; together with dilatation of the skin vessels, this caused arterial hypotension (collapse). Hypoxia and edema of the brain injured the thermoregulatory center, sweating stopped and the temperature rose even further (a vicious circle). Antipyretics lower the set point of the thermoregulatory center that has been changed by pyrogens; in hyperthermia, however, the set point is unchanged, and the problem is insufficient heat loss. Therefore physical cooling of the body (a cool place, wet wrapping, cold compresses) and restoration of the water-electrolyte balance are necessary.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 28-year-old mountaineer ascended from sea level to an altitude of 4500 m in one day. The next day he complained of headache, weakness, shortness of breath and insomnia. Later a cough with pink frothy sputum appeared.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? What is the main link of pathogenesis? How can this condition be prevented?
cases.answer: Mountain sickness has developed, complicated by pulmonary edema. The main link is hypoxic hypoxia and hypoxemia resulting from the decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the air. Hypoxemia causes hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, hypoxic spasm of the pulmonary arterioles and increased pressure in the pulmonary artery; as a result, capillary permeability increases and pulmonary edema develops. Prevention: stepwise ascent and time for acclimatization; when severe signs appear, immediate descent and oxygen therapy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In an experiment, students “raised” three mice in a pressure chamber. Convulsions appeared at 9000 m in the control mouse, at 7000 m in the mouse heated at +40 °C, and at 11,000 m in the cooled mouse whose body temperature had fallen to 30 °C.
cases.ask: Explain the results. What are the cause and the condition in this experiment? What is the clinical significance of the result?
cases.answer: The cause is the same in all the mice — a decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the air (hypoxic hypoxia). The condition is the ambient and body temperature. In the heated mouse, metabolism and the oxygen demand of tissues increased, so the signs of hypoxia appeared at a lower “altitude” (resistance decreased). In the hypothermic mouse, metabolism slowed, the central nervous system was inhibited and oxygen demand fell, so resistance increased. Clinical significance: febrile patients are more sensitive to hypoxia, and monitoring their oxygen supply is important; in heart and brain operations, artificial hypothermia is used to protect tissues from hypoxia.

cards.back: An environmental factor that amplifies or weakens the action of the cause
A rise in body temperature due to insufficient heat loss; the thermoregulatory set point does not change
Severe decompensation of hyperthermia: sweating stops, collapse, cerebral edema
A fall in body temperature below 35 °C; mild 32–35, moderate 28–32, severe below 28 °C
Controlled cooling to reduce the oxygen demand of tissues
Hypoxic hypoxia due to decreased pO2; in severe cases pulmonary and cerebral edema
Up to 2000 m indifferent, 2000–4000 m compensation, 4000–5500 m incomplete compensation, 5500–8000 m critical
Gas embolism by nitrogen bubbles during desaturation
The main factor is current strength; alternating current of 40–60 Hz is the most dangerous

topics.title: The importance of internal conditions in the development of pathological processes. Reactivity and resistance; the role of constitution and heredity in pathology

goals.text: To explain to the student the role of internal conditions — the reactivity and resistance of the organism, the state of the nervous and endocrine systems, constitution, heredity, age and sex — in the origin and course of disease; and to teach the student to observe the development of hypoxic hypoxia in an experiment under different functional states of the central nervous system (narcotic sleep and excitation) and to analyze the result.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the concepts of reactivity and resistance, their types and their interrelationship;
the forms of expression of reactivity (hyperergy, hypoergy, dysergy, anergy);
the biological barriers of the organism and their significance;
the role of the nervous and endocrine systems in shaping reactivity, and the types of higher nervous activity;
the classifications of constitution (Hippocrates, Sigaud, Kretschmer, Chernorutsky) and diatheses;
the types of hereditary diseases and the difference between the concepts “hereditary” and “congenital”;
the effect of age and sex on reactivity.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to model hypoxic hypoxia in anesthetized and excited animals and compare the results;
to assess changes in reactivity and resistance in concrete examples;
to determine a patient's constitutional type and indicate the predisposition to diseases characteristic of it.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Reactivity** is “how does it respond?”, **resistance** is “how much can it withstand?”. A decrease in reactivity does not always mean a decrease in resistance: in anesthesia and hypothermia, reactivity decreases while resistance to hypoxia increases. This is proved in the experimental part of this session.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain, but many drugs (for example, some antibiotics) cross it poorly. In the treatment of meningitis, drugs that cross the barrier well are chosen. In inflamed meninges the permeability of the barrier increases.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Thin — stomach, stout — vessels”**: people of the asthenic type are more prone to peptic ulcer and tuberculosis, whereas people of the hypersthenic type are prone to hypertension, atherosclerosis and diabetes.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **“Congenital”** and **“hereditary”** are not the same concept. A congenital disease is present at birth, but it may not be hereditary (for example, defects caused by the rubella virus or alcohol during pregnancy). A hereditary disease, in contrast, may appear long after birth (Huntington chorea — at the age of 30–50). Conditions that develop under the influence of external factors and resemble a hereditary disease but are not passed from generation to generation are called **phenocopies**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Although anesthesia increases resistance to hypoxia, narcotic substances in large doses depress the respiratory center and can themselves lead to hypoxia (respiratory hypoxia). That is why the dose is strictly fixed in the experiment, and in the clinic anesthesia is always performed under monitoring of respiration and blood oxygen.

blocks.text: **Internal conditions** are the properties of the organism itself that determine the result of the action of the cause of disease. Internal conditions are the main reason why the same cause (for example, an infection or hypoxia) produces different results in different people.

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Internal conditions
head: Group
Content
rows: The ability of the organism to respond to a stimulus and to resist it
Type of higher nervous activity, the balance of excitation and inhibition, sleep, anesthesia, stress
Levels of hormones of the pituitary, adrenal, thyroid and pancreatic glands
Hereditary and acquired, relatively stable morphological and functional features of the organism
Hereditary diseases and hereditary predisposition to diseases
Childhood, maturity and old age; features of the female and male organism
State of the skin, mucous membranes and blood-tissue barriers
Previous diseases, immunity, fatigue, nutritional status

blocks.text: **Reactivity** is the property of the organism to respond to influences of the external and internal environment by changing its vital activity. Reactivity is characteristic of all levels of the living organism — molecule, cell, tissue, organ, system and the whole organism.

The concept of “reactivity” was introduced into medicine at the beginning of the 20th century; in this period anaphylaxis and serum sickness were discovered, and C. Pirquet proposed the term “allergy” (altered reactivity). I.I. Mechnikov (immunological reactivity), A.A. Bogomolets and N.N. Sirotinin (constitutional and evolutionary approaches) made a great contribution to the doctrine of reactivity. Avicenna (Ibn Sina) emphasized the need to take into account the patient's “temperament” in treatment.

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Types of reactivity (based on data from N.H. Abdullaev, 2008)

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Types of reactivity
head: Type
Definition
Examples
rows: Hereditarily determined features of response characteristic of a particular biological species
Resistance of humans to cattle plague and of dogs to measles; hibernation in animals
Features characteristic of individuals belonging to one group
Differences related to age, sex, constitution and blood group
Reactivity of each organism determined by its hereditary and acquired features
Different course of the same infection in different people
Formation of antibodies and sensitized lymphocytes in response to a particular antigen
Responding in the same way to different factors
The normal response of a healthy organism
Adaptation to physical work, immunity after vaccination
An abnormal response with limited adaptive capacity under the influence of a disease factor
Allergy, immunodeficiency, decreased reactivity in traumatic shock

blocks.text: Forms of expression of reactivity

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Forms of expression of reactivity
head: Form
Essence
Clinical picture
rows: A normal response appropriate to the stimulus
The usual (typical) course of the disease
The disease runs a violent, severe course: high fever, intense inflammation, allergic reactions
The disease is sluggish, with vague signs; “asymptomatic” pneumonia in the elderly and in cachexia
Unexpected, unusual reactions (for example, a paradoxical response to drugs)
Almost complete absence of a response
Severe sepsis, AIDS, extreme cachexia, a negative tuberculin test

parts.text: A hypoergic course is particularly dangerous: in an elderly patient or a patient with diabetes mellitus, pneumonia may occur without fever or leukocytosis, with only weakness and clouding of consciousness. The “mildness” of the signs reflects not the mildness of the disease but the weakness of the organism's response, and it increases the risk of late diagnosis.

sections.title: 3. Resistance and its relationship to reactivity

blocks.text: **Resistance** is the ability of the organism to withstand and resist the action of pathogenic factors. Resistance is one of the important manifestations of reactivity.

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Types of resistance
head: Type
Content
Examples
rows: Resistance related to the structural features of the organism
The barrier of the skin, bones and mucous membranes; the thick skin of some animals
Due to active engagement of protective-adaptive mechanisms
Phagocytosis, antibody formation, detoxification of poisons
Immunity after disease or vaccination, hardening
Resistance of a hardened person to cold, hypoxia and infections

blocks.text: Reactivity and resistance do not always change in the same direction:

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Interrelationship of reactivity and resistance
head: State
Reactivity
Resistance
Example
rows: Increased resistance to infections and cold
Increases with respect to hypoxia and certain poisons and microbes
Resistance of a hibernating animal to hypoxia
Rapid death of an excited animal in hypoxia

parts.text: **Reactivity** is “how does it respond?”, **resistance** is “how much can it withstand?”. A decrease in reactivity does not always mean a decrease in resistance: in anesthesia and hypothermia, reactivity decreases while resistance to hypoxia increases. This is proved in the experimental part of this session.

blocks.text: **External barriers:** the skin (mechanical protection, acidic environment, bactericidal action of fatty acids, desquamation), mucous membranes (mucus, ciliated epithelium, lysozyme, secretory IgA), the acidic environment of gastric juice, and the normal microflora (competition with pathogenic microbes).
**Internal (blood-tissue) barriers:** the blood-brain, blood-ocular, blood-testis and blood-placental barriers, lymph nodes, and the liver (detoxifies toxic substances coming from the intestine).

parts.text: The blood-brain barrier protects the brain, but many drugs (for example, some antibiotics) cross it poorly. In the treatment of meningitis, drugs that cross the barrier well are chosen. In inflamed meninges the permeability of the barrier increases.

sections.title: 5. The role of the nervous system in reactivity

blocks.text: The nervous system is the main system that shapes and regulates reactivity. Its state sharply changes the organism's response to pathogenic influences.

items: **In ontogenesis:** in newborns the nervous system is immature, so their fever and inflammatory reactions are weak and infection rapidly becomes generalized.
**Inhibition of the central nervous system** (sleep, anesthesia, hibernation) reduces metabolism and oxygen demand — resistance to hypoxia and certain poisons increases.
**Excitation of the central nervous system** (stress, caffeine, amphetamine, hyperthyroidism) increases metabolism — resistance to hypoxia decreases.
**Injury of the nervous system** (spinal cord transection, denervation) leads to degenerative changes in tissues and impaired inflammation and regeneration.

blocks.title: Table 3.6. Types of higher nervous activity (I.P. Pavlov) and the temperaments of Hippocrates
head: Type according to Pavlov
Properties of the nervous processes
Temperament according to Hippocrates
Predisposition to pathology
rows: Excitation and inhibition are strong, equal and alternate quickly
The processes are strong and equal but alternate slowly
Arterial hypertension, ischemic heart disease, neurasthenia

parts.text: Anesthesia and controlled sedation are used in resuscitation practice to protect the brain from hypoxia (by reducing oxygen demand). Conversely, agitation, shivering and seizures sharply increase the patient's oxygen demand and aggravate hypoxia.

sections.title: 6. The role of the endocrine system in reactivity

blocks.text: The endocrine system regulates reactivity together with the nervous system.

items: **The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical system** provides the stress reaction. According to H. Selye's doctrine, the organism responds to strong stimuli with the **general adaptation syndrome**: the alarm stage, the stage of resistance and the stage of exhaustion. Glucocorticoids suppress inflammatory and allergic reactions, but in excess they lower immunity.
**Thyroid hormones** increase metabolism: in hyperthyroidism resistance to hypoxia decreases, whereas in hypothyroidism reactivity is weakened in general.
**Insulin deficiency** (diabetes mellitus) weakens phagocytosis and regeneration — susceptibility to purulent infections increases and wounds heal slowly.
**Sex hormones** determine sex differences in reactivity.

sections.title: 7. Constitution and its role in pathology

blocks.text: **Constitution** is the complex of hereditary and acquired, relatively stable morphological, functional and psychological features of the organism. Constitution determines the reactivity of the organism and its predisposition to certain diseases.

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Sigaud's constitutional types (labels а, б, в, г in the figure): respiratory, digestive, muscular and cerebral type (N.N. Zaiko, 2002, Fig. 6)

blocks.title: Table 3.7. Classifications of constitution
head: Author
Types
Main features
rows: Based on temperament (the ratio of the four humors)
Based on the predominant system in the body (shape of the face and trunk)
Relationship between body build and psychological features

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Kretschmer's constitutional types (labels а, б, в in the figure): asthenic, athletic, pyknic (N.N. Zaiko, 2002, Fig. 7)

parts.text: **“Thin — stomach, stout — vessels”**: people of the asthenic type are more prone to peptic ulcer and tuberculosis, whereas people of the hypersthenic type are prone to hypertension, atherosclerosis and diabetes.

blocks.text: Diatheses

**Diathesis** is an anomaly of constitution occurring in childhood, characterized by the organism's predisposition to respond abnormally to certain influences. Diathesis is not a disease but a state of predisposition to disease.

blocks.title: Table 3.9. Types of diathesis
head: Type
Essence
Predisposition to diseases
rows: Predisposition of the skin and mucous membranes to inflammatory and allergic reactions
Atopic dermatitis, eczema, allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma
Hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue (enlargement of the thymus), reduced adrenal function
Severe course of infections, risk of sudden death under stress
Impaired purine metabolism, increased excitability of the nervous system
Gout, urolithiasis, obesity, diabetes mellitus (in adulthood)

sections.title: 8. Heredity and its role in pathology

blocks.text: By the participation of heredity in their origin, diseases are divided into three groups:

blocks.title: Table 3.10. The ratio of hereditary and external factors in diseases
head: Group
Role of heredity and environment
Examples
rows: The mutation is decisive; the external environment affects only the course
Arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, bronchial asthma, peptic ulcer disease, atherosclerosis
Diseases caused mainly by external factors
The role of heredity is small

head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: A single mutant allele is sufficient
Phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anemia
Mainly boys are affected; their mothers are carriers

Change in the number or structure of chromosomes

parts.text: **“Congenital”** and **“hereditary”** are not the same concept. A congenital disease is present at birth, but it may not be hereditary (for example, defects caused by the rubella virus or alcohol during pregnancy). A hereditary disease, in contrast, may appear long after birth (Huntington chorea — at the age of 30–50). Conditions that develop under the influence of external factors and resemble a hereditary disease but are not passed from generation to generation are called **phenocopies**.

sections.title: 9. The effect of age and sex on reactivity

items: **Infancy and early childhood:** the nervous, endocrine and immune systems are immature, and the biological barriers are weak. Inflammatory and febrile reactions are weak, and infections quickly become generalized (predisposition to sepsis). At the same time, newborns are more resistant to hypoxia than older people (high activity of anaerobic glycolysis; fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen well).
**Maturity:** reactivity is at its highest level.

**Old age:** the immune response weakens, barriers become weaker, and the reserve capacity of organs decreases; diseases often run a hypoergic, asymptomatic course; neoplastic diseases become more frequent.

**Sex:** the female organism is more resistant to blood loss, hypoxia and starvation; autoimmune diseases are more common in women, whereas ischemic heart disease occurs more often at an early age in men (the protective effect of estrogens). In women, reactivity changes during the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause.

sections.title: 10. Experimental part: development of hypoxic hypoxia in different states of the central nervous system

blocks.text: **Aim:** to observe how an internal condition — the functional state of the central nervous system — changes the development and outcome of hypoxia.

**Equipment:** white mice (3, of the same weight), a Komovsky pressure chamber and a manometer, a solution of a narcotic agent (the drug and dose adopted at the department, for example urethane), 1% caffeine solution, physiological saline, syringes, a stopwatch.

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Scheme of the experiment

blocks.text: Procedure

items: Assess the initial state of all three mice: motor activity, respiratory rate, color of the skin, ears and tail.
Inject physiological saline into the peritoneal cavity of mouse 1 (control).
Inject the narcotic agent into mouse 2 and wait for signs of narcotic sleep (immobility, weakened reflexes, slower breathing) to appear.
Inject the caffeine solution into mouse 3 and wait for signs of excitation (increased motor activity, rapid breathing) to appear.
Place each mouse in turn in the pressure chamber and lower the pressure at the same rate.
Record the “altitude” and the time at which the stages of hypoxia appear: excitation, change in breathing, cyanosis, lying on the side, convulsions, agonal breathing.
As soon as agonal breathing appears, immediately restore the pressure and observe the animal's recovery.
Enter the results in the table and compare them.

blocks.title: Table 3.12. Sample table for recording the results of the experiment
head: Parameter
Control
Narcotic sleep
Caffeine (excitation)

blocks.text: Expected results and their analysis

items: **The mouse in narcotic sleep** is the most resistant to hypoxia: the signs of hypoxia appear at a much higher “altitude”, and convulsions are weak or absent. The reason is that the central nervous system is inhibited, and metabolism and the oxygen demand of neurons are reduced.
**The mouse given caffeine** is the least resistant to hypoxia: the signs appear at a lower “altitude” and sooner. The reason is that excited neurons and muscles consume much oxygen.
**The control mouse** shows an intermediate result.

parts.text: Although anesthesia increases resistance to hypoxia, narcotic substances in large doses depress the respiratory center and can themselves lead to hypoxia (respiratory hypoxia). That is why the dose is strictly fixed in the experiment, and in the clinic anesthesia is always performed under monitoring of respiration and blood oxygen.

blocks.text: **Conclusion:** the same cause (a decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the air) gives different results in different states of the central nervous system. Inhibition of the nervous system lowers reactivity but increases resistance to hypoxia, whereas excitation does the opposite. This confirms the role of internal conditions in the development of a pathological process.

skills.title: Skill: modeling hypoxia in narcotic sleep and in excitation

items: Match the animals by weight and label them.
Record the initial parameters.
Inject the drugs into the peritoneal cavity at the specified dose and wait for the effect to begin.
Lower the pressure in the pressure chamber at the same rate.
Record the “altitude” and the time at which each stage of hypoxia appears.
As soon as agonal breathing appears, restore the pressure.
Compare the results with the control group and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: determining the constitutional type (according to Chernorutsky)

items: Measure height and body weight and calculate the body mass index.
Assess the shape, length and width of the chest.
Determine the epigastric (costal) angle: less than 90° — asthenic, about 90° — normosthenic, more than 90° — hypersthenic.
Calculate the Pignet index: height (cm) − [body weight (kg) + chest circumference (cm)]. Less than 10 — hypersthenic, 10–30 — normosthenic, more than 30 — asthenic.
Take into account arterial pressure and pulse as additional signs.
Write a conclusion and indicate the predisposition to diseases characteristic of this type.
