cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: During an influenza epidemic in a kindergarten, 18 of 30 children fell ill. In 3 of them the disease was severe, with high fever and convulsions; in 2 children (one of whom was often ill and underweight) the disease ran a sluggish course without fever and was complicated by pneumonia. Twelve children did not fall ill at all.
cases.ask: How do you explain the different courses of the disease under the action of the same cause? Which forms of reactivity were observed? What played the decisive role in the children who did not fall ill?
cases.answer: The cause of the disease (the influenza virus) is the same, while the different courses depend on internal conditions — individual reactivity and resistance. The severe course with high fever and convulsions reflects hyperergic reactivity (in children, the immaturity and excitability of the nervous system create a predisposition to convulsions). The cases with a sluggish course without fever and with complications reflect hypoergic reactivity (low weight and frequent illness indicate a weakened immune response). The children who did not fall ill had high resistance: specific immunity resulting from vaccination or previous illness, and nonspecific resistance due to good nutrition and hardening.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 52-year-old man, height 168 cm, body weight 98 kg, with a broad and short chest and an obtuse epigastric angle. Arterial pressure is 160/100 mm Hg; blood cholesterol and glucose are elevated. His father died of myocardial infarction at the age of 55.
cases.ask: Determine the patient's constitutional type. To what diseases is he predisposed? Distinguish internal and external conditions.
cases.answer: Hypersthenic constitution according to Chernorutsky (the pyknic type according to Kretschmer). This type is characterized by a predisposition to arterial hypertension, atherosclerosis, ischemic heart disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus and gallstone disease; the patient already has arterial hypertension and metabolic disorders. Internal conditions: constitution, hereditary predisposition (the father's early myocardial infarction), male sex and age. External conditions (to be clarified): overeating, physical inactivity, smoking, stress. Prevention is aimed at eliminating the external factors: weight reduction, diet, physical activity, control of arterial pressure and lipids.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a student experiment in a pressure chamber, convulsions appeared at 9000 m in the control mouse. The mouse in narcotic sleep was “raised” to 11,500 m without convulsions, whereas in the mouse given caffeine convulsions began at 7500 m and agonal breathing developed rapidly.
cases.ask: Explain the results. How did reactivity and resistance change? What is the clinical significance of the result?
cases.answer: The cause is the same in all the mice — a decreased partial pressure of oxygen in the air. In the mouse in narcotic sleep, the central nervous system was inhibited, reactivity decreased, and metabolism and oxygen demand fell, so resistance to hypoxia increased. In the mouse given caffeine, the nervous system was excited and reactivity increased, but resistance decreased because oxygen consumption rose. This shows that reactivity and resistance do not always change in the same direction. Clinical significance: in patients at risk of hypoxia (after cardiac arrest, in severe brain injury), sedation and anesthesia are used to protect the brain; agitation, seizures and fever increase oxygen demand and aggravate hypoxia, so they must be eliminated.

topics.title: Arterial and venous hyperemia. Disorders of the microcirculation and peripheral circulation

goals.text: To explain to the student the significance of the microcirculation in health and disease and the mechanisms regulating peripheral circulation; to teach the causes, mechanisms of development, signs and outcomes of arterial and venous hyperemia; and to teach the student to induce arterial and venous hyperemia in the rabbit ear and the frog mesentery in an experiment and to observe the changes in the microcirculation.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the structure of the microcirculatory bed and the factors regulating blood flow;
the classification of disorders of peripheral circulation;
the types and mechanisms of development of arterial hyperemia (neurotonic, neuroparalytic, neuromyoparalytic, humoral);
the external signs of arterial hyperemia, the changes in the microcirculation and its outcomes;
the causes and signs of venous hyperemia, the changes in the microcirculation and its outcomes;
the distinguishing features of arterial and venous hyperemia.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to induce neuroparalytic arterial hyperemia and venous hyperemia in the rabbit ear;
to observe the microcirculation in the frog mesentery under a microscope and describe the changes;
to identify the type of hyperemia by its external signs and explain its mechanism.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Factors regulating the microcirculation: **neurogenic** — sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves (norepinephrine, alpha-adrenergic receptors) and vasodilator nerves in some regions; **humoral** — epinephrine, angiotensin II, vasopressin (constrict); histamine, bradykinin, prostacyclin (dilate); **local metabolic** — adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, lactate, oxygen deficiency (dilate); **endothelial** — nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (dilate), endothelin (constricts); **myogenic** — the response of smooth muscle to stretching of the vessel wall by contraction (the Bayliss effect).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Rapid removal of a large volume of ascitic fluid from the abdominal cavity or rapid removal of a large tumor leads to hyperemia ex vacuo: a large part of the blood moves into the abdominal organs, and relative anemia (ischemia) of the brain and fainting develop. That is why paracentesis is performed with slow removal of the fluid.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Arterial — “HOT & RED”**: red, warm, many open (working) capillaries, pulsation. **Venous — “BLUE & COLD”**: bluish (cyanotic), cold, slow flow, swelling (edema).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: This experiment can also be performed with hot water or by rubbing the skin of the ear with xylene — in this case **neuromyoparalytic** (local) hyperemia is observed. The student must be able to name the type of hyperemia correctly according to the method used to induce it.

blocks.text: **Microcirculation** is the movement of blood and lymph through the smallest vessels (less than 100 µm in diameter) and the exchange of substances between blood and tissue. The microcirculatory bed is the functional unit of an organ: it supplies tissues with oxygen and nutrients and removes metabolic products.

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Components of the microcirculatory bed
head: Segment
Function
rows: “Resistance vessels”: regulate blood flow through the tone of smooth muscle
Regulate the entry of blood into the capillaries (the number of working capillaries)
“Exchange vessels”: the wall consists of a single layer of endothelium; exchange of gases and substances
This is where the exit of fluid and leukocytes from the vessels mainly takes place
“Capacitance vessels”: collect and carry away the blood
Carry blood past the capillaries (important in thermoregulation)
Carry away interstitial fluid and proteins

blocks.text: Blood flow through a vessel obeys Poiseuille's law: flow is directly proportional to the pressure difference between the beginning and the end of the vessel and inversely proportional to vascular resistance. Vascular resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius — that is, doubling the radius of an arteriole increases blood flow about 16 times.

parts.text: Factors regulating the microcirculation:

items: **neurogenic** — sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves (norepinephrine, alpha-adrenergic receptors) and vasodilator nerves in some regions;
**humoral** — epinephrine, angiotensin II, vasopressin (constrict); histamine, bradykinin, prostacyclin (dilate);
**local metabolic** — adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, lactate, oxygen deficiency (dilate);
**endothelial** — nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (dilate), endothelin (constricts);
**myogenic** — the response of smooth muscle to stretching of the vessel wall by contraction (the Bayliss effect).

sections.title: 2. Classification of disorders of peripheral circulation

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Disorders of peripheral (local) circulation
head: Group
Types
rows: Intravascular (rheological properties of blood, “sludge”), vascular wall (increased permeability, diapedesis), extravascular (edema, impaired lymph flow)
Disruption of the integrity of the vascular wall

blocks.text: **Hyperemia** (Greek hyper — excess, haima — blood) is increased blood filling of an organ or tissue. When the inflow of blood increases, **arterial (active)** hyperemia develops; when the outflow of blood is impeded, **venous (passive, congestive)** hyperemia develops.

**Arterial hyperemia** is an increased inflow of blood through the arteries into an organ or tissue and increased blood filling as a result of arteriolar dilatation, while the outflow of blood remains normal.
Types of arterial hyperemia
**Physiological arterial hyperemia** is a normal phenomenon observed when the activity of an organ increases:

items: **working (functional)** — in a working muscle, in the gastrointestinal tract during digestion, in the brain during mental work;
**reflex** — reddening of the skin under the action of heat;
**emotional** — reddening of the face from embarrassment or anger.

blocks.text: **Pathological arterial hyperemia** develops under the action of pathogenic factors, is not related to increased activity of the organ and is disproportionate to the stimulus.
Mechanisms of development of arterial hyperemia

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Mechanisms of development of arterial hyperemia (based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009; N.H. Abdullaev, 2008)

blocks.title: Table 4.3. Mechanisms of arterial hyperemia
head: Mechanism
Essence
Examples
rows: Increased tone or stimulation of vasodilator nerves
Emotional reddening of the face, some reflex hyperemias, reddening of the skin under the action of heat
Loss of the influence of sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves; the tone of arteriolar smooth muscle decreases
C. Bernard's experiment: transection of the cervical sympathetic nerve of a rabbit; sympathectomy; injury of the vasoconstrictor centers
Decreased tone of smooth muscle in the vessel wall under the action of local metabolites
Working hyperemia, postischemic hyperemia, a hot compress, a mustard plaster
Action of vasoactive substances (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, NO)
Hyperemia in an inflammatory focus, allergic reddening

blocks.text: **Postischemic (reactive) hyperemia** develops after ischemia has been eliminated: metabolites accumulated during ischemia (adenosine, lactate, H+, K+) dilate the arterioles, and muscle tone is reduced. An example is reddening of a limb after removal of a tourniquet.

**Hyperemia ex vacuo** (Latin vacuus — empty) develops when the barometric pressure over a tissue decreases. Examples are the application of medical cups, or the movement of a large amount of blood into the vessels of the abdominal organs when ascitic fluid is rapidly removed from the abdominal cavity.

parts.text: Rapid removal of a large volume of ascitic fluid from the abdominal cavity or rapid removal of a large tumor leads to hyperemia ex vacuo: a large part of the blood moves into the abdominal organs, and relative anemia (ischemia) of the brain and fainting develop. That is why paracentesis is performed with slow removal of the fluid.

blocks.text: Signs of arterial hyperemia

blocks.title: Table 4.4. External signs of arterial hyperemia and their causes
head: Feature
Cause
rows: Increase in arterial blood rich in oxyhemoglobin in the dilated vessels; increased number of working capillaries
Increased inflow of warm arterial blood and increased metabolism
Increased blood filling, increased formation of interstitial fluid
Dilatation of the arterioles, smaller pressure drop up to the capillaries
Increased filtration pressure in the capillaries

blocks.text: Changes in the microcirculation

items: arterioles, precapillaries and capillaries dilate;
the number of working (open) capillaries increases — previously closed capillaries open;
the linear and volumetric velocities of blood flow increase;
hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries rises and filtration increases;
the arteriovenous oxygen difference decreases (venous blood is also rich in oxygen).

blocks.text: Outcomes of arterial hyperemia

**Beneficial outcomes:** the supply of the tissue with oxygen and nutrients improves, metabolism, regeneration and phagocytosis increase, and metabolites are rapidly removed. That is why arterial hyperemia is used in physiotherapy (hot compresses, UHF, mustard plasters, cups).

**Harmful outcomes:** rupture of the wall of altered (atherosclerotic, aneurysmal) vessels and hemorrhage (for example, cerebral hemorrhage in a hypertensive crisis); increased intracranial pressure (headache); relative ischemia in other organs when a large part of the blood collects in one region.

parts.text: Arterial hyperemia is often observed in the clinic: redness and heat in an inflammatory focus (rubor, calor), warm and moist skin in hyperthyroidism, “hot flashes” in menopause, flushing in carcinoid syndrome. Red, warm, pulsating tissue is always a sign of increased blood inflow.

blocks.text: **Venous hyperemia (congestion)** is increased blood filling of an organ or tissue when the outflow of blood through the veins is impeded; the inflow of blood is normal or reduced.
Causes of venous hyperemia

blocks.title: Table 4.5. Causes of venous hyperemia
head: Group of causes
Examples
rows: Tumor, scar, pregnant uterus, tight bandage (cast, tourniquet), edema
Occlusion of the venous lumen from within
Thrombosis, embolism, inflammation of the vein wall (phlebitis)
Insufficiency of the vein wall and valves
Congestion in the pulmonary circulation in left ventricular failure and in the systemic circulation in right ventricular failure
Reduced suction function of the chest
Prolonged standing; in the dependent regions of bedridden severely ill patients (hypostasis)

blocks.text: Signs of venous hyperemia

blocks.title: Table 4.6. External signs of venous hyperemia and their causes
head: Feature
Cause
rows: Due to slow blood flow, tissues extract more oxygen and the amount of reduced hemoglobin increases (cyanosis is visible when it exceeds 50 g/L)
Decreased inflow of warm arterial blood, weakened metabolism, increased heat loss
Increased hydrostatic pressure in capillaries and venules, increased permeability of the vessel wall

blocks.text: Changes in the microcirculation

items: venules and capillaries dilate and the amount of blood in them increases;
the velocity of blood flow decreases; in severe cases the blood moves in a **“pendulum-like”** manner (forward in systole, backward in diastole), and then **stasis** develops;
hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries rises — filtration predominates over reabsorption and edema develops;
red blood cells pass through the vessel wall (**diapedesis**) — small hemorrhages appear;
the rheological properties of blood are impaired (aggregation of red blood cells, “sludge”).

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of venous hyperemia (based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009, Fig. 9.4)

blocks.text: Outcomes of venous hyperemia
The main harmful factor of venous hyperemia is **hypoxia**. When prolonged, it leads to degeneration and atrophy of parenchymal cells and growth of connective tissue (**sclerosis, induration**).

blocks.title: Table 4.7. Outcomes of chronic venous hyperemia in various organs
head: Organ
Cause
Outcome
rows: “Nutmeg liver”: congestion in the centers of the lobules and atrophy of hepatocytes, later cardiac sclerosis (cirrhosis)
Brown induration of the lung: diapedesis, accumulation of hemosiderin (“heart failure cells”), sclerosis
Ascites, splenomegaly, varicose dilatation of the esophageal and rectal veins

parts.text: Venous hyperemia creates favorable conditions for thrombosis (part of Virchow's triad — slowing of blood flow). That is why measures to prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are taken in long-term bedridden patients, patients with varicose veins of the legs and postoperative patients: early mobilization, elastic bandaging, anticoagulants.

sections.title: 5. Comparative characteristics of arterial and venous hyperemia

blocks.title: Table 4.8. Differences between arterial and venous hyperemia
head: Feature
Arterial hyperemia
Venous hyperemia
rows: Increased inflow of blood (dilatation of arterioles)
Mostly beneficial; risk of vessel rupture

parts.text: **Arterial — “HOT & RED”**: red, warm, many open (working) capillaries, pulsation. **Venous — “BLUE & COLD”**: bluish (cyanotic), cold, slow flow, swelling (edema).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: neuroparalytic arterial hyperemia in the rabbit ear (C. Bernard's experiment)
**Aim:** to observe the development of arterial hyperemia when the sympathetic vasoconstrictor influence is lost.
**Equipment:** a white (albino) rabbit, surgical instruments, a local anesthetic, a thermometer (electric thermometer), a light source.

items: Fix the rabbit on a special table; hold both ears against the light and compare the vascular network, color and temperature.
Under local anesthesia, incise the skin and tissues on one side of the neck, find the cervical sympathetic nerve lying next to the carotid artery and transect it.
After 5–10 minutes, compare both ears: in the ear on the side of transection, the vessels dilate, the ear reddens, more small vessels become visible and the temperature rises.
Record the results in the protocol.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** when the cervical sympathetic nerve is transected, the constant vasoconstrictor impulses to the vessels of the ear stop, the tone of arteriolar smooth muscle decreases and the arterioles dilate — **neuroparalytic arterial hyperemia** develops.

parts.text: This experiment can also be performed with hot water or by rubbing the skin of the ear with xylene — in this case **neuromyoparalytic** (local) hyperemia is observed. The student must be able to name the type of hyperemia correctly according to the method used to induce it.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: venous hyperemia in the rabbit ear

items: Place a rubber ring or ligature at the base of the rabbit ear (where the vessels pass) so that it compresses only the veins and not the artery.
Observe for 10–15 minutes: the ear becomes bluish, the veins dilate and fill with blood, the temperature falls and the ear swells.
Remove the ring and observe the restoration of circulation.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: changes in the microcirculation in the frog mesentery

items: Under anesthesia (or after destruction of the spinal cord), fix the frog on a cork board, incise the abdominal wall from the side, bring out an intestinal loop, spread the mesentery over the opening and place it under the microscope.

In the normal state, observe blood flow in the arterioles, capillaries and venules: in the arterioles blood flows rapidly and pulsates, in the venules slowly and evenly; red blood cells are in the axis of the vessel, and there is a plasma layer next to the wall.
**Arterial hyperemia:** apply a drop of xylene (or warm physiological saline) to the mesentery — the arterioles dilate, previously invisible capillaries open and blood flow accelerates.

**Venous hyperemia:** tie a mesenteric vein with a ligature — the venules and capillaries dilate, blood flow slows, pendulum-like movement and stasis appear, and diapedesis of red blood cells is observed.
Draw your observations in the protocol.

blocks.title: Table 4.9. Sample table for recording the results of the experiment
head: Parameter
Normal
Arterial hyperemia
Venous hyperemia
rows: Velocity and character of blood flow

skills.title: Skill: identifying the type of hyperemia by its external signs

items: Assess the color of the tissue: scarlet-red or bluish.
Compare the local temperature with the symmetrical region using the back of the hand or a thermometer.
Check for edema (a pit remaining after pressing with a finger).
Detect pulsation of small arteries.
Determine the cause of hyperemia: whether the inflow of blood has increased or its outflow is impeded.
Write a conclusion: the type of hyperemia, its mechanism and probable outcome.

skills.title: Skill: assessing the microcirculation under a microscope

items: Find the preparation at low magnification and distinguish the arteriole, capillary and venule (by the direction and velocity of flow).
Measure the diameter of the vessels with an ocular micrometer.
Count the number of working capillaries in the field of view.
Describe the character of blood flow: fast, slow, pendulum-like, stasis.
Note aggregation of red blood cells, diapedesis and the marginal position of leukocytes.
Compare with the normal state and write a conclusion.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a 35-year-old woman, bleeding was stopped by a tourniquet applied to the right leg for a long time (1.5 hours). After the tourniquet was removed, the skin of the leg became sharply red and warm, and the pulsation of the vessels increased. At the same time, the patient's arterial pressure fell and dizziness appeared.
cases.ask: What type of hyperemia developed in the leg? What is its mechanism? Why did arterial pressure fall?
cases.answer: After removal of the tourniquet, postischemic (reactive) arterial hyperemia developed. During ischemia, metabolites (adenosine, lactate, H+, K+, CO2) accumulated in the tissue and the tone of arteriolar smooth muscle decreased — the neuromyoparalytic (metabolic) mechanism. When blood flow was restored, a large volume of blood passed into the dilated vessels. Because a considerable part of the blood collected in the vessels of the leg, the circulating blood volume decreased relatively, arterial pressure fell and the blood supply of the brain deteriorated. That is why a tourniquet is released gradually and the patient's hemodynamics are monitored.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old patient has had mitral stenosis for several years. He complains of shortness of breath, cough and sometimes blood-streaked sputum. Examination of the sputum revealed hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”).
cases.ask: What disorder has developed in the patient, and in which circulation? How do hemosiderin-laden macrophages appear? What is the outcome of this condition?
cases.answer: In mitral stenosis, the passage of blood from the left atrium into the left ventricle is impeded, and as a result venous hyperemia (congestion) develops in the pulmonary circulation. Increased pressure in the pulmonary capillaries leads to the exit of fluid and red blood cells into the alveoli (diapedesis) — that is why there is blood in the sputum. The red blood cells in the alveoli are phagocytosed by macrophages, and hemosiderin is formed from hemoglobin. Prolonged congestion and hypoxia lead to growth of connective tissue in the lungs — brown induration of the lung.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman, a shop assistant, works standing all day. Toward evening, heaviness and swelling appear in her legs. Examination revealed dilated, tortuous veins on the calves, a bluish-brown color of the skin in the ankle region and a trophic ulcer.
cases.ask: What circulatory disorder has developed? Explain the pathogenesis of the edema and the trophic ulcer. What dangerous complication can this condition cause?
cases.answer: As a result of venous valve insufficiency and gravity, chronic venous hyperemia has developed in the legs (varicose disease). Because the outflow of blood is impeded, hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries and venules rises — filtration predominates over reabsorption and edema appears. Prolonged congestion and edema lead to tissue hypoxia, diapedesis of red blood cells and accumulation of hemosiderin (brown pigmentation), impaired trophism of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, and a trophic ulcer. Slowing of blood flow increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

topics.title: Ischemia, stasis, thrombosis and embolism

goals.text: To explain to the student the causes, mechanisms of development, manifestations and outcomes of ischemia, stasis, thrombosis and embolism; to teach the significance of collateral circulation; and to teach the student to observe in an experiment local anemia in the frog tongue and the rabbit ear, thrombus formation caused by injury of the vessel wall, and fat embolism.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the causes (compression, obturation, angiospasm, redistribution), signs and outcomes of ischemia;
the types of collateral circulation and the factors determining the outcome of ischemia;
the mechanisms of reperfusion injury;
the types and mechanism of development of stasis;
the causes of thrombus formation (Virchow's triad), its stages, the types of thrombi and their outcomes;
the types of embolism (by the nature of the embolus and the path of its movement) and their outcomes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to induce and observe ischemia in the frog tongue and the rabbit ear using epinephrine;
to injure the vessel wall with a crystal of table salt and observe thrombus formation;
to model fat embolism and analyze its outcomes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: By their collateral circulation, organs are divided into three groups: **organs with absolutely sufficient collaterals** — many anastomoses (limbs, mesentery, chest wall): ischemia is slight when one artery is occluded; **organs with relatively sufficient (or relatively insufficient) collaterals** — anastomoses exist but open slowly (intestine, stomach, lungs, skin); **organs with absolutely insufficient collaterals** — “end” (terminal) arteries (myocardium, brain, kidney, spleen, retina): occlusion of an artery leads to infarction.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Massive PE often develops suddenly and unexpectedly: in the days after surgery, when the patient gets up for the first time or strains in the toilet, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, cyanosis and fainting are observed. Do not forget thromboprophylaxis in patients with risk factors (surgery, prolonged bed rest, cancer, pregnancy).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the frog, fat injected into the abdominal vein also enters the portal system and the liver; in humans, fat entering through a vein is first trapped in the pulmonary capillaries. This difference shows once again that interspecies differences must be taken into account when transferring the results of animal experiments to humans.

blocks.text: **Ischemia** (Greek ischo — I hold back, haima — blood) is local anemia that develops as a result of decreased or stopped inflow of blood through the arteries into an organ or tissue.
Causes of ischemia

blocks.title: Table 5.1. Types of ischemia by cause
head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Tumor, scar, tourniquet, edema, hematoma, tight bandage
Occlusion of the arterial lumen from within
Cold, stress, epinephrine, vasopressin; Raynaud syndrome; cocaine
Movement of a large amount of blood to another region
Cerebral ischemia during rapid removal of ascites; the “steal” syndrome

blocks.text: Signs of ischemia

blocks.title: Table 5.2. External signs of ischemia and their causes
head: Feature
Cause
rows: Less blood in the capillaries, fewer working capillaries
Decreased inflow of warm blood, weakened metabolism
Decreased amount of blood and interstitial fluid
Decreased inflow of blood into the artery
Hypoxia and stimulation of nerve endings by metabolites (H+, K+, lactate, bradykinin)

blocks.text: Changes in the microcirculation

items: the arterioles constrict or the inflow of blood into them decreases;
the number of working capillaries decreases and blood flow slows;
hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries falls — fluid passes from the tissue into the blood (the tissue “dries”);
lymph formation decreases;
the arteriovenous oxygen difference increases (the tissue extracts the maximum oxygen from the incoming blood).

blocks.text: Factors determining the outcome of ischemia
The outcome of ischemia can range from complete recovery to **infarction** (ischemic necrosis of the tissue). The outcome depends on the following:

items: **The development of collateral circulation** — the most important factor.
**The rate of development of ischemia** — with slow narrowing the collaterals have time to develop; with sudden occlusion they do not.
**The duration of ischemia.**
**The sensitivity of the tissue to hypoxia** and the intensity of its metabolism.
**The state of the general circulation** (heart failure and hypotension aggravate the outcome).

blocks.title: Table 5.3. Tolerance time of tissues to complete ischemia (approximate)
head: Tissue
Time at which irreversible changes begin

parts.text: By their collateral circulation, organs are divided into three groups:

items: **organs with absolutely sufficient collaterals** — many anastomoses (limbs, mesentery, chest wall): ischemia is slight when one artery is occluded;
**organs with relatively sufficient (or relatively insufficient) collaterals** — anastomoses exist but open slowly (intestine, stomach, lungs, skin);
**organs with absolutely insufficient collaterals** — “end” (terminal) arteries (myocardium, brain, kidney, spleen, retina): occlusion of an artery leads to infarction.

blocks.text: Cell injury in ischemia and reperfusion injury

The main mechanisms of cell injury in ischemia: cessation of oxidative phosphorylation → ATP deficiency → failure of the Na+/K+ pump → entry of sodium and water into the cell (cellular swelling) → anaerobic glycolysis and lactic acidosis → accumulation of Ca2+ inside the cell → activation of phospholipases and proteases → membrane injury → necrosis.

**Reperfusion injury** is a paradoxical increase in injury when blood flow is restored after ischemia. Its mechanisms: formation of large amounts of reactive oxygen species (free radicals), massive entry of Ca2+ into cells, activation of leukocytes and plugging of microvessels (the no-reflow phenomenon), reperfusion arrhythmias.

parts.text: In myocardial infarction, “time is myocardium”: the faster blood flow in the coronary artery is restored (thrombolysis or coronary angioplasty), the smaller the volume of necrosis. The same applies to ischemic stroke — thrombolysis is effective only in the first hours after the onset of symptoms (the “therapeutic window”). Along with reperfusion, measures are also taken to reduce its injurious effect.

blocks.text: **Stasis** is the slowing and cessation of blood flow in the vessels of the microcirculation (mainly in the capillaries).

blocks.title: Table 5.4. Types of stasis
head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Sharp decrease in the inflow of blood from the arteries
Impeded outflow of blood through the veins
The severe stage of venous hyperemia
Changes in the blood itself and in the capillary wall: aggregation of red blood cells, hemoconcentration

blocks.text: The main mechanism of true stasis is **aggregation of red blood cells (“sludge”)**: red blood cells stick together like “stacks of coins” and plug the capillaries. This is caused by a decrease in the negative surface charge of red blood cells, an increase in high-molecular-weight plasma proteins (fibrinogen, globulins), hemoconcentration (water loss) and increased permeability of the capillary wall.
If stasis is brief, it is a reversible process; if prolonged, it leads to tissue necrosis and thrombus formation.

**Thrombosis** is the clotting of blood in a vessel or heart cavity in the living organism with the formation of a clot called a thrombus. Unlike a blood clot, a **thrombus** (Greek thrombos — clot) is attached to the vessel wall and forms under conditions of blood flow.
Causes of thrombus formation — Virchow's triad

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Virchow's triad (based on N.H. Abdullaev, 2008; V. Kumar et al., 2015)

blocks.title: Table 5.5. Virchow's triad
head: Factor
Essence
Examples
rows: Subendothelial collagen is exposed, tissue factor is released, and the antithrombotic properties of the endothelium (prostacyclin, NO, thrombomodulin) are lost
Atherosclerosis, vasculitis, trauma, intravascular catheter, homocysteinemia, smoking
Slowing and turbulence: platelets come close to the wall, activated factors are not diluted
Venous congestion, atrial fibrillation, aneurysm, prolonged bed rest, long flights
Increased activity of the coagulation system or weakening of the anticoagulant system
Cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, oral contraceptives, hereditary thrombophilias (factor V Leiden mutation, antithrombin III deficiency), antiphospholipid syndrome

blocks.text: Stages of thrombus formation

items: **Platelet adhesion** — at the site of injury, platelets adhere to exposed collagen via von Willebrand factor.
**Platelet activation and aggregation** — platelets change shape and release ADP, thromboxane A2 and serotonin; they stick to one another via fibrinogen bridges (the white head of the thrombus).
**Activation of the coagulation cascade** — thrombin is generated via tissue factor (the extrinsic pathway) and factor XII (the intrinsic pathway).
**Conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin** — a fibrin network forms, in which red blood cells and leukocytes become trapped.
**Clot retraction** — the thrombus becomes denser owing to the contractile proteins of platelets.

blocks.text: Types of thrombi

blocks.title: Table 5.6. Types of thrombi
head: Type
Composition and conditions of formation
Location
rows: Mainly platelets and fibrin; forms slowly in fast flow
A fibrin network and many red blood cells; forms rapidly in slow flow
White head, mixed body, red tail
In microvessels; fibrin and fragments of red blood cells and platelets

blocks.text: By whether they completely occlude the vascular lumen, **occlusive** and **mural (parietal)** thrombi are distinguished.
Outcomes of a thrombus

items: **Aseptic autolysis** (dissolution) — the thrombus dissolves under the action of the fibrinolytic system (plasmin), and blood flow is restored.
**Organization** — connective tissue grows into the thrombus.
**Canalization and vascularization** — new channels form within the organized thrombus, and blood flow is partly restored.
**Petrification** — calcium salts are deposited in the thrombus (“phleboliths” in veins).
**Septic (purulent) dissolution** — the thrombus becomes infected; risk of septic embolism and sepsis.
**Detachment of the thrombus** — thromboembolism.

parts.text: Thrombus formation is a pathological manifestation of a protective mechanism (hemostasis). Arterial thrombosis leads to ischemia and infarction (myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke), whereas venous thrombosis leads to venous congestion and thromboembolism. Prevention: antiplatelet agents (acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) — in arterial thrombosis), anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin — in venous thrombosis and atrial fibrillation).

blocks.text: **Embolism** (Greek emballo — I throw in) is occlusion of a vascular lumen by particles not normally found in the blood or lymph flow (**emboli**) that are carried along by the flow.
Types of embolism by the nature of the emboli

blocks.title: Table 5.7. Types of embolism by the nature of the embolus
head: Type
Embolus
Conditions of origin
rows: A detached thrombus or part of it
Deep vein thrombosis of the legs, thrombi in the heart
Fractures of long bones, crushing of adipose tissue, accidental intravenous injection of oily solutions
Injury of the neck veins (negative pressure in the veins), violation of infusion technique, surgery
Decompression sickness, loss of sealing at altitude
During labor; severe shock and DIC syndrome
Clusters of bacteria, an infected thrombus
A bullet, a fragment of a catheter

blocks.text: Types of embolism by the path of movement of the emboli

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Paths of movement of emboli (based on N.H. Abdullaev, 2008)

blocks.title: Table 5.8. Types of embolism by the path of movement
head: Type
Path
rows: Systemic veins → right heart → branches of the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary veins, left heart (thrombi on the valves and in the atrial appendage), aorta → systemic arteries (brain, kidneys, spleen, intestine, legs)
Intestinal and splenic veins → portal vein → liver
Systemic veins → right heart → left heart through a septal defect between the atria or ventricles → systemic arteries
The embolus moves against the blood flow because of its weight (for example, a heavy embolus in the inferior vena cava descends)

blocks.text: Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the most dangerous types of embolism. The main source of emboli (about 90%) is deep vein thrombosis of the legs and the small pelvis.

Pathogenesis: the embolus occludes the pulmonary artery → pulmonary vascular resistance increases and the right ventricle is overloaded (acute cor pulmonale) → the return of blood to the left heart decreases, and cardiac output and arterial pressure fall → the ventilation-perfusion relationship is disturbed and hypoxemia develops. In addition, serotonin and thromboxane released from platelets cause reflex spasm of the bronchi and pulmonary vessels and spasm of the coronary vessels (the pulmonocoronary reflex).

parts.text: Massive PE often develops suddenly and unexpectedly: in the days after surgery, when the patient gets up for the first time or strains in the toilet, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, cyanosis and fainting are observed. Do not forget thromboprophylaxis in patients with risk factors (surgery, prolonged bed rest, cancer, pregnancy).

blocks.text: **Fat embolism** usually develops 24–72 hours after a fracture of a long bone (the femur): shortness of breath and hypoxemia (occlusion of the pulmonary capillaries), neurological disorders (brain), and a petechial rash on the skin of the chest and axillae.

In **air embolism**, entry of 10–20 mL of air into the blood is usually harmless, but a large volume entering rapidly (more than 100 mL) may form an “air lock” in the right ventricle and lead to cardiac arrest.
Experiment 1: ischemia in the frog tongue and the rabbit ear

items: Fix the anesthetized frog on a cork board with its belly down, pull out the tongue, spread it over the opening and observe the vessels under the microscope.
Apply 1–2 drops of epinephrine solution (1:1000) to the tongue.
Observe the constriction of the arterioles, the decrease in the number of working capillaries, the slowing of blood flow and the blanching of the tongue.
In the rabbit ear: press the ear artery with a finger or inject a small amount of epinephrine under the skin — the ear blanches, the vascular network becomes invisible and the temperature falls.
After the pressure is removed or the action of epinephrine ends, observe the development of postischemic hyperemia.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** epinephrine constricts the arterioles via alpha-adrenergic receptors — **angiospastic ischemia** develops. The reddening after ischemia has been eliminated is postischemic arterial hyperemia caused by metabolites.
Experiment 2: observing thrombus formation

items: Place the frog mesentery under the microscope and find a larger vessel (a venule or arteriole).
Place a crystal of table salt (sodium chloride) on the vessel wall.

Observe the injury of the vessel wall at the site of the crystal, the adhesion and accumulation of platelets (in the frog — cells that perform the function of platelets) on the wall, and then the growth of the thrombus and the narrowing of the blood flow.
Record the time of thrombus formation and the degree to which it has occluded the vascular lumen.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** the hypertonic solution injures the endothelium (the first factor of Virchow's triad), as a result of which platelet adhesion and aggregation begin.
Experiment 3: fat embolism

items: Fix the frog on the board and place the mesentery under the microscope.
Inject 0.2–0.5 mL of warm vegetable oil into the abdominal vein of the frog (v. abdominalis), taking care not to inject into the lymph sac.
After a few minutes, observe the movement of fat droplets in the mesenteric vessels, their becoming lodged in small vessels and the cessation of blood flow along that vessel.
Observe the general state of the frog (breathing, movement).

parts.text: In the frog, fat injected into the abdominal vein also enters the portal system and the liver; in humans, fat entering through a vein is first trapped in the pulmonary capillaries. This difference shows once again that interspecies differences must be taken into account when transferring the results of animal experiments to humans.

skills.title: Skill: assessing the signs of ischemia

items: Compare the color of the limb on the affected and healthy sides (pallor, mottling).
Compare skin temperature at symmetrical points with the back of the hand.
Check the pulse in the peripheral arteries (femoral, popliteal, foot arteries).
Assess capillary refill: press the nail plate for 5 seconds and release it — if the color returns more slowly than in 2 seconds, perfusion is reduced.
Detect pain and impaired sensation and movement.
Determine the type of ischemia (compression, obturation, angiospasm) and its probable cause.

skills.title: Skill: assessing the risk of thrombosis and embolism

items: Examine all three factors of Virchow's triad separately in the patient.
Identify factors of endothelial injury: trauma, surgery, catheter, atherosclerosis.
Identify factors of slowed blood flow: prolonged bed rest, varicose veins, heart failure, arrhythmia.
Identify factors of hypercoagulability: cancer, pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives, a family history of thrombosis.
Determine the source of the embolus and its probable path (pulmonary or systemic circulation).
Write a conclusion and indicate the direction of prevention.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man has smoked for 20 years and has diabetes mellitus. He complains of pain in the left calf that appears when walking and disappears when he stops (“intermittent claudication”). On examination, the left foot is pale and cold, and no pulse is detected in the foot arteries. Ultrasound revealed atherosclerotic narrowing of the femoral artery.
cases.ask: What circulatory disorder has developed? Why does the pain appear only when walking? What factors are important in the development of the disease?
cases.answer: Obturative ischemia has developed because of an atherosclerotic plaque. At rest, the blood arriving through the narrowed artery and the collaterals covers the needs of the muscle, but during walking the oxygen demand of the muscle increases while the inflow of blood does not — relative ischemia; products of anaerobic metabolism (lactate, H+, K+) accumulate, stimulate the nerve endings and cause pain. When the patient stops, demand decreases and the pain passes. Smoking (endothelial injury, vascular spasm) and diabetes mellitus (endothelial dysfunction, accelerated atherosclerosis) are important as etiologic factors and conditions. Because the disease developed slowly, the collaterals have had time to develop partially — that is why there is no necrosis at rest.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 67-year-old woman underwent surgery for a fracture of the femoral neck. On day 6, when she got up for the first time, she suddenly developed severe shortness of breath and chest pain, her lips turned blue, and arterial pressure fell to 80/50 mm Hg. The left calf is swollen and painful on palpation.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? What is the source of the embolus? Which factors of Virchow's triad took part in thrombus formation?
cases.answer: Pulmonary embolism has developed. The source of the embolus is a thrombus in the deep veins of the left leg (swelling and pain of the calf). All three factors of Virchow's triad took part: endothelial injury (trauma and surgery), slowing of blood flow (prolonged bed rest, old age) and hypercoagulability (the state after surgery and trauma). When the patient got up and her muscles contracted, the thrombus detached and was carried with venous blood through the right heart into the pulmonary artery. Occlusion of the pulmonary artery led to right ventricular strain, decreased cardiac output and arterial hypotension, and the ventilation-perfusion mismatch led to hypoxemia and cyanosis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 70-year-old patient has atrial fibrillation (permanent form) and does not take anticoagulants. Paralysis of the right arm and leg and a speech disorder suddenly appeared.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Where did the embolus come from and by what path? Could this condition have been prevented?
cases.answer: Ischemic stroke has developed as a result of thromboembolism of a cerebral artery (the territory of the left middle cerebral artery). In atrial fibrillation the left atrium does not contract effectively; blood flow slows and becomes turbulent, especially in the left atrial appendage, and a thrombus forms (the abnormal blood flow factor of Virchow's triad). The detached thrombus passed through the left ventricle and aorta into the arteries of the systemic circulation — into a cerebral artery. Because the cerebral arteries are “end” arteries with insufficient collaterals, ischemic necrosis developed. In atrial fibrillation, anticoagulant therapy significantly reduces the risk of such embolism.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of inflammation. Alteration and vascular reactions

goals.text: To explain to the student the essence and biological significance of inflammation, its etiology, components and stages; to teach alteration, inflammatory mediators, metabolism in the inflammatory focus and the changes in vascular reactions; and to teach the student to observe the stages of local circulation in inflammation in the frog mesentery using Cohnheim's experiment.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition, biological significance and classical signs of inflammation;
the etiology and classification of inflammation;
the components of inflammation: alteration, exudation (with vascular reactions), proliferation;
the mechanisms of primary and secondary alteration;
the origin and action of inflammatory mediators;
the metabolic and physicochemical changes in the inflammatory focus;
the stages of vascular reactions in inflammation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to perform Cohnheim's experiment and identify the stages of vascular reactions in the inflammatory focus under the microscope;
to explain the external signs of inflammation in relation to their mechanisms;
to group inflammatory mediators by origin and action.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The classical signs of inflammation: the four signs of **Celsus** — **rubor** (redness), **tumor** (swelling), **calor** (heat), **dolor** (pain); the fifth sign added by **Galen** (or Virchow) — **functio laesa** (loss of function).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Secondary alteration is often stronger than primary alteration and continues even after the phlogogenic factor has disappeared. For example, in acute pancreatitis the activated pancreatic enzymes themselves “digest” the gland tissue and its surroundings (autolysis). One of the goals of anti-inflammatory treatment is precisely to limit secondary alteration.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the main actions of mediators: **vasodilators** — “HPN” (Histamine, Prostaglandins, NO); **increase permeability** — “HBL” (Histamine, Bradykinin, Leukotrienes C4/D4); **chemotaxis** — “C5a, LTB4, IL-8”; **pain** — “BP” (Bradykinin, Prostaglandin E2); **fever** — “IL-1, TNF, IL-6, PGE2”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Arterial hyperemia in inflammation is short (from 10–30 minutes to several hours), whereas venous hyperemia lasts long and is the main vascular manifestation of inflammation. The main reasons for the transition to venous hyperemia are extravascular (pressure of the exudate), vascular wall (endothelial swelling, adhesion of leukocytes) and intravascular (hemoconcentration, aggregation, microthrombi) factors.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: For the experiment to succeed, the mesentery must not be stretched so as to compress the vessels, and it must not be allowed to dry. Otherwise venous hyperemia and stasis will appear not because of inflammation but as a result of mechanical compression or drying, and the experiment will be misinterpreted.

sections.title: 1. The concept of inflammation and its biological significance

blocks.text: **Inflammation** (Latin inflammatio) is a typical pathological process formed during evolution that manifests in response to injury by changes in local circulation and microcirculation in the tissue, exudation, emigration of leukocytes and proliferation of cells. Its goal is to delimit and eliminate the injurious factor and to clean and restore the injured tissue.

**The protective significance** of inflammation: delimiting the pathogenic factor and the injured tissue from the rest of the organism (forming a barrier), neutralizing and eliminating it, and creating conditions for regeneration. I.I. Mechnikov regarded inflammation as a protective reaction based on phagocytosis.

**The harmful side** of inflammation: it may itself intensify injury (secondary alteration), impair the function of vital organs (laryngeal edema, cerebral edema, injury of the heart valves), produce scars, and underlie chronic diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis).

parts.text: The classical signs of inflammation: the four signs of **Celsus** — **rubor** (redness), **tumor** (swelling), **calor** (heat), **dolor** (pain); the fifth sign added by **Galen** (or Virchow) — **functio laesa** (loss of function).

blocks.title: Table 6.1. External signs of inflammation and their mechanisms
head: Feature
Mechanism
rows: Arterial hyperemia, dilatation of arterioles and capillaries
Inflow of warm arterial blood, increased metabolism and heat production
Stimulation of nerve endings by mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandin E2, histamine) and by H+ and K+ ions; compression of tissues by edema
Tissue injury, pain, edema and disturbed microcirculation

blocks.text: **Phlogogenic factors** (Greek phlogosis — inflammation) are factors that cause inflammation:

items: **exogenous**: biological (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites — the most common), physical (trauma, burns, frostbite, radiation), chemical (acids, alkalis, turpentine, croton oil);
**endogenous**: foci of necrosis (infarction), hemorrhage, salt crystals (urate crystals in gout), immune complexes, tumor breakdown.

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Classification of inflammation
head: Basis of classification
Types
rows: Acute (from several days to 2–3 weeks), subacute, chronic (months, years)
Serous, fibrinous, purulent, putrefactive, hemorrhagic, mixed

blocks.text: **Specific inflammation** runs with morphological features characteristic of a particular causative agent (granulomas): tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, scleroma.

Inflammation consists of three interrelated components: **alteration** (injury), **exudation** (disturbed microcirculation, exit of fluid and cells from the vessels) and **proliferation** (multiplication of cells and repair). These components begin in sequence but then proceed simultaneously.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: General scheme of the pathogenesis of inflammation (based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009, Fig. 10.4)

blocks.text: **Alteration** (Latin alteratio — change) is injury of the structure, metabolism and function of a tissue. Alteration is the initial stage of inflammation.
**Primary alteration** is the direct injurious action of the phlogogenic factor on the tissue. Its extent depends on the strength, nature and duration of action of the factor.
**Secondary alteration** is the spread and deepening of injury under the action of factors formed as a result of primary alteration:

items: release of hydrolytic enzymes (proteases, lipases, glycosidases) from the lysosomes of injured cells;
release of reactive oxygen species and enzymes from activated leukocytes;
hypoxia due to disturbed microcirculation;
acidosis and hyperosmia;
excessive formation of mediators.

parts.text: Secondary alteration is often stronger than primary alteration and continues even after the phlogogenic factor has disappeared. For example, in acute pancreatitis the activated pancreatic enzymes themselves “digest” the gland tissue and its surroundings (autolysis). One of the goals of anti-inflammatory treatment is precisely to limit secondary alteration.

blocks.text: Disturbances of metabolism in the inflammatory focus

In the inflammatory focus, metabolism initially increases and oxygen consumption rises; then, as a result of disturbed microcirculation and mitochondrial injury, **anaerobic glycolysis** predominates.

blocks.title: Table 6.3. Metabolic and physicochemical changes in the inflammatory focus
head: Change
Essence and consequence
rows: Glycolysis increases, lactate and pyruvate accumulate
Breakdown of fats, accumulation of fatty acids and ketone bodies
Proteolysis increases, polypeptides and amino acids accumulate
First compensated, then decompensated; pH falls to 6.5–5.5 (in a purulent focus); it intensifies pain and permeability
The number of particles increases because of the breakdown of molecules, osmotic pressure rises — water is drawn into the focus
Oncotic pressure rises owing to proteins leaving the vessels and to protein breakdown
K+ leaves injured cells, and the ratio of K+ to H+ and Ca2+ in the tissue increases

blocks.text: **Inflammatory mediators** are biologically active substances that regulate the development of inflammation and determine its manifestations. They are divided into **cell-derived** and **plasma-derived** mediators.

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Cell-derived mediators
head: Mediator
Source
Main action
rows: Dilates arterioles, rapidly increases venular permeability (early phase), itching
Many cells (from arachidonic acid by the cyclooxygenase pathway)
Dilate vessels, intensify pain and fever
LTB4 — strong chemotaxis; LTC4 and LTD4 — increased permeability, bronchospasm
Activate the endothelium (adhesion molecules), fever, acute-phase proteins
Kill microbes but also injure the tissue

blocks.title: Table 6.5. Plasma-derived mediators
head: System
Mediators
Main action
rows: Dilate vessels, increase permeability, cause severe pain
C3a, C5a (anaphylatoxins), C3b, the membrane attack complex
C5a — strong chemotaxis; C3a and C5a — release histamine from mast cells; C3b — opsonization
Fibrinopeptides, fibrin degradation products, factor XIIa
Increase permeability, chemotaxis, activate the kinin system

parts.text: To remember the main actions of mediators: **vasodilators** — “HPN” (Histamine, Prostaglandins, NO); **increase permeability** — “HBL” (Histamine, Bradykinin, Leukotrienes C4/D4); **chemotaxis** — “C5a, LTB4, IL-8”; **pain** — “BP” (Bradykinin, Prostaglandin E2); **fever** — “IL-1, TNF, IL-6, PGE2”.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, diclofenac, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin)) block cyclooxygenase and reduce the synthesis of prostaglandins — that is why they weaken pain, fever and inflammation. Glucocorticoids inhibit phospholipase A2 (via lipocortin) and the synthesis of cytokines, that is, they reduce the formation of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

blocks.text: In the inflammatory focus, local circulation changes in a certain sequence. These changes were first described by J. Cohnheim (1867) in the frog mesentery.

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Stages of vascular reactions in inflammation (according to Cohnheim)

blocks.title: Table 6.6. Stages of vascular reactions in inflammation
head: Stage
Mechanism
Significance
rows: Reflex stimulation of vasoconstrictor nerves, action of catecholamines; lasts a few seconds
Dilatation of arterioles by neuroparalytic and metabolic mechanisms and under the action of mediators (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, NO)
Redness and heat; the inflow of blood, leukocytes and oxygen into the focus increases
Hemoconcentration due to exudation, aggregation of red blood cells, compression of venules by edema fluid, endothelial swelling, margination of leukocytes and microthrombi
Blood flow slows, conditions are created for the emigration of leukocytes
The inflammatory focus is delimited; but if prolonged, tissue necrosis

parts.text: Arterial hyperemia in inflammation is short (from 10–30 minutes to several hours), whereas venous hyperemia lasts long and is the main vascular manifestation of inflammation. The main reasons for the transition to venous hyperemia are extravascular (pressure of the exudate), vascular wall (endothelial swelling, adhesion of leukocytes) and intravascular (hemoconcentration, aggregation, microthrombi) factors.

blocks.text: Exudation
**Exudation** is the exit of the liquid part of blood (plasma), proteins and blood cells from the vessels into the inflammatory focus. The fluid that leaves the vessels is called **exudate**.
Mechanisms of exudation:

items: **Increased permeability of the vessel wall** — the main mechanism. Under the action of mediators (histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes), endothelial cells contract and gaps form between them (mainly in postcapillary venules); the endothelium is injured directly; activated leukocytes injure the endothelium.
**Increased hydrostatic pressure in capillaries and venules** — as a result of hyperemia.
**Increased osmotic and oncotic pressure in the tissue** — hyperosmia and hyperonkia draw fluid into the focus.

blocks.title: Table 6.7. Differences between exudate and transudate
head: Parameter
Exudate (in inflammation)
Transudate (in edema, without inflammation)

blocks.text: **Aim:** to observe under the microscope the stages of the changes in local circulation in the inflammatory focus in the frog mesentery.
**Equipment:** a frog, ether or urethane for anesthesia (or a needle for destroying the spinal cord), a cork board with an opening, pins, surgical instruments, a microscope, physiological saline.
Procedure

items: Under anesthesia (or after destruction of the spinal cord), fix the frog on its back on the board with an opening.
Make a 1–1.5 cm incision on the side of the abdominal wall and carefully pull out an intestinal loop.
Spread the mesentery over the opening in the board and fix it with pins (do not compress the vessels).
At low magnification, find the arterioles, capillaries and venules; describe normal blood flow (fast, axial flow, a plasma layer next to the wall).
Because the mesentery is in contact with air, inflammation gradually develops. Observe the changes every 5–10 minutes and record them in the protocol (1–1.5 hours in total).
Apply drops of physiological saline from time to time so that the mesentery does not dry.

blocks.text: Sequence of the changes observed

items: **Arterial hyperemia** (the first 10–20 minutes): arterioles and capillaries dilate, previously invisible capillaries open and blood flow accelerates.
**Venous hyperemia**: venules dilate, blood flow slows and the plasma layer disappears.
**Margination of leukocytes**: leukocytes roll along the venular wall and adhere to it.
**Emigration of leukocytes**: leukocytes pass through the venular wall into the surrounding tissue (in detail in the next topic).
**Prestasis and stasis**: in some capillaries blood moves in a pendulum-like manner and stops; diapedesis of red blood cells.

Otherwise venous hyperemia and stasis will appear not because of inflammation but as a result of mechanical compression or drying, and the experiment will be misinterpreted.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 25-year-old man got a thorn in his finger. Two days later the fingertip became red, swollen and warm, severe “throbbing” pain appeared, and bending the finger is difficult. Body temperature is 37.8 °C.
cases.ask: What pathological process has developed? Explain the mechanism of each local sign. What does the systemic sign indicate?
cases.answer: Acute inflammation of the finger (paronychia/felon) has developed; the phlogogenic factor is the microbes introduced with the thorn and the foreign body. Redness and heat — arterial hyperemia (dilatation of arterioles under the action of mediators, inflow of warm blood, increased metabolism). Swelling — exudation: increased permeability of the vessel wall, hyperosmia and hyperonkia. Pain — stimulation of nerve endings by bradykinin, prostaglandin E2, H+ and K+ ions, and compression of the nerve endings by exudate in the dense tissue of the fingertip (hence “throbbing”). Loss of function — due to pain and swelling. Fever — a systemic reaction under the action of cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) released from the inflammatory focus; it indicates that the local process is affecting the whole organism.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Students performed Cohnheim's experiment. After 40 minutes, one student saw that blood flow in the venules had slowed and leukocytes had accumulated along the wall. In the second student's preparation, stasis was observed in all vessels after only 10 minutes, and the stage of arterial hyperemia was not seen at all.
cases.ask: Which stage of inflammation did the first student observe? What does the second student's result indicate?
cases.answer: The first student observed the stage of venous hyperemia and the margination of leukocytes — the regular development of inflammation. In the second student's preparation, rapidly developing stasis and the absence of arterial hyperemia indicate a fault in the experimental technique: the mesentery was stretched and the vessels were compressed by the pins, or the mesentery dried. Such stasis developed not because of inflammation but as a result of a mechanical factor, so the preparation must be made again.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Fluid was obtained by puncture of the pleural cavity in a 40-year-old patient. The fluid is turbid, protein content 42 g/L, specific gravity 1.024, many neutrophils, positive Rivalta test.
cases.ask: Is this an exudate or a transudate? Explain the mechanism of its formation. What type of exudate could it be?
cases.answer: This is an exudate: protein more than 30 g/L, specific gravity above 1.018, many cells, positive Rivalta test, turbid. It formed as a result of inflammation of the pleura (pleurisy). Mechanism: under the action of mediators (histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes), venular permeability increases, hydrostatic pressure rises because of hyperemia, and hyperosmia and hyperonkia develop in the inflammatory focus — as a result, protein-rich fluid and leukocytes pass into the pleural cavity. Because there are many neutrophils, it may be a serous-purulent or purulent exudate (if it progresses — pleural empyema); this is characteristic of bacterial infection.

goals.text: To explain to the student the stages and molecular mechanisms of leukocyte emigration, the theories of emigration, and the significance of phagocytosis and chemotaxis in inflammation; to teach the role of inflammatory mediators in these processes, proliferation, and the systemic signs and outcomes of inflammation; and to teach the student to observe leukocyte emigration and the effect of physicochemical factors on it in an experiment and to assess phagocytic activity.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

the sequence of emigration (Mechnikov's law) and its causes;

goals.text: The student should be able to:

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The role of physicochemical factors in emigration: **acidosis** and **an increase in K^+^ ions** in the inflammatory focus change the surface properties of the endothelium and leukocytes and intensify emigration; **Ca^2+^ ions**, in contrast, make the vessel wall denser and weaken permeability and emigration. This rule is tested in the experimental part.

blocks.text: **Emigration** is the exit of leukocytes from a blood vessel into the inflammatory focus. Emigration takes place mainly in **postcapillary venules**, because here blood flow is slow, the endothelium has many adhesion molecules, and the junctions between endothelial cells are looser.

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: Stages of leukocyte emigration (based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009, Fig. 10.11)

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Stages of leukocyte emigration
head: Stage
Mechanism
Key molecules
rows: When blood flow slows, red blood cells collect along the axis, and leukocytes are pushed to the periphery, next to the wall
The leukocyte forms loose bonds with the endothelial surface and rolls slowly
Selectins: P-selectin (rapidly, under the action of histamine), E-selectin (under the action of IL-1 and TNF), L-selectin (on the leukocyte)
Leukocyte integrins are activated and bind firmly to endothelial ligands
Integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1, VLA-4) and ICAM-1, VCAM-1
The leukocyte extends pseudopodia, passes between endothelial cells and breaks down the basement membrane with enzymes
Directed movement in the tissue toward the focus along the concentration gradient of chemoattractants
C5a, LTB4, IL-8, bacterial N-formyl peptides

parts.text: **Leukocyte adhesion deficiency** is a rare disease associated with a hereditary defect of integrins (CD18). In such children leukocytes cannot leave the vessels: there are many neutrophils in the blood, but no pus is formed, the umbilical stump separates late, and recurrent severe bacterial infections are observed. This example clearly shows the protective significance of emigration.

blocks.text: Sequence of emigration
As I.I. Mechnikov established, in acute inflammation leukocytes leave the vessels in a certain order:

items: **Neutrophils** predominate in the first 6–24 hours (the most mobile, numerous and fast-responding).
**Monocytes (which turn into macrophages)** predominate after 24–48 hours.
**Lymphocytes** come later, especially in chronic and immune inflammation.

blocks.text: This sequence is not always maintained: in viral infections lymphocytes, and in allergic inflammation and helminthic infestations eosinophils, predominate early.
Theories of emigration

blocks.title: Table 7.2. Theories of emigration
head: Theory
Content
rows: Leukocytes are passively “squeezed out” through the vessel wall by the pressure difference
Leukocytes actively move toward chemical substances in the focus
Changes in pH, ionic composition and surface tension in the focus cause the leukocyte membrane to extend pseudopodia on one side
Emigration is a regulated process with the active participation of adhesion molecules, chemokines and the leukocyte cytoskeleton

parts.text: The role of physicochemical factors in emigration: **acidosis** and **an increase in K^+^ ions** in the inflammatory focus change the surface properties of the endothelium and leukocytes and intensify emigration; **Ca^2+^ ions**, in contrast, make the vessel wall denser and weaken permeability and emigration. This rule is tested in the experimental part.

blocks.text: **Chemotaxis** is the directed movement of cells along a concentration gradient of chemical substances. If leukocytes move toward the focus, it is **positive** chemotaxis; if they move away from it, **negative** chemotaxis.

blocks.title: Table 7.3. Main chemoattractants
head: Group
Substances
rows: Bacterial N-formyl peptides, components of the bacterial cell wall (lipopolysaccharide)
IL-8 (CXCL8) — for neutrophils; MCP-1 — for monocytes; eotaxin — for eosinophils
Breakdown products of fibrin and collagen

blocks.text: The chemoattractant binds to a receptor on the leukocyte membrane → a signal is transmitted via a G protein → intracellular Ca2+ increases and actin polymerizes → the leukocyte extends pseudopodia and moves toward the focus.

**Phagocytosis** (Greek phagein — to devour, kytos — cell) is the active engulfment and digestion of foreign particles, microorganisms and dead cells by specialized cells (phagocytes). Phagocytosis was discovered by I.I. Mechnikov in 1883, who regarded it as the main protective mechanism of inflammation.
Phagocytes:

items: **microphages** — neutrophil granulocytes (mainly phagocytose bacteria);
**macrophages** — monocytes and tissue macrophages (histiocytes, Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, microglia, osteoclasts); they engulf large particles and dead cells and present antigen.

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Stages of phagocytosis and mechanisms of killing microbes

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Stages of phagocytosis
head: Stage
Essence
rows: The phagocyte moves toward the object by chemotaxis
Phagocyte receptors recognize the object; opsonins (IgG, the C3b fragment of complement, lectins) sharply accelerate this process
The phagocyte surrounds the object with pseudopodia, and a phagosome forms
The microbe is killed by oxygen-dependent and oxygen-independent mechanisms and broken down by hydrolytic enzymes

blocks.text: Mechanisms of killing microbes

**Oxygen-dependent mechanism (“respiratory burst”):** oxygen consumption rises sharply during phagocytosis; NADPH oxidase forms the superoxide anion (O2−), from which hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and the hydroxyl radical arise; myeloperoxidase forms a very powerful bactericidal substance, hypochlorous acid (HOCl), from H2O2 and chloride ion.

**Oxygen-independent mechanism:** lysozyme (breaks down the bacterial wall), defensins (form pores in the membrane), lactoferrin (binds iron and stops bacterial growth), cationic proteins, proteases, the acidic environment in the phagolysosome.

parts.text: The myeloperoxidase system = “household bleach”: H2O2 + Cl− → HOCl. The greenish-yellow color of pus is due precisely to myeloperoxidase (an enzyme with a green pigment).

blocks.text: Completeness of phagocytosis

items: **Complete phagocytosis** — the engulfed microbe is killed and fully digested.

**Incomplete phagocytosis** — the engulfed microbe does not die; it survives and even multiplies inside the phagocyte (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, gonococcus, Brucella, Leishmania). In this case the phagocyte may spread the microbe throughout the organism.

blocks.text: Insufficiency of phagocytosis

blocks.title: Table 7.5. Causes of insufficient phagocytosis
head: Impaired stage
Causes and examples
rows: Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect), myeloperoxidase deficiency

parts.text: **In chronic granulomatous disease**, neutrophils engulf the microbe but cannot kill it because there is no “respiratory burst”. Patients develop recurrent abscesses and granulomas caused by catalase-positive microbes (staphylococcus, Aspergillus). The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test is used for diagnosis.

blocks.text: **Proliferation** is the multiplication of cells in the inflammatory focus; it is the final stage of inflammation and ensures the restoration of the injured tissue.

Proliferation mainly involves **local stem (cambial) cells** (fibroblasts, endothelium, epithelium) and monocytes arriving from the blood. Macrophages release growth factors: platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

**Granulation tissue** is young connective tissue consisting of newly formed capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells. It fills the bottom of the wound, and later, as collagen fibers increase, it turns into a scar.

blocks.title: Table 7.6. Types of repair
head: Type
Essence
Condition
rows: The injured tissue is restored by the same kind of tissue
The injury is small and the tissue is capable of regeneration (epithelium, liver)
The defect is filled with connective tissue — a scar
Extensive injury, tissue with low regenerative capacity (myocardium, neurons)

blocks.text: Although inflammation is a local process, it is accompanied by a response of the whole organism.

blocks.title: Table 7.7. Systemic signs of inflammation
head: Feature
Mechanism
rows: IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha → PGE2 in the hypothalamus → raised set point of the thermoregulatory center
Increased release and production of leukocytes in the bone marrow under the action of cytokines and colony-stimulating factors
An increase in blood fibrinogen and globulins enhances aggregation of red blood cells
Under the action of IL-6, the liver increases the synthesis of C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin
Change in the protein composition of blood
Alpha- and gamma-globulins increase, albumin decreases
Weakness, loss of appetite, drowsiness (the action of cytokines on the central nervous system)

sections.title: 6. Outcomes of inflammation and chronic inflammation

blocks.text: Outcomes of acute inflammation:

items: **complete resolution** — the phlogogenic factor disappears, the exudate is absorbed and the tissue is restored;
**scar formation (fibrosis)** — in extensive injury;
**abscess formation** — a delimited collection of pus in purulent infection;
**transition to chronic inflammation** — if the phlogogenic factor persists.

blocks.text: **Chronic inflammation** is long-lasting inflammation in which alteration, inflammation and repair proceed simultaneously. Macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells predominate in its cellular composition; fibrosis and angiogenesis are marked. Causes: microbes that are difficult to kill (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi), long-acting exogenous substances (silica dust — silicosis), autoimmune reactions.

**Granulomatous inflammation** is a special type of chronic inflammation in which **granulomas** consisting of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) and multinucleated giant cells are formed (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, around foreign bodies).
Experiment 1: observing leukocyte emigration in the frog mesentery

items: Prepare the frog mesentery by Cohnheim's method (see Topic 6).
Find a venule under the microscope and observe it for 40–60 minutes.

Record the following stages in sequence: movement of leukocytes to the wall (margination), slow rolling along the wall, adhesion to the wall, passage through the wall by extending pseudopodia, and accumulation outside the vessel.
Count the number of leukocytes that have left the vessel in the field of view every 10 minutes.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: the effect of a change in ionic composition on emigration (physicochemical factors)

This experiment appears in the department plan as “Danilevsky's experiment” and is aimed at studying the effect of physicochemical shifts in the inflammatory focus on emigration. The preparation and concentrations are specified according to the department's methodological guidelines.

items: Prepare mesentery preparations from two frogs.
Keep applying drops of potassium chloride solution (or a weakly acidic buffer solution) to the first preparation.
Keep applying drops of calcium chloride solution to the second preparation.
Compare the intensity of emigration (the number of leukocytes that have left the vessels) in both preparations over the same period of time.

blocks.text: **Expected results and analysis:** K+ ions and acidosis loosen the junctions between endothelial cells and increase the mobility of leukocytes — emigration increases. Ca2+ ions make the vessel wall denser and stabilize membranes — emigration weakens. This confirms that hyperkalia and acidosis in the inflammatory focus are factors that intensify emigration.

parts.text: Old ideas about the “anti-inflammatory” and “antiallergic” action of calcium preparations were based on experiments like this one. In modern clinical practice calcium preparations are not considered effective for this purpose; they are used only in hypocalcemia.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determining phagocytic activity

items: Place 0.2 mL of heparinized blood (or peritoneal exudate of an animal) and 0.1 mL of a microbial suspension (for example, killed staphylococci or yeast cells) in a test tube.
Keep it in a thermostat at 37 °C for 30 minutes, mixing from time to time.
Prepare a smear from the mixture, dry it, fix it and stain it by the Romanowsky–Giemsa method.
Under the oil immersion microscope, examine 100 neutrophils: count how many of them have engulfed microbes and how many microbes each contains.
Calculate the parameters.

blocks.title: Table 7.8. Parameters of phagocytosis
head: Parameter
Calculation
Norm (approximate)
rows: Percentage of neutrophils that have engulfed microbes
Average number of microbes per phagocyte
Ratio of killed microbes to engulfed microbes

parts.text: The reference values of phagocytosis parameters depend on the method used in the laboratory and on the test object (type of microbe, exposure time). Always compare the result with the control values of the same laboratory.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the stages of emigration under the microscope

items: Distinguish a venule from an arteriole and a capillary by the direction of flow and the diameter.
Note the disappearance of the plasma layer and the movement of leukocytes to the wall.
Observe the slow rolling of a leukocyte along the wall (slower movement than red blood cells).
Count the leukocytes firmly attached to the wall and immobile.
Find and draw a leukocyte passing through the wall by extending pseudopodia.
Describe the movement of leukocytes outside the vessel toward the focus.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the phagocytic index and phagocytic number

items: Examine 100 consecutive neutrophils in the stained smear.
Count the neutrophils that have engulfed at least one microbe — this number equals the phagocytic index (in percent).
Calculate the total number of microbes inside all neutrophils.
Divide the total number of microbes by the number of neutrophils that have engulfed microbes — the phagocytic number.
Compare the result with the norm and write whether phagocytic activity has decreased or increased.
