cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 3-year-old child has had recurrent severe bacterial infections (pneumonia, otitis, skin abscesses) since birth. Staphylococcus and Aspergillus were isolated from the abscesses. The neutrophil count in the blood is normal, and the neutrophils have preserved their ability for chemotaxis and engulfment, but the NBT test is negative.
cases.ask: What disease does the child have? Which stage of phagocytosis is impaired? Why are catalase-positive microbes particularly dangerous?
cases.answer: Chronic granulomatous disease — a hereditary defect of NADPH oxidase. Neutrophils engulf microbes, but because there is no “respiratory burst”, they cannot form the superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide; that is, the killing stage of phagocytosis is impaired, and the negative NBT test shows exactly this. Catalase-negative microbes “deliver” the hydrogen peroxide they produce into the phagolysosome, and myeloperoxidase uses it to kill the microbe. Catalase-positive microbes (staphylococcus, Aspergillus) break down their own peroxide, so in such patients they are not killed and cause recurrent abscesses and granulomas.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In a 60-year-old patient with diabetes mellitus, a small wound on a toe has not healed for a long time, and purulent inflammation is spreading to the surroundings. Glycated hemoglobin is 10%.
cases.ask: Why do inflammation and infections run a severe course in diabetes mellitus? Which stages of leukocyte function are impaired?
cases.answer: Prolonged hyperglycemia impairs several stages of leukocyte function: chemotaxis and adhesion of neutrophils weaken, phagocytosis and the “respiratory burst” decrease (NADPH deficiency — glucose is consumed by the polyol pathway), and opsonization is impaired. In addition, diabetic microangiopathy and macroangiopathy worsen the blood supply of the tissue, neuropathy causes the wound to go unnoticed, and regeneration and the formation of granulation tissue slow down. As a result, the infection is not delimited and the wound does not heal for a long time; control of glycemia is an important part of treatment.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old patient has acute appendicitis. Blood test: leukocytes 15 × 10^9^/L, band neutrophils 12%, ESR 28 mm/h, C-reactive protein elevated. Body temperature 38.1 °C.
cases.ask: What signs of inflammation are these changes? Explain their mechanism.
cases.answer: These are systemic signs of inflammation. Leukocytosis and an increase in band neutrophils (a left shift) result from the release of immature neutrophils from the bone marrow and increased granulopoiesis under the action of cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha) and colony-stimulating factors released from the inflammatory focus. Increased ESR — an increase in fibrinogen and globulins in the blood enhances aggregation of red blood cells. C-reactive protein is an acute-phase protein synthesized in the liver under the action of IL-6. Fever — cytokines increase the formation of PGE2 in the hypothalamus and raise the set point of the thermoregulatory center.

topics.title: Allergy: etiology, pathogenesis and types. Immunodeficiency states

goals.text: To explain to the student the concepts of allergy and sensitization, the types of allergens, the stages and types of allergic reactions (the Gell–Coombs classification), the pathogenesis of immediate and delayed allergic reactions, anaphylaxis and its local manifestations, the mechanisms of desensitization, and primary and secondary immunodeficiency states; and to teach the student to observe anaphylactic shock and desensitization in a guinea pig in an experiment.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the concepts of allergy, sensitization and allergen, and the classification of allergens;
the three stages of allergic reactions;
the mechanisms and examples of types I–IV (V) of allergic reactions according to Gell and Coombs;
the differences between immediate and delayed allergic reactions;
the pathogenesis of anaphylactic shock and the principles of emergency care;
the mechanisms of specific and nonspecific desensitization;
primary and secondary immunodeficiencies and the pathogenesis of AIDS.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: to model anaphylactic shock in a guinea pig and describe its stages;
to perform desensitization by Besredka's method and explain its mechanism;
to identify the type of allergic reaction in a clinical situation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the types: **“ACID”** — **A**naphylactic (I), **C**ytotoxic (II), **I**mmune complex (III), **D**elayed (IV). Only type IV proceeds without antibodies, via T lymphocytes.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Atopy** is a hereditary predisposition to IgE production. In atopic patients (those with a family history of asthma, hay fever, atopic dermatitis), allergic diseases are common. **Pseudoallergic reactions** resemble allergy in appearance but proceed without an immunological stage: mediators are released directly (radiocontrast agents, opiates, some foods — strawberries, chocolate). They develop even on first exposure and do not require sensitization.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Stages of HIV infection: acute infection (mononucleosis-like syndrome), a long clinically latent period (years), and the AIDS stage. In the AIDS stage, the CD4+ lymphocyte count is less than 200 cells/µL, and Pneumocystis pneumonia, tuberculosis, candidiasis, toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus infection, Kaposi sarcoma and lymphomas develop. Modern antiretroviral therapy stops viral replication and restores immunity.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Before administering preparations based on horse serum, an intradermal test and stepwise administration by Besredka's method are mandatory. At the same time, a resuscitation kit (epinephrine, glucocorticoids, infusion agents) must always be ready.

blocks.text: **Allergy** (Greek allos — other, ergon — action) is an altered (enhanced) immune response of the organism on repeated exposure to an allergen, accompanied by injury of its own tissues. The term was proposed in 1906 by the Austrian pediatrician C. Pirquet.

Immunity and allergy are based on the same immune mechanisms; the difference lies in the result: in immunity the antigen is neutralized and the tissues are not injured, whereas in allergy the immune response injures the organism's own tissues.

**Sensitization** is an increase in the organism's sensitivity to an allergen after its first entry (formation of specific antibodies or sensitized T lymphocytes). Sensitization itself gives no clinical signs; it forms in 7–14 days and can persist for years.

items: **Active sensitization** — formation of the organism's own antibodies when an allergen is introduced.
**Passive sensitization** — when the serum (antibodies) or lymphocytes of a sensitized organism are transferred to another organism.

blocks.text: Allergens and their classification

**An allergen** is an antigen that causes an allergic reaction. Complete antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) and haptens (small molecules that are not antigens themselves but become allergens when bound to a protein: drugs, nickel, chromium) are distinguished.

blocks.title: Table 8.1. Classification of allergens
head: Group
Examples
rows: Hair and dander of cats, dogs and horses; bird feathers
Cow's milk, eggs, fish, nuts, peanuts, citrus fruits
Penicillins, sulfonamides, local anesthetics, vaccines and sera
Formaldehyde, latex, chromium and nickel salts, dyes
Altered own proteins; “sequestered” tissues (lens of the eye, thyroid colloid, sperm)

blocks.text: According to A.D. Ado, every allergic reaction passes through three stages.

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Stages of allergic reactions (according to A.D. Ado; based on V.V. Novitsky, 2009)

blocks.title: Table 8.2. Stages of an allergic reaction
head: Stage
Essence
rows: On first entry of the allergen, antibodies (IgE, IgG, IgM) or sensitized T lymphocytes are formed; on repeated entry the allergen binds to them
As a result of antigen-antibody or antigen-lymphocyte binding, biologically active substances (mediators) are formed and released
Under the action of mediators, the function of tissues and organs is impaired: contraction of smooth muscle, increased permeability, edema, inflammation, itching

sections.title: 3. Types of allergic reactions (the Gell and Coombs classification)

blocks.text: P. Gell and R. Coombs (1963) divided allergic reactions into four types according to the mechanism of immune injury; type V (stimulatory) was added later.

head: Type
Mechanism

Examples

IgG or IgM binds to an antigen on the cell surface → cell lysis via complement, phagocytosis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
Hemolytic anemias (incompatible blood transfusion, hemolytic disease of the newborn), drug-induced thrombocytopenia, Goodpasture syndrome

parts.text: To remember the types: **“ACID”** — **A**naphylactic (I), **C**ytotoxic (II), **I**mmune complex (III), **D**elayed (IV). Only type IV proceeds without antibodies, via T lymphocytes.

blocks.text: Immediate and delayed allergic reactions

blocks.title: Table 8.4. Differences between immediate and delayed allergic reactions
head: Feature
Immediate (I–III)
Delayed (IV)

blocks.text: **Anaphylaxis** (Greek ana — reverse, phylaxis — protection) — the systemic (generalized) form of a type I allergic reaction. It was discovered in 1902 by Ch. Richet and P. Portier: dogs that had received a small dose of sea anemone toxin died instead of being protected when it was injected a second time.
**Anaphylactic shock** — the most severe, life-threatening form of a type I allergic reaction.

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of anaphylactic shock (based on Ataman A.V., 2000, figure 27)

blocks.text: Main mediators of anaphylactic shock and their effects:

items: **histamine** — dilates arterioles, increases venular permeability, constricts the bronchi, causes itching;
**leukotrienes C~4~, D~4~, E~4~** (formerly called the “slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis”) — strong and prolonged bronchospasm, increased permeability;
**platelet-activating factor** — hypotension, bronchospasm, platelet aggregation;
**prostaglandin D~2~** — bronchospasm, vasodilation;
**tryptase** — a laboratory marker of mast cell activation.

blocks.text: In humans the main “target organs” of anaphylactic shock are the cardiovascular system (hypotension, collapse) and the airways (laryngeal edema, bronchospasm). In the guinea pig, by contrast, bronchospasm and asphyxia predominate; in the dog — spasm of the hepatic veins and pooling of blood in the portal system; in the rabbit — spasm of the pulmonary arteries. This interspecies difference is explained by the concept of the “shock organ”.

parts.text: The first and main drug in anaphylactic shock is **epinephrine (adrenaline)** (0.1 % solution, 0.3–0.5 ml into the thigh muscle in adults, repeated after 5–15 minutes if needed). Via alpha-adrenoceptors it constricts vessels and raises arterial pressure; via beta2-receptors it dilates the bronchi and stops mediator release from mast cells. Additional measures: stop the allergen, lay the patient down with legs raised, oxygen, intravenous crystalloid solutions; antihistamines and glucocorticoids are second-line agents.

blocks.text: Local manifestations of allergy

items: **Hives (urticaria)** — itchy wheals on the skin; increased vascular permeability in the dermis.
**Quincke's edema (angioedema)** — circumscribed deep edema of the subcutaneous and submucosal tissue; risk of asphyxia if it develops in the larynx.
**Allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis (pollinosis)** — seasonal, occurring when plants are in bloom.
**Atopic bronchial asthma** — bronchial hyperreactivity, bronchospasm, mucus hypersecretion and eosinophilic inflammation.
**Arthus phenomenon** — when an allergen is re-injected subcutaneously into a sensitized animal, immune complexes deposit at that site and hyperemia, edema and necrosis develop (type III).

parts.text: **Atopy** is a hereditary predisposition to IgE production. In atopic patients (those with a family history of asthma, hay fever, atopic dermatitis), allergic diseases are common. **Pseudoallergic reactions** resemble allergy in appearance but proceed without an immunological stage: mediators are released directly (radiocontrast agents, opiates, some foods — strawberries, chocolate). They develop even on first exposure and do not require sensitization.

blocks.text: **Desensitization (hyposensitization)** — reduction or elimination of the body's sensitivity to an allergen.
**Specific desensitization** — directed at a particular allergen:

items: **Besredka method (rapid desensitization)** — the allergen (e.g. a therapeutic serum) is first given in very small doses, then in gradually increasing doses at 20–30-minute intervals. The small doses gradually “bind” the IgE on mast cells and release mediators in small, safe portions; the full dose then does not cause shock. The effect is temporary.

**Allergen-specific immunotherapy (slow desensitization)** — the allergen is given in increasing doses over months and years. Mechanism: formation of “blocking” IgG antibodies (they capture the allergen before IgE does), a shift of the Th2 response towards Th1 and regulatory T cells, and reduced IgE synthesis.

blocks.text: **Nonspecific desensitization** — acting on the common mechanisms of allergic reactions: antihistamines, mast cell membrane stabilizers (cromoglicate), glucocorticoids, leukotriene receptor antagonists, adrenomimetics, monoclonal anti-IgE antibodies (omalizumab).
**Immunodeficiency states** — reduced resistance of the body to infections and tumors as a result of a defect in one or more components of the immune system.

blocks.title: Table 8.5. Primary (congenital) immunodeficiencies
head: Affected component
Examples
Clinical features
rows: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease), selective IgA deficiency
Recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of life (once maternal antibodies are exhausted)
Viral and fungal infections, hypocalcemia (the parathyroid glands are also absent)
Chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency

blocks.text: **Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiencies** — far more common. Causes: HIV infection, starvation and protein deficiency, diabetes mellitus, tumors (especially lymphoproliferative), ionizing radiation, treatment with cytostatics and glucocorticoids, splenectomy, old age, severe burns and injuries, chronic kidney failure.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)

The causative agent of AIDS is the **human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)**, a member of the retrovirus family. The virus binds to the CD4 molecule (and the CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors) and mainly damages **CD4^+^ T helper cells**, as well as macrophages and dendritic cells.

Pathogenesis: the virus enters the cell → a DNA copy is made from RNA by reverse transcriptase → it is integrated into the cell genome by integrase → the virus replicates and CD4+ cells die → the number of CD4+ lymphocytes gradually falls → cellular and humoral immunity are profoundly impaired → opportunistic infections and tumors develop.

parts.text: Stages of HIV infection: acute infection (mononucleosis-like syndrome), a long clinically latent period (years), and the AIDS stage. In the AIDS stage, the CD4+ lymphocyte count is less than 200 cells/µL, and Pneumocystis pneumonia, tuberculosis, candidiasis, toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus infection, Kaposi sarcoma and lymphomas develop. Modern antiretroviral therapy stops viral replication and restores immunity.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: anaphylactic shock in the guinea pig
**Aim:** to model and observe the systemic form of a type I allergic reaction — anaphylactic shock.
**Equipment:** guinea pigs (at least 2 sensitized and 1 control), horse serum (allergen), syringes, stopwatch.

items: **Sensitization** (performed in advance by the teacher): 14–21 days earlier, 0.1 ml of horse serum (sensitizing dose) was injected subcutaneously or intraperitoneally into the guinea pig.
Assess the baseline state of the sensitized and control (non-sensitized) animals: movement, respiratory rate, condition of the fur.
Inject both animals intravenously (or intracardially) with 0.5–1 ml of horse serum (challenge dose).

In the sensitized animal, record in sequence the signs that develop within a few minutes: restlessness, rubbing the nose, sneezing, ruffled fur, passage of urine and feces, difficulty breathing (expiratory dyspnea), trembling, convulsions, falling onto its side.
Record that no such changes are observed in the control animal.
On autopsy of the animal that died, observe the markedly distended (emphysematous), non-collapsing lungs — air is trapped in the alveoli because of bronchospasm.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** in the sensitized guinea pig, IgE (and IgG1) antibodies are bound to mast cells.
When the challenge dose is given, mast cell degranulation and release of mediators (mainly histamine) cause severe bronchiolar spasm and asphyxia — the guinea pig's “shock organ” is the lung.
Experiment 2: desensitization by the Besredka method

items: Before the challenge dose, inject a second sensitized guinea pig subcutaneously with a very small dose (0.01–0.05 ml) of horse serum.
After 20–30 minutes give a larger dose, then after another 20–30 minutes inject the full challenge dose intravenously.
Observe the animal — anaphylactic shock does not develop or is mild.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** the small doses gradually bind the antibodies on mast cells, and mediators are released in small, harmless amounts; when the full dose is given, not enough active antibodies remain to cause shock.
This is the basis of the Besredka method, which was used clinically when administering therapeutic sera (e.g. antitetanus or antivenom serum).

parts.text: Before administering preparations based on horse serum, an intradermal test and stepwise administration by Besredka's method are mandatory. At the same time, a resuscitation kit (epinephrine, glucocorticoids, infusion agents) must always be ready.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of allergic reaction

items: Determine the time of onset of the reaction: minutes (type I), hours (types II–III) or 1–3 days (type IV).
Assess the main clinical picture: bronchospasm and hypotension (I), hemolysis or cytopenia (II), vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, arthralgia (III), contact dermatitis or infiltrate (IV).
Determine the nature of the allergen: soluble protein, cell-surface antigen, hapten.
Take laboratory findings into account: blood IgE and eosinophils (I), Coombs test (II), immune complexes and decreased complement (III).
Write a conclusion and indicate the main direction of treatment.

skills.title: Skill: emergency care algorithm for anaphylactic shock

items: Stop exposure to the allergen (stop the drug infusion, remove the bee sting).
Call for help; lay the patient on their back and raise the legs (semi-sitting position if breathing is difficult).
Inject epinephrine into the middle outer surface of the thigh muscle; if there is no effect, repeat after 5–15 minutes.
Ensure airway patency and give oxygen.
Establish venous access and infuse crystalloid solutions.
Give an antihistamine and a glucocorticoid (second line).
Monitor arterial pressure, pulse and breathing continuously; the patient must be observed for at least 24 hours (risk of a delayed wave).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman was given an anesthetic for local anesthesia at the dentist. After 5 minutes she complained of shortness of breath, tightness in the throat and itching all over the body. Red wheals appeared on the skin, her lips swelled, arterial pressure was 70/40 mm Hg, pulse 130 beats/min, breathing wheezy.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain its pathogenesis. In what order is emergency care provided?
cases.answer: Anaphylactic shock — the systemic form of a type I (IgE-mediated) allergic reaction. The patient had previously been sensitized to this anesthetic: IgE specific to it is present on the surface of mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure the allergen binds to IgE and causes mast cell degranulation; histamine, leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor are released. They sharply dilate the vessels and increase their permeability (hypotension, reduced circulating blood volume, compensatory tachycardia), constrict the bronchi (wheezing, dyspnea), and cause edema (lips, larynx) and urticaria. Care: stop the anesthetic, immediately inject epinephrine into the thigh muscle, lay the patient down with legs raised, oxygen, intravenous crystalloid solutions; then an antihistamine and a glucocorticoid; observation for at least 24 hours.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: 9 days after receiving antitetanus horse serum, a patient developed fever, skin rashes, joint pain and enlarged lymph nodes. Protein was found in the urine, and the blood complement level was decreased.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Which type of allergic reaction does it belong to? Why did the signs appear after 9 days?
cases.answer: Serum sickness — a type III (immune complex) allergic reaction. Foreign (horse) proteins persist in the body for a long time; within about a week antibodies (mainly IgG) are formed against them and create soluble immune complexes with the antigen still in the blood. These complexes deposit in vessel walls, renal glomeruli and joint synovium, activate complement (which is why blood complement falls), attract neutrophils and cause vasculitis, glomerulonephritis (proteinuria) and arthritis. The signs appeared after the time needed to form antibodies (7–14 days); because there was no prior sensitization, the reaction developed on the very first injection.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old patient has had weight loss, prolonged fever, oral candidiasis and recurrent pneumonias over a year. Pneumocystis was found in the latest pneumonia. Blood CD4+ lymphocytes are 120 cells/µl.
cases.ask: What condition can be suspected? Explain the mechanism of the immunodeficiency.
cases.answer: The AIDS stage of HIV infection (secondary immunodeficiency). HIV enters T helper cells via the CD4 molecule and coreceptors, inserts its genome into the cell DNA by means of reverse transcriptase, replicates and kills the cells. Loss of CD4+ T helper cells impairs cellular immunity (macrophage activation, cytotoxic T cells) and humoral immunity (help to B lymphocytes). When CD4+ cells fall below 200/µl, opportunistic infections develop — pneumocystis pneumonia, candidiasis, tuberculosis. The diagnosis should be confirmed by detecting antibodies to HIV and viral RNA, and antiretroviral therapy should be started.

topics.title: Disorders of water and electrolyte metabolism. Pathogenetic factors of edema

goals.text: To explain to the student the balance of water and electrolytes in the body, the mechanisms that regulate it, the types of water balance disorders (dehydration and hyperhydration), their causes, pathogenesis and consequences, disorders of the main electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium), and the pathogenetic factors and types of edema; to teach the student to observe experimentally the role of the osmotic and colloid-osmotic factors in edema formation in the frog lymph sac.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the distribution of water in the body, water balance and its regulation;
the types of dehydration and hyperhydration (iso-, hypo-, hyperosmolar), their causes and consequences;
the main manifestations of disorders of sodium, potassium and calcium metabolism;
the Starling forces and the pathogenetic factors of edema;
the pathogenesis of cardiac, renal, hepatic, starvation, inflammatory and allergic edema.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: observe the role of the osmotic factor in edema formation by introducing a hypertonic solution into the frog lymph sac;
determine the type of water balance disorder from clinical and laboratory signs;
determine the type of edema and its leading pathogenetic factor.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main systems regulating water–salt homeostasis: **antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** — formed in the hypothalamus when osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolarity and released from the posterior pituitary; it increases water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts; thirst appears at the same time; **renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS)** — renin is released when renal blood flow falls, angiotensin II constricts vessels and increases aldosterone secretion; aldosterone retains sodium and excretes potassium; **natriuretic peptides** — released when the atria and ventricles are stretched, they increase sodium and water excretion; **thirst mechanism** — regulates water intake.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Water always moves towards the side of **higher osmolarity**: “**water follows salt**”. If plasma salt increases, the cell “dries out” (hyperosmolar state); if plasma salt decreases, the cell “swells” (hypoosmolar state).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Most edemas develop with the participation of **several factors**, one of which is leading (initiating). For example, in cardiac edema the leading factor is hydrostatic, in nephrotic edema — oncotic, in inflammatory edema — membranogenic, in lymphedema — lymphogenic.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Edema is sometimes life-threatening: **laryngeal edema** leads to asphyxia, **cerebral edema** to herniation of the brainstem into the foramina of the skull, **pulmonary edema** to severe hypoxemia. Such edemas require emergency treatment.

sections.title: 1. Distribution of water in the body and water balance

blocks.text: In the adult body, water makes up about 60 percent of body weight (more in men, less in women and the elderly, up to 75–80 percent in newborns).

Share of body weight

rows: — transcellular fluid (CSF, pleural, synovial, digestive juices)

Volume

blocks.text: Normal plasma osmolarity is 280–295 mOsm/kg; most of it is provided by sodium (135–145 mmol/l) and its accompanying anions. Sodium is the main cation of the extracellular fluid, and potassium (140–150 mmol/l inside cells, 3.5–5.0 mmol/l in plasma) is the main cation of the intracellular fluid.
Regulation of water and electrolyte balance

parts.text: The main systems regulating water–salt homeostasis:

items: **antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** — formed in the hypothalamus when osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolarity and released from the posterior pituitary; it increases water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts; thirst appears at the same time;

**renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS)** — renin is released when renal blood flow falls, angiotensin II constricts vessels and increases aldosterone secretion; aldosterone retains sodium and excretes potassium;
**natriuretic peptides** — released when the atria and ventricles are stretched, they increase sodium and water excretion;
**thirst mechanism** — regulates water intake.

blocks.text: Water balance disorders are divided into **dehydration (hypohydration, water loss)** and **hyperhydration (excess water accumulation)**. Each is subdivided into three types according to the osmolarity of the extracellular fluid.
Dehydration (water loss)

blocks.title: Table 9.3. Types of dehydration

parts.text: In diarrhea (cholera, rotavirus infection), dehydration develops rapidly in children. Oral rehydration solution (a mixture of glucose and salts) is based on the co-absorption of sodium and glucose in the intestine and sharply reduces the risk of death. “Rehydrating” a dehydrated patient with plain water alone can lead to hypoosmolar dehydration.

parts.text: Water always moves towards the side of **higher osmolarity**: “**water follows salt**”. If plasma salt increases, the cell “dries out” (hyperosmolar state); if plasma salt decreases, the cell “swells” (hypoosmolar state).

blocks.text: **Disorders of calcium metabolism:** total plasma calcium is 2.2–2.6 mmol/l. **Hypocalcemia** (hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, acute pancreatitis) increases neuromuscular excitability: tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, laryngospasm. **Hypercalcemia** (hyperparathyroidism, bone metastases) causes weakness, constipation, polyuria, kidney stones and arrhythmias.

**Edema** — excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space. Accumulation of fluid in serous cavities is called **dropsy**: in the abdominal cavity — ascites, in the pleura — hydrothorax, in the pericardium — hydropericardium, in the testicular membranes — hydrocele. Widespread edema of the whole body is called **anasarca**.
Starling forces

Fluid exchange between capillary and tissue obeys E. Starling's law. The forces that **move** fluid out of the capillary into the tissue are capillary hydrostatic pressure and the oncotic pressure of tissue fluid; the forces that **return** it to the capillary are plasma oncotic pressure and tissue hydrostatic pressure.

blocks.text: Normally filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption; excess fluid and proteins are removed by the lymphatic vessels (2–4 l of lymph per day).

parts.text: Most edemas develop with the participation of **several factors**, one of which is leading (initiating). For example, in cardiac edema the leading factor is hydrostatic, in nephrotic edema — oncotic, in inflammatory edema — membranogenic, in lymphedema — lymphogenic.

blocks.text: Cardiac edema

blocks.label: Figure 9.2

blocks.text: In right ventricular failure, edema begins in the legs (ankles and shins), increases towards evening and decreases overnight; in bedridden patients it is located in the sacral and lumbar region (effect of gravity). The skin is cold and cyanotic. In severe cases ascites, hydrothorax and anasarca develop.

blocks.text: Renal edema is soft, the skin is pale and warm, and pressure easily leaves a pit; eyelid edema is especially marked in the morning (loose subcutaneous tissue).
Other types of edema

items: **Hepatic edema and ascites** (cirrhosis): portal hypertension (hydrostatic factor), reduced albumin synthesis in the liver (oncotic factor), secondary hyperaldosteronism (aldosterone is poorly broken down in the liver), increased lymph formation.
**Cachectic (starvation) edema**: protein deficiency — hypoalbuminemia; kwashiorkor in children.
**Inflammatory edema**: membranogenic, osmotic and oncotic factors (see topic 6).
**Allergic edema** (Quincke's edema, urticaria): a sharp increase in permeability under the action of histamine and other mediators.
**Toxic edema** (toxic pulmonary edema, edema after a snakebite): direct damage to the capillary endothelium.

parts.text: Edema is sometimes life-threatening: **laryngeal edema** leads to asphyxia, **cerebral edema** to herniation of the brainstem into the foramina of the skull, **pulmonary edema** to severe hypoxemia. Such edemas require emergency treatment.

blocks.text: Consequences of edema

Edema mechanically compresses tissues and impairs microcirculation and oxygen diffusion (the diffusion distance increases) — hypoxia, dystrophy and susceptibility to infection result; if prolonged, connective tissue overgrowth (sclerosis) develops. At the same time, inflammatory edema also has a protective role: it dilutes toxins and walls off the focus.

sections.title: 6. Experimental part: role of the osmotic and colloid-osmotic factors in edema formation

blocks.text: **Aim:** to observe how a rise in tissue osmotic pressure affects edema formation.
**Equipment:** frogs (of similar weight, 2–3), 10 % sodium chloride (hypertonic) solution, 0.6 % saline (isotonic for the frog), scales, syringes.
Procedure

items: Weigh the frogs and record their weights.
Inject 1–2 ml of hypertonic sodium chloride solution into the dorsal lymph sac of frog 1.
Inject the same volume of isotonic solution into the lymph sac of frog 2 (control).
Place both frogs in a container of water (the frog absorbs water through its skin).
For 1–2 hours, weigh the frogs every 30 minutes and record the change in weight and appearance (swelling of the lymph sac and legs).

blocks.text: **Expected results and analysis:** the weight of the frog given the hypertonic solution increases noticeably and its lymph sac and legs swell; the weight of the control frog hardly changes. Accumulation of an osmotically active substance — sodium — in the tissue (lymph sac) raises osmotic pressure, and water moves along the osmotic gradient from the vessels and the external medium into the tissue. This confirms the role of the **osmotic factor** in edema formation. By performing the same experiment with a protein solution (e.g. gelatin), the **colloid-osmotic (oncotic)** factor can also be demonstrated.

parts.text: The osmotic factor is used clinically in two ways: sodium retention aggravates edema (which is why table salt is restricted in cardiac and renal edema), while osmotically active agents (mannitol, hypertonic sodium chloride) are used in cerebral edema to draw water from the tissue into the vessels and reduce the edema.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of water balance disorder

items: From the history, identify the source of water and salt loss or excess intake (vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria, sweating, infusions).
Assess the clinical signs: thirst, mucous membranes, skin turgor, pulse, arterial pressure, diuresis, edema, neurological signs.
Determine plasma sodium and osmolarity (osmolarity ≈ 2 × Na + glucose + urea, mmol/l).
Assess hematocrit and total protein (increased in dehydration, decreased in hyperhydration).
Determine the type of disorder (dehydration or hyperhydration; iso-, hypo- or hyperosmolar).
Explain the movement of water between the intracellular and extracellular compartments and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of edema and the leading factor

items: Determine the location and extent of the edema (legs, face, generalized, local).
Ask how the edema changes over time (worse in the morning or in the evening).
Assess skin color, temperature and whether pressure leaves a pit.
Identify heart, kidney and liver diseases and nutritional status.
Analyze laboratory values: blood albumin, urine protein, creatinine, liver tests.
Indicate the leading pathogenetic factor and write a conclusion.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 1-year-old child has had liquid stools 10–12 times a day and vomiting for 2 days. The mother gave the child only boiled water to drink. On examination: the child is lethargic, not thirsty, the skin fold returns slowly, the fontanelle is sunken, muscle cramps are observed. Plasma sodium is 124 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What water–electrolyte disorder has developed? Explain its pathogenesis. Why is there no thirst?
cases.answer: Hypoosmolar (salt-deficit) dehydration. Water and sodium were lost with diarrhea and vomiting; because the losses were replaced only with plain water, sodium became more deficient than water — hyponatremia and plasma hypoosmolarity developed. Water moves along the osmotic gradient into the cells: extracellular fluid (and circulating blood volume) decreases further, and the cells, especially neurons, swell — lethargy and convulsions. Thirst is mainly triggered by a rise in plasma osmolarity; here osmolarity has fallen, so there is no thirst. Treatment — rehydration with saline solutions (oral rehydration solution or intravenous isotonic solutions).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: 3 weeks after tonsillitis, an 8-year-old child developed edema of the face and eyelids (especially in the morning), reduced urine output and “meat-washings”-colored urine. Arterial pressure 140/90 mm Hg. Urine: protein 1.2 g/l, many erythrocytes. Blood albumin is normal.
cases.ask: What type of edema is this? What are its leading factors? How does it differ from nephrotic edema?
cases.answer: Nephritic edema in acute glomerulonephritis. Leading factors: sodium and water retention due to reduced glomerular filtration (osmotic and neurohumoral factor — RAAS activation), as well as increased capillary permeability (membranogenic factor). Fluid retention has also led to arterial hypertension. Difference from nephrotic edema: proteinuria is moderate and blood albumin is normal, i.e. the oncotic factor is not leading; hematuria and hypertension are present. In nephrotic edema, by contrast, daily proteinuria exceeds 3.5 g, hypoalbuminemia is marked and the edema quickly progresses to anasarca.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 55-year-old patient has chronic heart failure. Edema in the legs increases towards evening and decreases somewhat in the morning. The neck veins are distended and the liver is enlarged. Furosemide was prescribed; a week later the patient developed muscle weakness and a heart rhythm disturbance.
cases.ask: Explain the pathogenesis of the edema. What are the changes after taking furosemide related to?
cases.answer: Cardiac edema: in right ventricular failure venous pressure rises and capillary hydrostatic pressure increases (leading factor). Reduced cardiac output lowers renal perfusion, RAAS is activated, and aldosterone and ADH secretion increase — sodium and water are retained, circulating blood volume increases and venous pressure rises further (a vicious circle). Under gravity the edema is located in the dependent parts and increases towards evening. Furosemide excretes large amounts of potassium along with sodium and water — hypokalemia has developed; it causes muscle weakness and arrhythmias. Therefore, during diuretic treatment potassium must be monitored and, if needed, replaced, or potassium-sparing diuretics added.

Leading — hydrostatic; starts in the legs, worse in the evening
Leading — oncotic (proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia)
Leading — lymphogenic

topics.title: Pathophysiology of carbohydrate metabolism. Hyper- and hypoglycemia, glucosuria

goals.text: To explain to the student the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism, the biological effects of insulin and counter-insulin hormones, the main manifestations of carbohydrate metabolism disorders (hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, glucosuria) and their causes, mechanisms and consequences; to teach the student to model and analyze hyper- and hypoglycemia and glucosuria experimentally.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the normal values of blood glucose and the mechanisms that regulate it;
the effect of insulin on metabolism and the counter-insulin hormones;
the classification of carbohydrate metabolism disorders by stage (digestion, absorption, storage, intermediate metabolism);
the types and mechanisms of hyperglycemia;
the causes and mechanism of hypoglycemia and the signs of hypoglycemic coma;
the types of glucosuria and the concept of the renal threshold;
how to interpret the glucose tolerance test.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: induce hyperglycemia in a rabbit with epinephrine and determine blood glucose;
induce hypoglycemia and hypoglycemic convulsions in a mouse with insulin and reverse them with glucose;
detect glucose in urine qualitatively;
interpret the results of a glucose tolerance test.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In fasting venous plasma the thresholds are different: normal up to 6.1 mmol/l, diabetes mellitus — 7.0 mmol/l and above. When making a diagnosis, note which blood sample (capillary blood or venous plasma) was used. Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 6.5 % or higher is also a criterion for diabetes mellitus.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Hypoglycemia is especially dangerous for the brain, because neurons do not store glucose and obtain their energy mainly from it. Prolonged severe hypoglycemia leads to irreversible changes in the brain. Hypoglycemic coma develops quickly (within minutes), the skin is moist, muscle tone is increased and there are convulsions — this distinguishes it from ketoacidotic coma, which develops slowly and in which the skin is dry.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the experiment, the fasting period of the animals and the insulin dose are chosen in strict accordance with the department's methodological guidelines. The glucose solution must be ready before the experiment begins.

blocks.text: Glucose is the main energy source for the body's cells; the brain obtains almost all its energy from glucose (partly from ketone bodies during prolonged fasting). Therefore blood glucose is kept within narrow limits.

blocks.title: Table 10.1. Normal and diagnostic blood glucose values (capillary blood, mmol/l)
head: State
Fasting
2 hours after a glucose load

parts.text: In fasting venous plasma the thresholds are different: normal up to 6.1 mmol/l, diabetes mellitus — 7.0 mmol/l and above. When making a diagnosis, note which blood sample (capillary blood or venous plasma) was used. Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 6.5 % or higher is also a criterion for diabetes mellitus.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Hormonal regulation of blood glucose

blocks.text: Biological effects of insulin

Insulin is the only hypoglycemic hormone; it is produced in the beta cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. Its secretion is stimulated mainly by glucose: glucose enters the beta cell via GLUT2 and is metabolized to form ATP, ATP-sensitive potassium channels close, the cell depolarizes, calcium enters and insulin granules are released.

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Effects of insulin on metabolism
head: Type of metabolism
Effect of insulin
rows: Increases glucose entry into muscle and adipose tissue (moves GLUT4 transporters to the membrane); stimulates glycogen synthesis; inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; activates glycolysis
Stimulates lipogenesis, inhibits lipolysis; reduces ketone body formation
Increases amino acid entry into cells and protein synthesis, reduces proteolysis (an anabolic hormone)

blocks.text: **Counter-insulin hormones** raise blood glucose: **glucagon** (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis), **epinephrine** (glycogenolysis, reduced insulin secretion), **glucocorticoids** (gluconeogenesis, reduced glucose use by tissues), **growth hormone** and **thyroid hormones**.

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Carbohydrate metabolism disorders by stage
head: Stage
Disorder
Examples
rows: Deficiency of amylase or disaccharidases, impaired absorption
Lactase deficiency (milk intolerance), pancreatitis, malabsorption syndrome
Glycogenoses (von Gierke disease — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; Pompe disease), liver cirrhosis
Impaired glycolysis, Krebs cycle and gluconeogenesis
Lactic acidosis in hypoxia, vitamin B1 deficiency (pyruvate accumulation), galactosemia, fructosemia
Imbalance between insulin and counter-insulin hormones

parts.text: **Lactase deficiency** is a common condition in adults. Undigested lactose passes into the colon, where bacteria ferment it, producing gas and organic acids; because of the osmotic effect, water is drawn into the intestine. As a result, bloating, pain and diarrhea occur after drinking milk.

blocks.text: **Hyperglycemia** — a rise in blood glucose above normal.

blocks.title: Table 10.4. Types of hyperglycemia
head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Intake of a large amount of rapidly absorbed carbohydrate
Activation of the sympathoadrenal system, release of epinephrine and increased glycogenolysis
Before an exam, pain, fear; “exam glucosuria”
Insulin deficiency or excess of counter-insulin hormones
Diabetes mellitus, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, glucagonoma
Damage to the central nervous system, irritation of the hypothalamus
Head injury, stroke; C. Bernard's “sugar puncture” (needle puncture of the floor of the fourth ventricle)

blocks.text: Consequences of hyperglycemia

items: **Glucosuria and osmotic diuresis** — when glucose exceeds the renal threshold it passes into the urine and takes water with it: polyuria, dehydration, thirst (polydipsia).
**Increased blood osmolarity** — dehydration of cells; in severe cases hyperosmolar coma.
**Glycation of proteins** — glucose binds non-enzymatically to the amino groups of proteins (glycated hemoglobin, collagen, crystallin); the basis of the long-term complications.
**Activation of the polyol (sorbitol) pathway** — in tissues that take up glucose independently of insulin (lens, nerves, kidney), sorbitol accumulates and damages the cells.

blocks.text: **Hypoglycemia** — a fall in blood glucose below 3.3 mmol/l (clinically often below 3.9 mmol/l).

blocks.title: Table 10.5. Causes of hypoglycemia
head: Group
Examples
rows: Overdose of insulin or sulfonylurea drugs, insulinoma (beta-cell tumor)
Prolonged fasting, malabsorption, a diabetic patient not eating after taking insulin
Heavy physical work, fever, some large tumors

blocks.text: Signs of hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia presents with two groups of signs:

items: **Adrenergic (autonomic) signs** — epinephrine release as a counter-insulin response: hunger, trembling, profuse sweating (cold sweat), tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, pallor.

**Neuroglycopenic signs** — insufficient glucose supply to the brain: headache, impaired concentration, strange behavior (resembling drunkenness), visual disturbances, convulsions, loss of consciousness — **hypoglycemic coma**.

parts.text: Hypoglycemia is especially dangerous for the brain, because neurons do not store glucose and obtain their energy mainly from it. Prolonged severe hypoglycemia leads to irreversible changes in the brain. Hypoglycemic coma develops quickly (within minutes), the skin is moist, muscle tone is increased and there are convulsions — this distinguishes it from ketoacidotic coma, which develops slowly and in which the skin is dry.

Care in hypoglycemia: if the patient is conscious — 15–20 g of rapidly absorbed carbohydrate (sugar, sweet juice); if unconscious — 40 % glucose solution intravenously or glucagon intramuscularly. In doubtful cases (when the type of coma is unclear) giving glucose is safer: it saves life in hypoglycemia and does not significantly worsen the condition in hyperglycemia.

blocks.text: **Glucosuria** — the appearance of glucose in the urine. Normally, glucose filtered in the glomeruli is completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubules together with sodium (via the SGLT2 and SGLT1 transporters).
**Renal threshold** — the blood glucose concentration above which the tubular transporters become saturated and glucose begins to appear in the urine. In adults it is about **8.9–10 mmol/l**.

blocks.title: Table 10.6. Types of glucosuria
head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold
Diabetes mellitus, alimentary and emotional hyperglycemia, after epinephrine injection
Blood glucose is normal, but tubular reabsorption is impaired (the renal threshold is lowered)
Hereditary renal glucosuria, Fanconi syndrome, pregnancy, phlorizin poisoning, treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors

parts.text: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are modern drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. They reduce glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules, causing a “drug-induced renal glucosuria”, and thereby lower glycemia. These agents also have cardio- and renoprotective properties.

blocks.text: The glucose tolerance test assesses the body's ability to handle a glucose load.

Procedure: after 3 days of usual diet and an 8–14-hour overnight fast, fasting blood glucose is measured in the morning; the patient drinks 75 g of glucose dissolved in 250–300 ml of water within 5 minutes; after 2 hours (every 30 minutes in the extended version) glucose is measured again.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Glucose tolerance test curves (approximate, drawn for explanation)

blocks.text: Normally glucose peaks at 30–60 minutes (not exceeding 8–9 mmol/l) and returns to the baseline level by 2 hours (below 7.8 mmol/l). In impaired glucose tolerance the 2-hour value is 7.8–11.0 mmol/l, and in diabetes mellitus it is 11.1 mmol/l or higher.
Experiment 1: epinephrine hyperglycemia and glucosuria in the rabbit

items: Take blood from the rabbit's ear vein and determine the baseline glucose level (with a glucometer or the glucose oxidase method).
Place the rabbit in a metabolic cage or catheterize the bladder, and test the baseline urine for glucose (test strip or Nylander/Fehling test).
Inject 0.1 % epinephrine solution (0.1–0.2 ml/kg) subcutaneously.
Measure blood glucose again after 30, 60 and 90 minutes.
Once glycemia exceeds the renal threshold, test the urine for glucose.

blocks.text: **Expected results and analysis:** via beta2- and alpha-adrenoceptors in the liver, epinephrine stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces insulin secretion — hyperglycemia develops.
When glucose exceeds the renal threshold, **hyperglycemic glucosuria** appears. This experiment is a model of emotional (stress) hyperglycemia.
Experiment 2: insulin hypoglycemia in the mouse

items: Fast two mice for 12–18 hours beforehand (their glycogen stores will be reduced).
Inject each of them intraperitoneally with insulin (at the dose given in the department's guidelines), and a third mouse with saline (control).
Observe the mice in a warm place and record the time at which signs appear: immobility, then restlessness, ruffled fur, loss of balance, convulsions, lying on the side.
As soon as convulsions begin, inject one mouse intraperitoneally with 0.5–1 ml of 40 % glucose solution; continue to observe the second one (with the teacher's permission if rescue is required).
Record the recovery of the glucose-treated mouse within a few minutes.

blocks.text: **Expected results and analysis:** insulin increases glucose uptake by tissues and stops glucose production in the liver; in the fasted mouse glycogen stores are low, so hypoglycemia develops quickly. The energy supply of neurons is impaired, and first excitation, then convulsions and coma develop. Giving glucose restores the energy supply of neurons and quickly rescues the animal — this proves that the cause of hypoglycemic convulsions is precisely the lack of glucose.

parts.text: In the experiment, the fasting period of the animals and the insulin dose are chosen in strict accordance with the department's methodological guidelines. The glucose solution must be ready before the experiment begins.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: qualitative detection of glucose in urine

items: Pour 2–3 ml of urine into a test tube.
Dip a test strip (glucose oxidase method) into the urine and, after the specified time, compare its color with the scale.
Alternative method — the Nylander test: when the reagent is added to urine and boiled, a black precipitate forms if glucose is present.
Compare normal urine, urine with added glucose and the urine of the experimental animal.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting the glucose tolerance test

items: Compare the fasting value with the normal range (3.3–5.5 mmol/l in capillary blood).
Determine the value 2 hours after drinking the glucose.
A 2-hour value below 7.8 mmol/l is normal; 7.8–11.0 — impaired glucose tolerance; 11.1 and above — diabetes mellitus.
Assess the shape of the curve: when and how high the peak is, and the time to return to the baseline level.
Write the result taking into account the type of blood sample (capillary blood or venous plasma).

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic coma

items: Determine the speed of onset: minutes (hypoglycemic) or hours to days (hyperglycemic).
Assess the skin: moist with cold sweat (hypoglycemic) or dry (ketoacidotic).
Assess breathing: normal, or deep noisy Kussmaul breathing with an acetone odor (ketoacidosis).
Check muscle tone and convulsions (increased tone and convulsions in hypoglycemia).
Measure glucose immediately with a glucometer.
Start first aid according to the diagnosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old man has type 1 diabetes mellitus. In the morning he took his usual dose of insulin but went to the gym without having breakfast. During the workout he developed intense hunger, trembling, cold sweat and palpitations, then began to behave inappropriately and lost consciousness; brief convulsions were observed.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain the mechanism of the signs. What is the first aid?
cases.answer: Hypoglycemic coma. Insulin was taken, but no glucose was taken in (he did not eat), and physical exertion sharply increased glucose consumption by the muscles — hypoglycemia developed. Hunger, trembling, cold sweat and tachycardia are adrenergic signs: in response to hypoglycemia the sympathoadrenal system is activated and epinephrine is released. Changed behavior, loss of consciousness and convulsions are neuroglycopenic signs: brain neurons do not store glucose, and their function is impaired by lack of energy. First aid: because he is unconscious, give nothing by mouth; give 40 % glucose solution intravenously or glucagon intramuscularly; once he regains consciousness, give carbohydrate food.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Glucose was found in the urine of a 30-year-old pregnant woman. Fasting blood glucose is 4.6 mmol/l and the glucose tolerance test is normal.
cases.ask: Which type of glucosuria can be considered? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: Renal glucosuria. Blood glucose is normal and the tolerance test is not impaired, so there is no hyperglycemia. In pregnancy glomerular filtration increases and more glucose reaches the proximal tubules, while the tubular reabsorptive capacity is relatively reduced — the renal threshold falls and glucose appears in the urine even when blood levels are normal. Nevertheless, glycemia is still monitored to rule out diabetes of pregnancy (gestational diabetes).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 40-year-old patient with a head injury has blood glucose of 11.5 mmol/l and glucose in the urine. He had no previous diabetes mellitus. After two weeks glycemia returned to normal.
cases.ask: What type of hyperglycemia is this? Explain the mechanism. Which classic experiment models this condition?
cases.answer: Neurogenic (and stress) hyperglycemia. Brain injury irritates the autonomic centers in the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata and activates the sympathoadrenal system and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: epinephrine and cortisol release increases, and glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are enhanced. Because glycemia exceeded the renal threshold, glucosuria appeared. After the acute period of the injury, the hyperglycemia resolved. This condition is modeled by C. Bernard's “sugar puncture” experiment: when a needle is inserted into the floor of the fourth ventricle, the animal develops hyperglycemia and glucosuria.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of acid–base balance. Acidosis and alkalosis

goals.text: To explain to the student the concept of acid–base balance (ABB), its main parameters, the buffer systems and physiological (lung, kidney) regulatory mechanisms, the types of ABB disorders (respiratory and nonrespiratory acidosis and alkalosis), their causes, compensatory mechanisms and consequences; to teach the student in practice to determine titratable acidity and ammonia in urine and the alkaline reserve in blood, and to interpret ABB parameters.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main parameters of ABB and their normal values (pH, pCO2, HCO3−, BE, anion gap);
the blood buffer systems and their significance;
the role of the lungs and kidneys in regulating ABB;
the classification, causes and compensatory mechanisms of acidosis and alkalosis;
the effects of ABB disorders on the body (heart, nervous system, electrolytes).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine and interpret titratable acidity and ammonia in urine;
assess the alkaline reserve of blood;
determine the type of disorder and the degree of compensation from blood gases and ABB parameters.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The largest share of blood buffer capacity is provided by the **hemoglobin** buffer system, but clinically the most important system, and the one that is assessed, is the **bicarbonate buffer system**, because both of its components are physiologically regulated (CO2 — by the lungs, HCO3− — by the kidneys), and it is exactly this system that is measured in blood gas analysis.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis: **“MUDLES”** (a short form of the classic MUDPILES) — **M**ethanol, **U**remia (kidney failure), **D**iabetic and other ketoacidosis, **L**actic acidosis, **E**thylene glycol (antifreeze), **S**alicylates.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A rule of ABB analysis: **the primary change and the compensatory change go in the same direction** (pCO2 and HCO3− both increase or both decrease). If they change in opposite directions (e.g. pCO2 raised, HCO3− decreased), this indicates a **mixed disorder** (respiratory and metabolic acidosis together) — for example, in cardiac arrest.

blocks.text: **Acid–base balance** — the relative constancy of the hydrogen ion concentration (pH) in the internal environment of the body. Arterial blood pH is kept within very narrow limits — 7.35–7.45. A pH below 6.8 or above 7.8 is incompatible with life.

Acids are constantly produced in the body: the **volatile acid** — carbon dioxide (about 15,000 mmol per day, excreted by the lungs) — and **nonvolatile (fixed) acids** — sulfuric, phosphoric, lactic and keto acids (50–100 mmol per day, excreted by the kidneys).

blocks.title: Table 11.1. Main ABB parameters (arterial blood)
head: Parameter
Normal
Meaning
rows: Active reaction; the final result of the balance
Partial pressure of carbon dioxide — the respiratory component
Deviation of buffer bases from normal; negative — base deficit

blocks.text: pH depends on the ratio of carbon dioxide (respiratory) to bicarbonate (metabolic) (Henderson–Hasselbalch equation):
Normally the ratio of HCO3− to dissolved CO2 is **20 : 1**. As long as this ratio is maintained, pH stays normal even when the absolute values change — this is the basis of compensation.
Buffer systems
Buffer systems act within seconds and convert a strong acid or base into a weak acid or base.

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Blood buffer systems
head: Buffer system
Share of blood buffer capacity
Feature
rows: The strongest; linked to CO2 transport
An “open” system: CO2 is regulated by the lungs and HCO3− by the kidneys; in practice the most important and quickly adaptable
Of great importance inside cells and in urine

parts.text: The largest share of blood buffer capacity is provided by the **hemoglobin** buffer system, but clinically the most important system, and the one that is assessed, is the **bicarbonate buffer system**, because both of its components are physiologically regulated (CO2 — by the lungs, HCO3− — by the kidneys), and it is exactly this system that is measured in blood gas analysis.

blocks.text: Role of the lungs

The respiratory center is very sensitive to pH and pCO2. In acidosis (increased H+) pulmonary ventilation increases, more CO2 is exhaled and pH rises; in alkalosis ventilation decreases. Pulmonary compensation starts within minutes to hours, but it is incomplete.
Role of the kidneys
The kidneys regulate ABB most powerfully, but slowly (over hours and days):

items: **Bicarbonate reabsorption** — almost all filtered HCO3− is reabsorbed (85 percent of it in the proximal tubules).
**Acidogenesis** — secretion of H+ ions and their excretion bound to the phosphate buffer (**titratable acidity**).
**Ammoniogenesis** — ammonia (NH3) is formed from glutamine in the tubular cells, binds H+ and is excreted as ammonium (NH4+).
In these processes a new HCO3− is formed for each H+ excreted and returned to the blood.

parts.text: In acidosis the kidneys can excrete up to 500 mmol of acid per day, with **ammoniogenesis** playing the main role, because it can increase many times over within a few days. Therefore, in kidney failure ammonia formation decreases and metabolic acidosis inevitably develops.

blocks.text: Other organs

Bone tissue (in prolonged acidosis, through calcium carbonate and phosphates — risk of osteoporosis), the liver (converts lactic acid to glucose, urea synthesis) and the stomach (HCl secretion) also take part in regulating ABB.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: Classification of ABB disorders

blocks.text: By compensation:

items: **compensated** — pH within the normal range (7.35–7.45), but pCO2 and HCO3− are altered;
**subcompensated and decompensated** — pH outside the normal range.

blocks.text: Respiratory (gas) acidosis
**Cause** — reduced elimination of CO2 through the lungs (alveolar hypoventilation):

items: depression of the respiratory center (opiates, barbiturates, anesthesia, head injury);
damage to the respiratory muscles and neuromuscular apparatus (myasthenia, poliomyelitis, paralysis of the respiratory muscles);
diseases of the lungs and airways (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe asthma attack, pulmonary edema, extensive pneumonia);
chest deformity, pneumothorax;
breathing CO2-rich air in a closed room.

blocks.text: **Compensation:** buffer systems (mainly intracellular and hemoglobin) and the kidneys — H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption increase, and blood HCO3− rises (in the chronic state this is fully developed in 3–5 days).
Nonrespiratory (metabolic) acidosis
**Causes** are divided into two groups according to the anion gap.

blocks.title: Table 11.3. Causes of metabolic acidosis
head: Group
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Excess production or intake of acids

Ketoacidosis (diabetes mellitus, starvation, alcohol), lactic acidosis (hypoxia, shock, metformin), kidney failure (retention of sulfates and phosphates), poisoning with methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates
Loss of bicarbonate or impaired renal acid excretion
Diarrhea, intestinal fistulas, proximal and distal renal tubular acidosis, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, infusion of large amounts of sodium chloride

parts.text: Causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis: **“MUDLES”** (a short form of the classic MUDPILES) — **M**ethanol, **U**remia (kidney failure), **D**iabetic and other ketoacidosis, **L**actic acidosis, **E**thylene glycol (antifreeze), **S**alicylates.

blocks.text: **Compensation:** buffer systems (HCO3− is consumed), **lungs** — hyperventilation, CO2 elimination increases (deep, noisy **Kussmaul breathing** in severe ketoacidosis), **kidneys** — acidogenesis and ammoniogenesis increase (unless the kidneys themselves are the cause).
Effects of acidosis on the body

items: **Cardiovascular system:** myocardial contractility decreases, vessels lose their sensitivity to catecholamines (hypotension), and the risk of arrhythmias increases.
**Nervous system:** depression, weakness, drowsiness, coma in severe cases (especially in respiratory acidosis — CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier rapidly; “CO2 narcosis”).
**Electrolytes: hyperkalemia** — H+ enters the cells and K+ leaves them; ionized calcium increases.
**Oxyhemoglobin dissociation:** the curve shifts to the right (Bohr effect) — oxygen delivery to tissues is facilitated.
**Bone:** in prolonged acidosis calcium leaves bone and osteoporosis develops.

blocks.text: Respiratory (gas) alkalosis
**Cause** — alveolar hyperventilation and excessive elimination of CO2:

items: psychogenic hyperventilation (hysteria, fear, pain);
hypoxemia (altitude, lung diseases, anemia) — reflex hyperventilation;
brain injury and inflammation (stimulation of the respiratory center);
fever, early sepsis, early stage of salicylate poisoning;
liver failure, pregnancy (progesterone stimulates the respiratory center);
incorrect settings of mechanical ventilation.

blocks.text: **Compensation:** the kidneys reduce bicarbonate reabsorption and H+ secretion, and more HCO3− is excreted in the urine.
Nonrespiratory (metabolic) alkalosis
Causes:

items: **loss of H^+^** — profuse vomiting (HCl is lost with gastric juice), prolonged gastric drainage through a tube;
**renal loss of H^+^ and K^+^** — thiazide and loop diuretics, hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), Cushing syndrome;
**hypokalemia** — K+ leaves the cells, H+ enters them;
**excessive intake of alkali** — excessive administration of sodium bicarbonate, “milk-alkali syndrome”.

blocks.text: **Compensation:** the lungs — hypoventilation (CO2 retention), but limited by the risk of hypoxemia; the kidneys — increase bicarbonate excretion (provided there is no hypovolemia, hypokalemia or hypochloremia).
Effects of alkalosis on the body

items: **Increased neuromuscular excitability:** ionized calcium decreases (more of it binds to albumin) — paresthesias, muscle cramps, tetany (“obstetrician's hand”), laryngospasm.
**Brain:** in respiratory alkalosis, hypocapnia constricts the cerebral vessels — dizziness, fainting.
**Electrolytes: hypokalemia** (K+ enters the cells and is lost through the kidneys), hypochloremia.
**Oxyhemoglobin dissociation:** the curve shifts to the left — hemoglobin gives up oxygen to the tissues less readily.
**Heart:** arrhythmias (especially together with hypokalemia).

blocks.title: Table 11.4. Changes in the main parameters in ABB disorders
head: Type of disorder
pH
pCO2
HCO3−
BE
Compensation

parts.text: A rule of ABB analysis: **the primary change and the compensatory change go in the same direction** (pCO2 and HCO3− both increase or both decrease). If they change in opposite directions (e.g. pCO2 raised, HCO3− decreased), this indicates a **mixed disorder** (respiratory and metabolic acidosis together) — for example, in cardiac arrest.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determining titratable acidity and ammonia in urine
**Aim:** to assess the role of the kidneys in regulating ABB.
Determining titratable acidity:

items: Put 10 ml of urine and 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein indicator into a flask.
Titrate with 0.1 N sodium hydroxide solution until a pale pink color appears.
Record the volume of alkali used and recalculate it for the daily urine volume.
Normal titratable acidity is about 10–30 mmol per day (part of the H+ excreted in the urine).

blocks.text: Determining ammonia (formol titration method):

items: Add neutralized formalin solution to the titrated urine — ammonium ions react with formalin, an equivalent amount of acid is released and the pink color disappears.
Titrate again with 0.1 N sodium hydroxide until the pink color returns.
The volume of alkali used in the second titration corresponds to the amount of ammonium.
Normally about 30–50 mmol of ammonium is excreted in the urine per day.

parts.text: If ammonium excretion in the urine is low in a patient with acidosis, the cause of the acidosis is related to the kidneys (renal tubular acidosis or kidney failure). If ammonium excretion is high, the kidneys are doing their job and the acidosis has developed for extrarenal reasons (e.g. diarrhea or ketoacidosis).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining the alkaline reserve of blood (Van Slyke method)
**Alkaline reserve** — the amount of CO2 that blood plasma can bind as bicarbonate when saturated with carbon dioxide (pCO2 = 40 mm Hg). Normally 50–65 vol % (22–29 mmol/l).

items: Saturate the plasma at a CO2 pressure close to that of alveolar air.
In the Van Slyke apparatus, add acid to the plasma and measure the volume of CO2 released from bicarbonate.
Correct the result for temperature and pressure and express it in volume percent.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** in metabolic acidosis the alkaline reserve decreases (bicarbonate is used up neutralizing acids), and in metabolic alkalosis it increases. In modern practice, standard bicarbonate and BE measured on a blood gas analyzer are used instead of this parameter.

skills.title: Skill: determining an ABB disorder from blood gases

items: **Assess pH:** below 7.35 — acidosis, above 7.45 — alkalosis; if normal, there may be a compensated or mixed disorder.
**Assess pCO~2~:** if it has changed in the opposite direction to pH (pH decreased, pCO2 increased), the primary disorder is respiratory.
**Assess HCO~3~^−^ and BE:** if they have changed in the same direction as pH (pH decreased, HCO3− decreased), the primary disorder is metabolic.
**Assess compensation:** has the second component changed in the same direction as the first?
**In metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap:** Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−).
Compare with the clinical data and indicate the cause.

skills.title: Skill: determining titratable acidity and ammonium in urine

items: Measure the volume of the urine sample accurately.
Perform the first titration with sodium hydroxide solution and phenolphthalein.
Add neutralized formalin and perform the second titration.
Recalculate both values for the daily urine.
Compare the result with the patient's ABB status and assess renal compensation.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus has not taken insulin for 2 days. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep noisy breathing, acetone odor on the breath. Blood: glucose 26 mmol/l, pH 7.12, pCO2 22 mm Hg, HCO3− 7 mmol/l, BE −20 mmol/l, Na+ 136, Cl− 100 mmol/l, K+ 5.6 mmol/l.
cases.ask: Determine the type of ABB disorder. Calculate and interpret the anion gap. Explain the changes in breathing and potassium.
cases.answer: Decompensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12; HCO3− and BE markedly decreased) with partial respiratory compensation (pCO2 22 mm Hg — hyperventilation). Anion gap = 136 − (100 + 7) = 29 mmol/l — increased: in insulin deficiency, lipolysis and the formation of ketone bodies (acetoacetic and beta-hydroxybutyric acids) are sharply increased, and these are unmeasured anions. Deep noisy Kussmaul breathing is compensatory hyperventilation resulting from stimulation of the respiratory center by H+; CO2 elimination increases. Hyperkalemia — in acidosis H+ enters the cells and K+ leaves them; in addition, in insulin deficiency potassium does not move into the cells. During treatment with insulin, potassium returns to the cells and there is a risk of hypokalemia, so potassium is monitored.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old patient has had profuse vomiting for 1 week due to narrowing of the gastric outlet (pyloric stenosis). The patient is weak and has cramps in the hands (“obstetrician's hand”). Blood: pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mm Hg, HCO3− 36 mmol/l, K+ 2.9 mmol/l, Cl− 85 mmol/l.
cases.ask: Determine the type of ABB disorder. Explain its pathogenesis and the cause of the cramps.
cases.answer: Metabolic alkalosis (pH and HCO3− increased) with partial respiratory compensation (pCO2 48 — hypoventilation). With vomiting, HCl (H+ and Cl−) is lost in the gastric juice — hypochloremia. Dehydration and hypovolemia increase aldosterone secretion: the kidneys retain sodium and excrete K+ and H+ — hypokalemia and maintenance of the alkalosis. In hypokalemia K+ leaves the cells and H+ enters them, which deepens the alkalosis. The cramps (“obstetrician's hand”) are due to increased neuromuscular excitability, because in alkalosis more calcium binds to albumin and ionized calcium decreases. Treatment — restore water and electrolyte balance with sodium chloride and potassium chloride solutions.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 62-year-old patient has had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease for many years. His condition is stable. Blood: pH 7.37, pCO2 60 mm Hg, HCO3− 34 mmol/l.
cases.ask: Determine the type of ABB disorder. Why is the pH normal? Why is it dangerous to give such a patient high-concentration oxygen?
cases.answer: Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis. The primary disorder is a rise in pCO2 (60 mm Hg) due to hypoventilation. Over several days the kidneys have increased H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, raising HCO3− to 34 mmol/l; the HCO3−/CO2 ratio has approached 20 : 1, so the pH is within the normal range. In such patients the respiratory center has adapted to prolonged hypercapnia and lost its sensitivity to CO2, and breathing is driven mainly by hypoxemia (via the carotid bodies). High-concentration oxygen removes the hypoxic stimulus, reduces ventilation further and creates the risk of a sharp rise in pCO2, decompensation of the respiratory acidosis and hypercapnic coma. Therefore oxygen is given to them under monitoring, at a low flow rate.
