topics.title: Main metabolic diseases: diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, obesity, metabolic syndrome (seminar)

goals.text: To explain to the student the etiology, pathogenesis, main manifestations and complications of the most common metabolic diseases — diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, obesity and metabolic syndrome; to teach the student to distinguish the types of diabetic coma and to assess lipid parameters and body mass index.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of diabetes mellitus and the etiology and pathogenesis of types 1 and 2;
the metabolic disorders in diabetes mellitus and the mechanisms of its clinical signs;
the pathogenesis of diabetic comas (ketoacidotic, hyperosmolar, lactic acidotic, hypoglycemic);
the mechanisms of the late complications of diabetes mellitus (micro- and macroangiopathies, neuropathy);
the definition, risk factors and pathogenesis of atherosclerosis;
the types, causes and pathogenesis of obesity;
the concept of metabolic syndrome and its criteria.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish the types of diabetic coma by clinical and laboratory signs;
assess lipid profile parameters and the atherogenic index;
determine the degree of obesity from body mass index and waist circumference.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The “three P's” of diabetes mellitus: **P**olyuria, **P**olydipsia, **P**olyphagia. The fourth is weight loss (mainly in type 1).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: There is no ketoacidosis in hyperosmolar coma, because in type 2 diabetes the residual insulin is enough to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis in the liver, but not enough to ensure glucose uptake by the tissues. The main dangers in this coma are severe dehydration, hypernatremia and thrombosis; mortality is higher than in ketoacidotic coma.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The most dangerous type of atherosclerotic plaque is the **unstable plaque**: a large lipid core, a thin fibrous cap and many macrophages. Its rupture leads to platelet adhesion and thrombus formation — this is the main mechanism of acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, myocardial infarction) and ischemic stroke.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The criteria for metabolic syndrome differ slightly between international organizations (WHO, NCEP ATP III, IDF): for example, in NCEP ATP III abdominal obesity is not mandatory and the waist circumference thresholds are higher. When making the diagnosis, the criteria used should be stated.

blocks.text: **Diabetes mellitus** — a group of metabolic diseases characterized by chronic hyperglycemia resulting from impaired insulin secretion, impaired insulin action, or both. It is accompanied by disturbed carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism and damage to the vessels, nervous system, kidneys and eyes.

blocks.title: Table 12.1. Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO)
head: Type
Main mechanism
Features
rows: Destruction of beta cells (mainly autoimmune) → absolute insulin deficiency
Usually in childhood and youth; acute onset; prone to ketoacidosis; insulin is essential for life
Insulin resistance + secretory dysfunction of beta cells (relative insulin deficiency)
About 90 percent of diabetes; usually after 40 years of age, with obesity; gradual onset
Insulin resistance in pregnancy (due to placental hormones)
Usually resolves after delivery; later risk of type 2 is high
Genetic defects of beta-cell function (MODY), diseases of the pancreas, endocrinopathies, drugs

blocks.text: Pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes mellitus

items: **Genetic predisposition** — certain alleles of the HLA system (DR3, DR4).
**Triggering factor** — viral infections (Coxsackie B, rubella, mumps), toxins.
**Autoimmune process** — autoantibodies and cytotoxic T lymphocytes against beta-cell antigens (insulin, glutamate decarboxylase, tyrosine phosphatase) are formed; insulitis develops.
Clinical signs appear **after 80–90 percent of beta cells have died**.

blocks.text: Pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus

items: **Insulin resistance** — reduced sensitivity of target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) to insulin; its main cause is abdominal (visceral) obesity: visceral adipose tissue releases large amounts of free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6), and adiponectin decreases; these disrupt post-receptor insulin signaling.
At first the beta cells overcome the resistance by producing more insulin (compensatory hyperinsulinemia).
Later **beta-cell dysfunction** (gluco- and lipotoxicity, amylin deposition) develops, insulin secretion becomes insufficient and hyperglycemia appears.

blocks.title: Table 12.2. Differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus
head: Feature
Type 1
Type 2
rows: Diet, physical activity, oral agents, later insulin

sections.title: 2. Metabolic disorders and clinical signs in diabetes mellitus

blocks.title: Table 12.3. Main signs of diabetes mellitus and their mechanisms
head: Feature
Mechanism
rows: Reduced glucose uptake by tissues, increased glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Glycemia exceeding the renal threshold (8.9–10 mmol/l)
“Energy starvation” of cells, increased lipolysis and proteolysis
Conversion of fatty acids released by lipolysis into ketone bodies in the liver
Increased lipolysis, decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
Susceptibility to infections, slow wound healing

parts.text: The “three P's” of diabetes mellitus: **P**olyuria, **P**olydipsia, **P**olyphagia. The fourth is weight loss (mainly in type 1).

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of diabetic ketoacidosis (based on Novitskiy V.V., 2009, figure 12.29)

blocks.title: Table 12.4. Comparative characteristics of diabetic comas
head: Feature
Ketoacidotic
Hyperosmolar
Lactic acidotic
Hypoglycemic
rows: Severe hyperglycemia and dehydration, no ketosis (a small amount of insulin is enough to suppress lipolysis)
Lack of glucose supply to neurons

parts.text: There is no ketoacidosis in hyperosmolar coma, because in type 2 diabetes the residual insulin is enough to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis in the liver, but not enough to ensure glucose uptake by the tissues. The main dangers in this coma are severe dehydration, hypernatremia and thrombosis; mortality is higher than in ketoacidotic coma.

blocks.text: The main cause of late complications is prolonged hyperglycemia. The main mechanisms are:

items: **Non-enzymatic glycation of proteins** and accumulation of advanced glycation end products (AGE) — basement membranes thicken, the vessel wall stiffens, and inflammation and oxidative stress are enhanced via AGE receptors.

**Activation of the polyol (sorbitol) pathway** — in cells that take up glucose independently of insulin (Schwann cells, lens, endothelium), sorbitol accumulates, causing osmotic damage and NADPH deficiency (weakened antioxidant defense).
**Activation of protein kinase C** — impaired vascular permeability and contractility.
**Oxidative stress** and endothelial dysfunction.

blocks.title: Table 12.5. Late complications of diabetes mellitus
head: Complication
Manifestation
Outcome
rows: Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, growth of new vessels
One of the main causes of blindness
Thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, microalbuminuria, then proteinuria
Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (“stocking and glove” type), autonomic neuropathy
Loss of sensation, painless ulcers, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis
Ischemic heart disease, stroke, obliterative disease of the leg arteries

parts.text: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) reflects the average glycemia over the last 2–3 months (the erythrocyte lifespan is about 120 days). Large clinical trials have shown that keeping HbA1c below 7 percent significantly reduces the risk of microangiopathic complications.

blocks.text: **Atherosclerosis** — a chronic disease characterized by accumulation of lipids (mainly cholesterol) in the intima of large and medium-sized arteries of the elastic and muscular-elastic type, connective tissue overgrowth and formation of atherosclerotic plaques. It underlies ischemic heart disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease — the leading causes of death worldwide.
Lipoproteins and their role

blocks.title: Table 12.6. Blood lipoproteins
head: Lipoprotein
Main function
Atherogenicity
rows: Transport dietary triglycerides from the intestine
Transport triglycerides formed in the liver
Transport cholesterol from the liver to the tissues
Return cholesterol from the tissues to the liver

blocks.title: Table 12.7. Risk factors
head: Non-modifiable
Modifiable
rows: Male sex (estrogen protection in women before menopause)

blocks.text: Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis
According to the modern view, atherosclerosis is a **chronic inflammatory process** that develops in response to lipid accumulation in the vessel wall (the “response to injury” theory).

blocks.label: Figure 12.2
blocks.caption: Stages of atherosclerotic plaque formation (based on Kumar V. et al., 2015)

parts.text: The most dangerous type of atherosclerotic plaque is the **unstable plaque**: a large lipid core, a thin fibrous cap and many macrophages. Its rupture leads to platelet adhesion and thrombus formation — this is the main mechanism of acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, myocardial infarction) and ischemic stroke.

blocks.text: **Obesity** — excess accumulation of adipose tissue in the body that poses a risk to health. The main cause is a long-term excess of energy intake over expenditure.

blocks.title: Table 12.8. Assessment by body mass index (BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)2) (WHO)
head: BMI, kg/m^2^
Assessment

blocks.title: Table 12.9. Types of obesity
head: Basis of classification
Types
rows: Primary (alimentary-constitutional — more than 90 percent); secondary (hypothalamic, endocrine — hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome; genetic syndromes; drug-induced)
Abdominal (android, “apple” type) — high metabolic and cardiovascular risk; gluteofemoral (gynoid, “pear” type)
Hypertrophic (adipocytes enlarge — in adults); hyperplastic (the number of adipocytes increases — when onset is in childhood)

blocks.text: **Regulation of appetite and body weight:** the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus regulates appetite. **Leptin** (secreted by adipocytes) and insulin give the satiety signal and reduce appetite; **ghrelin** (stomach) increases appetite. Most obese people have high leptin levels but reduced sensitivity to it (**leptin resistance**).

parts.text: A simple method of assessing abdominal obesity is **waist circumference**: the risk increases if it exceeds 94 cm in men and 80 cm in women (102 and 88 cm respectively in some guidelines). Visceral adipose tissue is metabolically active: free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines from it pass directly to the liver via the portal vein and increase insulin resistance.

blocks.text: **Metabolic syndrome** — the combination of abdominal obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension and impaired glucose metabolism. It is based on insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia; the syndrome sharply increases the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.

blocks.title: Table 12.10. Criteria for metabolic syndrome (International Diabetes Federation, 2005)
head: Criterion
Value
rows: Waist circumference: more than 94 cm in men, more than 80 cm in women (for Europeans)
+ at least two of the following:
Below 1.03 mmol/l in men, below 1.29 mmol/l in women
130/85 mm Hg or higher, or antihypertensive treatment
5.6 mmol/l or higher, or type 2 diabetes mellitus

parts.text: The criteria for metabolic syndrome differ slightly between international organizations (WHO, NCEP ATP III, IDF): for example, in NCEP ATP III abdominal obesity is not mandatory and the waist circumference thresholds are higher. When making the diagnosis, the criteria used should be stated.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 72-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes mellitus and takes oral agents. She has had diarrhea for a week and drank little fluid. She was brought to hospital with clouded consciousness. The skin and mucous membranes are very dry, breathing is rapid and shallow, there is no acetone odor. Blood: glucose 48 mmol/l, Na+ 152 mmol/l, K+ 4.8 mmol/l, urea 18 mmol/l, pH 7.36; no ketone bodies in the urine.
cases.ask: What coma has developed? Calculate the plasma osmolarity. Why is there no ketoacidosis?
cases.answer: Hyperosmolar (hyperglycemic, non-ketoacidotic) coma. Plasma osmolarity = 2 × (152 + 4.8) + 48 + 18 ≈ 380 mOsm/kg (normal 280–295) — markedly increased. Diarrhea and low fluid intake started the dehydration, hyperglycemia aggravated it through osmotic diuresis, and reduced renal perfusion cut glucose excretion, raising glycemia further. Hyperosmolarity led to dehydration of neurons and impaired consciousness. In type 2 diabetes the residual insulin secretion, although insufficient to ensure glucose uptake by tissues, is enough to suppress lipolysis in adipose tissue and ketogenesis in the liver — which is why there are no ketone bodies and no acidosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 48-year-old man, height 175 cm, weight 100 kg, waist circumference 112 cm. Arterial pressure 145/90 mm Hg. Blood: fasting glucose 6.3 mmol/l, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/l, total cholesterol 6.2 mmol/l, HDL 0.9 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What syndrome does the patient have? Calculate the atherogenic index. Explain the pathogenesis.
cases.answer: Metabolic syndrome: abdominal obesity (waist circumference 112 cm; BMI ≈ 32.7 kg/m^2^ — class I obesity) and four additional criteria — raised triglycerides, low HDL, arterial hypertension and raised fasting glycemia. Atherogenic index = (6.2 − 0.9) / 0.9 ≈ 5.9 — the risk of atherosclerosis is high. Pathogenesis: visceral adipose tissue releases large amounts of free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines, which cause insulin resistance; compensatory hyperinsulinemia increases renal sodium retention and sympathetic activity, causing arterial hypertension; in the liver, synthesis of VLDL and triglycerides increases and HDL decreases. Because the beta-cell reserve is beginning to be exhausted, glycemia is rising — the risk of type 2 diabetes is high.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old patient has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 12 years, with poor glycemic control (HbA1c 10.5 %). Recently his vision has deteriorated, he has numbness in his feet and reduced sensation in a “stocking” distribution, and persistent protein is found in the urine.
cases.ask: What complications have developed in the patient? What is their common pathogenetic mechanism?
cases.answer: Late microangiopathic and neuropathic complications of diabetes: diabetic retinopathy (deteriorating vision), diabetic nephropathy (proteinuria) and distal symmetric polyneuropathy (sensory loss in a “stocking” distribution). The common mechanism is many years of poorly controlled hyperglycemia (HbA1c 10.5 %): non-enzymatic glycation of proteins and accumulation of advanced glycation end products (thickening of basement membranes), activation of the polyol pathway and sorbitol accumulation in cells that take up glucose independently of insulin, activation of protein kinase C, oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction. Good glycemic control slows the development of these complications.

topics.title: Cell pathophysiology. General mechanisms of cell injury (seminar)

goals.text: To explain to the student the causes, general mechanisms and main manifestations of cell injury, damage to the cell membrane and organelles, disturbances of energy supply and ion balance, damage to the genetic apparatus, the forms of cell death (necrosis and apoptosis), and the protective and adaptive mechanisms of the cell.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the classification of factors that injure cells;
the general mechanisms of cell injury: disturbances of energy supply, membranes, ion and water balance, the genetic apparatus and regulatory mechanisms;
free-radical (peroxide) oxidation of lipids and the antioxidant defense systems;
the damaging effect of calcium overload in the cell;
the signs of reversible and irreversible injury;
the differences between necrosis and apoptosis;
the mechanisms by which the cell adapts to injury.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the leading mechanism of cell injury in a specific pathological condition;
distinguish necrosis from apoptosis by morphological and biochemical signs;
identify the injured organ from blood markers of cell injury (enzymes).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Oxidative stress** — a shift in the balance between free radical formation and antioxidant defense in favor of the radicals. It plays an important role in reperfusion injury, atherosclerosis, the complications of diabetes mellitus, aging, radiation injury and many inflammatory diseases.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The “**4P**” effects of calcium overload: **P**hospholipases (break down the membrane), **P**rotein- and DNA-cleaving enzymes — proteases (disrupt the cytoskeleton) and endonucleases (cleave DNA), **P**hosphorylation uncoupling (mitochondria are damaged, ATP falls), **P**ulling of fibrils (contracture of myofibrils).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Both **decreased** and **increased** apoptosis cause disease. Insufficient apoptosis — tumors (p53 mutation, Bcl-2 excess), autoimmune diseases (autoreactive lymphocytes are not eliminated). Excessive apoptosis — neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer, Parkinson), death of CD4+ lymphocytes in AIDS, part of ischemic injury.

blocks.text: **Cell injury** — a change in the structure, metabolism, physicochemical properties and function of a cell that disrupts its vital activity. Every disease is ultimately linked to cell injury.

blocks.title: Table 13.1. Factors that injure cells
head: Group
Examples
rows: Ischemia, anemia, respiratory failure, carbon monoxide poisoning
Mechanical trauma, high and low temperature, ionizing radiation, electric current
Poisons (cyanides, heavy metals), drugs (a large dose of paracetamol), alcohol, excess oxygen
Viruses, bacteria and their toxins, parasites
Autoimmune reactions, allergic reactions, cytotoxic T lymphocytes
Enzyme defects, mutations of structural proteins, chromosomal abnormalities
Deficiency or excess of protein, vitamins, trace elements

blocks.text: Injury can be **primary** (direct action of the factor on the cell) or **secondary** (the effect of changes resulting from the primary injury, e.g. hypoxia or accumulation of toxins). **Specific** changes (characteristic of a particular factor) and **nonspecific** changes (repeated in any injury) are also distinguished.

blocks.label: Figure 13.1
blocks.caption: General mechanisms of cell injury (based on Novitskiy V.V., 2009, figure 3.15)

blocks.text: Disturbance of energy supply
The main source of cell energy is ATP, formed by oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria. Energy supply can be disturbed at the following stages:

items: **reduced ATP formation** — hypoxia, inhibitors of the respiratory chain (cyanides block cytochrome oxidase), uncoupling of oxidation and phosphorylation (excess thyroid hormones, 2,4-dinitrophenol), lack of substrates (hypoglycemia);
**impaired ATP transport** — damage to the creatine phosphokinase system;
**impaired ATP use** — reduced ATPase activity.

blocks.text: Consequences of ATP deficiency: the Na+/K+ pump stops → Na+ and water enter the cell (cell swelling) and K+ leaves; anaerobic glycolysis increases → lactate accumulates and pH falls; Ca2+ pumps stop → cytoplasmic Ca2+ rises; protein synthesis decreases (ribosomes detach).
Membrane damage

blocks.label: Figure 13.2
blocks.caption: Elements of the biological membrane that are subject to damage: 1 — lipid bilayer, 2 — lipid monolayer, 3 — glycolipids, 4 — glycoproteins, 5 — microfilaments, 6 — microtubules, 7 — ion channel, 8 — ion pump (Novitskiy V.V., 2009, figure 3.1)

blocks.title: Table 13.2. Main mechanisms of membrane damage
head: Mechanism
Essence
rows: Reactive oxygen species oxidize unsaturated fatty acids; a chain reaction creates “holes” in the membrane
When Ca2+ rises, phospholipase A2 is activated and breaks down phospholipids; lysophospholipids with a detergent action and free fatty acids accumulate
Damage to membrane proteins and enzymes
Excessive stretching and rupture of the membrane in cell swelling
The membrane attack complex of complement (C5b–C9), perforins of cytotoxic T lymphocytes

blocks.text: Free-radical oxidation of lipids and antioxidant defense

**Free radicals** — highly reactive molecules with an unpaired electron in the outer orbital. The main oxygen radicals are the superoxide anion (O2−) and the hydroxyl radical (OH•); hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and singlet oxygen are also reactive oxygen species.

Sources of radicals: the mitochondrial respiratory chain (electron “leakage”, especially during reperfusion), NADPH oxidase of phagocytes, xanthine oxidase (accumulates in ischemia), ionizing radiation, metabolism of drugs and poisons.

blocks.title: Table 13.3. Antioxidant defense systems
head: Group
Representatives
Effect
rows: Converts O2− to H2O2 Breaks down H2O2 into water and oxygen
Breaks the chain reaction in membranes
Bind free iron and copper, reducing radical formation

parts.text: **Oxidative stress** — a shift in the balance between free radical formation and antioxidant defense in favor of the radicals. It plays an important role in reperfusion injury, atherosclerosis, the complications of diabetes mellitus, aging, radiation injury and many inflammatory diseases.

blocks.text: Disturbance of ion and water balance

items: Entry of Na+ and water into the cell → **cell swelling** (hydropic degeneration) and swelling of organelles;
Loss of K+ from the cell → change in membrane potential, impaired excitability;
**Rise of cytoplasmic Ca^2+^** — the “final common pathway” of cell injury.

parts.text: The “**4P**” effects of calcium overload: **P**hospholipases (break down the membrane), **P**rotein- and DNA-cleaving enzymes — proteases (disrupt the cytoskeleton) and endonucleases (cleave DNA), **P**hosphorylation uncoupling (mitochondria are damaged, ATP falls), **P**ulling of fibrils (contracture of myofibrils).

blocks.text: Damage to the genetic apparatus

DNA damage (mutations, breaks, chromosomal aberrations) occurs under the action of ionizing radiation, chemical mutagens, viruses and free radicals. Consequences: impaired protein synthesis, arrest of cell division, apoptosis (via the p53 protein), tumor transformation. The cell has DNA repair systems; their hereditary defects (e.g. xeroderma pigmentosum) sharply increase the risk of tumors.
Disturbance of regulatory mechanisms

Disturbance of the systems that regulate cell activity: changes in the number and sensitivity of receptors, impaired G-protein function (e.g. cholera toxin permanently activates the Gs protein, raising cAMP in intestinal cells and causing severe secretory diarrhea), impaired function of second messengers and protein kinases.

blocks.title: Table 13.4. Manifestations of organelle damage
head: Organelle
Manifestation of damage
Outcome
rows: Swelling, destruction of cristae, calcium deposition in the matrix; increased membrane permeability
Decreased ATP; release of cytochrome C and initiation of apoptosis
Decreased protein synthesis; accumulation of misfolded proteins (“ER stress”)
Loss of membrane stability, release of enzymes into the cytoplasm
Autolysis; sometimes they escape from the cell and damage the tissue
Impaired cell shape, movement and division

sections.title: 4. Reversible and irreversible injury. Cell death

blocks.text: Signs of **reversible injury**: swelling of the cell and organelles, blebs on the membrane surface, detachment of ribosomes, accumulation of fat droplets (fatty degeneration). If the injuring factor is removed, the cell recovers.

Signs of **irreversible injury**: marked swelling of mitochondria with dense calcium deposits in the matrix, extensive damage to the plasma membrane, rupture of lysosomes, nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis).

parts.text: When the cell membrane is damaged, the enzymes and proteins inside it are released into the blood — they are used diagnostically as **markers of cell injury**: troponins and the MB fraction of creatine phosphokinase in myocardial injury, aminotransferases (ALT, AST) in the liver, creatine phosphokinase in skeletal muscle, amylase and lipase in the pancreas.

blocks.title: Table 13.5. Differences between necrosis and apoptosis
head: Feature
Necrosis
Apoptosis
rows: “Forced”, disorderly death of the cell under the action of an injuring factor
Genetically programmed, energy-dependent active cell death
Physiological (embryogenesis, replacement of aged cells) and pathological (DNA damage, viruses, cytotoxic T lymphocytes, hormone deficiency)
A group of cells, an area of tissue
Remains intact for a long time; phosphatidylserine appears on the outer surface
Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis; DNA is degraded randomly
Chromatin condensation; DNA is cleaved between nucleosomes into regular fragments (a “ladder” on electrophoresis)
Membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, rapidly engulfed by macrophages

blocks.text: Pathways of apoptosis:

items: **intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway** — DNA damage, oxidative stress, lack of growth factors → imbalance of Bcl-2 family proteins (Bax and Bak are activated) → cytochrome C is released from the mitochondria → apoptosome → caspase-9 → effector caspases (caspase-3);
**extrinsic (receptor) pathway** — “death receptors” (Fas, TNF receptor) bind their ligand → caspase-8 → effector caspases.

parts.text: Both **decreased** and **increased** apoptosis cause disease. Insufficient apoptosis — tumors (p53 mutation, Bcl-2 excess), autoimmune diseases (autoreactive lymphocytes are not eliminated). Excessive apoptosis — neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer, Parkinson), death of CD4+ lymphocytes in AIDS, part of ischemic injury.

sections.title: 5. Mechanisms of cell adaptation to injury

blocks.title: Table 13.6. Protective and adaptive mechanisms at the cellular level
head: Mechanism
Essence
rows: Increased glycolysis, increased number and activity of mitochondria
Activation of antioxidant systems, membrane repair (resynthesis)
Restoration of ion and water balance
Increased activity of ion pumps, buffer systems
Refold damaged proteins or direct them to degradation
Repair of damaged DNA segments; if repair is impossible — apoptosis (p53)
Digestion and recycling of damaged organelles

blocks.title: Table 13.7. Forms of cell adaptation
head: Form
Definition
Examples
rows: Myocardium in arterial hypertension, skeletal muscles in athletes
Uterus in pregnancy, endometrium with excess estrogen
Decrease in cell size and function
Muscles in prolonged immobility, ischemia, starvation
Replacement of one differentiated cell type by another
Transformation of bronchial epithelium into stratified squamous epithelium in smokers, Barrett esophagus

items: Why is hypoxia the most common cause of cell injury?

items: Determine the type of injuring factor (hypoxia, toxin, radiation, immune, etc.).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 25-year-old man took a total of 15 g of paracetamol over one day because of toothache. In the first 24 hours he had only nausea. On day 3 jaundice and pain under the right costal margin appeared; blood ALT and AST were sharply raised (50 times the normal value) and the prothrombin time was prolonged.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of hepatocyte injury. What does the rise in ALT and AST indicate? Why is acetylcysteine an antidote?
cases.answer: A large dose of paracetamol forms a toxic metabolite in the liver via cytochrome P450 — N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine. Normally it is neutralized by glutathione; at a large dose the glutathione stores are exhausted and the metabolite binds covalently to proteins, enhances oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation and damages the mitochondria — hepatocyte necrosis develops. The sharp rise in ALT and AST indicates damage to the hepatocyte membrane and release of enzymes from these cells into the blood — extensive necrosis; prolonged prothrombin time shows that the synthetic function of the liver is impaired. Acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis and restores glutathione stores, i.e. it restores the capacity to neutralize the toxic metabolite; it is most effective in the first 8–10 hours.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient who had been in a closed room during a fire was brought in unconscious. The skin and mucous membranes are pinkish-red and breathing is rapid. Blood carboxyhemoglobin is 40 %.
cases.ask: What is the main mechanism of cell injury? Which tissues are damaged first, and why?
cases.answer: Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin about 200–250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin; the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood decreases and the remaining oxyhemoglobin gives up oxygen less readily (the dissociation curve shifts to the left). In addition, CO partly blocks cytochrome oxidase. The result is tissue hypoxia → ATP deficiency → ion pumps stop, cell swelling, calcium accumulation and necrosis. The tissues with the highest oxygen demand and the greatest sensitivity to hypoxia — the brain and myocardium — are damaged first. The pinkish-red color is due to the color of carboxyhemoglobin and masks the severity of the hypoxia.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with cancer received a course of radiotherapy. After treatment the tumor decreased in size, but the patient developed leukopenia and diarrhea.
cases.ask: How does ionizing radiation kill tumor cells? Why are the complications related specifically to the bone marrow and intestine?
cases.answer: Ionizing radiation damages DNA directly and through free radicals formed by radiolysis of water (breaks in DNA strands). Damaged DNA triggers apoptosis via the p53 protein, or the cell dies during division (mitotic death). Tumor cells divide rapidly and are therefore sensitive to radiation. According to the Bergonié–Tribondeau law, the rapidly renewing tissues of the body — the bone marrow and intestinal epithelium — are also sensitive to radiation: death of bone marrow cells leads to leukopenia, and damage to the epithelium of the intestinal crypts leads to impaired absorption and diarrhea.

cards.back: A change in cell structure, metabolism and function that disrupts its vital activity
Hypoxia
Na+/K+ pump stops, cell swelling, lactic acidosis, Ca2+ rise
O2−, OH•, H2O2 — damage lipids, proteins and DNA
Superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, vitamins E and C
Radical formation outweighs antioxidant defense
Activation of phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases; mitochondrial damage
Calcium deposits in mitochondria, membrane rupture, nuclear changes
Forced death: the cell swells, the membrane ruptures, inflammation
Programmed death: the cell shrinks, caspases, no inflammation
Intrinsic (mitochondria, cytochrome C) and extrinsic (Fas, TNF receptor)
Troponin — myocardium, ALT — liver, lipase — pancreas
Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia

topics.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of tumor development in the body

goals.text: To explain to the student the nature of tumor growth, the differences between malignant and benign tumors, carcinogenic factors and their mechanisms of action, the stages and molecular basis of carcinogenesis (oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes), the types of tumor atypia, the stages of metastasis, the local and systemic changes caused by a tumor in the body, and the mechanisms of antiblastoma defense.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the concept of a tumor and the differences between malignant and benign tumors;
the classification of carcinogenic factors (chemical, physical, biological) and their mechanism of action;
the stages of carcinogenesis: initiation, promotion, progression;
the role of proto-oncogenes, oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes;
the types of tumor atypia (growth, metabolic, functional, morphological);
the stages and routes of metastasis;
the effects of the tumor on the body (cachexia, paraneoplastic syndromes) and antiblastoma defense.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: explain the methods of studying tumors experimentally;
identify the carcinogenic factor and the likely mechanism of tumor growth in a clinical situation;
distinguish a malignant from a benign tumor by its features.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A “benign” tumor can also be life-threatening depending on its location: a meningioma in the brain compresses the brain, and hormone-producing adenomas (pheochromocytoma, insulinoma) cause severe hormonal disturbances. Some benign tumors can become malignant (adenomatous polyps of the colon).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main hallmarks of the tumor cell (D. Hanahan and R. Weinberg, “Hallmarks of cancer”): independence from growth signals, insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals, evasion of apoptosis, unlimited replication (telomerase), sustained angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis; additional ones — reprogramming of energy metabolism, evasion of immune surveillance, genome instability and tumor-promoting inflammation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Tumors that frequently metastasize to bone: “**P**rostate, **B**reast, **K**idney, **T**hyroid, **L**ung” — “**Pb KTL**” (“lead kettle”). Prostate cancer usually gives osteoblastic metastases (bone becomes denser), the others give osteolytic metastases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In immunodeficiency states (AIDS, immunosuppression after transplantation), tumors are common, especially virus-associated tumors (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, cervical cancer) — this confirms the important role of immune surveillance in antiblastoma defense.

blocks.text: **Tumor (neoplasia, blastoma)** — a typical pathological process characterized by unlimited proliferation of cells that escapes the body's control and by impaired differentiation, resulting from changes in their genetic apparatus. These properties of tumor cells are passed on to subsequent cell generations.
The main features of a tumor:

items: **autonomous (uncontrolled) growth** — tumor cells do not obey the signals that regulate growth;
**atypia** — structure and function that differ from normal cells;
**anaplasia** — loss of differentiation, resemblance to embryonic cells;
**unlimited proliferation (“immortality”)** — due to telomerase activity;
in malignant tumors, **invasive growth** and **metastasis**.

blocks.title: Table 14.1. Differences between benign and malignant tumors
head: Feature
Benign tumor
Malignant tumor
rows: High, resembling the tissue of origin
Expansive (pushing the surrounding tissue aside), has a capsule

parts.text: A “benign” tumor can also be life-threatening depending on its location: a meningioma in the brain compresses the brain, and hormone-producing adenomas (pheochromocytoma, insulinoma) cause severe hormonal disturbances. Some benign tumors can become malignant (adenomatous polyps of the colon).

blocks.text: **Carcinogens** — factors that cause tumor development.

blocks.title: Table 14.2. Classification of carcinogenic factors
head: Group
Examples
Associated tumors
rows: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (benzo(a)pyrene — tobacco smoke, charred food), aromatic amines (aniline dyes), nitrosamines, aflatoxin B1, asbestos, benzene, arsenic, vinyl chloride
Cancer of the lung, bladder, stomach, liver; mesothelioma; leukemias
Leukemias, thyroid cancer; skin cancer and melanoma
Human papillomavirus (types 16, 18), Epstein–Barr virus, hepatitis B virus, Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (HHV-8)
Cervical cancer; Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal cancer; liver cancer; Kaposi sarcoma
Hepatitis C virus, human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-1)
Hormones (excess estrogens), chronic inflammation, hereditary mutations
Endometrial and breast cancer; colon cancer in ulcerative colitis

blocks.text: **Chemical carcinogens** by their mode of action:

items: **direct-acting** — react with DNA themselves (alkylating agents, some cytostatics);
**indirect-acting (procarcinogens)** — become carcinogenic after metabolic activation in the body (mainly in the liver by the cytochrome P450 system) (benzo(a)pyrene, aflatoxin, nitrosamines).

parts.text: Historical examples: in 1775 P. Pott linked the high frequency of scrotal skin cancer in London chimney sweeps to an occupational factor — soot. In 1915 K. Yamagiwa and K. Ichikawa first induced a tumor experimentally by applying coal tar to rabbits' ears for a long time. Today tobacco smoking is associated with 80–90 percent of lung cancer.

sections.title: 3. Stages and molecular mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Stages of carcinogenesis (based on Novitskiy V.V., 2009, figure 14.9)

blocks.text: Oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes

blocks.title: Table 14.3. Genes involved in carcinogenesis
head: Gene group
Normal function
Change in tumors
Examples
rows: Stimulate cell growth and division (growth factors, their receptors, signaling proteins, transcription factors)
Activated (dominant effect — one allele is enough): point mutation, amplification, translocation
RAS (many tumors), HER2/neu (breast cancer), MYC (Burkitt lymphoma), BCR-ABL (chronic myeloid leukemia)

TP53 (“guardian of the genome” — in more than half of tumors), RB (retinoblastoma), APC (familial adenomatous polyposis), BRCA1/2 (breast and ovarian cancer)

parts.text: The main hallmarks of the tumor cell (D. Hanahan and R. Weinberg, “Hallmarks of cancer”): independence from growth signals, insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals, evasion of apoptosis, unlimited replication (telomerase), sustained angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis; additional ones — reprogramming of energy metabolism, evasion of immune surveillance, genome instability and tumor-promoting inflammation.

blocks.text: Theories of carcinogenesis

items: **Mutation theory** — a tumor is the result of the accumulation of several successive mutations (in colon cancer: APC → KRAS → TP53 mutations, the adenoma–carcinoma sequence).
**Viral-genetic theory** (L.A. Zilber) — oncogenic viruses insert their genome into the cell DNA and transform it.
**Epigenetic theory** — disturbed gene expression without changes in the DNA sequence (DNA methylation, histone modification).
**Cancer stem cell theory** — a tumor develops from a small group of self-renewing cells, which are resistant to treatment.

blocks.title: Table 14.4. Types of tumor atypia
head: Type
Essence
rows: Uncontrolled proliferation, loss of contact inhibition, invasion and metastasis

Warburg effect: glycolysis predominates even when oxygen is sufficient (“aerobic glycolysis”) — high glucose consumption and lactate production; the tumor “draws” glucose, amino acids and lipids from the body (“nitrogen trap”, “glucose trap”)
Loss or alteration of the function of the tissue of origin; ectopic hormone production
Cellular atypia (nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, abnormal mitoses) and tissue atypia (disordered architecture)
Tumor-specific antigens, reappearance of embryonic antigens (alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen)

parts.text: Metabolic atypia is used in diagnosis: in **positron emission tomography** (PET), radiolabeled glucose (18F-FDG) accumulates in the tumor and its metastases because they consume glucose rapidly. **Tumor markers** (alpha-fetoprotein — liver cancer, carcinoembryonic antigen — colon cancer, PSA — prostate cancer, CA-125 — ovarian cancer) are used to monitor treatment response and recurrence.

blocks.text: **Metastasis** — detachment of tumor cells from the primary focus, their migration to other organs and formation of new tumor foci (metastases) there. It is the main cause of death from malignant tumors.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Stages of metastasis

blocks.title: Table 14.5. Routes of metastasis
head: Path
Feature
Examples
rows: First to the regional lymph nodes
Most carcinomas (gastric cancer — Virchow's metastasis to the left supraclavicular node)
Via the blood, often to the lungs, liver, bone, brain
Sarcomas, kidney cancer, melanoma, breast cancer
Gastric and ovarian cancer — peritoneal carcinomatosis, Krukenberg tumor

parts.text: Tumors that frequently metastasize to bone: “**P**rostate, **B**reast, **K**idney, **T**hyroid, **L**ung” — “**Pb KTL**” (“lead kettle”). Prostate cancer usually gives osteoblastic metastases (bone becomes denser), the others give osteolytic metastases.

sections.title: 6. Effects of the tumor on the body

blocks.text: **Local effects:** compression of surrounding tissues and organs, obstruction of vessels and ducts (jaundice, intestinal obstruction), tissue destruction (bleeding, perforation), pain.
Systemic effects:

items: **Tumor cachexia** — loss of appetite and marked weight loss; mechanism: cytokines released by the tumor and immune cells (TNF-alpha — “cachectin”, IL-1, IL-6), proteolysis-inducing factor, the metabolic “trap” of the tumor, anorexia.
**Paraneoplastic syndromes** — manifestations not related to the direct spread of the tumor, arising through substances it secretes or through immune reactions.
**Anemia**, immunodeficiency, fever, tendency to thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome — migratory thrombophlebitis).

blocks.title: Table 14.6. Examples of paraneoplastic syndromes
head: Syndrome
Mechanism
Commonly associated tumor
rows: Squamous cell lung cancer, kidney cancer

blocks.text: **Antiblastoma resistance** — the system of the body's defense mechanisms against the emergence and development of tumors.

blocks.title: Table 14.7. Mechanisms of antiblastoma defense
head: Group
Mechanisms
rows: Neutralization and excretion of carcinogens (liver enzymes), antioxidant systems
DNA repair systems, elimination of mutated cells by apoptosis (p53)
NK cells (natural killers), cytotoxic T lymphocytes, macrophages, antibodies, interferons, TNF

blocks.text: A tumor can escape immune surveillance: it reduces expression of HLA molecules, secretes immunosuppressive factors (TGF-beta, IL-10) and expresses immune “brake” molecules (PD-L1). Modern immunotherapy (PD-1 and CTLA-4 inhibitors) is based precisely on removing these “brakes”.

parts.text: In immunodeficiency states (AIDS, immunosuppression after transplantation), tumors are common, especially virus-associated tumors (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas, cervical cancer) — this confirms the important role of immune surveillance in antiblastoma defense.

sections.title: 8. Practical part: methods of studying tumors experimentally

blocks.title: Table 14.8. Methods of studying tumors experimentally
head: Method
Essence
Examples
rows: Inducing a tumor with a carcinogen
Applying coal tar to rabbits' ears (Yamagiwa and Ichikawa); applying benzo(a)pyrene to mouse skin; viral tumors (Rous sarcoma — in chickens)
Transferring tumor cells from one animal to another
Ehrlich ascites carcinoma, Walker carcinosarcoma, Lewis carcinoma
Growing tumor cells outside the body
p53 knockout mice, mice expressing an oncogene

blocks.text: Modeling two-stage carcinogenesis (analysis using a scheme)

items: A small dose of a carcinogen is applied once to mouse skin (initiator) — no tumor develops.
Then a promoter (not itself carcinogenic, croton oil or phorbol esters) is applied to the same area for a long time — papillomas and then cancer develop.
If the promoter is applied **before** the initiator, or only the promoter is used, no tumor develops.

blocks.text: **Analysis:** initiation is an irreversible genetic change (DNA mutation); promotion is a process that stimulates the proliferation of initiated cells, requires prolonged and repeated exposure and is reversible up to a certain point. This experiment proves the multistage nature of carcinogenesis and explains why quitting smoking or treating chronic inflammation reduces the risk of tumors.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing tumor risk factors

items: Identify exposure to occupational and household carcinogens (smoking, asbestos, dyes, radiation).
Identify chronic infections (hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, human papillomavirus).
Identify chronic inflammation and precancerous conditions (Barrett esophagus, ulcerative colitis, adenomatous polyps).
Check the family history (signs of BRCA, Lynch syndrome).
Take immunodeficiency states into account.
Write a conclusion and indicate the direction of screening or prevention.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing a malignant from a benign tumor

items: Assess the growth rate (history).
Determine the borders and whether there is a capsule (palpation, imaging).
Check for infiltration of surrounding tissues and mobility.
Palpate the regional lymph nodes.
Assess systemic signs: weight loss, weakness, anemia.
Indicate that histological examination is needed for the final diagnosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 62-year-old man has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 40 years. In recent months: cough, hemoptysis, 8 kg weight loss, weakness. Blood sodium 124 mmol/l, urine osmolarity high. Bronchoscopy revealed small cell lung cancer.
cases.ask: Which carcinogenic factor is leading in the development of the tumor? What is the mechanism of the hyponatremia? What is the weight loss due to?
cases.answer: The leading factor is the chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke (benzo(a)pyrene and other polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines). After metabolic activation in the liver and lungs, they cause mutations in the DNA of the bronchial epithelium (TP53, KRAS and others) — initiation; many years of repeated exposure and chronic inflammation provide promotion and progression. The hyponatremia is the paraneoplastic syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion: the tumor cells produce ectopic ADH, excess water is retained by the kidneys, the plasma is diluted and the urine is concentrated. The weight loss is tumor cachexia: anorexia and increased proteolysis and lipolysis under the action of TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6, and the metabolic “trap” of the tumor.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman's mother died of breast cancer at the age of 42, and her maternal aunt died of ovarian cancer. Genetic testing found a mutation in the BRCA1 gene, but so far there is no tumor.
cases.ask: To which group of genes does BRCA1 belong? Why is there no tumor yet despite the mutation?
cases.answer: BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene (involved in repairing DNA double-strand breaks). In a hereditary mutation, one allele is defective from birth in all cells (the “first hit”). For a tumor to develop, the second allele must also be damaged somatically in a particular cell (the “second hit”) — Knudson's hypothesis. Therefore the tumor does not develop immediately, but it develops much earlier and with a much higher probability than in the general population. Such patients are advised to undergo regular screening (MRI, mammography) and preventive measures.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 55-year-old patient has had chronic hepatitis B for 20 years, with liver cirrhosis. The latest examination found a sharp rise in blood alpha-fetoprotein and a focus typical of a tumor in the liver.
cases.ask: By what mechanisms has the tumor developed? To which type of tumor atypia does the rise in alpha-fetoprotein belong?
cases.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis B virus DNA integrates into the hepatocyte genome and causes insertional mutagenesis; the viral protein HBx blocks p53 and stimulates cell growth (viral carcinogenesis). In addition, chronic inflammation, cycles of necrosis and regeneration, and cirrhosis create conditions for the accumulation of mutations through repeated cell division (promotion). Alpha-fetoprotein is an embryonic protein; its renewed synthesis by tumor cells is a manifestation of antigenic (biochemical) atypia and is used as a tumor marker.

topics.title: Changes in the leukocyte differential in disease. Leukocytosis and leukopenia

goals.text: To explain to the student the functional and morphological features of the formed elements of the blood, hematopoiesis and leukopoiesis, the normal leukocyte count and differential, the types, causes and mechanisms of leukocytosis and leukopenia, the types of nuclear shift and the nuclear shift index; to teach the student to determine the leukocyte differential in blood smears and interpret it in various diseases.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main stages of hematopoiesis and the factors that regulate leukopoiesis;
the types of leukocytes, their functions and morphological features;
the normal leukocyte count and the leukocyte differential;
the types, causes and mechanisms of leukocytosis and leukopenia;
agranulocytosis and its consequences;
the left and right nuclear shifts and the nuclear shift index;
the changes in the leukocyte differential in various diseases (pneumonia, viral infections, helminth infestations, atopy, trauma, myocardial infarction).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish the types of leukocytes in a blood smear;
calculate the leukocyte differential and convert it to absolute counts;
calculate and assess the nuclear shift index;
interpret the leukogram in relation to the clinical situation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Neutrophils exist in three “pools” in the body: the **bone marrow pool** (maturing and reserve cells — the largest), the **circulating pool** (free in the bloodstream — measured in the blood test) and the **marginal (wall) pool** (close to the vessel wall, not measured in the blood test). Neutrophils circulate in the blood for only 6–10 hours and then move into the tissues.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Assessing the leukocyte differential only in percentages can lead to a wrong conclusion. For example, in leukopenia the percentage of lymphocytes may be increased while their absolute count is normal — this is **relative lymphocytosis**. Always calculate the absolute count: absolute count = total leukocyte count × percentage / 100.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Causes of eosinophilia — “**PAD**”: **P**arasites (helminths), **A**llergy (asthma, pollinosis, drugs), **D**ermatoses. Lymphocytosis — “**VTP**”: **V**iruses, **T**uberculosis, **P**ertussis (whooping cough).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Disappearance of eosinophils (aneosinophilia)** is seen in acute infection and stress (effect of glucocorticoids), and their reappearance is a sign of recovery (the “dawn of recovery”). Prolonged absence of eosinophils and lymphopenia in severe pneumonia or sepsis are signs of a poor prognosis.

blocks.text: **Hematopoiesis** — the formation of blood cells. In adults it takes place mainly in the red bone marrow of the flat bones and the epiphyses of the long bones. All blood cells arise from a **pluripotent (stem) cell**, which gives rise to progenitor cells of the myeloid and lymphoid lineages.

The main factors regulating leukopoiesis are the **colony-stimulating factors**: granulocyte (G-CSF), granulocyte-macrophage (GM-CSF) and macrophage (M-CSF), as well as interleukins (IL-3 — multipotential, IL-5 — for eosinophils, IL-7 — for lymphocytes).

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Maturation of granulocytes and nuclear shift (based on Abdullayev N.H., 2008; Zayko N.N., 2002)

parts.text: Neutrophils exist in three “pools” in the body: the **bone marrow pool** (maturing and reserve cells — the largest), the **circulating pool** (free in the bloodstream — measured in the blood test) and the **marginal (wall) pool** (close to the vessel wall, not measured in the blood test). Neutrophils circulate in the blood for only 6–10 hours and then move into the tissues.

blocks.text: In adults the normal leukocyte count in peripheral blood is **4.0–9.0 × 10^9^/l**.
**Leukocyte differential (leukogram)** — the percentage ratio of the individual types of leukocytes in a blood smear.

head: Cell type
Percentage

parts.text: Assessing the leukocyte differential only in percentages can lead to a wrong conclusion. For example, in leukopenia the percentage of lymphocytes may be increased while their absolute count is normal — this is **relative lymphocytosis**. Always calculate the absolute count: absolute count = total leukocyte count × percentage / 100.

In children the leukocyte differential changes with age: at birth neutrophils predominate; on day 4–6 of life neutrophils and lymphocytes become equal (**first crossover**); then lymphocytes predominate; at 4–6 years they become equal again (**second crossover**), after which the adult differential is established. Assessing a child's blood test against adult norms is a mistake.

blocks.text: **Leukocytosis** — a rise in the peripheral blood leukocyte count above 9.0 × 10^9^/l.

blocks.text: Nuclear shift
The nuclear shift is assessed according to the degree of maturity of the neutrophils.

blocks.title: Table 15.4. Types of nuclear shift
head: Type
Essence
Clinical significance
rows: Band forms and metamyelocytes increase, with leukocytosis
Active response of the bone marrow to infection; prognosis relatively good
no leukocytosis or leukopenia; degenerative changes in neutrophils (toxic granulation, vacuolization)
Hypersegmented neutrophils with 5 or more segments, fewer band forms
Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency, radiation sickness
Blast cells and mature neutrophils are present, intermediate forms are absent

blocks.text: **Nuclear shift index (NSI)** = (myelocytes + metamyelocytes + band forms) / segmented neutrophils. Normally **0.05–0.08**. 0.3–1.0 — moderately severe, above 1.0 — severe process.
Toxic changes in neutrophils

In severe infections, neutrophils show **toxic granulation** (large dark granules), **vacuolization of the cytoplasm**, **Döhle bodies** and nuclear pyknosis — these indicate the severity of the intoxication.
**Leukopenia** — a fall in the peripheral blood leukocyte count below 4.0 × 10^9^/l. It usually develops through a decrease in neutrophils (**neutropenia**).

blocks.title: Table 15.5. Mechanisms and causes of leukopenia
head: Mechanism
Causes
rows: Ionizing radiation, cytostatics, benzene, aplastic anemia, infiltration of the bone marrow by tumor (leukemia, metastases), vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency, hereditary neutropenias
Immune (autoimmune, drug-induced — antibodies), hypersplenism (enlarged spleen), increased consumption in severe infections (sepsis)
Accumulation of leukocytes in the capillaries of the lungs and other organs in the early stage of anaphylactic and transfusion shock

blocks.text: Agranulocytosis
**Agranulocytosis** — a sharp decrease or disappearance of granulocytes (neutrophils): granulocytes **below 0.75 × 10^9^/l** or total leukocytes **below 1.0 × 10^9^/l**.

items: **Myelotoxic** — direct toxic action on the bone marrow (cytostatics, radiation); other blood cells also decrease.
**Immune** — antibodies against granulocytes (hapten mechanism: metamizole sodium (analgin), thiamazole, sulfonamides, clozapine) or autoimmune.

blocks.text: Consequences: severe bacterial and fungal infections, necrotic tonsillitis, ulcers of the oral cavity, sepsis; fever is often the only sign.

parts.text: If fever develops in a patient receiving cytostatic chemotherapy (**febrile neutropenia**), this is an emergency: because neutrophils are low, signs of inflammation (pus, infiltrate) may be absent, and the infection quickly progresses to sepsis. Such patients are immediately given broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Prolonged absence of eosinophils and lymphopenia in severe pneumonia or sepsis are signs of a poor prognosis.

sections.title: 6. Experimental part: studying a blood smear and determining the leukocyte differential

blocks.text: **Aim:** to distinguish the types of leukocytes in blood smears from a healthy person and from patients with various diseases, and to calculate and interpret the leukocyte differential.

**Equipment:** ready-stained blood smears (healthy person and patients with pneumonia, viral infection, helminth infestation, atopy, trauma, myocardial infarction), immersion microscope, immersion oil, 11-key counter (or a table).
Procedure

items: Place the smear under the immersion objective (stained by the Romanowsky–Giemsa or Pappenheim method).
At the edge of the smear (where leukocytes are evenly distributed), moving in a meander (zigzag) pattern, count at least **100** consecutive leukocytes, preferably 200.
Identify each cell by its morphological features (see the table) and record it on the counter.
Calculate the percentage of each type.
If the total leukocyte count is known, calculate the absolute counts.
Calculate the nuclear shift index.
Record toxic changes and atypical cells.
Compare the result with the normal values and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: calculating and interpreting the leukocyte differential

items: Count at least 100 leukocytes in the smear using the meander method.
Determine the percentage of each type.
Calculate the absolute count: (leukocyte count × percentage) / 100.
Compare the absolute values with the normal ranges: which type is truly increased or decreased.
Calculate the nuclear shift index and determine the type of shift.
Record toxic and atypical changes.
Relate the findings to the clinical situation and write a conclusion (e.g. “neutrophilic leukocytosis with a regenerative left shift — typical of acute bacterial inflammation”).

skills.title: Skill: calculating the nuclear shift index

items: Add up the percentages of myelocytes, metamyelocytes and band neutrophils.
Divide the sum by the percentage of segmented neutrophils.
Compare the result with the normal value (0.05–0.08).
Assess it together with the leukocyte count: with leukocytosis — regenerative; with leukopenia — degenerative shift.
Write a conclusion about the severity of the process and its prognosis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: On day 5 after surgery for acute appendicitis, a 30-year-old patient has a fever of 39 °C and increasing abdominal pain. Blood test: leukocytes 18.5 × 10^9^/l; myelocytes 2 %, metamyelocytes 6 %, band forms 18 %, segmented forms 60 %, eosinophils 0 %, lymphocytes 10 %, monocytes 4 %. Toxic granulation in neutrophils.
cases.ask: Interpret the leukogram. Calculate the nuclear shift index. What complication can be suspected?
cases.answer: Neutrophilic leukocytosis (absolute neutrophils ≈ 15.9 × 10^9^/l), hyperregenerative left shift (myelocytes and metamyelocytes have appeared), aneosinophilia, relative lymphopenia, toxic granulation. NSI = (2 + 6 + 18) / 60 ≈ 0.43 — increased, indicating a severe purulent inflammatory process. A purulent complication (abdominal abscess or peritonitis) can be suspected. Cytokines and colony-stimulating factors released from the purulent focus have sharply increased neutrophil production and the release of young forms from the bone marrow; aneosinophilia reflects the effect of stress and glucocorticoids.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-year-old child has itchy skin, restless sleep and abdominal pain. Blood test: leukocytes 8.2 × 10^9^/l; eosinophils 18 %, other values close to normal. Ascaris eggs were found in the stool.
cases.ask: Assess the change in the leukogram. What is the mechanism of the eosinophilia?
cases.answer: Absolute eosinophilia: 8.2 × 18 / 100 ≈ 1.48 × 10^9^/l (normal up to 0.3 × 10^9^/l). Helminth antigens induce a Th2-type immune response: Th2 lymphocytes secrete IL-5, which enhances the production and maturation of eosinophils in the bone marrow; IL-4 and IL-13 increase IgE synthesis. Eosinophils adhere to helminths coated with IgE and IgG and damage them by releasing major basic protein and other toxic substances. The itching is the allergic (IgE-mediated) component.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 60-year-old woman is taking thiamazole for an overactive thyroid. In week 6 of treatment she developed a fever of 39.5 °C, severe sore throat and necrotic ulcers on the tonsils. Blood test: leukocytes 1.1 × 10^9^/l, granulocytes 0.2 × 10^9^/l, erythrocytes and platelets normal.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? What are its mechanism and danger?
cases.answer: Drug-induced immune agranulocytosis (granulocytes far below 0.75 × 10^9^/l; erythrocytes and platelets normal — not a myelotoxic but an immune mechanism). Thiamazole, acting as a hapten, binds to proteins on the neutrophil surface and causes the formation of antibodies against them and destruction of neutrophils in the blood and bone marrow. Because of the absence of phagocytes, the oral microflora has caused necrotic tonsillitis; the infection can quickly progress to sepsis. The drug is stopped immediately, the patient is placed in an isolated (aseptic) ward, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor are prescribed.

topics.title: Leukemias: definition, etiology, pathogenesis and types. Leukemoid reactions

goals.text: To explain to the student the definition, etiology and pathogenesis of leukemias, their classification, the features of acute and chronic leukemias, the changes in peripheral blood and bone marrow in leukemia, the main hematological phenomena, the local and systemic changes in the body, and the difference between leukocytosis and leukemia (leukemoid reactions); to teach the student to study and analyze peripheral blood smears in acute and chronic myeloid leukemia, lymphocytic leukemia and undifferentiated leukemia.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition of leukemia and its neoplastic nature;
the etiological factors and pathogenesis of leukemias (clonal theory);
the classification of leukemias (acute and chronic, myeloid and lymphoid);
the changes in blood and bone marrow in acute leukemias, the leukemic “gap”;
the hematological signs of chronic myeloid leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia;
the main clinical syndromes of leukemias and their mechanisms;
leukemoid reactions and how they differ from leukemia.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify blast cells and the leukemic “gap” by studying the blood smear in leukemias;
distinguish smears of chronic myeloid leukemia and lymphocytic leukemia;
distinguish leukemia from a leukemoid reaction by the blood test.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The three main features of leukemia: **neoplastic nature** — leukemic cells have all the properties of tumor cells (uncontrolled proliferation, atypia, metastasis — leukemic infiltrates); **clonal origin** — all leukemic cells are descendants of a single mutated cell; **location** — the tumor starts in the bone marrow and spreads to the blood (leukemic cells do not have to be numerous in the blood).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The terms “acute” and “chronic” leukemia refer not to the duration of the disease but to the degree of maturity of the tumor cells. Acute leukemia never turns into chronic leukemia, whereas chronic myeloid leukemia may pass into an “acute leukemia-like” state with a blast crisis in its final stage.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Distinguishing chronic leukemias in a smear: **myeloid leukemia** — “all the steps of the granulocyte ladder + the eosinophil–basophil pair”; **lymphocytic leukemia** — “a sea of small lymphocytes + Botkin–Gumprecht shadows”.

blocks.text: **Leukemia (hemoblastosis)** — a neoplastic disease of the hematopoietic tissue, characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of tumor cells (a leukemic clone) derived from a single mutated hematopoietic cell in the bone marrow and other organs, and by displacement of normal hematopoiesis.

parts.text: The three main features of leukemia:

items: **neoplastic nature** — leukemic cells have all the properties of tumor cells (uncontrolled proliferation, atypia, metastasis — leukemic infiltrates);
**clonal origin** — all leukemic cells are descendants of a single mutated cell;
**location** — the tumor starts in the bone marrow and spreads to the blood (leukemic cells do not have to be numerous in the blood).

blocks.text: The term “leukemia” (“white blood”) is historical: it refers to the whitish color the blood takes on when leukocytes are greatly increased (R. Virchow, 1845). However, only some leukemias have leukocytosis in the blood.

blocks.title: Table 16.1. Etiological factors of leukemias
head: Group
Examples
rows: Leukemias increased among the population of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, after the Chernobyl accident and after radiotherapy
Benzene and its derivatives, cytostatics (alkylating agents), some pesticides, smoking
HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukemia), Epstein–Barr virus (Burkitt lymphoma)
Down syndrome (10–20 times higher risk of acute leukemia), Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia

blocks.text: According to the modern **clonal theory**, leukemia begins with a mutation (often a chromosomal translocation) in a single hematopoietic stem or progenitor cell. As a result of the mutation:

items: **proliferation** of the cell escapes control (oncogenes are activated);
**differentiation** (maturation) is blocked — in acute leukemias the cells “get stuck” at the blast stage;
**apoptosis** is impaired — the cells live long (especially in chronic lymphocytic leukemia).

blocks.text: As the leukemic clone develops, new mutations accumulate and the tumor becomes more malignant — **tumor progression**: transition from the monoclonal to the polyclonal stage, emergence of resistance to cytostatics, and development of a **blast crisis** in chronic leukemias.

parts.text: An example of a common chromosomal change in leukemias is the **Philadelphia chromosome** t(9;22): the ABL gene on chromosome 9 fuses with the BCR gene on chromosome 22, producing a permanently active tyrosine kinase. It is found in almost all cases of chronic myeloid leukemia. Imatinib, which selectively blocks this kinase, was the first successful example of targeted therapy in cancer.

blocks.label: Figure 16.1
blocks.caption: Main clinical syndromes of leukemias and their mechanisms

blocks.text: Leukemias are classified by two main criteria: **the degree of cell maturity** (acute and chronic) and **the cell lineage** (myeloid and lymphoid).

blocks.title: Table 16.2. Classification of leukemias
head: Criterion
Groups
rows: Acute — the tumor substrate consists of immature blast cells; chronic — the tumor substrate consists mainly of maturing and mature cells
Myeloid (myeloblast, monoblast, erythroblast, megakaryoblast lineage), lymphoid (B- and T-lymphocyte lineage), undifferentiated
Leukemic (above 50–100 × 10^9^/l), subleukemic (slightly increased), leukopenic (decreased), aleukemic (no leukemic cells in the blood)

parts.text: The terms “acute” and “chronic” leukemia refer not to the duration of the disease but to the degree of maturity of the tumor cells. Acute leukemia never turns into chronic leukemia, whereas chronic myeloid leukemia may pass into an “acute leukemia-like” state with a blast crisis in its final stage.

blocks.text: In acute leukemias the leukemic cells have lost the ability to mature and have stopped at the blast stage. The bone marrow contains **more than 20 percent blast cells** (WHO criterion).

blocks.title: Table 16.3. Main types of acute leukemia
head: Type
Features
rows: The most common leukemia in children (2–5 years); lymph nodes, liver and spleen enlarge, the meninges are often involved; with modern treatment the cure rate in children exceeds 80–90 percent
More common in adults; Auer rods in blasts
t(15;17) translocation; accompanied by severe DIC; differentiation therapy with a vitamin A derivative (all-trans retinoic acid) is effective
The blasts show no features of any lineage

blocks.text: Peripheral blood in acute leukemia

items: the leukocyte count may vary — from leukopenia to high leukocytosis;
**blast cells** appear;

**leukemic “gap” (hiatus leucaemicus)** — the blood contains blast cells and mature (segmented) neutrophils, while the intermediate stages of maturation (promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte) are absent or very few; this reflects the immaturity of the leukemic clone and the remnants of normal hematopoiesis;
**normochromic anemia** and **thrombocytopenia**.

blocks.title: Table 16.4. Morphological features of a blast cell
head: Feature
Feature
rows: Round, occupies most of the cell; chromatin delicate, reticular
Narrow, sky-blue to blue (basophilic); Auer rods may be present in myeloblasts

blocks.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia
Chronic myeloid leukemia is a myeloproliferative disease arising from a stem cell and characterized by the Philadelphia chromosome.

**Peripheral blood:** high leukocytosis (50–200 × 10^9^/l or more); **all stages of granulocyte maturation** are present in the blood (myeloblasts, promyelocytes, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, band and segmented neutrophils) — a “marked left nuclear shift”, with **no** leukemic “gap”; **eosinophil–basophil association** (eosinophils and basophils increase together); thrombocytosis may be present at the onset; neutrophil alkaline phosphatase activity is reduced.
Clinical signs: marked enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly), enlargement of the liver, weakness, sweating.

blocks.title: Table 16.5. Phases of chronic myeloid leukemia
head: Stage
Feature
rows: Few blasts in blood and bone marrow (below 10 percent); mature cells predominate; good response to treatment
Blasts and basophils increase, resistance to treatment appears
Blasts above 20 percent; course resembling acute leukemia; poor prognosis

blocks.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a tumor characterized by the accumulation of mature-looking but functionally defective B lymphocytes; it occurs mainly in the elderly (the most common leukemia in adults in Western countries).

**Peripheral blood:** leukocytosis; **absolute lymphocytosis** (lymphocytes up to 80–90 percent), mainly small mature lymphocytes; **Botkin–Gumprecht shadows** (smudge cells) — remnants of lymphocyte nuclei destroyed during smear preparation (because of the fragility of the lymphocytes).
Clinical signs: enlargement of lymph nodes in many regions (painless, soft-elastic), splenomegaly; recurrent infections due to hypogammaglobulinemia; autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia.

parts.text: Distinguishing chronic leukemias in a smear: **myeloid leukemia** — “all the steps of the granulocyte ladder + the eosinophil–basophil pair”; **lymphocytic leukemia** — “a sea of small lymphocytes + Botkin–Gumprecht shadows”.

sections.title: 7. Changes in the body in leukemias

Mechanism
Manifestations
rows: Thrombocytopenia, DIC (in promyelocytic leukemia), infiltration of the vessel wall
Petechiae, ecchymoses, nose and gum bleeding, cerebral hemorrhage

parts.text: **Tumor lysis syndrome** develops when chemotherapy for leukemia is started, as a result of the simultaneous breakdown of many tumor cells: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia and acute kidney failure. To prevent it, plenty of fluid and agents that reduce uric acid formation are given before treatment begins.

blocks.text: **Leukemoid reactions** — changes in the peripheral blood resembling leukemia (high leukocytosis, appearance of young cells), but they are not neoplastic in nature and disappear when the underlying disease is eliminated.

rows: Severe bacterial infections (sepsis, pneumonia), tumor metastases, severe burns, acute hemolysis

sections.title: 9. Experimental part: studying peripheral blood smears in leukemias

blocks.text: **Aim:** to identify the characteristic features of blood smears in acute and chronic leukemias.

**Equipment:** stained blood smears (acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, undifferentiated leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, myeloid leukemoid reaction), immersion microscope, hematology atlas.
Procedure

items: Examine each smear first at low magnification, then under immersion.
Roughly estimate the density of leukocytes (many or few).
Prepare a leukogram of at least 100 cells; count the blast cells separately.
Check whether the stages of granulocyte maturation are present (whether there is a leukemic “gap”).
Record eosinophils and basophils, Botkin–Gumprecht shadows and Auer rods.
Assess the state of the erythrocytes and platelets.
Write a conclusion for each smear and enter the main distinguishing features in a table.

blocks.title: Table 16.9. Main features of the peripheral blood picture in leukemias
head: Feature
Acute leukemia

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of leukemia from the smear

items: Determine the percentage of blast cells: if high — acute leukemia or blast crisis.
Check whether the intermediate stages of granulocytes are present (leukemic “gap”).
If granulocytes of all stages and an eosinophil–basophil association are present, suspect chronic myeloid leukemia.
If small lymphocytes predominate and Botkin–Gumprecht shadows are present, suspect chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Assess the degree of anemia and thrombocytopenia.
Indicate that bone marrow examination, immunophenotyping and cytogenetic analysis are needed for the final diagnosis.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing leukemia from a leukemoid reaction

items: Assess the clinical situation: is there an obvious infection or other cause?
Check for toxic granulation and an eosinophil–basophil association.
Take into account the degree of splenomegaly.
Assess the results of neutrophil alkaline phosphatase and the Philadelphia chromosome.
Follow the change in the blood picture as the underlying disease is treated.
Write a conclusion.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 4-year-old child has had weakness, pallor, fever, leg pain and bruises on the skin for 3 weeks. The cervical lymph nodes, liver and spleen are enlarged. Blood test: hemoglobin 72 g/l, platelets 25 × 10^9^/l, leukocytes 32 × 10^9^/l, blast cells 68 %, segmented neutrophils 8 %, no intermediate stages, lymphocytes 24 %.
cases.ask: What disease can be suspected? Explain the changes in the blood test and the clinical signs.
cases.answer: Acute leukemia; given the child's age and enlarged lymph nodes, probably acute lymphoblastic leukemia (bone marrow examination and immunophenotyping are needed for confirmation). The blood contains many blast cells and mature neutrophils, with no intermediate stages — the leukemic “gap”: the leukemic clone does not mature, while the mature neutrophils come from the remnants of normal hematopoiesis. Anemia and thrombocytopenia — the bone marrow is filled with blasts and normal erythro- and thrombopoiesis are displaced; pallor and weakness — the anemic syndrome; bruises — the hemorrhagic syndrome. Fever — infectious complications and intoxication. Bone pain — bone marrow infiltration; enlargement of the lymph nodes, liver and spleen — the hyperplastic (infiltrative) syndrome.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 50-year-old man complains of heaviness under the left costal margin, sweating and weakness. The spleen is markedly enlarged. Blood test: leukocytes 150 × 10^9^/l; myeloblasts 2 %, promyelocytes 4 %, myelocytes 15 %, metamyelocytes 12 %, band forms 16 %, segmented forms 38 %, eosinophils 6 %, basophils 5 %, lymphocytes 2 %. Platelets 520 × 10^9^/l.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Which signs confirm it? By what test can the diagnosis be confirmed?
cases.answer: Chronic myeloid leukemia, chronic phase. Signs confirming it: very high leukocytosis; all stages of granulocyte maturation in the blood (from myeloblast to segmented form), no leukemic “gap”; eosinophil–basophil association (eosinophils 6 %, basophils 5 %); thrombocytosis; few blasts; marked splenomegaly (infiltration of the spleen by leukemic cells). The diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) on cytogenetic testing or the BCR-ABL gene on molecular testing; neutrophil alkaline phosphatase is reduced.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old patient has severe right-sided pneumonia and sepsis. Blood test: leukocytes 48 × 10^9^/l, myelocytes 6 %, metamyelocytes 10 %, band forms 22 %, segmented forms 54 %, lymphocytes 6 %, monocytes 2 %, no eosinophils or basophils. Toxic granulation in neutrophils. The spleen is not enlarged.
cases.ask: Is this leukemia or a leukemoid reaction? Justify your answer.
cases.answer: Myeloid (neutrophilic) leukemoid reaction. Reasons: an obvious cause — severe pneumonia and sepsis; toxic granulation in neutrophils (a sign of a reactive process); no eosinophil–basophil association (on the contrary, aneosinophilia — a sign of stress and infection); no splenomegaly. Neutrophil alkaline phosphatase is expected to be increased and the Philadelphia chromosome absent. After the infection is treated, the blood picture returns to normal.
