topics.title: Pathophysiology of erythrocytes. Classification of anemias. Posthemorrhagic and hemolytic anemias

goals.text: To explain to the student the stages of erythropoiesis and its regulation, the criteria for assessing cells of the erythroid series, the pathological forms of erythrocytes, the concept and classification of anemia, and the etiology, pathogenesis and blood picture of acute and chronic posthemorrhagic anemias and hemolytic anemias; to teach the student to identify pathological forms of erythrocytes in blood smears, to detect reticulocytes by supravital staining and to measure hemoglobin concentration by the colorimetric method.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the stages of erythropoiesis and the factors that regulate it (erythropoietin, iron, B12, folic acid);
the red blood cell indices and their normal values;
the pathological forms of erythrocytes (anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, anisochromia, regenerative and degenerative forms);
the definition and classification of anemia (by pathogenesis, color index, regeneration);
the stages of compensation and the blood picture in acute posthemorrhagic anemia;
the types of hemolytic anemia and the signs of intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify pathological forms of erythrocytes in a blood smear;
count reticulocytes with supravital staining and assess the result;
determine hemoglobin concentration and calculate the red blood cell indices;
determine the type of anemia from the blood test.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The general signs of anemia are related to hypoxia and compensatory reactions: weakness, fatigue, dizziness, tinnitus, “floaters” before the eyes, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia, pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, a functional systolic murmur at the cardiac apex (reduced blood viscosity and increased flow velocity).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the first hours of acute blood loss, hemoglobin and hematocrit may be normal, because plasma and erythrocytes are lost in the same proportion. Relying on these values and underestimating the volume of blood loss is dangerous: at this time pulse, arterial pressure, the shock index (pulse / systolic pressure) and clinical signs are more important.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The reticulocyte count is the simplest indicator of the erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow. **Reticulocytosis** occurs after hemolysis and acute blood loss (from day 4–5); **reticulocytopenia** occurs in aplastic anemia and in iron, B12 and folate deficiency (before treatment). The “**reticulocyte crisis**” seen on day 5–7 of treatment of B12 deficiency is a sign of treatment effectiveness.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The old Sahli method (converting hemoglobin to hematin with hydrochloric acid and comparing it visually with a standard color) is subjective and of low accuracy; today the hemiglobincyanide photometric method and automated analyzers are the standard. The reagents of the hemiglobincyanide method are toxic (cyanides) — observe safety precautions when working with them.

blocks.text: **Erythropoiesis** — the formation of erythrocytes; in adults it takes place in the red bone marrow. Sequence: stem cell → erythroid progenitors (BFU-E, CFU-E) → proerythroblast → basophilic, polychromatophilic and oxyphilic (orthochromic) normoblasts (the nucleus is extruded) → **reticulocyte** (1–2 days in the bone marrow, 1 day in the blood) → **mature erythrocyte** (lifespan about 120 days).

blocks.text: **Erythrocytosis** — an increase in the erythrocyte count and hemoglobin in the blood.

items: **Primary (polycythemia vera, Vaquez disease)** — a myeloproliferative neoplastic disease (JAK2 mutation), independent of erythropoietin; accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis.
**Secondary absolute** — increased erythropoietin: hypoxia (high altitude, chronic lung diseases, cyanotic congenital heart defects, smoking), kidney diseases and tumors (ectopic erythropoietin).
**Relative (hemoconcentration)** — reduced plasma volume (dehydration, burns); the total erythrocyte mass is unchanged.

sections.title: 4. The concept and classification of anemia

blocks.text: **Anemia** — a decrease in hemoglobin (and often erythrocytes) per unit volume of blood. WHO criterion: hemoglobin below 130 g/l in men, below 120 g/l in women, below 110 g/l in pregnant women.

blocks.title: Table 17.4. Classification of anemias
head: Basis of classification
Groups
rows: 1) Due to blood loss (posthemorrhagic — acute and chronic); 2) due to impaired erythropoiesis (iron, B12, folate deficiency, aplastic, anemia of chronic disease); 3) due to increased destruction of erythrocytes (hemolytic)
Microcytic (below 80 fl), normocytic (80–100 fl), macrocytic (above 100 fl)
By the regenerative capacity of the bone marrow (reticulocytes)
Regenerative (0.5–2 %), hyperregenerative (above 2 percent), hyporegenerative (below 0.5 percent), aregenerative (reticulocytes almost absent)
Mild (Hb above 90 g/l), moderate (70–90 g/l), severe (below 70 g/l)

blocks.text: **Color index** = (Hb, g/l × 3) / the first three digits of the erythrocyte count. For example, if Hb is 120 g/l and erythrocytes 4.0 × 10^12^/l: (120 × 3) / 400 = 0.9.

parts.text: The general signs of anemia are related to hypoxia and compensatory reactions: weakness, fatigue, dizziness, tinnitus, “floaters” before the eyes, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia, pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, a functional systolic murmur at the cardiac apex (reduced blood viscosity and increased flow velocity).

blocks.text: Acute posthemorrhagic anemia

Develops as a result of losing a large amount of blood in a short time. Loss of 10–15 percent of the circulating blood volume (CBV) is usually well tolerated, 25–30 percent is a severe condition, and more than 40–50 percent is life-threatening (hemorrhagic shock).

blocks.label: Figure 17.1
blocks.caption: Stages of compensation after acute blood loss (based on Abdullayev N.H., 2008)

blocks.title: Table 17.5. Dynamics of the blood picture in acute posthemorrhagic anemia
head: Stage
Hemoglobin and erythrocytes
Other changes
rows: Not yet changed (blood volume is reduced, but its composition is “proportional”)
Reticulocytosis (up to 5–10 percent), polychromatophilia, normoblasts, slight decrease in the color index (hypochromia — iron consumption)

parts.text: In the first hours of acute blood loss, hemoglobin and hematocrit may be normal, because plasma and erythrocytes are lost in the same proportion. Relying on these values and underestimating the volume of blood loss is dangerous: at this time pulse, arterial pressure, the shock index (pulse / systolic pressure) and clinical signs are more important.

blocks.text: Chronic posthemorrhagic anemia

Develops as a result of repeated loss of small amounts of blood over a long time (from the gastrointestinal tract — ulcer, tumor, hemorrhoids; heavy and prolonged menstruation; helminths — ancylostomiasis). The body's iron stores are exhausted and **iron deficiency anemia** (hypochromic, microcytic, hyporegenerative) develops (see topic 18).

**Hemolytic anemias** — anemias resulting from increased destruction of erythrocytes (shortened lifespan); even though the bone marrow increases erythropoiesis, it cannot keep up with the rate of destruction.

blocks.label: Figure 17.2

head: Group
Type
Examples
rows: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency
Sickle cell anemia (HbS), thalassemias (reduced synthesis of globin chains)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn, incompatible blood transfusion
Prosthetic heart valves, microangiopathic (DIC, hemolytic uremic syndrome), “march hemoglobinuria”
Hemolytic poisons (snake venom, arsine, lead), malaria, clostridial sepsis

blocks.text: General signs of hemolytic anemias

items: **anemia** — normochromic, hyperregenerative (reticulocytosis);
**jaundice** — increased indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin; stercobilin and urobilin increase in the stool and urine;
**splenomegaly** — in extravascular hemolysis;
**gallstone disease** — pigment stones;
in intravascular hemolysis — **hemoglobinemia**, **hemoglobinuria** (black or red-brown urine), decreased haptoglobin, hemosiderinuria;
erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow; in children with chronic hemolysis — skull deformity (“tower” skull).

blocks.text: Hereditary spherocytosis (Minkowski–Chauffard disease)

Inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. As a result of a defect in erythrocyte membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin), membrane is lost and the erythrocyte becomes spherical (a **spherocyte**). Spherocytes are small, lack central pallor and have low deformability; they cannot pass through the splenic sinuses and are destroyed by macrophages (extravascular hemolysis).

Signs: anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, gallstones; microspherocytes and reticulocytosis in the blood; **decreased osmotic resistance** of erythrocytes (they hemolyze quickly in hypotonic solutions). Treatment — splenectomy (almost stops the hemolysis, but the membrane defect remains).
G6PD deficiency

Inherited in an X-linked manner. With the enzyme deficiency, little NADPH and reduced glutathione are formed in erythrocytes, and the erythrocytes become unable to withstand oxidative stress. **Hemolytic crises** develop after oxidizing drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurans), infections and **eating legumes (fava beans)** (favism). Heinz bodies (precipitated hemoglobin) are found in the blood.
Sickle cell anemia

A point mutation of the beta-globin gene (glutamic acid is replaced by valine at position 6) produces HbS. When oxygen falls, HbS polymerizes, the erythrocytes become sickle-shaped, block small vessels (vaso-occlusive crises, pain, infarcts) and undergo hemolysis. Heterozygous carriers are more resistant to falciparum malaria — which is why the mutation is common in areas where malaria is widespread.

parts.text: **Hemolytic disease of the newborn** — when the mother is Rh-negative and the fetus Rh-positive (or with ABO incompatibility), maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal erythrocytes (a type II allergic reaction). In severe cases indirect bilirubin accumulates in the brain nuclei — **bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus)**. Prevention — giving anti-D immunoglobulin to the Rh-negative woman within 72 hours after delivery.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: studying pathological forms of erythrocytes in a blood smear

items: Take stained smears from a healthy person and from patients with acute posthemorrhagic anemia, hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell anemia and thalassemia.
Under the immersion objective, assess the size, shape and staining of the erythrocytes.
Find regenerative (polychromatophils, normoblasts) and degenerative (Howell–Jolly bodies, basophilic stippling) forms.
Draw each smear and write down the main changes.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: detecting reticulocytes by supravital staining

items: Put a few drops of brilliant cresyl blue (or new methylene blue) dye solution and an equal volume of blood into a test tube and mix.
Leave for 20–30 minutes at room temperature (or at 37 °C) — the living cells are stained (supravital staining).
Prepare a thin smear from the mixture and let it dry.
Under the immersion objective, count the reticulocytes among 1000 erythrocytes: their cytoplasm shows a blue network or granules (remnants of ribosomal RNA — the “granulofilamentous substance”).
Express the result in per mille (‰) or percent.
Compare with the normal value (5–12 ‰) and assess the regenerative activity of the bone marrow.

parts.text: The reticulocyte count is the simplest indicator of the erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow. **Reticulocytosis** occurs after hemolysis and acute blood loss (from day 4–5); **reticulocytopenia** occurs in aplastic anemia and in iron, B12 and folate deficiency (before treatment). The “**reticulocyte crisis**” seen on day 5–7 of treatment of B12 deficiency is a sign of treatment effectiveness.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determining hemoglobin concentration by the colorimetric (photometric) method

items: Put 5 ml of transforming solution (which converts hemoglobin into a stable compound — hemiglobincyanide) into a test tube.
Add 0.02 ml of blood with a micropipette, mix and leave for 10–20 minutes.
Measure the optical density in a photoelectric colorimeter (wavelength about 540 nm).
Calculate the hemoglobin concentration (g/l) using a calibration curve prepared with a standard solution, or a formula.
Determine hemoglobin and the color index in the blood of a patient with hemolytic anemia and assess the type of anemia.

parts.text: The old Sahli method (converting hemoglobin to hematin with hydrochloric acid and comparing it visually with a standard color) is subjective and of low accuracy; today the hemiglobincyanide photometric method and automated analyzers are the standard. The reagents of the hemiglobincyanide method are toxic (cyanides) — observe safety precautions when working with them.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of anemia from the blood test

items: Determine from hemoglobin whether anemia is present and its severity.
Calculate the color index (or MCH): hypo-, normo- or hyperchromic.
Determine from MCV whether it is micro-, normo- or macrocytic.
Assess the regenerative activity from reticulocytes.
Examine the morphology of erythrocytes in the smear (spherocytes, target cells, megalocytes).
Assess bilirubin (indirect), haptoglobin and LDH as signs of hemolysis.
Determine the pathogenetic type and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: counting reticulocytes

items: Examine the supravitally stained smear under the immersion objective.
Moving from field to field in sequence, count 1000 erythrocytes.
Count the reticulocytes among them separately.
Record the result in per mille.
Compare with the normal value and write a conclusion about erythropoietic activity.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 35-year-old man lost blood from the femoral artery in a car accident. In hospital 1 hour after the accident: pulse 125 beats/min, arterial pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pale skin, cold sweat. Blood test: Hb 138 g/l, erythrocytes 4.4 × 10^12^/l, hematocrit 42 %. The next day: Hb 92 g/l, hematocrit 28 %. On day 6, reticulocytes 6 %.
cases.ask: Why is the first test close to normal? Explain the subsequent changes stage by stage.
cases.answer: In the first hour, the reflex (vascular) stage: plasma and erythrocytes have been lost in equal proportion, so although blood volume has decreased, hemoglobin and hematocrit per unit volume have not yet changed; at the same time, the hemodynamic signs (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, cold sweat) indicate severe blood loss. The next day, the hydremic stage: tissue fluid moves into the blood vessels and restores circulating blood volume, the blood is diluted — hemoglobin and hematocrit fall (normochromic anemia). From day 4–5, the bone marrow stage: in response to hypoxia, renal erythropoietin increases and erythropoiesis is enhanced — reticulocytosis (6 %), the anemia is hyperregenerative.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 12-year-old child has had episodes of jaundice and heaviness under the left costal margin since early childhood. His father has similar signs. The spleen is enlarged. Blood: Hb 95 g/l, color index 1.0, reticulocytes 8 %, microspherocytes in the smear, indirect bilirubin raised. Osmotic resistance of erythrocytes is decreased.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its pathogenesis and the type of hemolysis. What treatment is effective?
cases.answer: Hereditary spherocytosis (Minkowski–Chauffard disease) — inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (the father is also affected). Because of a defect in erythrocyte membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin), membrane is lost, the erythrocyte becomes spherical and fragile, loses its deformability and, unable to pass through the splenic sinuses, is destroyed by macrophages — extravascular hemolysis. This is why splenomegaly and raised indirect bilirubin (jaundice) are seen; the bone marrow has increased erythropoiesis (reticulocytosis 8 %). Splenectomy almost stops the hemolysis, although the membrane defect persists.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 25-year-old man was prescribed a sulfonamide drug for pneumonia. 2 days later his urine turned black, and weakness and jaundice appeared. Blood: Hb 78 g/l, haptoglobin markedly decreased, Heinz bodies in the smear. A similar episode had occurred previously after eating fava beans.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: An acute hemolytic crisis due to G6PD deficiency. With the enzyme deficiency, little NADPH is formed in the pentose phosphate pathway, reduced glutathione is not regenerated and erythrocytes are not protected from oxidative stress. Under the action of an oxidizing drug (sulfonamide) or substances in fava beans, hemoglobin is oxidized and precipitates (Heinz bodies), the membrane is damaged and the erythrocytes are destroyed mainly within the vessels: hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria (black urine), decreased haptoglobin; raised indirect bilirubin leads to jaundice. The oxidizing drug must be stopped and such drugs avoided.

topics.title: Etiology and pathogenesis of deficiency anemias. Iron, vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency anemias

goals.text: To explain to the student the importance of iron, vitamin B12 and folic acid in erythropoiesis, the causes, pathogenesis, hematological signs and clinical manifestations of iron deficiency and megaloblastic (B12 and folate deficiency) anemias, as well as aplastic anemia and anemia of chronic disease; to teach the student to study blood smears of patients with iron and folate deficiency anemias, to determine hemoglobin concentration and to calculate the color index.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: iron metabolism in the body and its regulation (hepcidin);
the causes and stages of iron deficiency and the signs of iron deficiency anemia;
the metabolism of vitamin B12 and folic acid and their role in DNA synthesis;
the causes, pathogenesis and blood picture of megaloblastic anemias;
the nature of pernicious (Addison–Biermer) anemia and the mechanism of funicular myelosis;
the main features of aplastic anemia and anemia of chronic disease;
how to distinguish deficiency anemias by laboratory values.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: distinguish smears of iron deficiency and megaloblastic anemia;
determine hemoglobin concentration and calculate the color index;
interpret iron metabolism parameters (serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The body has **no** physiological mechanism for actively excreting iron — iron balance is maintained only by regulating intestinal absorption. Daily loss (epithelial shedding, sweating) is 1–2 mg, with an additional 0.5–1 mg in menstruating women. **Hepcidin** (produced in the liver) degrades ferroportin and stops iron absorption from the intestine and its release from macrophages; hepcidin increases with iron overload and inflammation (IL-6) and decreases with iron deficiency and hypoxia.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Funicular myelosis (subacute combined degeneration)** — a neurological complication specific to B12 deficiency: demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Signs: paresthesias in the legs, loss of deep (vibration and joint-position) sensation, ataxia, spastic paresis, memory impairment. Folic acid deficiency does not cause such neurological signs.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Treating a patient with B12 deficiency with folic acid alone is dangerous: blood values may partly improve, but the neurological disturbances worsen and become irreversible. In megaloblastic anemia, B12 and folate levels should be determined first, and folic acid alone should not be given until B12 deficiency has been ruled out.

blocks.text: The adult body contains 3–5 g of iron: 65–70 percent in hemoglobin, 20–30 percent in stores (ferritin and hemosiderin), and the rest in myoglobin and enzymes (cytochromes, catalase).

blocks.label: Figure 18.1
blocks.caption: Iron metabolism in the body (based on Novitskiy V.V., 2009; Kumar V. et al., 2015)

parts.text: The body has **no** physiological mechanism for actively excreting iron — iron balance is maintained only by regulating intestinal absorption. Daily loss (epithelial shedding, sweating) is 1–2 mg, with an additional 0.5–1 mg in menstruating women. **Hepcidin** (produced in the liver) degrades ferroportin and stops iron absorption from the intestine and its release from macrophages; hepcidin increases with iron overload and inflammation (IL-6) and decreases with iron deficiency and hypoxia.

blocks.text: Heme iron (meat, liver) is well absorbed (20–30 %); non-heme iron (plant foods) is poorly absorbed. Vitamin C, gastric hydrochloric acid and animal proteins improve absorption; tea (tannins), phytates, calcium and antacids reduce it.

**Iron deficiency anemia (IDA)** — a hypochromic microcytic anemia characterized by impaired hemoglobin synthesis due to iron deficiency in the body. It is the most common anemia in the world (about 80 percent of all anemias).

blocks.title: Table 18.1. Causes of iron deficiency
head: Group
Examples
rows: Chronic blood loss (the main cause in adults)
Heavy and prolonged menstruation, occult gastrointestinal bleeding (ulcer, tumor, hemorrhoids, erosions, NSAID use), ancylostomiasis, frequent blood donation
Pregnancy and breastfeeding, periods of rapid growth in children and adolescents
Vegetarian diet, prolonged feeding of children with milk alone, starvation
Gastric resection, atrophic gastritis (achlorhydria), celiac disease, small intestinal diseases, H. pylori

blocks.title: Table 18.2. Stages of iron deficiency
head: Stage
Essence
Laboratory signs
rows: Ferritin decreased; serum iron and Hb normal
Stores are exhausted, the transport pool decreases
Ferritin, serum iron and transferrin saturation decreased; Hb normal

blocks.text: Signs of IDA
**Anemic syndrome** (general signs) and **sideropenic syndrome** (tissue iron deficiency — reduced activity of iron-containing enzymes):

items: dry skin, hair loss and brittleness, thin, spoon-shaped concave nails (**koilonychia**);
**disturbed taste and smell** — eating chalk, clay, rice, ice (**pica chlorotica**), liking the smell of gasoline or acetone;
**angular stomatitis** (cracks at the corners of the mouth), glossitis, difficulty swallowing (sideropenic dysphagia);
muscle weakness, urinary incontinence (weakened sphincters);
delayed psychomotor development in children.

blocks.text: **Blood picture:** hypochromic (color index below 0.85, MCH decreased), microcytic (MCV below 80 fl) anemia; anisocytosis (microcytosis), poikilocytosis, ring-shaped erythrocytes (annulocytes — with a wide pale center); reticulocytes normal or decreased (hyporegenerative); serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation decreased, total iron-binding capacity of serum increased.

parts.text: When iron deficiency anemia is found in adults, especially men and postmenopausal women, its cause — above all occult gastrointestinal bleeding (colon cancer, gastric cancer, ulcer) — must always be sought. Treating with iron preparations without identifying the cause is a dangerous mistake.

sections.title: 3. Metabolism of vitamin B12 and folic acid

blocks.label: Figure 18.2
blocks.caption: Absorption of vitamin B12

blocks.text: **Vitamin B~12~ (cobalamin)** is found only in animal products (meat, liver, eggs, milk). The daily requirement is 2–3 µg; the store in the liver lasts 3–5 years — which is why deficiency develops very slowly.
**Folic acid** is found in green leaves, liver and legumes; it is quickly destroyed by cooking. The daily requirement is 200–400 µg; the store lasts only 3–4 months.

**Role in DNA synthesis:** folic acid (as tetrahydrofolate) carries one-carbon groups in the synthesis of thymidylate (the thymine nucleotide for DNA). B12, as methylcobalamin, takes the methyl group from methyltetrahydrofolate and converts homocysteine to methionine, thereby “freeing” tetrahydrofolate. In B12 deficiency, folic acid is “trapped” in the methyl form (the **folate trap**) and DNA synthesis is impaired.

In addition, B12 (as adenosylcobalamin) takes part in the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; in its deficiency methylmalonate accumulates and myelin synthesis is impaired — **neurological disturbances** are specific to B12 deficiency.

**Megaloblastic anemias** — hyperchromic macrocytic anemias characterized by impaired DNA synthesis due to vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency and a switch of erythropoiesis to the megaloblastic type.

blocks.title: Table 18.3. Causes of B12 and folic acid deficiency
head: Cause
B12 deficiency
Folic acid deficiency
rows: Few fresh vegetables and fruits, alcoholism, diet of the elderly

Pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor deficiency), gastric resection (gastrectomy), resection or diseases of the ileum (Crohn), fish tapeworm (diphyllobothriasis), bacterial overgrowth in “blind loop” syndrome
Metformin, proton pump inhibitors (long-term), nitrous oxide (anesthesia)
Methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin (act on dihydrofolate reductase or absorption)

blocks.text: Pernicious (Addison–Biermer) anemia

As a result of autoimmune atrophic gastritis, the gastric parietal cells die: autoantibodies against **parietal cells** and **Castle's intrinsic factor** are formed → intrinsic factor and hydrochloric acid are not produced (achlorhydria) → B12 is not absorbed. It occurs mainly after the age of 50–60; the risk of gastric cancer is increased.
Pathogenesis of megaloblastic anemia

items: DNA synthesis slows down while RNA and protein synthesis continue → **asynchrony of nuclear and cytoplasmic maturation** (the nucleus is “young”, the cytoplasm “mature”).
Large cells — **megaloblasts** — form in the bone marrow.
Most megaloblasts die in the bone marrow itself — **ineffective erythropoiesis** (intramedullary hemolysis); therefore indirect bilirubin and LDH rise.
The **megalocytes** released into the blood are large and saturated with hemoglobin, but fragile and short-lived.
Leukopoiesis and thrombopoiesis are also impaired — **pancytopenia**, hypersegmented neutrophils, large platelets.
All rapidly dividing cells (gastrointestinal epithelium) are affected — **Hunter's glossitis** (a smooth, “lacquered”, bright red tongue), dyspepsia.

blocks.text: **Blood picture:** hyperchromic (color index above 1.05, often 1.2–1.5) macrocytic (MCV above 100 fl) anemia; megalocytes (oval), megaloblasts; Howell–Jolly bodies, Cabot rings, basophilic stippling; aniso- and poikilocytosis; reticulocytes decreased (aregenerative); leukopenia, **hypersegmentation of neutrophils** (right nuclear shift), thrombocytopenia.

parts.text: **Funicular myelosis (subacute combined degeneration)** — a neurological complication specific to B12 deficiency: demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Signs: paresthesias in the legs, loss of deep (vibration and joint-position) sensation, ataxia, spastic paresis, memory impairment. Folic acid deficiency does not cause such neurological signs.

Treating a patient with B12 deficiency with folic acid alone is dangerous: blood values may partly improve, but the neurological disturbances worsen and become irreversible. In megaloblastic anemia, B12 and folate levels should be determined first, and folic acid alone should not be given until B12 deficiency has been ruled out.

blocks.text: **Aplastic anemia** — a sharp depression of the hematopoietic function of the bone marrow (hypoplasia or aplasia) with damage to stem cells. Causes: autoimmune (T lymphocytes damage the stem cells), drugs (chloramphenicol, cytostatics), benzene, radiation, viruses (hepatitis, parvovirus B19), hereditary (Fanconi anemia). Blood picture: pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), normochromic anemia, reticulocytes markedly decreased; the bone marrow is replaced by adipose tissue.

**Anemia of chronic disease** (anemia of inflammation) — in chronic infections, autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis) and tumors. Mechanism: under the action of IL-6, hepcidin increases → iron is “locked” in macrophages and its intestinal absorption decreases (functional iron deficiency); erythropoietin production and sensitivity to it decrease; erythrocyte lifespan is shortened. Blood picture: normo- or hypochromic anemia; serum iron decreased, but **ferritin normal or increased** (iron is present in the stores).
**Anemia in chronic kidney failure** — mainly due to reduced erythropoietin production; treatment — erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

blocks.title: Table 18.4. Comparative characteristics of deficiency anemias
head: Parameter
Iron deficiency anemia
B12 and folate deficiency anemia
Anemia of chronic disease
Aplastic anemia

blocks.text: Experiment 1: studying blood smears of patients with iron and folate (B12) deficiency anemias

items: Take stained smears from a healthy person and from patients with iron deficiency anemia and B12 (folate) deficiency anemia.
Under the immersion objective, assess the size (microcytes, megalocytes), staining (hypochromia, hyperchromia) and shape of the erythrocytes.
Find annulocytes, megaloblasts, Howell–Jolly bodies and Cabot rings.
Count the segments of the neutrophils (5 or more — hypersegmentation).
Draw the smears and write the distinguishing features in a table.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining hemoglobin concentration and calculating the color index

items: Determine the hemoglobin concentration in the patient's blood by the hemiglobincyanide method (see topic 17).
Determine the erythrocyte count (in a Goryaev chamber or on an automated analyzer).
Calculate the color index: (Hb, g/l × 3) / the first three digits of the erythrocyte count.
Calculate the mean corpuscular hemoglobin (pg) using the formula MCH = Hb (g/l) / erythrocytes (× 10^12^/l).
Assess the anemia as hypo-, normo- or hyperchromic.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting iron metabolism parameters

items: Assess serum iron (normal: 11.6–30.4 µmol/l in men, 8.9–30.4 µmol/l in women).
Assess ferritin (the main indicator of the body's iron stores; below 15–30 µg/l — stores exhausted).
Assess transferrin saturation with iron (normal 20–45 %; below 16 percent — iron deficiency).
Assess the total iron-binding capacity of serum (increased in iron deficiency).
Compare with markers of inflammation (C-reactive protein): ferritin, as an acute-phase protein, may rise in inflammation.
Distinguish true from functional iron deficiency and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: determining the cause of megaloblastic anemia

items: Confirm hyperchromic macrocytic anemia and hypersegmentation in the blood picture.
Determine serum B12 and folate levels.
Check for neurological signs (paresthesia, impaired deep sensation).
Clarify diet, alcohol, drugs and gastrointestinal surgery from the history.
In pernicious anemia, indicate the need to detect antibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor and atrophic gastritis on gastroscopy.
Write a conclusion.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 38-year-old woman has weakness, dizziness, hair loss and brittle nails; she craves chalk and likes the smell of acetone. Her periods last 8–9 days and are heavy. Blood test: Hb 78 g/l, erythrocytes 3.6 × 10^12^/l, MCV 68 fl, reticulocytes 0.8 %, serum iron 4.2 µmol/l, ferritin 6 µg/l.
cases.ask: What anemia is this? Calculate the color index. Explain the mechanism of the clinical signs.
cases.answer: Iron deficiency anemia due to chronic blood loss (heavy and prolonged periods — menorrhagia). Color index = (78 × 3) / 360 ≈ 0.65 — hypochromic; MCV 68 fl — microcytic; ferritin markedly decreased (stores exhausted), serum iron low; reticulocytes normal — hyporegenerative. Weakness and dizziness — the anemic syndrome (hypoxia). Hair loss, brittle nails and disturbed taste and smell (eating chalk, liking the smell of acetone) — the sideropenic syndrome: reduced activity of iron-containing enzymes in the tissues and impaired trophism of the epithelium and its derivatives. Treatment — iron preparations, plus identifying and eliminating the cause of the menorrhagia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old man has weakness, dyspnea, numbness in the legs and an unsteady gait. His tongue is smooth, bright red and burning. The skin is slightly yellowish. Blood test: Hb 70 g/l, erythrocytes 1.7 × 10^12^/l, MCV 118 fl, leukocytes 3.1 × 10^9^/l, platelets 110 × 10^9^/l, reticulocytes 0.2 %; megalocytes, Howell–Jolly bodies and hypersegmented neutrophils in the smear. Indirect bilirubin is raised. Antibodies to parietal cells are positive.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain the pathogenesis of the signs.
cases.answer: Pernicious (Addison–Biermer) anemia — absence of intrinsic factor and failure of B12 absorption due to autoimmune atrophic gastritis. Color index = (70 × 3) / 170 ≈ 1.24 — hyperchromic, macrocytic. In B12 deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired and erythropoiesis switches to the megaloblastic type; megaloblasts die in the bone marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) — indirect bilirubin rises and causes the yellowish skin; leuko- and thrombopoiesis are also impaired — pancytopenia, hypersegmentation of neutrophils. Hunter's glossitis — damage to the rapidly dividing epithelium of the tongue. Numbness in the legs and ataxia — funicular myelosis: accumulation of methylmalonyl-CoA and impaired myelin synthesis damage the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Treatment — lifelong parenteral (intramuscular) B12.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 55-year-old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years. Blood test: Hb 98 g/l, MCV 82 fl, serum iron 7 µmol/l, ferritin 240 µg/l, C-reactive protein raised.
cases.ask: What anemia is this? Why is serum iron low but ferritin high? Will iron preparations be effective?
cases.answer: Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation). In chronic inflammation, IL-6 increases hepcidin synthesis in the liver; hepcidin degrades ferroportin and stops the release of iron from macrophages and its absorption from the intestine. As a result, iron is “locked” in the stores (macrophages) — ferritin is high, but there is not enough iron in the blood for erythropoiesis — serum iron is low (functional iron deficiency). In addition, cytokines reduce erythropoietin production and sensitivity to it. Oral iron preparations are of little benefit because their absorption is blocked by hepcidin; the main treatment is to reduce the inflammatory activity (treat the underlying disease).

topics.title: Arrhythmias due to disturbances of cardiac automaticity and excitability

goals.text: To explain to the student the regulation of cardiovascular function, the properties and metabolism of the myocardium, the parameters of central hemodynamics, the main elements of the ECG and their origin, the classification of cardiac rhythm disturbances, and the causes, mechanisms and consequences of disturbances of automaticity and excitability (sinus tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmia, extrasystoles); to teach the student to record a normal ECG and to analyze the ECG in various disturbances of automaticity and excitability.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main properties of the myocardium (automaticity, excitability, conductivity, contractility) and the structure of the conduction system;
the parameters of central hemodynamics;
the origin, amplitude and duration of the ECG waves, segments and intervals;
the classification and mechanisms of arrhythmias (abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, re-entry);
the causes and ECG signs of sinus tachycardia, bradycardia and arrhythmia;
the types, causes, theories and ECG signs of extrasystoles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: record an ECG and calculate its main parameters (heart rate, intervals);
identify sinus rhythm;
identify disturbances of automaticity and extrasystoles on the ECG.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: At the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s: 1 mm (small square) = 0.04 s, 5 mm (large square) = 0.2 s. Heart rate = 60 / RR (in seconds) or 300 / the number of large squares between R waves. **Criteria of sinus rhythm:** a P wave before each QRS, P positive in lead II, constant PQ (0.12–0.20 s), equal RR intervals (difference below 10 percent), rate 60–90 beats/min.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: “Dangerous” signs of ventricular extrasystoles: multifocal, paired and grouped, early (“R on T”) extrasystoles, especially against the background of acute myocardial infarction — they indicate a risk of progression to ventricular fibrillation. The contraction that follows the prolonged pause after an extrasystole is stronger (Frank–Starling law) — the patient feels this as “the heart stopped and then beat hard”.

sections.title: 1. Properties of the myocardium and regulation of cardiac function

blocks.title: Table 19.1. Main properties of the myocardium
head: Property
Essence
Disturbance
rows: Ability to generate impulses without external stimulation (mainly in the sinus node)
Sinus tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmia, sick sinus syndrome, ectopic rhythms
Ability to be excited in response to a stimulus
Conduction of the impulse through the heart

blocks.title: Table 19.2. Centers of the conduction system
head: Center
Location
Rate of automaticity
rows: Right atrium, at the entry of the superior vena cava
Lower part of the interatrial septum
Third order — bundle branches of His and Purkinje fibers

blocks.text: Cardiac activity is regulated by **sympathetic** nerves (norepinephrine, beta1-receptors: heart rate, force, conductivity and excitability increase) and **parasympathetic** nerves (vagus nerve, acetylcholine: heart rate and AV conduction decrease); humoral factors (catecholamines, thyroid hormones, K+, Ca2+) also have an effect.

**Parameters of central hemodynamics:** stroke volume (60–80 ml), cardiac output (4.5–5.5 l/min) = stroke volume × heart rate, cardiac index (2.5–4.0 l/min/m^2^), total peripheral vascular resistance, central venous pressure (5–10 cm H2O). The myocardium obtains its energy mainly from aerobic oxidation of fatty acids; oxygen extraction is high even at rest (70–75 %), so increased demand is met mainly by increased coronary blood flow.

**Electrocardiography (ECG)** — a method of recording from the body surface the electrical potentials generated during cardiac excitation. There are 12 standard leads: 3 standard limb leads (I, II, III), 3 augmented leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and 6 chest leads (V1–V6).

blocks.label: Figure 19.1
blocks.caption: Normal sinus rhythm (schematic ECG)

blocks.title: Table 19.3. ECG elements and their normal values
head: Element
What it reflects
Normal
rows: 0.08–0.10 s, amplitude up to 2.5 mm; positive in lead II
Time for the impulse to pass from the atria to the ventricles
Shorter than 0.03 s, smaller than 1/4 of R
Fully excited state of the ventricles
On the isoelectric line (deviation of 0.5–1 mm is possible)
Depends on heart rate, usually 0.35–0.44 s

parts.text: At the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s: 1 mm (small square) = 0.04 s, 5 mm (large square) = 0.2 s. Heart rate = 60 / RR (in seconds) or 300 / the number of large squares between R waves. **Criteria of sinus rhythm:** a P wave before each QRS, P positive in lead II, constant PQ (0.12–0.20 s), equal RR intervals (difference below 10 percent), rate 60–90 beats/min.

blocks.text: **Arrhythmia** — a disturbance of the rate, regularity or source of cardiac excitation or of the sequence of impulse conduction.

blocks.title: Table 19.4. Classification of arrhythmias (by myocardial properties)
head: Group
Types
rows: Sinus tachycardia, sinus bradycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sick sinus syndrome
Escape (replacement) rhythms and complexes: atrial, AV junctional, idioventricular rhythms
Blocks (sinoatrial, intra-atrial, AV, bundle branch), pre-excitation syndromes (WPW)
Atrial and ventricular fibrillation and flutter (topic 20)

blocks.title: Table 19.5. Electrophysiological mechanisms of arrhythmias
head: Mechanism
Essence
Examples
rows: Change in the rate of diastolic depolarization in the sinus node or in an ectopic focus
Early or delayed afterdepolarizations (an “extra wave” after the preceding potential)
Glycoside toxicity, “torsades de pointes” tachycardia in long QT syndrome
The impulse is blocked in one pathway, returns through another pathway and re-excites a previously excited area; requires unidirectional block and slow conduction
Most extrasystoles and paroxysmal tachycardias, atrial flutter

blocks.text: Sinus tachycardia
An increase in the rate of impulses from the sinus node at rest above **90 (100) beats/min**.

**Causes:** physiological — physical exertion, excitement; pathological — fever (about 8–10 beats/min for every 1 °C), anemia, hypoxia, hypovolemia, hypotension, thyrotoxicosis, heart failure, myocarditis, pheochromocytoma, drugs (atropine, adrenomimetics, caffeine).
**Mechanism:** increased sympathetic or decreased parasympathetic influence — diastolic depolarization in the sinus node cells accelerates.
**ECG:** sinus rhythm preserved, RR intervals shortened, rate above 90.

blocks.label: Figure 19.2
blocks.caption: Sinus tachycardia

blocks.text: **Consequences:** diastole shortens → ventricular filling and coronary blood flow (which occurs mainly in diastole) decrease, myocardial oxygen demand increases → attacks of angina in patients prone to ischemia.
Sinus bradycardia
A decrease in the rate of sinus node impulses below **60 beats/min**.

**Causes:** physiological — in athletes (vagotonia), during sleep; pathological — increased vagal tone (raised intracranial pressure, obstructive jaundice — effect of bile acids), hypothyroidism, hypothermia, sick sinus syndrome, myocardial infarction (inferior wall), drugs (beta-blockers, cardiac glycosides, verapamil).
**ECG:** sinus rhythm, RR intervals prolonged, rate below 60.

blocks.label: Figure 19.3
blocks.caption: Sinus bradycardia

blocks.text: Sinus arrhythmia
**Irregular** discharge of impulses from the sinus node: the difference between RR intervals exceeds 0.1–0.15 s (or 10 percent).

items: **Respiratory arrhythmia** — the rate increases on inspiration and decreases on expiration (variation of vagal tone with the phases of respiration); physiological in children and adolescents.
**Non-respiratory arrhythmia** — organic myocardial changes, intoxications.

blocks.label: Figure 19.4
blocks.caption: Sinus arrhythmia

parts.text: **Sick sinus syndrome** — reduced automaticity resulting from organic damage to the sinus node (ischemia, fibrosis, cardiomyopathies): persistent bradycardia, sinoatrial blocks, sinus arrest, alternation of bradycardia with tachyarrhythmias (“tachy-brady syndrome”). During long pauses there are attacks of fainting due to cerebral ischemia (**Morgagni–Adams–Stokes**); treatment — a permanent pacemaker.

blocks.text: Escape (replacement) rhythms

When sinus node activity is depressed or impulses fail to be conducted, lower-order centers begin to generate impulses: AV junctional rhythm (40–60 beats/min, P inverted or merged with QRS), idioventricular rhythm (20–40 beats/min, wide deformed QRS). This is a protective (compensatory) mechanism — it prevents asystole.
**Extrasystole** — a premature (out-of-turn) contraction of the heart or part of it; the impulse arises from an ectopic focus (outside the sinus node).
Causes:

items: **functional** — excitement, smoking, strong tea and coffee, alcohol, autonomic dysfunction, gastrointestinal diseases (reflex);
**organic** — ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, myocarditis, cardiomyopathies, heart defects, arterial hypertension;
**toxic and electrolyte** — cardiac glycoside toxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, adrenomimetics, thyrotoxicosis.

blocks.text: **Theories and mechanisms of extrasystole:** re-entry of the excitation wave, increased automaticity of an ectopic focus, triggered activity (afterdepolarizations).
**Compensatory pause** — the prolonged interval after an extrasystole until the next normal contraction:

items: **full compensatory pause** — the sum of the RR intervals before and after the extrasystole equals two normal RR intervals; typical of ventricular extrasystoles (the sinus node is not “discharged” and its rhythm is not disturbed; the sinus impulse following the extrasystole reaches refractory ventricles);
**incomplete compensatory pause** — the sum is less than two RR intervals; typical of atrial and AV extrasystoles (the ectopic impulse also excites the sinus node and “resets” its cycle).

blocks.title: Table 19.6. ECG signs of extrasystoles
head: Feature
Atrial extrasystole
AV junctional extrasystole
Ventricular extrasystole
rows: Inverted P (before or after QRS) or absent
Directed opposite to the main deflection of QRS

blocks.label: Figure 19.5
blocks.caption: Atrial extrasystole

blocks.label: Figure 19.6
blocks.caption: Ventricular extrasystole

blocks.text: Types of extrasystole: **single**, **paired** (two in succession), **grouped** (three or more — “runs”, progressing to paroxysmal tachycardia); **allorhythmia** — regularly repeating: **bigeminy** (an extrasystole after every normal contraction), **trigeminy** (after every two); **monofocal** (from one focus) and **multifocal** (of different shapes, from different foci); early (“R on T” — falling on the T wave of the preceding contraction).

parts.text: “Dangerous” signs of ventricular extrasystoles: multifocal, paired and grouped, early (“R on T”) extrasystoles, especially against the background of acute myocardial infarction — they indicate a risk of progression to ventricular fibrillation. The contraction that follows the prolonged pause after an extrasystole is stronger (Frank–Starling law) — the patient feels this as “the heart stopped and then beat hard”.

blocks.text: **Hemodynamic consequences:** during an extrasystole the ventricles do not fill adequately with blood — the stroke volume is small, and the pulse wave may not be felt at the periphery (**pulse deficit**); frequent extrasystoles reduce cardiac output and coronary blood flow.

sections.title: 6. Experimental part: recording and analyzing the ECG

blocks.text: **Aim:** to record a normal ECG and analyze the ECGs of patients with disturbances of automaticity and excitability.
**Equipment:** electrocardiograph, electrodes, contact gel, calipers (measuring tool), a set of ECG samples of various arrhythmias.
ECG recording procedure

items: Lay the subject on their back, with relaxed muscles and calm breathing.
Moisten the electrode sites with gel.
Apply the limb electrodes: red — right arm, yellow — left arm, green — left leg, black (ground) — right leg.

Apply the chest electrodes: V1 — fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border; V2 — fourth space at the left sternal border; V4 — fifth space on the left midclavicular line; V3 — midway between V2 and V4; V5 — anterior axillary line at the level of V4; V6 — midaxillary line at the same level.
Check the calibration signal (1 mV = 10 mm) and the paper speed (25 or 50 mm/s).
Record all 12 leads; record lead II for longer (for rhythm analysis).

blocks.text: ECG analysis plan

items: Determine the rhythm: sinus or non-sinus, regular or irregular.
Calculate the heart rate.
Measure the duration of P, PQ, QRS and QT.
Determine the electrical axis of the heart.
Assess the shape of the P wave, QRS complex, ST segment and T wave.
Write a conclusion.

blocks.title: Table 19.7. Example of recording the analysis results
head: Parameter
ECG 1
ECG 2
ECG 3

skills.title: Skill: calculating heart rate from the ECG

items: Determine the paper speed (25 mm/s).
Measure the distance between two adjacent R waves in mm.
Multiply the distance by 0.04 to obtain RR in seconds.
Heart rate = 60 / RR.
If the rhythm is irregular, multiply the number of QRS complexes in a 6-second strip by 10.

skills.title: Skill: identifying an extrasystole on the ECG and determining its type

items: Find the premature complex (shortened RR).
Check whether there is a P wave before it and what its shape is.
Measure the width of the QRS: below 0.12 s — supraventricular, above — ventricular.
Assess the direction of the T wave.
Measure the compensatory pause: compare the sum of the RR intervals before and after the extrasystole with two normal RR intervals.
Write a conclusion about the number, sequence (bigeminy, pairs) and shape (monofocal or multifocal) of the extrasystoles.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 24-year-old woman has frequent palpitations, trembling hands, sweating and weight loss. Pulse 118 beats/min, regular. ECG: a positive P before each QRS, PQ 0.14 s, QRS 0.08 s, RR 0.51 s. Blood thyroid hormones are raised.
cases.ask: Analyze the ECG. What are the type and mechanism of the arrhythmia? What is the danger for the heart?
cases.answer: Heart rate = 60 / 0.51 ≈ 118 beats/min; a P before each QRS, normal PQ, narrow QRS — sinus rhythm. This is sinus tachycardia (a nomotopic disturbance of automaticity). The cause is thyrotoxicosis: thyroid hormones increase the number of beta-adrenoceptors in the sinus node cells and their sensitivity to catecholamines, and act directly on ion channels to accelerate diastolic depolarization; in addition, metabolism increases. In tachycardia diastole shortens, ventricular filling and coronary blood flow decrease, and myocardial oxygen demand increases; if prolonged, atrial fibrillation and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy may develop.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On day 2 of myocardial infarction, a 58-year-old man's cardiac monitor shows frequent premature wide QRS complexes: they have two different shapes, sometimes come in pairs, and some fall on the T wave of the preceding complex.
cases.ask: What arrhythmia is this? Why is it dangerous? What is the mechanism of its development?
cases.answer: Multifocal, paired and early (“R on T”) ventricular extrasystoles. In the ischemic myocardium of the infarct zone and its border, the membrane potential changes, conduction slows and refractoriness becomes uneven — conditions for re-entry are created; potassium leakage from damaged cells, increased catecholamines and reperfusion enhance triggered activity. Early extrasystoles falling into the relative refractory period of the ventricles (the “vulnerable phase”) can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Therefore the patient should be under monitor observation, electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) should be corrected and a defibrillator should be ready.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 72-year-old woman has had several attacks of sudden loss of consciousness, each lasting a few seconds and preceded by dizziness. 24-hour ECG monitoring revealed a heart rate of 38–42 beats/min, pauses of 4–5 seconds and episodes of atrial fibrillation between them.
cases.ask: What syndrome can be suspected? What is the mechanism of the fainting?
cases.answer: Sick sinus syndrome (the “tachy-brady” variant): as a result of organic damage to the sinus node (fibrosis in old age, ischemia), automaticity is reduced — persistent bradycardia and sinus arrest pauses, alternating with atrial tachyarrhythmia. During long pauses, if the escape centers do not start in time, cardiac output stops and cerebral ischemia develops — Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attacks (fainting). Treatment — implantation of a permanent pacemaker.

topics.title: Disturbances of cardiac conduction. Heart blocks. Atrial fibrillation

goals.text: To explain to the student the structure and function of the cardiac conduction system, the causes, mechanisms and ECG signs of conduction disturbances (sinoatrial, intra-atrial, atrioventricular and intraventricular blocks, pre-excitation syndromes), and the pathogenesis and consequences of atrial fibrillation (atrial fibrillation and flutter) and ventricular fibrillation; to teach the student to analyze the ECG in conduction disturbances and atrial fibrillation.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the parts of the conduction system and the sequence of impulse spread through the heart;
the causes and mechanisms of conduction disturbances;
the degrees and ECG signs of AV blocks;
the ECG signs of bundle branch block;
the nature of the pre-excitation (WPW) syndrome;
the mechanisms and hemodynamic consequences of atrial fibrillation and flutter and ventricular fibrillation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the degree of AV block by measuring the PQ interval on the ECG;
identify an intraventricular conduction disturbance by the width of the QRS;
distinguish atrial fibrillation from atrial flutter on the ECG.

sections.title: 1. The conduction system and impulse spread

blocks.text: The impulse arises in the sinus node and reaches the **AV node** through the atrial myocardium and internodal pathways. In the AV node the impulse is physiologically **delayed** (about 0.1 s) — this is necessary so that atrial contraction is completed and the ventricles fill with blood. The impulse then spreads rapidly to the ventricular myocardium through the **bundle of His**, its right and left bundle branches (the left branch divides into anterior and posterior fascicles) and the **Purkinje fibers**.
**Conduction disturbances** are of two kinds:

items: **slowing or arrest (block)** — the impulse is delayed in some part of the conduction system or does not pass at all;
**acceleration** — the impulse reaches the ventricles prematurely via accessory (abnormal) pathways (pre-excitation syndromes).

blocks.text: Causes of conduction disturbances:

items: organic — ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction, myocarditis (rheumatic, diphtheritic), cardiosclerosis, cardiomyopathies, heart defects, idiopathic fibrosis of the conduction system (Lenègre and Lev diseases), surgical injuries;
functional — a sharp increase in vagal tone;
toxic and drug-induced — cardiac glycosides, beta-blockers, verapamil, antiarrhythmic drugs;
electrolyte — hyperkalemia.

blocks.text: **Mechanism:** reduction of the resting potential of the cells (ischemia, hyperkalemia) leading to inactivation of sodium channels and reduced rate of rise and amplitude of the action potential; prolongation of the refractory period; replacement of conducting fibers by fibrosis.

blocks.title: Table 20.1. Classification of heart blocks
head: By location
By degree
rows: Second degree — some impulses are not conducted (incomplete block)
Third degree — no impulses are conducted (complete block)
Intraventricular block (bundle branches and fascicles of His)

blocks.text: Sinoatrial block

The impulse generated in the sinus node does not pass to the atria. In second-degree sinoatrial block the ECG shows **dropping of the whole P–QRS–T complex**, and the resulting pause equals (or is close to) twice the preceding RR.
First-degree AV block
Conduction of the impulse from the atria to the ventricles is slowed, but all impulses are conducted.
**ECG:** PQ interval **longer than 0.20 s**, a QRS follows every P. It has almost no effect on hemodynamics.

blocks.label: Figure 20.1
blocks.caption: First-degree AV block

blocks.text: Second-degree AV block
Some atrial impulses are not conducted to the ventricles.

items: **Mobitz type I (Samoilov–Wenckebach periods)** — the PQ interval gradually lengthens with each cycle, then one QRS is dropped (P present, no QRS); the cycle then starts again with a short PQ. Usually at the level of the AV node; prognosis relatively good (vagotonia, glycosides, inferior wall infarction).

blocks.label: Figure 20.2
blocks.caption: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I

items: **Mobitz type II** — the PQ interval is constant (normal or prolonged), but after some P waves the QRS complex is suddenly dropped; the ratio may be 2:1 or 3:1. Usually at or below the bundle of His — high risk of progression to third-degree block.

blocks.label: Figure 20.3
blocks.caption: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II

blocks.text: Third-degree (complete) AV block
Not a single impulse is conducted from the atria to the ventricles. The atria are excited from the sinus node, and the ventricles from their own escape center — **atrioventricular dissociation**.

**ECG:** P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated to each other; the P waves occur at their own rate (60–80), the QRS complexes slowly (40–60 with a narrow QRS if from the AV junction; 20–40 with a wide deformed QRS if from the ventricles).

blocks.label: Figure 20.4
blocks.caption: Third-degree (complete) AV block

parts.text: When complete AV block appears, the ventricular escape center starts a few seconds late (the “preautomatic pause”). During this time the brain is not supplied with blood — a **Morgagni–Adams–Stokes** attack: dizziness, loss of consciousness, pallor, then convulsions. Persistent bradycardia (30–40 beats/min) reduces cardiac output and leads to heart failure. Treatment — a pacemaker.

blocks.text: Bundle branch block

If the impulse is not conducted along one bundle branch, the ventricle on that side receives the excitation slowly through the myocardium from the other ventricle — ventricular depolarization is prolonged and becomes asynchronous.

blocks.title: Table 20.3. ECG signs of complete bundle branch block
head: Feature
Right bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block
rows: Wide R with a notched peak, no Q
May also occur in healthy people; pulmonary embolism, right ventricular strain
Almost always organic disease (infarction, hypertension, aortic defect)

parts.text: A new left bundle branch block in the setting of acute coronary syndrome is regarded as a sign as dangerous as myocardial infarction; left bundle branch block “masks” the signs of infarction on the ECG.

blocks.text: Pre-excitation syndrome (Wolff–Parkinson–White, WPW)

There is an accessory conducting pathway (the **Kent bundle**) between the atria and ventricles. The impulse passes through this pathway without the physiological delay of the AV node and excites part of the ventricles early.
**ECG:** shortened PQ (below 0.12 s), a **delta wave** (sloping upstroke) at the beginning of the QRS, widened QRS, discordant ST–T changes.

**Significance:** the accessory pathway and the AV node form a closed loop — attacks of paroxysmal tachycardia by **re-entry**; if atrial fibrillation develops, impulses can pass very rapidly to the ventricles via the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation.

**Atrial fibrillation** (“ciliary arrhythmia”) — uncoordinated, very rapid (350–700 per minute) excitation of the atria; the atria do not contract effectively, and the ventricles contract irregularly. Two types are distinguished: **atrial fibrillation** and **atrial flutter**.

**Causes:** mitral defects (especially mitral stenosis — dilation of the left atrium), ischemic heart disease, arterial hypertension, thyrotoxicosis, cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, alcohol intoxication (“holiday heart”), chronic lung diseases, old age.
Mechanism:

items: many small **re-entry** circuits in the atrial myocardium (the “multiple wavelet” theory) — excitation waves circulate chaotically in a dilated and fibrosed atrium;
rapid impulses from **ectopic foci** at the mouths of the pulmonary veins (trigger);
the AV node acts as a “filter” — it conducts only some of the impulses to the ventricles, which is why the ventricular rhythm is irregular.

blocks.text: **ECG:** no P waves; instead, small irregular **f waves** on the isoelectric line, completely irregular RR intervals, QRS usually narrow.

blocks.label: Figure 20.5
blocks.caption: Atrial fibrillation

blocks.text: **Atrial flutter** — regular, rapid (250–350 per minute) excitation of the atria; mainly a single large re-entry circuit in the right atrium (macro re-entry). On the ECG there are regular “**sawtooth**” F waves, usually conducted to the ventricles in a 2:1, 3:1 or 4:1 ratio.

blocks.label: Figure 20.6
blocks.caption: Atrial flutter with 4:1 conduction

blocks.title: Table 20.4. Distinguishing atrial fibrillation from atrial flutter
head: Feature
Fibrillation
Flutter
rows: Often regular (if the ratio is constant)
Many small re-entry circuits, ectopic foci

blocks.text: Consequences of atrial fibrillation

items: **Loss of atrial systole** — ventricular filling decreases by about 20–30 percent; cardiac output falls significantly, especially in mitral stenosis and myocardial hypertrophy.
**Tachysystole** — diastole shortens, the ventricles do not fill adequately, coronary blood flow decreases and myocardial oxygen demand increases; if prolonged — heart failure.
**Pulse deficit** — contractions with a small stroke volume do not produce a pulse wave at the periphery: the number of contractions at the cardiac apex exceeds the radial pulse.

**Thromboembolism** — blood stagnates in the non-contracting atrium (especially the left atrial appendage) and a thrombus forms; a fragment of the thrombus enters the systemic circulation and causes **ischemic stroke** and embolism of the renal, intestinal and leg arteries.

parts.text: Consequences of atrial fibrillation — “**STEP**”: **S**ystole (atrial) loss, **T**achysystole, **E**mbolism (thrombus), **P**ulse deficit.

blocks.text: Ventricular fibrillation and flutter

**Ventricular fibrillation** — chaotic, uncoordinated excitation and contraction of individual fibers of the ventricular myocardium; the pumping function of the heart stops — this is the most common mechanism of **clinical death**. The ECG shows chaotic waves of varying shape and amplitude, with no distinguishable QRS or T. **Ventricular flutter** — regular, high-amplitude “sinusoidal” waves (200–300 per minute), which quickly turn into fibrillation.
**Causes:** acute myocardial infarction and ischemia, electric shock, hyper- and hypokalemia, glycoside toxicity, long QT syndrome, hypothermia, severe hypoxia.

**Care:** immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and **electrical defibrillation** — a strong electrical impulse depolarizes all myocardial cells simultaneously, after which the sinus node may restore the rhythm.
Stannius ligatures (on the frog heart)
**Aim:** to demonstrate the hierarchy of the centers of automaticity and the consequences of arrested impulse conduction.

items: Immobilize the frog, open the chest and leave the heart exposed; count the heart contractions.

**First ligature** — tie a thread at the border between the sinus venosus and the atria: the sinus venosus continues to contract at its previous rhythm, the atria and ventricle stop temporarily, then begin to contract at a slower rhythm (automaticity of the AV center).
**Second ligature** — tie a thread at the border between the atria and the ventricle (tightening it stimulates the AV region): the ventricle begins to contract at its own rhythm.
**Third ligature** — separate the lower third of the ventricle: the apical part does not contract (no center of automaticity), but it responds if stimulated.
At each stage, record the contraction rate of each part in a table and draw a conclusion.

blocks.text: Analyzing ECG samples
On the ECGs provided, measure the PQ interval, the P to QRS ratio, the QRS width and the regularity of RR, and determine the type of conduction disturbance.

Simultaneously count the contractions at the cardiac apex (auscultation) and the radial pulse in the patient for 1 minute.
Pulse deficit = heart rate – pulse rate.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 66-year-old man has had several sudden losses of consciousness; when he fell his face turned pale, then convulsions occurred, and he came round after 20–30 seconds. Pulse 34 beats/min, regular. ECG: P waves 76 per minute, QRS 34 per minute, wide (0.14 s), no constant relationship between P and QRS.
cases.ask: What is the ECG conclusion? Explain the mechanism of the fainting attacks. What treatment is needed?
cases.answer: Third-degree (complete) AV block; the escape rhythm is ventricular (wide QRS, 34 beats/min — idioventricular rhythm). The atria are excited by the sinus node and the ventricles independently by their own center (AV dissociation). When the block appears or deepens, the ventricular center starts a few seconds late; during this time cardiac output stops and cerebral ischemia develops — Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attacks (loss of consciousness, then hypoxic convulsions). Persistent bradycardia reduces cardiac output and leads to heart failure. Treatment — a permanent pacemaker.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old woman has had mitral stenosis for many years. Over the last month irregular heartbeat and dyspnea have increased. Suddenly weakness of the left arm and leg and a speech disturbance appeared. Heart rate 118 beats/min, radial pulse 92 beats/min. ECG: no P, small irregular waves, RR intervals varying.
cases.ask: What arrhythmia is this? Calculate the pulse deficit and explain its mechanism. What are the neurological signs related to?
cases.answer: Atrial fibrillation (tachysystolic form). In mitral stenosis the left atrium dilates under pressure and becomes fibrotic — a substrate for many re-entry circuits is formed. Pulse deficit = 118 – 92 = 26: in contractions following a short diastole the ventricles do not fill adequately, the stroke volume is small and the pulse wave does not reach the wrist. Because the atrium does not contract effectively, blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage and a thrombus forms; a fragment of the thrombus has entered the right middle cerebral artery and caused an ischemic stroke (left-sided hemiparesis, speech disturbance) — a cardioembolic stroke. Such patients need anticoagulant prophylaxis and rhythm or rate control.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 20-year-old student has episodes of severe palpitations that start and end suddenly. ECG between attacks: PQ 0.10 s, a sloping upstroke at the beginning of the QRS, QRS 0.12 s.
cases.ask: What syndrome is this? What is the mechanism of the attacks? What dangerous complication may occur?
cases.answer: Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome: the impulse passes to the ventricles via an accessory pathway (the Kent bundle) without the delay of the AV node — shortened PQ, delta wave and wide QRS. The accessory pathway and the AV node form a closed loop — attacks of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia develop by the re-entry mechanism. If atrial fibrillation develops, very rapid impulses can pass to the ventricles via the accessory pathway (without the AV node “filter”) and lead to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. Radical treatment — catheter ablation of the accessory pathway.

topics.title: Typical forms of cardiovascular dysfunction. Compensatory mechanisms (seminar)

goals.text: To explain to the student the typical forms of cardiovascular dysfunction — heart failure, heart defects, coronary insufficiency, arterial hypertension and hypotension, pericardial pathology — their causes, hemodynamic changes, cardiac and extracardiac compensatory mechanisms and the development of decompensation; to teach the student to apply this knowledge to clinical cases.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition and classification of circulatory failure;
the causes (overload, myocardial damage, impaired diastolic filling) and pathogenesis of heart failure;
the cardiac (rapid and long-term) and extracardiac compensatory mechanisms of the heart;
the stages of myocardial hypertrophy and the features of the hypertrophied heart;
the hemodynamic changes in heart defects;
the pathogenesis of coronary insufficiency, myocardial infarction and arterial hypertension.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: explain the signs of heart failure in relation to their pathogenesis;
depict the hemodynamic changes in heart defects as a diagram;
distinguish signs of compensation and decompensation in clinical cases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The hypertrophied myocardium is “imperfect” — **unbalanced growth**: the mass of cardiomyocytes increases, but the number of capillaries, nerve endings, mitochondria and the sarcoplasmic reticulum lag behind the growth of the myocardium. As a result the diffusion distance lengthens (relative coronary insufficiency), energy supply and calcium handling are impaired, the rates of contraction and relaxation decrease and fibrosis develops. This is why, in the long term, hypertrophy leads to decompensation and arrhythmias.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Stenosis is like “**a queue in front of a narrow door**”: the load falls on the chamber in front of the door (pressure). Insufficiency is like “**guests who keep coming back**”: both chambers receive an excess volume (volume).

blocks.text: **Circulatory failure** — a state in which the cardiovascular system is unable to supply tissues and organs with blood in accordance with their needs. It develops for cardiac, vascular or mixed reasons.

**Heart failure** — a clinical syndrome in which, because of impaired pumping function of the heart, cardiac output cannot meet the needs of the tissues, or can do so only at the cost of increased ventricular filling pressure.

blocks.text: Cardiac compensatory mechanisms
Rapid (emergency) mechanisms:

items: **Heterometric mechanism (Frank–Starling law)** — if myocardial fibers are stretched more in diastole (increased preload), the next contraction is stronger. It is effective up to a certain limit; with excessive stretching (myogenic dilation) the force of contraction decreases.
**Homeometric mechanism (Anrep phenomenon)** — without a change in fiber length, the force of contraction gradually increases when aortic resistance rises (through greater release of calcium ions).

**Tachycardia** — resulting from sympathetic influence and the Bainbridge reflex (stretching of the venae cavae and right atrium). If the rate rises excessively, diastole shortens, filling and coronary blood flow decrease, and the effect is lost.
**Inotropic effect** — catecholamines increase myocardial contractility.

blocks.text: **Long-term mechanism — myocardial hypertrophy.** With constant overload, cardiomyocyte size (hypertrophy) and heart mass increase; this normalizes the work and wall stress per unit mass.

items: **Concentric hypertrophy** — with pressure overload (aortic stenosis, hypertension): the wall thickens, the cavity is unchanged or smaller (sarcomeres are added in parallel).
**Eccentric hypertrophy** — with volume overload (valvular insufficiency): the cavity dilates and the wall thickens relatively (sarcomeres are added in series).

blocks.label: Figure 21.1
blocks.caption: Stages of compensatory myocardial hypertrophy (according to F. Z. Meerson)

parts.text: The hypertrophied myocardium is “imperfect” — **unbalanced growth**: the mass of cardiomyocytes increases, but the number of capillaries, nerve endings, mitochondria and the sarcoplasmic reticulum lag behind the growth of the myocardium. As a result the diffusion distance lengthens (relative coronary insufficiency), energy supply and calcium handling are impaired, the rates of contraction and relaxation decrease and fibrosis develops. This is why, in the long term, hypertrophy leads to decompensation and arrhythmias.

blocks.text: **Cardiac reserve mechanisms of compensation** — increases in heart rate, stroke volume and oxygen extraction; athletes show physiological hypertrophy (balanced growth).
Extracardiac compensatory mechanisms

items: activation of the **sympathoadrenal system** — tachycardia, inotropic effect, constriction of arterioles (maintaining pressure), increased venous tone (increasing venous return), redistribution of blood in favor of vital organs;
**renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system** — vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, increased blood volume;
**antidiuretic hormone** — water retention;

**natriuretic peptides** (atrial and brain natriuretic peptides) — released from the stretched atria and ventricles, they enhance natriuresis and vasodilation (a counter-regulatory system; their blood level is used in the diagnosis of heart failure);
**increased erythropoiesis** (due to hypoxia), increased oxygen extraction in the tissues, increased anaerobic glycolysis.

blocks.label: Figure 21.2
blocks.caption: Neurohumoral activation and the vicious circle in heart failure

blocks.text: At first, neurohumoral mechanisms maintain blood pressure and perfusion of vital organs, but with prolonged activation they increase preload and afterload on the heart and have a direct harmful effect on the myocardium (remodeling, fibrosis, apoptosis) — a **vicious circle** forms. This is why the basis of treatment of chronic heart failure is drugs that block these systems (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists).
**Decompensation** — exhaustion of the compensatory mechanisms, so that the heart can no longer meet the needs of the tissues.

blocks.title: Table 21.3. Signs of left and right ventricular failure
head: Type of sign
Left ventricular failure
Right ventricular failure
rows: Dyspnea, orthopnea, nocturnal attacks of suffocation (cardiac asthma), moist rales in the lungs, pulmonary edema
Distended neck veins, enlarged liver, leg edema, ascites, raised central venous pressure
Increased hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary capillaries → interstitial and alveolar edema
Increased venous pressure → fluid moves into tissues, hepatic congestion
Weakness, fatigue, acrocyanosis, reduced renal perfusion (oliguria), cerebral hypoperfusion
Less blood reaches the pulmonary circulation — the preload on the left ventricle decreases

parts.text: **Orthopnea** — the patient's dyspnea increases when lying down and he is forced to sit up: in the lying position more blood returns to the heart from the legs and abdominal cavity, the weak left ventricle cannot pump it, and pulmonary congestion increases. **Acrocyanosis** — increased oxygen extraction at the periphery due to slowed blood flow, with more reduced hemoglobin.

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis of edema in chronic heart failure:** increased venous pressure (hydrostatic factor), reduced renal perfusion with RAAS activation and sodium and water retention, increased ADH, reduced albumin synthesis due to hepatic congestion (oncotic factor), impaired lymph flow. Edema first appears in the dependent parts (legs, ankles) and increases in the evening (topic 9).

**Heart defect** — a permanent change in the structure of the heart valves, septa or great vessels that leads to disturbed blood flow. Defects are **congenital** (atrial and ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy of Fallot) and **acquired** (mainly rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis, atherosclerosis, degenerative changes).
Two types of valvular defect:

items: **stenosis (narrowing)** — the orifice narrows and resistance to blood flow increases → the preceding chamber is overloaded **by pressure** (concentric hypertrophy);
**insufficiency** — the cusps do not close completely and part of the blood flows back (regurgitation) → the receiving chambers are overloaded **by volume** (eccentric hypertrophy and dilation).
