rows: Passage of blood from the left atrium to the left ventricle is impeded
Left atrium (hypertrophy, dilation), then the right ventricle
Pulmonary congestion, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular failure; atrial fibrillation
In systole blood returns from the left ventricle to the left atrium
Left ventricle and left atrium (by volume, eccentric hypertrophy)
Ejection from the left ventricle into the aorta is impeded
Left ventricle (concentric hypertrophy) — compensated for a long time
Angina, fainting (on exertion), left ventricular failure
In diastole blood returns from the aorta to the left ventricle
Left ventricle (by volume, eccentric hypertrophy — the largest heart, “cor bovinum”)
Diastolic pressure falls — coronary perfusion decreases; left ventricular failure
In systole blood returns from the right ventricle to the right atrium

parts.text: Stenosis is like “**a queue in front of a narrow door**”: the load falls on the chamber in front of the door (pressure). Insufficiency is like “**guests who keep coming back**”: both chambers receive an excess volume (volume).

blocks.text: Peripheral signs in **aortic insufficiency**: large pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic), a “quick and high” pulse, pulsation of the carotid arteries, head bobbing (de Musset sign).
**Coronary insufficiency** — a mismatch between the oxygen demand of the myocardium and the oxygen delivered by coronary blood flow.
Causes:

items: reduced coronary blood flow — atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries (the main cause), spasm, thrombosis, embolism, fall in diastolic pressure (aortic insufficiency, hypotension), shortening of diastole in tachycardia;
increased myocardial oxygen demand — physical and emotional stress (catecholamines), hypertrophy, tachycardia, thyrotoxicosis;
reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood — anemia, hypoxemia, carbon monoxide poisoning.

blocks.text: **Consequences of myocardial ischemia:** within seconds aerobic oxidation stops and is replaced by anaerobic glycolysis, lactate accumulates, ATP falls — contractility decreases; ion pumps fail, intracellular Na+ and Ca2+ increase and K+ leaves — electrical instability and arrhythmias; after 20–40 minutes irreversible injury — **necrosis (infarction)**. Pain arises from the action of ischemic metabolites (adenosine, lactate, bradykinin, K+).

blocks.title: Table 21.5. Main complications of myocardial infarction
head: Complication
Mechanism
rows: Re-entry and triggered activity at the border of the ischemic and necrotic zones
Acute left ventricular failure, pulmonary edema
Death of more than 40 percent of the left ventricular myocardium
Replacement of the necrotic zone by connective tissue and its bulging
Fever, leukocytosis, raised ESR, raised cardiac-specific markers (troponins, CK-MB)

blocks.text: **Arterial hypertension** — a persistent arterial pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher. Arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.

items: **Primary (essential) hypertension** — 90–95 percent of cases; hereditary predisposition, high salt intake, stress, obesity, insulin resistance, reduced renal sodium excretion, increased sympathetic and RAAS activity, endothelial dysfunction (decreased NO, increased endothelin).

**Secondary (symptomatic) hypertension** — renal (glomerulonephritis, renal artery stenosis — renovascular), endocrine (primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis), hemodynamic (coarctation of the aorta), neurogenic, drug-induced.

blocks.text: **Target organ damage:** heart (left ventricular hypertrophy, ischemic heart disease, heart failure), brain (stroke, encephalopathy), kidney (nephrosclerosis), retina (retinopathy), vessels (atherosclerosis, aortic aneurysm).

**Arterial hypotension** — pressure below 100/60 (95/60 in women) mm Hg: physiological (athletes), acute (shock, collapse, blood loss), chronic (adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, neurocirculatory dystonia), **orthostatic** (a sharp fall in pressure on standing — autonomic nervous system disorders, hypovolemia, drugs).

**Collapse** — acute vascular insufficiency resulting from an acute fall in vascular tone and a decrease in circulating blood volume: arterial and venous pressure fall, with hypoxia of the brain, heart and other organs.

**Pericardial tamponade** — rapid accumulation of fluid (blood, exudate) in the pericardial cavity, compressing the heart. The ventricles cannot expand in diastole — filling and stroke volume decrease sharply and venous pressure rises. **Beck's triad:** arterial hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds. **Pulsus paradoxus** — a fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration. Care — emergency pericardiocentesis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man has had arterial hypertension for 15 years without regular treatment. Over the last year he has had dyspnea when walking, and at night he wakes up suffocating and has to sit up. On examination: moist rales in the lower parts of the lungs, BP 170/105 mm Hg. Echocardiography: left ventricular wall thickened, cavity dilated, ejection fraction 35 %.
cases.ask: What pathological condition has developed? By what mechanism was compensation achieved and why did decompensation develop? Explain the pathogenesis of the signs.
cases.answer: Chronic left ventricular (systolic) failure resulting from many years of arterial hypertension. The left ventricle was overloaded by pressure and was compensated for a long time by concentric hypertrophy. In the hypertrophied myocardium the capillaries, mitochondria and innervation lagged behind, and relative coronary insufficiency and fibrosis developed; in addition, prolonged activation of RAAS and the sympathetic system enhanced remodeling — the stage of exhaustion: the ventricle has dilated and its contractility has fallen. The weak left ventricle cannot pump the blood out — congestion in the pulmonary circulation: dyspnea, moist rales in the lungs; when lying down venous return increases and congestion worsens — orthopnea and nocturnal attacks of suffocation (cardiac asthma).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 34-year-old woman had rheumatic fever in childhood. She has dyspnea on exertion, cough and sometimes blood-streaked sputum. On her face there is a “mitral flush” (bluish-red cheeks), and her heart beats irregularly. Leg edema, liver enlarged by 4 cm.
cases.ask: Which defect can be suspected? Explain the sequence of hemodynamic changes.
cases.answer: Rheumatic mitral stenosis. The passage of blood from the left atrium to the left ventricle is impeded — the left atrium, overloaded by pressure, has hypertrophied and dilated (the dilated atrium is a substrate for atrial fibrillation, which is why the heart beats irregularly). Because the left atrium is weak, it cannot compensate for long — the pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary veins: pulmonary congestion (dyspnea, cough), rupture of capillaries (hemoptysis). Reflex spasm of the pulmonary arterioles (Kitaev reflex) increases pulmonary hypertension — the right ventricle, overloaded by pressure, hypertrophies and then decompensates: congestion in the systemic circulation (enlarged liver, leg edema). The left ventricle, for its part, does not receive enough blood — cardiac output is reduced.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old man was brought in after a car accident with a chest injury. His condition is deteriorating: BP 75/50 mm Hg, pulse 130 beats/min and weak, neck veins distended, heart sounds very muffled, the pulse almost disappears on inspiration.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain the mechanism of the hemodynamic disturbance. What care is needed?
cases.answer: Acute pericardial tamponade due to hemopericardium. Blood accumulates rapidly in the pericardial cavity and compresses the heart — the ventricles cannot expand in diastole (impaired diastolic filling), stroke volume and cardiac output fall sharply — hypotension, compensatory tachycardia. Venous blood cannot return to the heart — the neck veins are distended and central venous pressure rises; the fluid damps the sound — muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). On inspiration the right ventricle fills more and pushes the interventricular septum to the left, further reducing left ventricular filling — pulsus paradoxus. Emergency care — pericardiocentesis (pericardial puncture) and surgical control of the source of bleeding.

Neurohumoral activation increases the load and damages the myocardium
Pulmonary congestion: dyspnea, orthopnea, cardiac asthma

Left atrium → pulmonary hypertension → right ventricle
“Cor bovinum”, large pulse pressure

topics.title: Pathophysiology of the respiratory system. Hypoxia and its types

goals.text: To explain to the student the functions of the external respiration system, the definition, types and mechanisms of respiratory failure (disturbances of ventilation, diffusion, perfusion and ventilation–perfusion relationships), disturbances of respiratory regulation and pathological types of breathing, and the etiology, types, mechanisms of development and adaptive and compensatory reactions of hypoxia; to teach the student to assess external respiration parameters and to determine the type of hypoxia.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main parameters of external respiration and their normal values;
the definition, classification and stages of respiratory failure;
the causes of and difference between obstructive and restrictive ventilatory disorders;
the mechanisms of diffusion and perfusion disturbances and ventilation–perfusion mismatch;
the pathological types of breathing and their causes;
the classification of hypoxia, the changes in blood gases in each type, the adaptive mechanisms and the consequences.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the type of ventilatory disorder from spirogram parameters;
determine the type of hypoxia from blood gases;
distinguish the pathological types of breathing.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **K**ussmaul — **K**etoacidosis (“blowing off” acid with deep breaths). **C**heyne–Stokes — **C**rescendo–decrescendo cycles (deepening and becoming shallow, then a pause). **B**iot — **B**ursts (equal breaths separated by long pauses).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Hypoxic vasoconstriction (**Euler–Liljestrand reflex**) — the arterioles constrict in a poorly ventilated part of the lung, and blood is directed to well-ventilated parts. This is a protective reaction that normalizes V/Q, but in chronic hypoxia of the whole lung (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, high altitude) it leads to **pulmonary hypertension** and right ventricular hypertrophy — **cor pulmonale**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The doses and animal species used in the experiments follow the department's methodological guidelines; bioethics rules are observed when working with animals.

blocks.text: **External respiration** — gas exchange between atmospheric air and the blood of the pulmonary capillaries. It consists of three processes: **ventilation** (movement of air into and out of the alveoli), **diffusion** (passage of gases across the alveolar–capillary membrane) and **perfusion** (blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries).

blocks.title: Table 22.1. Main parameters of external respiration
head: Parameter
Normal value
rows: 3.5–5 l in men, 3–3.5 l in women (more than 80 percent of the predicted value)
Forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1)
More than 80 percent of the predicted value

blocks.text: **Respiratory failure** — a state in which the external respiration system cannot maintain the normal blood gas composition, or maintains it only through the strain of compensatory mechanisms. The criterion is arterial pO2 below 60 mm Hg and (or) pCO2 above 45–50 mm Hg.

blocks.title: Table 22.2. Classification of respiratory failure
head: Criterion
Types
rows: Hypoxemic (type I — low pO2, normal or low pCO2), hypercapnic (type II — low pO2, high pCO2)
Latent (only on exertion), compensated (dyspnea at rest, blood gases normal), decompensated (hypoxemia and hypercapnia even at rest)

blocks.text: **Dyspnea** — a change in the rate, depth and rhythm of breathing accompanied by difficulty breathing and a sensation of air hunger. **Inspiratory** dyspnea (difficulty breathing in — narrowing of the upper airways, pulmonary edema), **expiratory** dyspnea (difficulty breathing out — bronchial asthma, emphysema), **mixed**.
Obstructive type
Impaired airway patency — resistance to air flow increases.

**Causes:** bronchospasm (bronchial asthma), swelling and inflammation of the mucosa, accumulation of sputum in the bronchi (chronic bronchitis), external compression of the bronchial wall, early closure of small bronchi on expiration in emphysema (reduced elastic recoil), obstruction of the upper airways by a foreign body, edema, tumor or laryngospasm.
**Spirogram:** FEV1 and the **Tiffeneau index decreased** (below 70 percent), VC normal or slightly decreased, residual volume increased.
Restrictive type
The ability of the lungs to expand is limited.
Causes:

items: extrapulmonary — fluid (hydrothorax) or air (pneumothorax) in the pleural cavity, pleural adhesions, chest deformities (kyphoscoliosis), paralysis of the respiratory muscles (poliomyelitis, myasthenia), obesity, increased intra-abdominal pressure;
intrapulmonary — pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, surfactant deficiency, lung resection.

blocks.text: **Spirogram: VC decreased**, FEV1 also decreased, but the Tiffeneau index normal or increased.

blocks.title: Table 22.3. Distinguishing obstructive and restrictive disorders
head: Parameter
Obstructive
Restrictive

blocks.text: Disturbances of respiratory regulation

When respiratory center function is impaired (brain trauma, stroke, tumors, encephalitis, poisoning with morphine and barbiturates, deep hypoxia, uremia, ketoacidosis), alveolar hypoventilation and pathological types of breathing are observed. When the excitability of the center increases (hysteria, pain, fever, metabolic acidosis) — hyperventilation and hypocapnia.

blocks.label: Figure 22.1
blocks.caption: Pathological types of breathing (schematic pneumograms)

blocks.title: Table 22.4. Pathological types of breathing
head: Type
Description
Causes and mechanism
rows: Fever, pain, pneumonia, pulmonary edema (stimulation of stretch receptors)
Inhibition of the respiratory center (raised intracranial pressure, narcotic substances), stenosis of the upper airways
Metabolic acidosis (diabetic ketoacidosis, uremia): H+ ions stimulate chemoreceptors, CO2 elimination increases
The depth of breathing gradually increases, then decreases, followed by apnea; this repeats

Reduced sensitivity of the respiratory center to CO2 (impaired cerebral circulation, heart failure, intoxications, elderly people during sleep): during apnea CO2 accumulates and stimulates the center; during hyperventilation CO2 falls and the center is inhibited again
Breaths of equal depth separated by long apneic pauses
Organic damage to the respiratory center (meningitis, encephalitis, brain trauma) — a more serious prognosis
Terminal state: the last activity of the bulbar centers

parts.text: **K**ussmaul — **K**etoacidosis (“blowing off” acid with deep breaths). **C**heyne–Stokes — **C**rescendo–decrescendo cycles (deepening and becoming shallow, then a pause). **B**iot — **B**ursts (equal breaths separated by long pauses).

blocks.text: Disturbance of diffusion

Passage of gases across the alveolar–capillary membrane is impeded. According to Fick's law, diffusion is directly proportional to the membrane area and the gas pressure difference and inversely proportional to the membrane thickness.

**Causes:** thickening of the membrane (interstitial pulmonary edema, pulmonary fibrosis, pneumoconioses, alveolitis), reduction of the diffusion area (emphysema, lung resection, atelectasis), too rapid passage of blood through the capillary (physical exertion).

**Feature:** CO2 crosses the membrane about 20 times more easily than O2 — which is why in diffusion disturbances **hypoxemia** develops first, while pCO2 remains normal for a long time or falls because of hyperventilation.
Disturbance of perfusion
Reduced blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries: pulmonary thromboembolism, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, shock, right-to-left shunts in congenital defects.
Disturbance of the ventilation–perfusion relationship
Normally the ratio of alveolar ventilation to blood flow (V/Q) is about **0.8–1.0**.

items: **Decreased V/Q** (alveoli that are not ventilated but are perfused — atelectasis, pneumonia, bronchial obstruction) — the **shunt** effect: venous blood not saturated with oxygen is added to arterial blood; hypoxemia is poorly corrected even by breathing oxygen.
**Increased V/Q** (ventilated but not perfused — pulmonary embolism) — **dead space** increases: ventilation is wasted.

parts.text: Hypoxic vasoconstriction (**Euler–Liljestrand reflex**) — the arterioles constrict in a poorly ventilated part of the lung, and blood is directed to well-ventilated parts. This is a protective reaction that normalizes V/Q, but in chronic hypoxia of the whole lung (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, high altitude) it leads to **pulmonary hypertension** and right ventricular hypertrophy — **cor pulmonale**.

blocks.text: **Hypoxia** — a typical pathological process resulting from inadequate oxygen supply to tissues or impaired use of oxygen by them. **Hypoxemia** — a decrease in the oxygen content of the blood.

blocks.label: Figure 22.2
blocks.caption: Types of hypoxia (by etiology)

blocks.text: Exogenous hypoxia
A decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen in the inspired air.

items: **Hypobaric** — on ascent to altitude (mountain sickness, in pilots): total atmospheric pressure and pO2 decrease.
**Normobaric** — little oxygen in the air at normal pressure (mine, well, closed room, malfunction of a breathing apparatus).

blocks.text: **Blood gases:** arterial pO2 and SaO2 decreased; because of hyperventilation, **hypocapnia** and respiratory alkalosis (inhibition of the respiratory center, spasm of the cerebral vessels).
Respiratory hypoxia

Resulting from failure of external respiration: disturbances of ventilation, diffusion and perfusion and V/Q mismatch (sections 3 and 5). **Blood gases:** arterial pO2 and SaO2 decreased, often **hypercapnia** and respiratory acidosis (if ventilation is impaired).
Hemic (blood) hypoxia
The oxygen capacity of the blood decreases:

items: **anemias** — decreased hemoglobin;

**carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning** — carboxyhemoglobin is formed; CO binds to hemoglobin about 200–300 times more strongly than oxygen and also shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, impeding oxygen release; the skin is “cherry-red”;
**methemoglobin-forming agents** (nitrites, nitrates, aniline, sulfonamides) — the iron passes into the Fe3+ state and does not carry oxygen; the blood is brown, the skin gray-bluish.

blocks.text: **Blood gases:** arterial pO2 is **normal**, but the oxygen capacity and oxygen content of the blood are decreased; the arteriovenous difference is decreased.
Circulatory hypoxia
Reduced blood flow to the tissues:

items: **ischemic** — reduced arterial blood flow (vascular spasm, thrombosis, blood loss, shock, heart failure);
**congestive** — impaired venous outflow (heart failure, venous thrombosis).

blocks.text: **Blood gases:** arterial pO2 and blood oxygen content normal (if the lungs are not damaged); because blood flows slowly in the capillaries, the tissue extracts more oxygen — the **arteriovenous difference increases**, venous pO2 decreases; cyanosis.
Tissue (histotoxic) hypoxia
The tissues cannot use oxygen:

items: inhibition of respiratory chain enzymes — **cyanides** (bind to the Fe3+ of cytochrome oxidase), sulfides, arsenic;
uncoupling of oxidation and phosphorylation — excess thyroid hormones, 2,4-dinitrophenol, some toxins;
impaired enzyme synthesis — deficiency of B vitamins (B1, B2, PP);
damage to mitochondrial membranes — ionizing radiation, lipid peroxidation, alcohol.

blocks.text: **Blood gases:** arterial pO2 normal, **venous pO~2~ increased** — oxygen remains unused, **arteriovenous difference decreased**; the skin is pink.
Load (exertional) and mixed hypoxia

**Exertional hypoxia** — during heavy physical work the oxygen demand exceeds the delivery capacity (oxygen debt). **Mixed** — several types together (e.g. circulatory, respiratory and tissue hypoxia in shock; hemic and circulatory in blood loss).

head: Type
Arterial pO2
O2 capacity of the blood
Venous pO2
Arteriovenous difference
pCO2

sections.title: 7. Adaptive reactions and consequences of hypoxia

blocks.text: Emergency adaptive mechanisms

items: **external respiration** — hyperventilation (stimulation of the chemoreceptors of the aortic and carotid bodies), opening of reserve alveoli;
**circulation** — tachycardia, increased stroke volume, release of blood from depots, redistribution of blood in favor of vital organs (brain, heart) (**centralization of the circulation**);
**blood** — release of erythrocytes from the spleen and other depots, enhanced oxyhemoglobin dissociation (acidosis, increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate — the curve shifts to the right);
**tissue** — increased oxygen extraction, increased anaerobic glycolysis.

blocks.text: Long-term adaptive mechanisms

items: increased erythropoietin → **erythrocytosis** (in highlanders);
hypertrophy of the lungs and respiratory muscles, increased number of alveoli;
myocardial hypertrophy, increased capillary density (angiogenesis, the HIF-1 factor);
increased number of mitochondria and activity of respiratory enzymes, increased tissue resistance to oxygen deficiency.

blocks.text: Consequences of hypoxia

Tissues differ in their sensitivity to hypoxia: the most sensitive is the **cerebral cortex** (irreversible changes after 4–6 minutes of complete ischemia), followed by the myocardium, kidney and liver; the most resistant are bone, cartilage and connective tissue.

At the cellular level: decreased ATP → impaired ion pumps → entry of Na+ and water into the cell (cell swelling), Ca2+ accumulation → activation of phospholipases and proteases, lipid peroxidation → membrane damage; anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acidosis.

parts.text: **Cyanosis** (bluish discoloration) appears when reduced (deoxygenated) hemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds 50 g/l. Therefore in severe anemia (low total hemoglobin) there may be no cyanosis even with deep hypoxia, while in polycythemia cyanosis may appear even with mild hypoxemia. In carbon monoxide poisoning the skin is pink, and in methemoglobinemia gray-bluish — the degree of cyanosis does not accurately reflect the severity of hypoxia.

blocks.text: Studying exogenous hypobaric hypoxia
**Aim:** to compare the resistance to lowered atmospheric pressure of animals of different ages and of the body in different functional states.

items: Place mice (or a frog) in a Komovsky chamber (a glass bell jar with a pump).
Gradually pump out the air to lower the pressure; record the “altitude” from the manometer.
Observe the respiratory rate and pattern, motor activity, skin color, and the time of onset of convulsions and respiratory arrest.
Record the appearance of pathological types of breathing (Cheyne–Stokes, gasping).
Restore the pressure immediately and observe the recovery of the animal.
Record the results in a table and draw a conclusion.

blocks.text: Studying hemic hypoxia
**Aim:** to observe the formation of methemoglobin under the action of sodium nitrite.

items: Inject sodium nitrite solution intraperitoneally into a mouse.
Observe the respiratory rate, the color of the skin and mucous membranes, and motor activity.
Compare a drop of blood with a drop of control blood — in methemoglobinemia the blood turns brown.

parts.text: The doses and animal species used in the experiments follow the department's methodological guidelines; bioethics rules are observed when working with animals.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of ventilatory disorder from the spirogram

items: Compare VC with the predicted value (below 80 percent — decreased).
Compare FEV1 with the predicted value.
Calculate the Tiffeneau index: FEV1 / VC × 100 percent.
Tiffeneau below 70 percent — obstructive type.
VC markedly decreased, Tiffeneau normal or increased — restrictive type.
Both values impaired — mixed type.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of hypoxia from blood gases

items: Assess arterial pO2: if decreased — exogenous or respiratory hypoxia.
Assess blood pCO2: if decreased — exogenous (hyperventilation); if increased — respiratory (hypoventilation).
If arterial pO2 is normal, assess the oxygen capacity of the blood: decreased — hemic.
If the oxygen capacity is normal, assess venous pO2 and the arteriovenous difference: difference increased, venous pO2 low — circulatory; difference decreased, venous pO2 high — tissue hypoxia.
Compare the conclusion with the clinical data.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In winter, members of a family who had fallen asleep in a closed room with a coal stove burning were found in the morning with headache, nausea and severe weakness. One of them was unconscious, with pinkish-red skin and mucous membranes and shallow, rapid breathing. Arterial pO2 92 mm Hg, carboxyhemoglobin 45 percent.
cases.ask: What type of hypoxia has developed? Explain its mechanism. Why is there no cyanosis and why is pO2 normal?
cases.answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning — hemic hypoxia. CO binds to hemoglobin about 200–300 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin — the oxygen capacity of the blood falls sharply; the dissociation curve of the remaining oxyhemoglobin shifts to the left, impeding oxygen delivery to the tissues; CO also partly inhibits cytochrome oxidase (a tissue component). Arterial pO2 is determined by the oxygen dissolved in plasma and remains normal because lung function is not impaired — which is why pulse oximetry and pO2 can be misleading. Because carboxyhemoglobin is bright red, the skin is pinkish-red and there is no cyanosis. Treatment — removal to fresh air, 100 percent oxygen (hyperbaric oxygenation if needed), which accelerates the dissociation of carboxyhemoglobin.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 64-year-old man has smoked for 40 years and has had a productive cough and expiratory dyspnea for many years. His lips are bluish, the neck veins distended, and there is leg edema. Spirogram: VC 78 percent of predicted, FEV1 42 percent, Tiffeneau index 48 percent. Arterial pO2 55, pCO2 54 mm Hg. Hemoglobin 178 g/l.
cases.ask: What is the type of ventilatory disorder? Determine the type of respiratory failure. How did the right ventricular failure and erythrocytosis develop?
cases.answer: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: Tiffeneau index below 70 percent, FEV1 markedly decreased — obstructive type. Hypoxemia and hypercapnia — type II (hypercapnic) chronic decompensated respiratory failure (respiratory hypoxia, respiratory acidosis). Chronic alveolar hypoxia causes persistent spasm of the pulmonary arterioles (Euler–Liljestrand reflex) and then their remodeling — pulmonary hypertension; the right ventricle, overloaded by pressure, hypertrophies and decompensates — cor pulmonale: distended neck veins, edema. Hypoxia increases erythropoietin production in the kidney — secondary erythrocytosis (an adaptive reaction, but it increases blood viscosity); cyanosis is due to the large amount of reduced hemoglobin.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 28-year-old mountaineer developed headache, insomnia, dyspnea and palpitations after a rapid ascent to 4500 m. At night his breathing is periodic: several deep breaths followed by a pause. Pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SaO2 80 percent.
cases.ask: What type of hypoxia is this? How do blood gases change? Explain the adaptive reactions and the cause of the periodic breathing at night.
cases.answer: Exogenous hypobaric hypoxia (acute mountain sickness). Atmospheric pressure and the pO2 of the air are decreased — arterial pO2 and SaO2 are decreased. The chemoreceptors are stimulated and hyperventilation develops — a lot of CO2 is exhaled: hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis; hypocapnia leads to constriction of the cerebral vessels and inhibition of the respiratory center. Emergency adaptation: hyperventilation, tachycardia, release of blood from depots, centralization of the circulation. Periodic (Cheyne–Stokes-type) breathing at night: during hyperventilation CO2 falls and the stimulus to the respiratory center is lost — apnea; during apnea CO2 accumulates and O2 falls, and the center is stimulated again. Long-term adaptation (over several weeks): erythropoietin and erythrocytosis, increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate, increased capillary density and number of mitochondria. Gradual ascent (acclimatization) prevents mountain sickness.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of the digestive system

goals.text: To explain to the student the general etiology and pathogenesis of digestive disorders, the disturbances of secretory, motor-evacuatory and absorptive function of the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, intestine and pancreas, disturbances of luminal and membrane (parietal) digestion, peptic ulcer disease, the maldigestion and malabsorption syndromes, intestinal obstruction and the features of digestive disorders in children; to teach the student to interpret the results of gastric juice analysis.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the causes and main syndromes of digestive disorders;
the types of gastric secretion disorders and their consequences;
disorders of the motor-evacuatory function of the stomach (vomiting, belching, heartburn);
the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease (balance of aggressive and protective factors);
disorders of luminal and membrane digestion and of absorption (maldigestion, malabsorption);
disorders of intestinal motility (diarrhea, constipation, intestinal obstruction) and pancreatic insufficiency;
the features of digestive disorders in children.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: assess the acidity of gastric juice and the type of secretion;
identify digestive disorder syndromes by clinical signs.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Lactase deficiency:** undigested lactose enters the colon and is broken down by bacteria into lactic acid and gases — osmotic diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal pain. The osmotic pressure of the colonic contents rises and draws water into the intestinal lumen.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The indicators, reagents and calculation procedure should be checked against the department's methodological manual; in modern practice gastric secretion is assessed mainly by (intragastric) pH-metry.

blocks.text: **Digestive insufficiency** — a state in which digestion and absorption of nutrients do not meet the needs of the body.
Causes:

items: **dietary factors** — irregular eating habits, poor-quality, very hot or spicy food, alcohol, dry food;
**infections and parasites** — Helicobacter pylori, intestinal infections (Shigella, Salmonella, rotaviruses), Giardia, helminths;
**drugs and toxins** — nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, antibiotics (dysbiosis), cytostatics, radiation;
**disturbances of nervous and humoral regulation** — stress, autonomic dysfunction, endocrine diseases (diabetes, thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism);
**hereditary factors** — enzyme deficiencies (lactase, disaccharidases), celiac disease (gluten enteropathy), cystic fibrosis;
**diseases of other organs** — liver, kidney (uremic gastroenteritis), heart failure (venous congestion), autoimmune processes;
**tumors, surgical interventions** (gastric resection, intestinal resection).

sections.title: 2. Digestive disorders in the oral cavity and esophagus

blocks.text: Disorders of salivation:

items: **hypersalivation (ptyalism)** — stomatitis, helminths, toxemia of pregnancy, mercury poisoning, parkinsonism; large amounts of swallowed saliva reduce gastric acidity;

**hyposalivation (xerostomia)** — fever, dehydration, diabetes mellitus, Sjögren syndrome, atropine; dry mouth, difficulty chewing and swallowing, development of caries and stomatitis (loss of the bactericidal properties of saliva).

blocks.text: Disorders of the esophagus:

items: **dysphagia** — difficulty swallowing: mechanical (stenosis, tumor, post-burn scar, diverticulum) or functional (achalasia — failure of the lower sphincter to relax, esophageal spasm);

**gastroesophageal reflux** — incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter, increased intragastric pressure, hiatal hernia; acidic contents flow back into the esophagus — **heartburn**, reflux esophagitis, and if prolonged, Barrett esophagus (metaplasia, a precancerous condition).

blocks.text: Gastric juice secretion is regulated in three phases: **complex reflex (cephalic)** — via the vagus nerve; **gastric (neurohumoral)** — gastrin, histamine (H2 receptors), acetylcholine; **intestinal** — secretin, cholecystokinin and somatostatin inhibit gastric secretion.

blocks.title: Table 23.1. Normal values of gastric juice
head: Parameter
Normal value

blocks.label: Figure 23.1
blocks.caption: Types of gastric secretion (schematic curves, based on textbooks)

blocks.text: **Types of secretion** (by the form of the response to a stimulant): **normal**; **excitable** — secretion rises quickly and strongly and lasts long; **asthenic** — rises quickly and declines quickly (the glands tire quickly);
**inhibited (inert)** — rises slowly and late and lasts long; **depressed** — secretion is low and does not rise adequately.
Secretion disorders are assessed quantitatively (increased or decreased juice volume) and qualitatively (changes in acidity and enzyme activity); they often occur together.

blocks.title: Table 23.2. Disorders of gastric secretion
head: Type
Causes
Consequences
rows: Increased vagal tone, increased parietal cell mass, increased gastrin (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome — gastrinoma), Helicobacter pylori (antral gastritis), hypercalcemia
Heartburn, sour belching, pyloric spasm and delayed evacuation, constipation, peptic ulcer disease (duodenal)
Hypoacidity, anacidity (achylia — absence of acid and pepsin)
Atrophic gastritis (autoimmune — antibodies to parietal cells), gastric cancer, resection, chronic intoxications, hypothyroidism, cachexia

Protein digestion is impaired, the bactericidal effect is lost (fermentation, putrefaction, dysbiosis), the pylorus stays open — rapid evacuation and diarrhea, reduced iron absorption (iron deficiency); if Castle's intrinsic factor is lost — B12 deficiency anemia

items: **Hypertonus and hyperkinesia** — rapid emptying of food from the stomach, strong contractions and pain; **pylorospasm** — delayed evacuation.
**Hypotonus and hypokinesia** — dilation of the stomach, stagnation of food, fermentation and putrefaction.
**Disturbed evacuation**: accelerated (achylia, after resection) and delayed (pyloric stenosis — ulcer scar, tumor; pyloric spasm in hyperacidity; diabetic gastroparesis).

blocks.text: **Belching (eructation)** — expulsion of air or food from the stomach through the mouth; in cardiac incompetence and increased gastric pressure. Belching smelling of “rotten eggs” — putrefaction of proteins in pyloric stenosis (hydrogen sulfide).

**Nausea and vomiting** — a protective reflex resulting from stimulation of the **vomiting center** in the medulla oblongata. The center is stimulated via the **trigger (chemoreceptor) zone** in the floor of the fourth ventricle by blood-borne toxins, drugs (cytostatics, morphine, glycosides), uremia and ketoacidosis, as well as by impulses from the gastrointestinal tract, vestibular apparatus and cerebral cortex, and by raised intracranial pressure.

parts.text: **Consequences of repeated vomiting:** dehydration (hypovolemia), **hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis** due to loss of hydrochloric acid, hypokalemia (renal potassium loss), possible alkalotic tetany; tearing of the mucosa at the esophagogastric junction (**Mallory–Weiss syndrome**), aspiration pneumonia.

blocks.text: **Gastric and duodenal peptic ulcer disease** — a disease characterized by the formation of a chronic recurrent ulcer in the mucosa. Its pathogenesis is explained by an **imbalance between aggressive and protective factors**.

blocks.label: Figure 23.2
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease: balance of aggressive and protective factors

blocks.text: **Role of Helicobacter pylori:** using the enzyme **urease**, the bacterium breaks down urea, forms a “cloud” of ammonia around itself and survives in the acidic environment; with its flagella it penetrates the mucus layer and produces cytotoxins (CagA, VacA) — inflammation (gastritis); somatostatin-releasing D cells in the antrum decrease → gastrin increases → hyperacidity → gastric metaplasia in the duodenum and ulcer.
**NSAIDs** inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce the synthesis of protective prostaglandins — mucus, bicarbonate and blood supply decrease.
**Stress ulcers** (severe burns — Curling, brain trauma — Cushing, shock) — mucosal ischemia and the effects of catecholamines and glucocorticoids.
**Complications:** bleeding, perforation (peritonitis), penetration (into a neighboring organ), pyloric stenosis, malignant transformation (in gastric ulcer).

sections.title: 6. Disorders of intestinal digestion and absorption

blocks.text: Luminal and membrane digestion

items: **Luminal digestion** — breakdown of large molecules in the intestinal lumen by the enzymes of pancreatic and intestinal juice and by bile.

**Membrane (parietal) digestion** — the stage associated with final breakdown and absorption by enzymes located on the surface of the microvilli of the intestinal epithelium, in the glycocalyx (disaccharidases, peptidases) (A. M. Ugolev).

blocks.text: **Maldigestion syndrome** — impaired digestion: pancreatic insufficiency, failure of bile acids to reach the intestine (obstructive jaundice), disaccharidase deficiency (lactase — milk intolerance), change in intestinal pH.

**Malabsorption syndrome** — impaired absorption: damage to the intestinal mucosa (celiac disease — villous atrophy, Crohn disease, enteritis), reduced absorptive surface (intestinal resection — “short bowel” syndrome), impaired lymph flow, impaired blood circulation in the intestinal wall.

**Consequences:** steatorrhea (fat in the stool), creatorrhea (undigested muscle fibers), amylorrhea (starch), weight loss, hypoproteinemic edema, anemia (iron, B12, folate), deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) — hypocalcemia, osteomalacia, impaired blood clotting.

parts.text: **Lactase deficiency:** undigested lactose enters the colon and is broken down by bacteria into lactic acid and gases — osmotic diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal pain. The osmotic pressure of the colonic contents rises and draws water into the intestinal lumen.

blocks.text: Disorders of intestinal motility
**Diarrhea** — frequent passage of liquid stools. Mechanisms:

items: **secretory** — increased secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen (cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP — several liters of fluid are lost per day);
**osmotic** — non-absorbable osmotically active substances in the intestine (lactase deficiency, magnesium sulfate);
**exudative (inflammatory)** — inflammation and ulceration of the mucosa, with discharge of blood, mucus and protein (dysentery, ulcerative colitis);
**motor (hyperkinetic)** — accelerated peristalsis (thyrotoxicosis, irritable bowel syndrome).

blocks.text: **Consequences:** dehydration, hypokalemia, **metabolic acidosis** due to loss of bicarbonate, hypovolemic shock (especially in children).

**Constipation** — retention of stool for more than 3 days: alimentary (little fiber and fluid), hypokinetic (physical inactivity, hypothyroidism, old age), spastic (autonomic dysfunction, lead poisoning), mechanical obstruction (tumor, scar), proctogenic (anal fissure, hemorrhoids — reflex inhibition due to pain). Consequences: intoxication (absorption of putrefaction products — indole, skatole, phenol), hemorrhoids.
Intestinal obstruction
**Intestinal obstruction (ileus)** — arrest of the movement of intestinal contents.

items: **Mechanical** — obturation (tumor, gallstone, a ball of worms, foreign body), strangulation (volvulus, knotting, incarcerated hernia — the mesenteric vessels are also compressed, rapid necrosis), intussusception (more common in children).
**Dynamic** — paralytic (peritonitis, after abdominal surgery, hypokalemia) and spastic (lead poisoning, hysteria).

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis:** above the obstruction the intestine is distended and the circulation in its wall is impaired; fluid and electrolytes accumulate in the intestinal lumen and are lost with vomiting — **dehydration and hypovolemia**; bacteria multiply, and toxins and bacteria pass through the wall into the blood (**endotoxemia**), peritonitis; pain impulses — pain shock. The result is water–electrolyte disturbances, intoxication and shock.

**Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency** — chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, resection and tumors of the gland. Lipase deficiency manifests first: **steatorrhea** (fatty, shiny, bulky stools), creatorrhea, amylorrhea, weight loss.
**Acute pancreatitis** — activation of the gland's enzymes within the gland and digestion of its own tissue (autolysis).

items: **Causes:** gallstones (obstruction of the common bile–pancreatic duct and bile reflux), alcohol, large fatty meals, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, infections, drugs.

**Pathogenesis:** trypsinogen is converted to trypsin within the gland → it activates other enzymes: **phospholipase A~2~** and **lipase** — fat necrosis (steatonecrosis, formation of soaps with calcium — hypocalcemia), **elastase** — damage to vessel walls and bleeding, activation of the **kallikrein–kinin system** — vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, pain, shock. The enzymes pass into the blood (**enzymemia** — amylase and lipase rise) and damage distant organs (lungs, kidneys).

sections.title: 8. Features of digestive disorders in children

items: The acidity of digestive juices and enzyme activity are low and the permeability of the intestinal mucosa is high — infections and allergens pass through easily.
The lower esophageal sphincter is immature and the stomach lies horizontally — **regurgitation** is frequent.
**Pyloric stenosis** — congenital hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle: projectile (“fountain”) vomiting from 2–4 weeks of age, hypochloremic alkalosis, weight loss.
**In diarrhea** water and electrolyte balance is disturbed quickly — exsiccosis and toxicosis; the risk of hypovolemic shock is much higher than in adults.
Hereditary enzymopathies (lactase deficiency, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis) often manifest when switching to formula feeding or introducing complementary foods.
Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children.

blocks.text: Determining the acidity of gastric juice (titration method)
**Aim:** to determine the total acidity and free hydrochloric acid of gastric juice.

items: Put 5 ml of filtered gastric juice into a flask.
Add the indicators: dimethylaminoazobenzene (for free hydrochloric acid) and phenolphthalein (for total acidity).
Titrate with 0.1 N sodium hydroxide solution: when the red color turns yellowish-orange — free hydrochloric acid; when a pink color appears — total acidity.
Multiply the milliliters of alkali used by 20 (calculating per 100 ml of juice) and express the result in titration units.
Compare the result with the normal values and write a conclusion (hyperacid, normacid, hypoacid, anacid).

blocks.text: Studying the activity of digestive enzymes

In test tubes, observe the breakdown of starch by salivary amylase (iodine test) and the digestion of protein (fibrin, egg white) by gastric juice, and the effect of various factors (temperature, pH, bile) on them.

parts.text: The indicators, reagents and calculation procedure should be checked against the department's methodological manual; in modern practice gastric secretion is assessed mainly by (intragastric) pH-metry.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting gastric juice analysis

items: Compare the volumes of basal and stimulated secretion with the normal values.
Assess total acidity and the amount of free hydrochloric acid.
No free hydrochloric acid and very low total acidity — anacid state; if pepsin is also absent — achylia.
Determine the type of secretion from the shape of the secretion curve.
Relate the result to the clinical signs (ulcer, atrophic gastritis, anemia) and write a conclusion.

skills.title: Skill: determining the mechanism of diarrhea

items: Assess the volume and character of the stools (watery, mixed with blood and mucus, fatty).
Does the diarrhea stop with fasting? If it stops — osmotic mechanism; if not — secretory.
If blood, mucus and leukocytes are present — exudative (inflammatory).
Fatty, shiny, bulky stools — maldigestion or malabsorption (steatorrhea).
Assess the degree of dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 32-year-old man has had epigastric pain on an empty stomach and at night for 3 years; the pain decreases after eating; heartburn, sour belching, constipation. He smokes heavily. Endoscopy: an ulcer in the duodenal bulb, positive urease test. Gastric juice: acidity increased.
cases.ask: Which aggressive and protective factors were involved in the development of the ulcer? Explain the constipation and the reduction of pain after eating.
cases.answer: Duodenal ulcer. Aggressive factors: Helicobacter pylori (antral gastritis, loss of D cells → decreased somatostatin and increased gastrin → hyperacidity), hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsin, smoking (reduces prostaglandin and bicarbonate secretion and worsens blood supply). The protective factors (mucus–bicarbonate barrier, blood supply) are weakened. On an empty stomach, highly acidic contents enter the duodenum and cause pain; food neutralizes the acid — the pain decreases. Hyperacidity causes pyloric spasm and reflex slowing of intestinal motility — constipation. Treatment — eradication of Helicobacter pylori and reduction of acid secretion.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 4-year-old child at a kindergarten has contracted cholera: watery stools resembling “rice water” 15–20 times a day and vomiting. The skin is dry, the skin fold returns slowly, the eyeballs are sunken, urine is scanty, BP is decreased, the pulse rapid and weak. Blood: hematocrit raised, K+ decreased, pH 7.26, bicarbonate decreased.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the diarrhea. Interpret the water–electrolyte and acid–base disturbances. Why is this condition especially dangerous in children?
cases.answer: Cholera toxin permanently activates adenylate cyclase in the intestinal epithelium and raises cAMP — chloride and bicarbonate ions, and water with them, are secreted into the intestinal lumen in large amounts and sodium absorption decreases — secretory diarrhea (the mucosa is not damaged, which is why there is no blood in the stool). The result is isotonic dehydration (hypovolemia — raised hematocrit, oliguria, hypotension, hypovolemic shock), potassium loss (hypokalemia), and metabolic acidosis due to loss of bicarbonate and lactate accumulation with tissue hypoperfusion. In children the proportion of body water and of extracellular fluid is higher, water turnover is faster and the concentrating ability of the kidneys is lower — dehydration and shock develop very quickly. The main treatment is oral or intravenous administration of water–electrolyte solutions (rehydration).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a festive meal (much fatty food, alcohol), a 48-year-old man developed severe girdle-like epigastric pain and repeated vomiting. BP 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min, bluish patches on the abdominal skin. Blood amylase and lipase are sharply raised, calcium decreased, leukocytosis.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its pathogenesis. By what mechanism did the hypotension and hypocalcemia develop?
cases.answer: Acute pancreatitis. Alcohol and fatty food stimulate the gland's secretion, cause spasm of the sphincter of Oddi and increased duct pressure, and premature activation of trypsinogen in the acinar cells — trypsin activates the other enzymes and self-digestion of the gland (autolysis) begins. Lipase and phospholipase A2 cause fat necrosis; in the necrotic foci fatty acids form soaps with calcium — hypocalcemia (a sign of a severe course). Elastase damages vessel walls and causes hemorrhages (the patches on the abdominal skin). Activation of the kallikrein–kinin system leads to vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity and retroperitoneal tissue, and water loss with vomiting — hypovolemia, which together with pain and enzymemia causes shock (hypotension, tachycardia). The enzymes pass into the blood (raised amylase and lipase) and may damage the lungs and kidneys.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of the hepatobiliary system

goals.text: To explain to the student the main functions of the liver, the causes, types and pathogenesis of liver failure, the changes in metabolism, blood clotting and detoxification when liver function is impaired, the mechanisms of hepatic coma, portal hypertension and liver cirrhosis, the types of jaundice and their laboratory differentiation, disorders of bile formation and excretion, and the features in children; to teach the student to detect bile pigments in urine and to determine the type of jaundice from laboratory parameters.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the main functions of the liver and the signs of their impairment;
the causes, types and pathogenesis of liver failure;
the types and pathogenesis of hepatic coma;
the syndromes that develop in portal hypertension and liver cirrhosis;
bilirubin metabolism and the types of jaundice, and their laboratory differences;
the cholestasis and acholia syndromes;
the features of neonatal jaundice.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: detect bilirubin and urobilin in urine;
determine the type of jaundice from blood, urine and stool parameters.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember obstructive jaundice: “urine the color of **beer**, stool the color of **clay**, the skin **itches**, the blood **does not clot**” (bilirubinuria, acholia, cholemia, vitamin K deficiency).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The concentrations of reagents and the procedure of the tests should be checked against the department's methodological manual; in a modern laboratory bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine are detected with test strips.

sections.title: 1. Main functions of the liver and their impairment

Normal
In failure

blocks.text: **Liver failure** — a condition with impairment of one or more functions of the liver.
Causes:

items: **infectious** — viral hepatitis (B, C, D, A, E), leptospirosis, echinococcosis, alveococcosis, opisthorchiasis;
**toxic** — alcohol, hepatotropic poisons (carbon tetrachloride, phosphorus, poisonous mushrooms — death cap), drugs (a large dose of paracetamol, antituberculosis and cytostatic drugs);
**circulatory disturbance** — chronic heart failure (“nutmeg liver”), shock, hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd–Chiari syndrome);
**impaired bile outflow** — gallstones, tumors (secondary biliary cirrhosis);
**hereditary metabolic disorders** — hemochromatosis (iron), Wilson–Konovalov disease (copper), alpha1-antitrypsin deficiency;
**autoimmune** — autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis;
**tumors** — hepatocellular carcinoma, metastases;
**nutritional** — protein deficiency, obesity (fatty hepatosis).

blocks.title: Table 24.2. Types of liver failure
head: Criterion
Types
rows: Hepatocellular (death of liver cells), portosystemic shunting (blood bypasses the liver), mixed

blocks.text: Syndromes of hepatocellular failure

items: **Cytolysis syndrome** — the hepatocyte membrane is damaged and enzymes are released into the blood: **ALT and AST** rise (ALT is more specific to the liver).
**Mesenchymal-inflammatory syndrome** — increased gamma globulins, positive thymol test.
**Hepatodepressive (synthetic failure)** syndrome — decreased albumin, prothrombin, cholinesterase, cholesterol.
**Cholestasis syndrome** — increased alkaline phosphatase, GGT (gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase), direct bilirubin, bile acids and cholesterol.

blocks.text: **Hepatic encephalopathy** — impaired function of the central nervous system under the action of toxic substances that are not neutralized in liver failure; its severe degree is **hepatic coma**.
Types:

items: **endogenous (hepatocellular)** — extensive necrosis of the liver parenchyma (fulminant hepatitis, poisoning);
**exogenous (portosystemic, bypass)** — in portal hypertension, blood from the intestine bypasses the liver through portocaval anastomoses and enters the systemic circulation directly;
**mixed**.

blocks.text: Pathogenesis:

items: **Ammonia** — formed mainly from the breakdown of proteins by bacteria in the intestine; it must be converted to urea in the liver. In the brain, excess ammonia binds alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate and then glutamine — **alpha-ketoglutarate in the Krebs cycle decreases and ATP formation falls**; glutamine accumulates in astrocytes and causes their swelling (cerebral edema); GABA-ergic inhibition increases.

**False neurotransmitters** — aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan) increase and branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine) decrease; **octopamine** and **phenylethylamine** are formed in the brain and replace the true transmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine).
Other toxins — mercaptans (“fetor hepaticus” from the mouth), short-chain fatty acids, phenols, endogenous benzodiazepines.
Additional factors — hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, alkalosis (ammonia passes into the brain easily), hypoxia.

parts.text: Factors that precipitate hepatic encephalopathy: gastrointestinal bleeding (blood in the intestine is a source of protein — ammonia increases), a high-protein diet, constipation, infections, diuretics (hypokalemia and alkalosis), sedatives, alcohol. Clinical signs: disturbed sleep rhythm, behavioral changes, “flapping” tremor (asterixis), stupor, coma.

blocks.text: **Portal hypertension** — a rise in pressure in the portal vein system above 10–12 mm Hg.

blocks.title: Table 24.3. Types of portal hypertension
head: Type
Causes
rows: Liver cirrhosis (the most common), schistosomiasis, tumors
Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd–Chiari), constrictive pericarditis, right ventricular failure

blocks.text: Consequences:

items: **dilation of portocaval anastomoses** — varicose veins of the esophagus and gastric cardia (dangerous bleeding), rectal veins (hemorrhoids), periumbilical veins (“caput medusae”);
**splenomegaly and hypersplenism** — anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia;
**ascites**;
portosystemic encephalopathy.

blocks.text: Pathogenesis of ascites

items: Portal hypertension — hydrostatic pressure in the hepatic sinusoids and intestinal capillaries rises and fluid passes into the abdominal cavity; hepatic lymph increases.
Hypoalbuminemia — oncotic pressure decreases.

Dilation of the visceral arteries (increased NO) — the effective blood volume decreases → **activation of RAAS, the sympathetic system and ADH** → sodium and water are retained by the kidneys; aldosterone inactivation in the liver decreases (secondary hyperaldosteronism).

blocks.text: **Liver cirrhosis** — a chronic diffuse disease of the liver characterized by death of hepatocytes, fibrosis and replacement of the normal architecture by **regenerative nodules**. The main causes are chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease, and autoimmune and biliary diseases.
Fibrosis develops as a result of activation of hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) and their production of collagen. Cirrhosis combines the syndromes of liver failure and portal hypertension.

blocks.label: Figure 24.1
blocks.caption: Bilirubin metabolism (diagram)

blocks.text: Aged erythrocytes are broken down in macrophages: the heme of hemoglobin is converted via **biliverdin** into **indirect (free) bilirubin**. It is insoluble in water, is carried in the blood by albumin and does not pass the renal filter (it is absent from urine). In the liver it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to form **direct bilirubin**, is excreted with bile into the intestine and is converted by bacteria to **urobilinogen** and then to **stercobilinogen** (which colors the stool). Part of the urobilinogen is absorbed and returns to the liver; a healthy liver retains it almost completely.
**Normally** total blood bilirubin is 8.5–20.5 µmol/l, mainly the indirect fraction (about 75 percent).

**Jaundice (icterus)** — yellow coloring of the skin, mucous membranes and sclerae due to increased blood bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia). Yellowing of the sclerae becomes visible when bilirubin exceeds about 34 µmol/l.

blocks.label: Figure 24.2
blocks.caption: Types of jaundice and their laboratory signs

blocks.text: Prehepatic (hemolytic) jaundice

**Cause:** increased breakdown of erythrocytes (hemolytic anemias, incompatible blood transfusion, hemolytic poisons, malaria, hemolytic disease of the newborn) — formation of indirect bilirubin exceeds the conjugating capacity of the liver.

**Signs:** indirect bilirubin raised in the blood; no bilirubin in the urine (indirect bilirubin is not filtered); a lot of bilirubin enters the intestine — **urobilin** in the urine and **stercobilin** in the stool are increased (dark stool); the skin is lemon-yellow, no itching; anemia, reticulocytosis.
Hepatic (parenchymal) jaundice
**Cause:** damage to hepatocytes — viral and toxic hepatitis, cirrhosis, leptospirosis.

**Mechanism:** uptake, conjugation and excretion of bilirubin into the bile capillaries are impaired in the liver cells; the cells die and conjugated bilirubin returns to the blood (the barrier between the bile capillaries and blood vessels is broken); the liver cannot retain urobilinogen coming from the intestine.

**Signs:** **both fractions** raised in the blood; direct bilirubin present in the urine (urine “the color of beer”) and urobilin increased; stool decolorized (less stercobilin); ALT and AST sharply raised, synthetic function of the liver impaired; the skin is saffron-yellow.
**By stage of hepatitis:** urobilinuria in the initial (prodromal) period; at the peak, if cholestasis develops, urobilin may temporarily disappear; it reappears during recovery.
Posthepatic (obstructive, mechanical) jaundice
**Cause:** obstruction of bile outflow — bile duct stones, cancer of the head of the pancreas, tumor of the papilla of Vater, cicatricial narrowing of the bile ducts, helminths, external compression.

**Mechanism:** pressure in the bile ducts rises, the bile capillaries rupture and conjugated bilirubin, bile acids and cholesterol pass into the blood (**cholemia**); bile does not enter the intestine (**acholia**).

**Signs:** **direct bilirubin** sharply raised in the blood; much bilirubin in the urine (dark urine, “the color of beer”), **no urobilin** (since bile does not enter the intestine, no urobilinogen is formed); stool **white-gray (acholic)**, fatty (steatorrhea); alkaline phosphatase, GGT and cholesterol raised; the skin is greenish-yellow, with severe itching.

blocks.text: **Cholemia** — entry of bile components (mainly bile acids) into the blood:

items: skin itching (action of bile acids and other pruritogens on nerve endings);
bradycardia and arterial hypotension (action of bile acids on the sinus node and the vagal nuclei, reduced vascular tone);
depression of the CNS — weakness, depression, drowsiness;
hemolysis of erythrocytes, reduced leukocyte activity;
hypercholesterolemia, xanthomas on the skin.

blocks.text: **Acholia** — bile does not enter the intestine:

items: emulsification and digestion of fats are impaired — **steatorrhea**;
fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are not absorbed — **vitamin K deficiency** (reduced synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X, bleeding), osteomalacia, night blindness;
intestinal peristalsis and the bacteriostatic action of bile decrease — putrefaction and fermentation in the intestine, flatulence, dysbiosis;
the stool is decolorized.

parts.text: To remember obstructive jaundice: “urine the color of **beer**, stool the color of **clay**, the skin **itches**, the blood **does not clot**” (bilirubinuria, acholia, cholemia, vitamin K deficiency).

sections.title: 7. Features of hepatobiliary disorders in children

blocks.text: **Physiological jaundice of the newborn** — appears on day 2–3 and disappears by day 7–10 (by 2–3 weeks in premature infants). Causes:

items: the short life of erythrocytes containing fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and their massive breakdown after birth;
low activity of hepatic **UDP-glucuronyltransferase** (immaturity of the enzyme);
absence of bacteria in the intestine and intense enterohepatic circulation.

blocks.text: Pathological jaundice:

items: **Hemolytic disease of the newborn** — maternal antibodies against the fetus's Rh-positive (or AB0) antigens destroy fetal erythrocytes; it appears on the first day and increases rapidly.

**Bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus)** — in newborns the permeability of the blood–brain barrier is high and albumin is low; indirect bilirubin (which is fat-soluble) accumulates in the subcortical nuclei of the brain and damages them. The risk is high when bilirubin exceeds about 340 µmol/l (even lower in premature infants). Treatment — phototherapy, exchange transfusion.

**Hereditary pigmentary hepatoses: Gilbert syndrome** (mild impairment of bilirubin uptake and conjugation — indirect bilirubin rises with fasting and stress, harmless), **Crigler–Najjar syndrome** (glucuronyltransferase absent or markedly reduced — severe indirect hyperbilirubinemia, risk of kernicterus), **Dubin–Johnson syndrome** (impaired excretion of direct bilirubin).
**Biliary atresia** — congenital obstructive jaundice; early surgery is required.

sections.title: 8. Experimental part: detecting bile pigments in urine

blocks.text: Detecting bilirubin in urine (Rosin test)

items: Pour 4–5 ml of urine into a test tube.
Carefully layer 1 percent alcoholic iodine solution along the wall of the test tube.
If a **green ring** appears at the boundary of the two liquids, bilirubin is present in the urine (positive test).

blocks.text: Detecting urobilin in urine

A reagent for urobilinogen (e.g. Ehrlich's reagent) is added to the urine: the appearance of a red color indicates increased urobilinogen (urobilin); normally the color is very faint or appears only on heating.
Interpreting the results
Detect bilirubin and urobilin in the urine samples of the “patients” provided, compare the results with the blood and stool parameters and determine the type of jaundice.

parts.text: The concentrations of reagents and the procedure of the tests should be checked against the department's methodological manual; in a modern laboratory bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine are detected with test strips.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of jaundice from laboratory parameters

items: Assess total blood bilirubin and its fractions: which fraction predominates?
Determine whether bilirubin is present in the urine: if present, direct bilirubin is raised (hepatic or posthepatic).
Assess urobilin in the urine: much — prehepatic or hepatic; absent — posthepatic.
Assess the stool color: dark — prehepatic; acholic — posthepatic.
Assess the enzymes: ALT and AST predominate — hepatic; alkaline phosphatase and GGT predominate — posthepatic.
Write a conclusion and suggest the underlying disease.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the syndromes of liver failure

items: Assess the signs of cytolysis (ALT, AST).
Assess synthetic function (albumin, prothrombin index or INR, cholesterol).
Assess the signs of cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase, GGT, direct bilirubin).
Identify the signs of portal hypertension (ascites, splenomegaly, varicose veins).
Assess the signs of encephalopathy (consciousness, sleep, asterixis).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 62-year-old man has had gradually increasing jaundice for 2 months, severe skin itching, loss of appetite and weight loss. The skin is greenish-yellow with scratch marks; pulse 56 beats/min. Blood: total bilirubin 280 µmol/l (direct 230), alkaline phosphatase and GGT sharply raised, ALT slightly raised, prothrombin index decreased. Urine dark, bilirubin positive, urobilin negative. Stool white-gray and fatty. CT: a tumor in the head of the pancreas.
cases.ask: Determine the type of jaundice and explain the laboratory signs. What is the mechanism of the itching, bradycardia and decreased prothrombin index?
cases.answer: Posthepatic (obstructive) jaundice — a tumor of the head of the pancreas has compressed the common bile duct. Pressure in the bile ducts rises and conjugated bilirubin and bile acids pass into the blood (cholemia): direct bilirubin predominates and the cholestatic enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, GGT) are sharply raised; direct bilirubin is water-soluble and is excreted by the kidneys — dark urine, bilirubin positive. Bile does not enter the intestine (acholia) — no urobilinogen is formed (no urobilin in the urine), and the stool is acholic and fatty (steatorrhea). Itching and bradycardia — the action of bile acids on the nerve endings of the skin, the sinus node and the vagal centers. Vitamin K is not absorbed without bile acids — synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X decreases and the prothrombin index falls (vitamin K is given parenterally before surgery).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 25-year-old student developed jaundice a week after fever and weakness. Urine dark, stool pale. The liver is enlarged and tender. Blood: bilirubin 140 µmol/l (direct 80, indirect 60), ALT 1800 U/l (normal up to 40), AST 1200 U/l. Urine: bilirubin and urobilin positive. HBsAg positive.
cases.ask: Determine the type of jaundice. Why are both fractions raised in the blood? Explain the mechanism of urobilinuria.
cases.answer: Hepatic (parenchymal) jaundice — acute viral hepatitis B. Hepatocytes are damaged (cytolysis — ALT and AST sharply raised): uptake and conjugation of indirect bilirubin are impaired — the indirect fraction rises; excretion of conjugated bilirubin into the bile capillaries is impaired and direct bilirubin returns to the blood through the dead cells — the direct fraction also rises and is found in the urine. Part of the bile still enters the intestine, urobilinogen is formed and absorbed, but the damaged liver cannot capture and reprocess it — urobilinogen passes into the systemic circulation and is excreted in the urine (urobilinuria). Because less bile enters the intestine, the stool is pale.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 55-year-old man has drunk alcohol for 20 years and has been diagnosed with liver cirrhosis. In recent days he has had black (tarry) stools, followed by drowsiness, confusion, a “flapping” tremor when he stretches out his hands and a characteristic sweetish-musty odor from the mouth. The abdomen is enlarged (ascites), with dilated veins around the navel.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? Explain the precipitating factor and the pathogenesis. How did the ascites and the periumbilical veins arise?
cases.answer: Hepatic encephalopathy (precoma) — mixed (hepatocellular failure and portosystemic shunting). The precipitating factor is bleeding from esophageal varices (black stools): bacteria form large amounts of ammonia from blood proteins in the intestine; the cirrhotic liver cannot convert it into urea, and in addition blood bypasses the liver through portocaval anastomoses. In the brain, ammonia binds alpha-ketoglutarate and reduces energy production, and glutamine accumulates in astrocytes and causes swelling; false neurotransmitters (octopamine) and mercaptans (“fetor hepaticus”) also accumulate — impaired consciousness, asterixis. Ascites is the result of portal hypertension (increased hydrostatic pressure), hypoalbuminemia (decreased oncotic pressure), secondary hyperaldosteronism and sodium and water retention. The periumbilical veins (“caput medusae”) are dilated portocaval anastomoses.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of the kidneys

goals.text: To explain to the student the causes and mechanisms of renal dysfunction — disturbances of glomerular ultrafiltration and of tubular reabsorption and secretion, changes in diuresis and urine composition, extrarenal signs (edema, hypertension, anemia), the nephrotic and nephritic syndromes, the pathogenesis of acute and chronic kidney failure and uremia, and the features in children; to teach the student the concept of clearance and to interpret renal function tests, especially the Zimnitsky test.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the functions of the nephron and the methods of examining renal function (clearance, functional tests);
the causes and mechanisms of impaired glomerular filtration;
disturbances of tubular reabsorption and secretion (tubulopathies);
changes in diuresis and urine composition (polyuria, oliguria, proteinuria, hematuria, etc.);
the pathogenesis of the nephrotic and nephritic syndromes;
the causes and stages of acute and chronic kidney failure and the pathogenesis of uremia.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: interpret the results of the Zimnitsky test;
calculate the glomerular filtration rate from clearance;
interpret pathological changes in urinalysis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Mechanisms of oliguria in acute tubular necrosis:** spasm of the afferent arterioles (RAAS, tubuloglomerular feedback — the macula densa senses an increased sodium load and reduces filtration), obstruction of the tubules by dead cells and casts (intratubular pressure rises and filtration falls), back-leak of filtrate through the damaged tubular wall into the blood, interstitial edema.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Other functional tests: the **Rehberg–Tareev test** (determining GFR and tubular reabsorption from endogenous creatinine clearance), the **Nechiporenko test** (number of leukocytes, erythrocytes and casts in 1 ml of urine), the concentration test (dry diet) and the dilution test (water load). In modern practice GFR is usually calculated from blood creatinine using formulas (CKD-EPI).

blocks.text: **Main functions of the kidneys:** excretory (excretion of nitrogenous waste, drugs and toxins), homeostatic (water–electrolyte balance, osmotic pressure, acid–base balance), endocrine (renin, erythropoietin, calcitriol — the active form of vitamin D, prostaglandins, kinins), metabolic (gluconeogenesis, breakdown of protein hormones).
**Urine formation** consists of three processes:

items: **Glomerular ultrafiltration** — primary urine is filtered from the capillaries into Bowman's capsule (about 180 l per day). Effective filtration pressure = capillary hydrostatic pressure – (plasma oncotic pressure + intracapsular pressure) ≈ 70 – (30 + 20) = 20 mm Hg.
**Tubular reabsorption** — 99 percent of the water and solutes are returned to the blood.
**Tubular secretion** — certain substances (H+, K+, ammonia, drugs) are transferred from the blood into the urine.

blocks.text: **Clearance** — the volume of plasma cleared of a given substance by the kidneys in 1 minute: C = (U × V) / P, where U is the urine concentration of the substance, V is the minute diuresis and P is the plasma concentration.

The clearance of a substance that is only filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted (inulin; in practice **endogenous creatinine** — the Rehberg–Tareev test) equals the **glomerular filtration rate (GFR)**.

blocks.text: **Consequences of reduced filtration:** oliguria, accumulation of nitrogenous substances (creatinine, urea, uric acid) in the blood — **azotemia**, sodium and water retention.

**Increased permeability of the filtering membrane** (immune damage, podocyte injury, loss of the negative charge of the membrane) — protein (**proteinuria**) and erythrocytes (**hematuria**) pass into the urine.

**Causes:** ischemia, nephrotoxins (mercury, lead, aminoglycosides, radiocontrast agents), interstitial inflammation (pyelonephritis), hereditary enzymopathies and transporter protein defects, disturbed hormonal regulation (deficiency of ADH or aldosterone, or insensitivity to them).

blocks.text: Disturbance of the urine-concentrating function:

items: **hyposthenuria** — urine specific gravity constantly low (below 1012), reduced concentrating ability;
**isosthenuria** — urine specific gravity fixed and equal to that of primary urine (plasma filtrate) (about 1010); neither concentration nor dilution — a sign of chronic kidney failure;
**hypersthenuria** — high specific gravity (glucosuria, protein, dehydration, oliguria).

blocks.text: Pathological changes in urine composition:

items: **Proteinuria** — protein in the urine: **glomerular** (increased membrane permeability; selective — mainly albumin, nonselective — larger proteins as well), **tubular** (impaired reabsorption of low-molecular-weight proteins), **overflow** (increased small proteins in the blood — Bence Jones protein in myeloma), **postrenal** (inflammation of the urinary tract). Functional proteinuria — heavy physical exertion, fever, orthostatic.
**Hematuria** — erythrocytes in the urine: glomerular (altered, dysmorphic erythrocytes — glomerulonephritis) and non-glomerular (unaltered erythrocytes — stones, tumors, trauma).
**Leukocyturia** — increased leukocytes in the urine (pyelonephritis, cystitis); **pyuria** — a large amount of pus.
**Cylindruria** — “casts” formed in the tubules from protein and cells: hyaline, granular, waxy, erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis).
**Glucosuria** — when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (about 8.9–10 mmol/l) or in a tubular defect.

blocks.text: Renal edema

items: **Nephrotic edema** — massive proteinuria → hypoalbuminemia → oncotic pressure falls → fluid moves into the tissues → circulating blood volume decreases → RAAS and ADH are activated → sodium and water are retained. The edema is large and soft, starting on the face and progressing to anasarca.
**Nephritic edema** — reduced filtration and primary retention of sodium and water (hypervolemia), increased capillary permeability. The edema is on the face and eyelids, more in the morning.

blocks.text: Renal hypertension

items: **Renovascular** — renal ischemia → increased renin → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (sodium and water retention).
**Renoparenchymal** — sodium and water retention (hypervolemia), RAAS activation, reduction of the renal depressor systems (prostaglandins, kinins).

blocks.text: Renal anemia
Reduced **erythropoietin** production as renal parenchyma decreases; additional factors — the effect of uremic toxins on the bone marrow, shortened erythrocyte lifespan, bleeding.
Renal osteodystrophy

Reduced calcitriol synthesis (hypocalcemia) and phosphate retention (hyperphosphatemia) → increased parathyroid hormone (**secondary hyperparathyroidism**) → release of calcium from bones, osteomalacia, osteoporosis.

Damage to the filtering membrane (podocytes), sharp increase in protein permeability
On the face and eyelids, moderate
