blocks.text: **Pathogenesis of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis:** 1–3 weeks after infection with group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (tonsillitis, pyoderma), **immune complexes** formed from streptococcal antigens and antibodies are deposited on the glomerular basement membrane (a type III allergic reaction) → complement is activated (C3 decreases) and neutrophils accumulate → the capillaries are damaged and inflamed → filtration falls (oliguria, azotemia), erythrocytes and protein pass into the urine, and sodium and water are retained (edema, hypertension).

**Hyperlipidemia in nephrotic syndrome** — increased hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins in response to hypoalbuminemia and reduced lipoprotein lipase activity; **hypercoagulation** — urinary loss of antithrombin III and increased hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (risk of thrombosis).
Acute kidney failure (acute kidney injury)
**Acute kidney failure** — a sudden (within hours or days) sharp decline in renal function, characterized by a rise in blood creatinine and (or) a decrease in diuresis.

blocks.label: Figure 25.1
blocks.caption: Types of acute kidney failure

blocks.text: Stages:

items: **Initial** — action of the cause (shock, poisoning), hours or days.

**Oligoanuric** (1–3 weeks) — oliguria or anuria; **azotemia**, **hyperkalemia** (risk of arrhythmia and cardiac arrest — the most dangerous complication), metabolic acidosis, hyperhydration (pulmonary and cerebral edema), hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, uremic intoxication.

**Polyuric (recovery of diuresis)** — filtration recovers, but the tubular epithelium is still immature, reabsorption and concentration are low — polyuria, hyposthenuria; risk of dehydration, **hypokalemia** and hyponatremia.
**Recovery** — from several months to a year.

parts.text: **Mechanisms of oliguria in acute tubular necrosis:** spasm of the afferent arterioles (RAAS, tubuloglomerular feedback — the macula densa senses an increased sodium load and reduces filtration), obstruction of the tubules by dead cells and casts (intratubular pressure rises and filtration falls), back-leak of filtrate through the damaged tubular wall into the blood, interstitial edema.

blocks.text: Chronic kidney failure (chronic kidney disease)

**Chronic kidney failure** — a progressive decline in renal function resulting from a gradual, irreversible reduction in the number of functioning nephrons (GFR below 60 ml/min or signs of kidney damage for more than 3 months).

**Causes:** diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy), arterial hypertension (nephrosclerosis), chronic glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, polycystic disease, urinary tract obstruction, amyloidosis.

**Pathogenesis:** as nephrons are lost, the remaining nephrons work in a hyperfiltration mode (**adaptive hyperfiltration**) — glomerular pressure rises and they gradually become sclerotic (**progressive nephrosclerosis**) — a “vicious circle”. Proteinuria and angiotensin II enhance interstitial fibrosis.

**Stages (by GFR):** latent (GFR 90–60) → compensated → polyuria, nocturia, isosthenuria (GFR 60–30; osmotic diuresis in the surviving nephrons) → increasing azotemia (GFR 30–15) → **terminal (uremic)** stage (GFR below 15) — oliguria; hemodialysis or kidney transplantation is required.
Pathogenesis of uremia
**Uremia** — poisoning of the body by metabolic products in end-stage kidney failure:

items: **uremic toxins** — urea, creatinine, guanidines, phenols, indole, “middle molecules”, parathyroid hormone (one of the most important “uremic toxins”);
**nervous system** — uremic encephalopathy (weakness, drowsiness, coma), polyneuropathy;
**cardiovascular** — hypertension, uremic pericarditis (pericardial friction rub), heart failure;
**respiratory** — Kussmaul breathing (acidosis), uremic pneumonitis, ammonia odor from the mouth;
**digestive** — uremic gastroenteritis (urea is broken down to ammonia in the intestine and irritates the mucosa), nausea, vomiting;
**blood** — anemia, platelet dysfunction (bleeding), immunodeficiency;
**skin** — dryness, itching, “uremic frost” (urea crystals excreted through the skin);
**bone** — renal osteodystrophy;
**water–electrolyte** — hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia.

sections.title: 8. Features of renal disorders in children

items: In infants GFR and concentrating ability are low (they mature by 1–2 years) — they are sensitive to dehydration and to excessive fluid administration.
Tubular bicarbonate reabsorption and H+ secretion are low — a tendency to metabolic acidosis.
Congenital defects (urinary tract anomalies, vesicoureteral reflux) are the main cause of pyelonephritis.
The main cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is **minimal change disease** (responds well to glucocorticoids).
Hereditary tubulopathies (Fanconi syndrome, phosphate diabetes, renal tubular acidosis) often present in childhood with rickets-like changes and growth retardation.
A frequent cause of acute kidney failure in children is **hemolytic uremic syndrome** (after diarrhea associated with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli).

sections.title: 9. Renal function tests. The Zimnitsky test

blocks.text: **Zimnitsky test** — a method of assessing the **concentrating and diluting** ability of the kidneys under an ordinary drinking regimen.
Procedure:

items: The patient follows the usual diet and drinking regimen (diuretics are stopped); the fluid intake is recorded.
At 6 a.m. the bladder is emptied (this urine is discarded).
Then urine is collected every 3 hours into separate containers: at 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 3 and 6 o'clock — 8 portions in total.
The volume and specific gravity (with a urometer) of each portion are determined.
Day (9–18) and night (21–6) diuresis and daily diuresis are calculated.

blocks.text: Normally:

items: daily diuresis is 70–80 percent of the fluid intake;
day diuresis is about 2/3 of the daily total, night diuresis — 1/3;
portion volumes vary within 40–350 ml;
the difference between the highest and lowest specific gravity is 8–10 or more (e.g. 1008–1025), and the maximum specific gravity is above 1020.

parts.text: Other functional tests: the **Rehberg–Tareev test** (determining GFR and tubular reabsorption from endogenous creatinine clearance), the **Nechiporenko test** (number of leukocytes, erythrocytes and casts in 1 ml of urine), the concentration test (dry diet) and the dilution test (water load). In modern practice GFR is usually calculated from blood creatinine using formulas (CKD-EPI).

skills.title: Skill: interpreting the results of the Zimnitsky test

items: Calculate the daily diuresis and compare it with the fluid intake.
Calculate day and night diuresis and determine their ratio.
Find the highest and lowest specific gravity among the portions.
If the maximum specific gravity is below 1020 — concentrating ability is reduced (hyposthenuria).
If the difference in specific gravity is 1–2 units and the values are around 1010 — isosthenuria.
Write a conclusion: polyuria or oliguria, nocturia, hypo- or isosthenuria.

skills.title: Skill: calculating creatinine clearance

items: Determine the minute diuresis: V = daily urine (ml) / 1440.
Take the urine (U) and blood (P) creatinine concentrations in the same units.
Calculate GFR = (U × V) / P.
Compare the result with the normal value (80–120 ml/min) and determine the stage of kidney failure.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: 2 weeks after tonsillitis, a 9-year-old child's face and eyelids are swollen, urine output has decreased and the urine is “meat-washings”-colored. BP 145/95 mm Hg. Urine: protein 1.5 g/l, altered erythrocytes covering the whole field of view, erythrocyte casts. Blood: creatinine slightly raised, high ASO titer, complement C3 decreased.
cases.ask: What syndrome and disease is this? Explain the pathogenesis. What is the mechanism of the edema and hypertension?
cases.answer: Nephritic syndrome — acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Group A streptococcal antigens and antibodies against them form immune complexes that are deposited on the glomerular basement membrane (a type III allergic reaction); complement is activated (C3 is consumed and decreases) and neutrophils accumulate and damage the capillaries. Membrane permeability increases and erythrocytes (altered, with casts — glomerular hematuria) and protein pass into the urine. Filtration falls in the inflamed glomeruli — oliguria, azotemia; because tubular sodium reabsorption is preserved, sodium and water are retained — hypervolemia: edema (on the face and eyelids — loose tissue) and hypertension (increased circulating blood volume, RAAS activation).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 56-year-old woman has had diabetes mellitus for 20 years. Weakness, loss of appetite, nausea, skin itching, frequent urination at night. The skin is pale-yellowish and dry. BP 170/100. Blood: Hb 82 g/l, creatinine 520 µmol/l, urea 28 mmol/l, K+ 5.8 mmol/l, pH 7.28, phosphates raised, calcium decreased, parathyroid hormone raised. Zimnitsky test: specific gravity 1008–1011, night diuresis exceeds day diuresis.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Interpret the laboratory values. What is the mechanism of the anemia and bone disorders?
cases.answer: Chronic kidney failure resulting from diabetic nephropathy, uremic stage. The number of functioning nephrons is sharply reduced — azotemia (raised creatinine and urea), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis (reduced excretion of H+ and ammonium), hyperphosphatemia. Isosthenuria and nocturia in the Zimnitsky test — the remaining nephrons work in an osmotic diuresis mode and cannot concentrate the urine. Anemia — reduced erythropoietin production, the effect of uremic toxins on erythropoiesis and shortened erythrocyte lifespan. Calcitriol synthesis decreases and calcium absorption falls, phosphates are retained — hypocalcemia stimulates parathyroid hormone (secondary hyperparathyroidism) — renal osteodystrophy. Nausea and itching — the effect of uremic toxins. Hypertension — sodium and water retention, RAAS activation. The patient needs hemodialysis or kidney transplantation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 35-year-old man's legs were trapped for a long time in a car accident. After rescue his BP fell, his urine became brown-red, and over the following days daily diuresis was 150 ml. Blood: creatinine 480 µmol/l, K+ 6.9 mmol/l, CK sharply raised, myoglobinuria. ECG: tall peaked T waves.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain the mechanism of the acute kidney failure. Which disturbance is the most life-threatening?
cases.answer: Acute kidney failure (renal, acute tubular necrosis) due to crush syndrome, oligoanuric stage. Myoglobin, potassium, phosphates and toxins pass from the damaged muscles into the blood (rhabdomyolysis — raised CK). Myoglobin precipitates in the tubules in an acidic environment, obstructs them and has a direct toxic effect on the epithelium; hypovolemia and shock aggravate renal ischemia (spasm of the afferent arterioles). As a result filtration falls sharply — anuria, azotemia. The most dangerous is hyperkalemia (release of potassium from muscles and failure of renal excretion): myocardial excitability and conduction are disturbed, there are tall peaked T waves on the ECG and the risk of cardiac arrest is high. Emergency measures: calcium preparations, glucose–insulin, hemodialysis.

topics.title: Pathophysiology of the endocrine system

goals.text: To explain to the student the structure and regulatory hierarchy of the endocrine system, the mechanisms of hormone action, the general etiology and pathogenesis of endocrine disorders (central, glandular and extraglandular mechanisms), the main forms of dysfunction of the hypothalamic–pituitary system, the adrenal glands, the thyroid and parathyroid glands and the gonads, and the methods of examining the endocrine system, including the Galli Mainini test.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the hierarchy of endocrine regulation and the feedback principle;
the mechanisms of hormone action and the types of receptors;
the central, glandular and peripheral mechanisms of endocrine disorders;
the main forms of hypothalamic–pituitary disorders (gigantism, acromegaly, pituitary dwarfism, panhypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus, Cushing disease);
hyper- and hypofunction of the adrenal, thyroid and parathyroid glands;
the methods of examining the endocrine system and the essence of the Galli Mainini test.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the level of the disorder (primary or secondary) from hormone levels and functional tests;
relate the clinical signs of endocrinopathies to their pathogenesis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The feedback principle is the key to determining the level of a disorder. In **primary** (peripheral gland) insufficiency the peripheral hormone is low and the tropic hormone is **high** (the inhibition is lost). In **secondary** (pituitary) insufficiency both are **low**. For example: in primary hypothyroidism T4 ↓, TSH ↑; in secondary hypothyroidism T4 ↓, TSH ↓.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The exact procedure of the Galli Mainini test (animal species, urine volume, observation time) should be checked against the department's methodological manual. Other experiments demonstrated in class: comparing basal metabolism and resistance to an oxygen-free environment in animals given thyroid preparations; observing hypoglycemic convulsions after insulin administration (topic 10).

blocks.text: The endocrine system is organized **hierarchically**: cerebral cortex and limbic system → **hypothalamus** (liberins and statins) → **pituitary** (tropic hormones) → **peripheral glands** (adrenal cortex, thyroid, gonads) → target tissues. Glands that are independent of the pituitary (pancreatic islets, parathyroid glands, adrenal medulla) are regulated mainly by the controlled variable itself (glucose, calcium) or by the nervous system.

blocks.label: Figure 26.1
blocks.caption: The hypothalamic–pituitary system and feedback

blocks.text: **Feedback principle:** when the level of a peripheral hormone rises, it inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary (**negative feedback**) — the hormone level is kept normal. In some cases positive feedback operates (in the menstrual cycle the estrogen peak triggers a surge of LH release).

parts.text: The feedback principle is the key to determining the level of a disorder. In **primary** (peripheral gland) insufficiency the peripheral hormone is low and the tropic hormone is **high** (the inhibition is lost). In **secondary** (pituitary) insufficiency both are **low**. For example: in primary hypothyroidism T4 ↓, TSH ↑; in secondary hypothyroidism T4 ↓, TSH ↓.

blocks.text: Endocrine disorders manifest as **hyperfunction** (excess hormone action), **hypofunction** (deficiency) and **dysfunction** (imbalance between different hormones).

blocks.caption: Main mechanisms of endocrine disorders

head: Degree
Mechanisms
Examples
rows: Altered secretion of liberins and tropic hormones: tumors, trauma, hemorrhage, infections, autoimmune processes, nervous system disorders (stress)
Cushing disease, acromegaly, pituitary dwarfism, Sheehan syndrome
Destruction of glandular tissue (autoimmune, infection, hemorrhage), tumor (adenoma — hyperfunction), hereditary defect of hormone-synthesizing enzymes, lack of raw material (iodine)

Altered binding of the hormone to transport proteins; impaired inactivation of the hormone in the liver and kidney; impaired conversion to the active form (T4 → T3); antibodies against the hormone; receptor defects or resistance; ectopic hormone production (tumors)

blocks.text: Hyperfunction of the adenohypophysis

items: **Excess somatotropin (growth hormone)** (usually a somatotroph adenoma) before closure of the bone growth plates (childhood and adolescence) — **gigantism** (height above 200 cm in men, above 190 cm in women).

**Excess growth hormone after closure of the growth plates** — **acromegaly**: the hands, feet, nose, lower jaw, ears and tongue enlarge, the internal organs enlarge (splanchnomegaly), and the facial features coarsen; counter-insulin effect — **hyperglycemia** (secondary diabetes), arterial hypertension, cardiomyopathy. The effects are mediated mainly by **IGF-1**, produced in the liver.
**Excess ACTH** — **Cushing disease** (pituitary adenoma): secondary hypercortisolism.
**Excess prolactin** (prolactinoma) — in women galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility; in men impotence, gynecomastia (prolactin inhibits GnRH).

blocks.text: Hypofunction of the adenohypophysis

items: **Pituitary dwarfism** — growth hormone deficiency in childhood: marked growth retardation, but body proportions are preserved and mental development is normal (unlike hypothyroid dwarfism); sexual development is also often delayed.

**Panhypopituitarism** — deficiency of all hormones of the adenohypophysis: tumors, trauma, surgery, radiation, postpartum pituitary necrosis (**Sheehan syndrome** — ischemia of the pituitary, enlarged during pregnancy, due to heavy blood loss at delivery), **Simmonds disease** (pituitary cachexia). Signs: secondary hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism (amenorrhea, loss of libido, loss of body hair), failure of lactation, weakness, hypoglycemia, hypotension.

blocks.text: Disorders of the neurohypophysis

items: **Diabetes insipidus** — ADH deficiency (**central**: tumors of the hypothalamus and pituitary, trauma, infections, surgery) or insensitivity of the kidney to ADH (**nephrogenic**). Water reabsorption in the collecting ducts decreases — **polyuria** (5–20 l per day), very low urine specific gravity (1001–1005), intense thirst (polydipsia), risk of dehydration and hypernatremia.

**Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion** (Parhon syndrome) — tumors (small cell lung cancer — ectopic ADH), CNS diseases, lung diseases, drugs: water is retained — **water intoxication**, dilutional **hyponatremia**, cerebral edema; the urine specific gravity is high, and there is usually no edema.

blocks.text: Hyperfunction of the adrenal cortex
**Hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome)** — excess glucocorticoids.
Signs and mechanisms:

items: **centripetal obesity** (“moon face”, fat on the back of the neck — “buffalo hump”, abdominal obesity, thin limbs) — different sensitivity of adipose tissue in different regions to cortisol and insulin;
**protein catabolism** — muscle atrophy and weakness, thinning of the skin, purple-red striae (stretch marks), osteoporosis (pathological fractures), slow wound healing;
**steroid diabetes** — increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance;
**arterial hypertension** — mineralocorticoid effect, increased angiotensinogen, increased vascular sensitivity to catecholamines;
**immunosuppression** — lymphopenia, eosinopenia, susceptibility to infections;
mental changes; in women, hirsutism and menstrual disorders (increased androgens).

blocks.text: **Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)** — an aldosterone-producing adenoma: sodium and water retention → **hypertension**; potassium loss → **hypokalemia** (muscle weakness, arrhythmias, polyuria), metabolic alkalosis; renin is **decreased** (the difference from secondary hyperaldosteronism, in which renin is increased).

**Adrenogenital syndrome** — a hereditary defect of cortisol-synthesizing enzymes (most often 21-hydroxylase): cortisol decreases → ACTH increases → hyperplasia of the adrenal cortex and excess androgen production → virilization of the external genitalia in girls, precocious puberty in boys; in the severe form aldosterone is also low — salt-wasting syndrome.
Hypofunction of the adrenal cortex
**Primary chronic insufficiency (Addison disease)** — destruction of more than 90 percent of the adrenal cortex: autoimmune adrenalitis (the main cause), tuberculosis, metastases, hemorrhage.

items: glucocorticoid deficiency — weakness, weight loss, **hypoglycemia**, hypotension, intolerance of stress;
mineralocorticoid deficiency — loss of sodium and water (hypovolemia, hypotension), **hyperkalemia**, craving for salty food;

**hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes** (“bronze disease”) — the fall in cortisol, through feedback, leads to an increase in **ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone** (whose common precursor is proopiomelanocortin). In secondary (pituitary) insufficiency there is no hyperpigmentation.

blocks.text: **Acute adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis)** — Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal hemorrhage in meningococcal sepsis), sudden withdrawal of glucocorticoids, stress in Addison disease: collapse, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, dehydration — life-threatening.
Hyperfunction of the adrenal medulla

**Pheochromocytoma** — a tumor of the chromaffin cells with excess catecholamines: paroxysmal (crisis) or persistent **arterial hypertension**, tachycardia, headache, sweating, pallor, hyperglycemia, weight loss.

Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis)
Hypothyroidism
rows: Diffuse toxic goiter (Graves–Basedow disease — autoantibodies that stimulate TSH receptors), toxic adenoma, early phase of thyroiditis
Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto), iodine deficiency, thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy; secondary — pituitary
↑ (uncoupling of oxidation and phosphorylation, increased Na+/K+-ATPase activity)
Cold intolerance, dry and cold skin
Tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, systolic hypertension (increased sensitivity of beta-receptors)
Mucous edema (myxedema) — accumulation of glycosaminoglycans under the skin

blocks.text: **Congenital hypothyroidism in children — cretinism:** thyroid hormones are essential for brain development, so if it is not detected early — severe mental retardation, dwarfism (with disproportionate body), delayed teething, a large tongue and prolonged jaundice. This is why **neonatal screening** (TSH) is performed in all newborns.

**Endemic goiter** — iodine deficiency (some regions of Uzbekistan are also iodine-deficient areas): thyroid hormone synthesis decreases → TSH increases → the glandular tissue undergoes compensatory hyperplasia (goiter). Prevention — iodized salt.

items: **Hyperparathyroidism** — excess parathyroid hormone: primary (adenoma), secondary (chronic kidney failure, vitamin D deficiency — in response to hypocalcemia). In the primary form: **hypercalcemia**, hypophosphatemia, release of calcium from bones (osteoporosis, osteitis fibrosa, fractures), kidney stones, peptic ulcer, muscle weakness, polyuria. To remember: “**bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans**”.

**Hypoparathyroidism** — most often damage to the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery: **hypocalcemia** → increased neuromuscular excitability → **tetany** (cramps, “obstetrician's hand”, laryngospasm), positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, QT prolongation.

**Hypogonadism** — primary (damage to the gonads: Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY; Shereshevsky–Turner syndrome 45,X0; orchitis, trauma, radiation — LH and FSH increased) and secondary (damage to the hypothalamus–pituitary — LH and FSH decreased).
Androgen deficiency before puberty — **eunuchoidism** (long limbs, undeveloped secondary sexual characteristics).
**Precocious puberty** — true (hypothalamic tumors, early activation of GnRH) and pseudo- (adrenal and gonadal tumors, adrenogenital syndrome).

sections.title: 9. Methods of examining the endocrine system

items: **Determining hormone levels** — radioimmune, enzyme immunoassay and chemiluminescent methods (in blood, urine, saliva).
**Stimulation tests** — when hypofunction is suspected (ACTH test — adrenal reserve; insulin hypoglycemia test — growth hormone and ACTH reserve).
**Suppression tests** — when hyperfunction is suspected (dexamethasone test — distinguishing Cushing disease from Cushing syndrome; suppression of growth hormone by a glucose load — acromegaly).
**Glucose tolerance test** (topic 10).
**Imaging** — US, CT, MRI (pituitary adenoma), scintigraphy (thyroid gland).
**Detecting autoantibodies** (to thyroid peroxidase, TSH receptors, the adrenal cortex).
**Biological tests** — assessing hormone activity in animals (historical methods; e.g. the Galli Mainini test).
**Experimental methods** — removal of the gland (extirpation), administration of a gland extract or hormone, transplantation of glandular tissue.

blocks.text: The Galli Mainini test

**The Galli Mainini test** (1947) — a biological method for the early detection of pregnancy. The urine of a pregnant woman contains **chorionic gonadotropin** (produced by the placenta); it acts on the germ cells of a male frog (or toad) and stimulates the **release of spermatozoa**.
Procedure:

items: Examine the fluid from the cloaca of a male frog (toad) under the microscope and confirm that it contains no spermatozoa.
Inject a few milliliters of the morning urine of the woman being tested into the dorsal lymph sac of the frog.
After 1–2 hours, take fluid from the cloaca with a pipette and examine it under the microscope.
**If spermatozoa are found, the test is positive** (chorionic gonadotropin is present in the urine — pregnancy is likely); if not — negative.

blocks.text: **Diagnostic significance:** chorionic gonadotropin rises sharply in pregnancy, as well as in **trophoblastic tumors** (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) and some testicular tumors. The test is of historical importance; today it has been replaced by **immunological detection of β-chorionic gonadotropin** in blood and urine (test strips, enzyme immunoassay) — these are more sensitive and faster.

parts.text: The exact procedure of the Galli Mainini test (animal species, urine volume, observation time) should be checked against the department's methodological manual. Other experiments demonstrated in class: comparing basal metabolism and resistance to an oxygen-free environment in animals given thyroid preparations; observing hypoglycemic convulsions after insulin administration (topic 10).

skills.title: Skill: determining the level of an endocrine disorder by the feedback principle

items: Assess the level of the peripheral hormone (increased or decreased).
Assess the level of the corresponding tropic hormone.
Peripheral hormone low, tropic hormone high — primary (glandular) insufficiency.
Peripheral hormone and tropic hormone both low — secondary (pituitary or hypothalamic) insufficiency.
Peripheral hormone high, tropic hormone low — primary hyperfunction (gland tumor or autoimmune stimulation).
Both high — central (pituitary) hyperfunction or ectopic secretion.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting the result of the Galli Mainini test

items: Before injecting the urine, confirm that there are no spermatozoa in the cloacal fluid.
After the specified time, examine the cloacal fluid under the microscope.
Spermatozoa present — positive result; absent — negative.
Compare the result with the clinical data (pregnancy, suspected trophoblastic tumor).
Write down the limitations of the method (possibility of false-positive and false-negative results) and modern alternatives.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Over the last 2 years a 38-year-old woman has gained weight, mainly on the face and abdomen, while her arms and legs have become thinner. Broad purple-red striae on the abdominal skin, a round, flushed face, increased hair growth, menstrual disturbance. BP 165/100 mm Hg, blood glucose 8.2 mmol/l, potassium slightly decreased, lymphopenia. Cortisol high, ACTH high. A low dose of dexamethasone does not suppress cortisol, but a high dose does. MRI: a pituitary microadenoma.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Determine the level of the disorder. Explain the pathogenesis of the main signs.
cases.answer: Cushing disease — central (pituitary) hypercortisolism: a pituitary corticotroph adenoma produces excess ACTH, which stimulates both adrenal cortices (cortisol and ACTH both raised; the adenoma is partly sensitive to feedback — a high dose of dexamethasone suppresses it). Centripetal obesity — different sensitivity of adipose tissue in different regions to cortisol and insulin; striae, thin skin, thin limbs — protein catabolism; steroid diabetes — increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance; hypertension and hypokalemia — the mineralocorticoid effect of cortisol and increased vascular sensitivity; lymphopenia — immunosuppression; hirsutism and menstrual disturbance — increased adrenal androgens under the action of ACTH.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 42-year-old man has weakness, fatigue, weight loss, lack of appetite, dizziness and a craving for salty food. The skin, especially the palmar creases and elbows, and the oral mucosa are dark brown. BP 90/55 mm Hg. Blood: Na+ 128, K+ 5.9 mmol/l, glucose 3.2 mmol/l, cortisol low, ACTH sharply raised, antibodies to the adrenal cortex positive.
cases.ask: What is the disease? What is the level of the disorder? How did the hyperpigmentation, hypotension, electrolyte disturbances and hypoglycemia develop?
cases.answer: Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease), autoimmune adrenalitis. The gland itself is destroyed — cortisol is low and, through feedback, ACTH is sharply raised (primary level). ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone are formed from a common precursor — proopiomelanocortin; their increase stimulates melanocytes — hyperpigmentation. Aldosterone deficiency leads to loss of sodium and water (hyponatremia, hypovolemia, hypotension) and potassium retention (hyperkalemia); craving for salt — sodium deficiency. In cortisol deficiency gluconeogenesis decreases — hypoglycemia; vascular sensitivity to catecholamines falls — hypotension worsens. With stress, infection or surgery an Addisonian crisis (collapse) may develop — the patient needs lifelong hormone replacement therapy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 29-year-old woman has had palpitations, sweating, hand tremor, nervousness and insomnia for several months, and has lost 8 kg despite a good appetite; diarrhea. Her eyes are protruding and the thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged. Pulse 120 beats/min, BP 150/70 mm Hg. Blood: free T4 and T3 sharply raised, TSH very low, antibodies to TSH receptors positive.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its pathogenesis. What is the mechanism of the weight loss, tachycardia and large pulse pressure?
cases.answer: Diffuse toxic goiter (Graves–Basedow disease). Autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptors continuously stimulate the gland in place of TSH — the gland enlarges diffusely and produces excess hormones; excess T3 and T4 suppress TSH through feedback (primary hyperfunction). Exophthalmos — autoimmune inflammation of the orbital tissues. Thyroid hormones increase basal metabolism (Na+/K+-ATPase activity, partial uncoupling of oxidation and phosphorylation, heat production) and enhance protein and fat catabolism — weight loss despite a good appetite, sweating. The number and sensitivity of beta-adrenoceptors increase — tachycardia, tremor, nervousness; stroke volume increases (systolic pressure rises) and peripheral vessels dilate (diastolic pressure falls) — large pulse pressure. Intestinal peristalsis accelerates — diarrhea.

Excess cortisol: centripetal obesity, striae, diabetes
Aldosterone ↑, renin ↓: hypertension, hypokalemia
Cortisol and aldosterone ↓, ACTH ↑: hyperpigmentation
Antibodies that stimulate TSH receptors
Congenital hypothyroidism; mental retardation and dwarfism
Hypocalcemia — tetany
Chorionic gonadotropin — release of spermatozoa in the male frog

topics.title: Pathophysiology of extreme states (seminar)

goals.text: To explain to the student the concept of extreme and terminal states, the general pathogenesis of conditions associated with exhaustion of the body's adaptive mechanisms, the causes, stages and mechanisms of shock, collapse, coma, crush syndrome and terminal states (preagony, agony, clinical and biological death), and the pathophysiological basis of resuscitation and post-resuscitation disease; to teach the student to apply this knowledge to clinical cases.
By the end of the session, the student should know:

items: the definition of extreme and terminal states and their common features;
the types, stages and general pathogenesis of shock;
the mechanisms of impaired microcirculation and multiple organ failure in shock;
the difference between collapse and shock;
the types, general pathogenesis and degrees of depth of coma;
the pathogenesis of crush syndrome;
the stages of terminal states, the factors affecting the duration of clinical death, and post-resuscitation disease.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the shock index and assess the severity of shock;
assess the level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale;
determine the type of shock and coma in clinical cases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Multiple organ failure syndrome** — the main cause of death in shock: **shock lung** (acute respiratory distress syndrome — damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia), **shock kidney** (acute kidney failure — prerenal, then acute tubular necrosis), shock liver (cytolysis, jaundice), intestine (mucosal ischemia, translocation of bacteria and endotoxins), heart (reduced coronary perfusion, myocardial depression), CNS (encephalopathy), blood (DIC).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Collapse is not shock, but prolonged collapse can progress to shock through tissue hypoxia and impaired microcirculation. **Fainting (syncope)** — a brief (seconds, minutes) loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery, resulting from short-term cerebral hypoperfusion (vasovagal, orthostatic, cardiogenic — arrhythmias).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The duration of clinical death: “**cold prolongs it, heat shortens it, a long agony steals it**”.

blocks.text: **Extreme state** — a state resulting from extraordinarily strong influences on the body (injury, blood loss, infection, poisoning, etc.) with excessive strain and exhaustion of the adaptive mechanisms and a risk of profound disturbance of vital functions. These include **shock, collapse, coma**, crush syndrome and acute organ failure.
**Terminal state** — states on the border between life and death that do not resolve spontaneously and lead to death without special help: preagony, terminal pause, agony and clinical death.
Common features of extreme states:

items: disturbance of vital functions (circulation, respiration, CNS activity);
initial hyperactivity of the adaptive mechanisms followed by their exhaustion (stress reaction → exhaustion);
**hypoxia** — the common pathogenetic link of all extreme states;
metabolic acidosis, endogenous intoxication;
formation of **vicious circles** and multiple organ failure.

blocks.text: **Shock** — an acute, severe generalized pathological process developing as a result of extremely strong influences, characterized by a sharp decrease in the blood supply (perfusion) of organs and tissues, cellular hypoxia and metabolic disturbance, followed by multiple organ failure.

blocks.title: Table 27.1. Types of shock (by pathogenesis)
head: Type
Main mechanism
Examples
rows: Blood loss (hemorrhagic), plasma loss (burns), dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea)
Sharp decline in the pumping function of the heart
Extensive myocardial infarction, severe arrhythmias, acute valvular insufficiency
Pericardial tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax
Sharp fall in vascular tone, redistribution of blood to the periphery
Mixed: pain, blood and plasma loss, toxemia

blocks.text: General pathogenesis of shock

blocks.label: Figure 27.1
blocks.caption: Pathogenesis of shock and the vicious circle

blocks.text: Stages of shock (according to N. I. Pirogov):

items: **Erectile (excitation) stage** — short (minutes), especially marked in traumatic and burn shock: strong pain impulses, excitation of the CNS and the sympathoadrenal system — the patient is restless, agitated and talkative, BP normal or raised, tachycardia, pale skin.

**Torpid (inhibition) stage** — inhibition of the CNS: the patient is apathetic, immobile and shows no interest in the surroundings, BP decreased, pulse rapid and weak (thready), skin pale-gray, cold sweat, oliguria.

blocks.text: Stages by circulatory changes:

items: **Compensated shock** — under the action of catecholamines, angiotensin II and vasopressin the vessels of the skin, muscles and internal organs (intestine, kidney) constrict and blood is directed mainly to the brain and heart — **centralization of the circulation**; BP is maintained.

**Decompensated (progressive) shock** — with prolonged ischemia, lactate, H+, adenosine and histamine accumulate in the tissues; the **precapillary sphincters**, being sensitive to them, relax, while the **postcapillary venules** remain constricted — blood enters the capillaries but cannot leave (**stasis**, “sequestration”); hydrostatic pressure rises and plasma leaks into the tissue, the blood thickens, erythrocytes aggregate (**sludge**) and DIC develops. Venous return decreases and BP falls — **decentralization**: the brain and heart also become ischemic.

**Irreversible shock** — cells die en masse, and lysosomal enzymes, myocardial depressant factor (formed in pancreatic ischemia) and endotoxins (which enter the blood when the intestinal barrier fails) accumulate; treatment is ineffective.

parts.text: **Multiple organ failure syndrome** — the main cause of death in shock: **shock lung** (acute respiratory distress syndrome — damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia), **shock kidney** (acute kidney failure — prerenal, then acute tubular necrosis), shock liver (cytolysis, jaundice), intestine (mucosal ischemia, translocation of bacteria and endotoxins), heart (reduced coronary perfusion, myocardial depression), CNS (encephalopathy), blood (DIC).

blocks.text: **Shock index (Allgöwer index)** = pulse / systolic BP. Normally about 0.5–0.7; around 1.0 — moderately severe shock (about 20–30 percent of blood volume lost); 1.5 or higher — severe shock.
Some types of shock

items: **Hemorrhagic shock** — when more than 20–25 percent of the circulating blood volume is lost rapidly (topic 17).

**Burn shock** — with deep burns of more than 15–20 percent of the body surface (more than 10 percent in children): severe pain, **plasma loss** due to a sharp increase in capillary permeability — hemoconcentration (hematocrit and hemoglobin rise), hypovolemia; toxins from the burned tissues (burn toxemia).

**Septic shock** — bacterial endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) activates macrophages → cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) → activation of **inducible NO synthase** → excess NO formation → marked vasodilation and hypotension; endothelial damage, increased capillary permeability, DIC, mitochondrial dysfunction. There is an initial “warm” phase (hyperdynamic — warm skin, increased cardiac output) and a later “cold” phase (hypodynamic).

**Anaphylactic shock** — a type I allergic reaction: histamine, leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor are released from mast cells and basophils → marked vasodilation, increased vascular permeability (plasma leakage), bronchospasm, laryngeal edema (topic 8). Care — immediate epinephrine.

**Cardiogenic shock** — when more than 40 percent of the left ventricular myocardium is damaged (topic 21): cardiac output falls, with pulmonary congestion (pulmonary edema) together with peripheral hypoperfusion.

blocks.text: **Collapse** — acute vascular insufficiency resulting from an acute fall in vascular tone and (or) a decrease in circulating blood volume: arterial and venous pressure fall sharply, with hypoxia of the brain, heart and other organs.

**Causes:** infections and intoxications (critical fall of fever, typhoid fever, pneumonia), blood loss, orthostatic position (standing up quickly, antihypertensive drugs), adrenal insufficiency, severe hypoxia, poisoning.

blocks.title: Table 27.2. Distinguishing shock from collapse
head: Feature
Shock
Collapse
rows: Strain of compensatory reactions, followed by impaired microcirculation
Primary fall in vascular tone and (or) decrease in blood volume
Excitation in the erectile stage, inhibition in the torpid stage
Usually recovers quickly if the cause is removed

parts.text: Collapse is not shock, but prolonged collapse can progress to shock through tissue hypoxia and impaired microcirculation. **Fainting (syncope)** — a brief (seconds, minutes) loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery, resulting from short-term cerebral hypoperfusion (vasovagal, orthostatic, cardiogenic — arrhythmias).

blocks.text: **Coma** — an extremely severe state resulting from profound inhibition of the CNS, with complete loss of consciousness, weakening or loss of responses to external stimuli, and disturbed reflexes and regulation of vital functions (respiration, circulation).

blocks.title: Table 27.3. Types of coma
head: Group
Types
rows: Traumatic, stroke (hemorrhagic, ischemic), tumors, meningitis and encephalitis, epileptic
Diabetic ketoacidotic, hyperosmolar, lactic acidotic, hypoglycemic (topic 10), hypothyroid (myxedema), adrenal (Addisonian crisis), thyrotoxic crisis
Endogenous: uremic (topic 25), hepatic (topic 24); exogenous: poisoning with alcohol, opioids, barbiturates, carbon monoxide, organophosphorus compounds
Comas due to water–electrolyte and thermal disturbances
Hypo- and hypernatremic, heat stroke (topic 2), hypothermic

blocks.text: General pathogenesis of coma:

items: **disturbed energy supply of neurons** — hypoxia, hypoglycemia (the brain depends mainly on glucose for energy), mitochondrial damage;
**direct action of toxins** — ammonia, uremic toxins, ketone bodies, alcohol, drugs;
**water–electrolyte and acid–base disturbances** — osmotic imbalance between the intracellular and extracellular compartments (cerebral edema or dehydration of brain cells), acidosis;
**cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure** — reduced cerebral blood flow, compression of the brainstem (herniation);
**disturbed neurotransmitter metabolism** (false neurotransmitters, increased GABA-ergic inhibition);

as a result, the activity of cortical and subcortical structures is inhibited and the activating influence of the reticular formation is lost — consciousness is lost; if the process deepens, the respiratory and vasomotor centers in the medulla oblongata are damaged.

blocks.text: **Degrees of impaired consciousness:** clear consciousness → obtundation (somnolence, pre-sopor) → **sopor** (protective movements only in response to strong painful stimuli) → **coma** (I — moderate, II — deep, III — terminal, transcendental coma).

blocks.title: Table 27.4. Glasgow Coma Scale (abbreviated)
head: Criterion
Response and score
rows: Spontaneous — 4; to speech — 3; to pain — 2; none — 1
Oriented — 5; confused — 4; inappropriate words — 3; incomprehensible sounds — 2; none — 1
Obeys commands — 6; localizes pain — 5; withdraws from pain — 4; abnormal flexion — 3; abnormal extension — 2; none — 1
15 — clear consciousness; 13–14 — obtundation; 9–12 — sopor; 8 or less — coma; 3 — terminal coma

blocks.text: **Crush syndrome** — a severe condition that develops after soft tissues (mainly limb muscles) have been compressed for a long time (more than 4–6 hours) and then released (earthquakes, car accidents, building collapses).
Main links of the pathogenesis:

items: **Pain factor** — prolonged pain impulses during compression, elements of traumatic shock.

**Plasma loss** — after release, blood flows into the damaged muscles and, because capillary permeability is increased, plasma leaks into the tissue — the limb swells sharply, with **hypovolemia** and hemoconcentration.

**Toxemia** — **myoglobin**, **potassium**, phosphates, creatine, lactate and other toxins are released from the ischemic muscles into the blood (**rhabdomyolysis**); **hyperkalemia** can cause cardiac arrest.
**Acute kidney failure** — myoglobin precipitates in the tubules in an acidic environment, obstructs them and damages the epithelium; hypovolemia aggravates renal ischemia (topic 25).

blocks.text: **Periods:** early (days 1–3, shock and hemodynamic disturbances predominate), intermediate (days 3–12, acute kidney failure), late (recovery, local complications — infection, muscle atrophy, contractures).

parts.text: Care: start intravenous fluids **before** releasing the compressed limb; at the moment of release, bandage the limb and cool it (to reduce the rapid absorption of toxins), give analgesia and alkaline solutions (alkalinizing the urine reduces myoglobin precipitation), monitor for hyperkalemia, and use hemodialysis if needed.

blocks.label: Figure 27.2
blocks.caption: Sequence of terminal states

blocks.title: Table 27.5. Stages of terminal states
head: Stage
Signs
Pathophysiological essence
rows: Consciousness clouded or absent, BP sharply low (systolic below 60–70 mm or undetectable), thready pulse, breathing rapid and shallow or slow, skin pale-bluish
Increasing hypoxia, inhibition of the higher parts of the CNS
Breathing stops for a few seconds up to 2–4 minutes, bradycardia, the pupils dilate
Extinction of cortical activity, predominance of vagal influence
Gasping (agonal) breathing, a brief slight rise in BP, temporary increase in cardiac activity, convulsions, relaxation of the sphincters
The last activity of the bulbar centers, released from the control of the higher parts; anaerobic glycolysis predominates
Breathing and cardiac activity have stopped, no reflexes, the pupils dilated and unresponsive to light
Metabolism continues at a minimal level; the changes are still reversible
Irreversible changes; then signs of death (livor mortis, rigor mortis, algor mortis, the “cat's eye” sign)
Death of the neurons of the cerebral cortex first of all

blocks.text: Clinical death
**Duration** — **4–6 minutes** at normal temperature: during this time the cerebral cortex tolerates complete ischemia.

**Factors that increase its duration: hypothermia** (metabolism and oxygen demand decrease — in drowning in cold water clinical death may last 30 minutes or more), early childhood, sudden death (electric current, arrhythmia — the preagony is short and energy reserves are preserved).
**Factors that shorten its duration:** prolonged preagony and agony (severe chronic diseases, prolonged blood loss — energy reserves exhausted), hyperthermia, old age.
Resuscitation and post-resuscitation disease
**Resuscitation** — restoration of vital functions: opening the airway, artificial ventilation, closed-chest cardiac massage, defibrillation (in ventricular fibrillation), drugs (epinephrine).
**Post-resuscitation disease** (V. A. Negovsky) — a specific pathological state after successful recovery from clinical death:

items: **reperfusion injury** — when blood flow is restored, large amounts of reactive oxygen species are formed and damage membranes through lipid peroxidation; massive entry of Ca2+ into the cells;
cerebral edema and posthypoxic encephalopathy, delayed death of some neurons (apoptosis);
cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmias;
multiple organ failure (lungs, kidneys, liver);
translocation of endotoxins from the intestine, DIC, immunodepression.

parts.text: The duration of clinical death: “**cold prolongs it, heat shortens it, a long agony steals it**”.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the shock index and assessing the severity of shock

items: Count the patient's pulse rate for 1 minute.
Measure the systolic arterial pressure.
Shock index = pulse / systolic BP.
Assess the result: 0.5–0.7 — normal; about 1.0 — moderately severe; 1.5 or more — severe shock.
Assess additional signs: skin color and temperature, level of consciousness, hourly diuresis (below 0.5 ml/kg/h — renal hypoperfusion), capillary refill time (more than 2 seconds).

skills.title: Skill: assessing the level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale

items: Assess the eye-opening response (1–4 points).
Assess the verbal response (1–5 points).
Assess the motor response (1–6 points).
Add up the points (3–15).
Determine the degree of impaired consciousness: 15 — clear, 13–14 — obtundation, 9–12 — sopor, 8 or less — coma.
To determine the cause of the coma, assess the history, glucose, breath odor, pupils and other signs.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 30-year-old man suffered second- and third-degree burns over 40 percent of his body surface at work. In the first minutes he was agitated and shouting, BP 140/90. 2 hours later he is apathetic and answers questions slowly, BP 85/50, pulse 128 beats/min, pale skin, cold sweat, hourly diuresis 15 ml. Blood: hematocrit 0.58, hemoglobin 190 g/l, K+ raised.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Determine its stages. Explain the mechanism of the hemoconcentration, oliguria and hyperkalemia. Calculate the shock index.
cases.answer: Burn shock: first the erectile stage (pain impulses, sympathoadrenal excitation — restlessness, raised BP), then the torpid stage (CNS inhibition, hypotension, thready pulse). In the burned area capillary permeability increases sharply — plasma leaks into the tissue and out through the burn surface — hypovolemia and hemoconcentration (raised hematocrit and hemoglobin). Under the action of hypovolemia and catecholamines the renal vessels constrict and filtration decreases — oliguria (risk of shock kidney). Hyperkalemia — release of potassium from the breakdown of burned tissues and erythrocytes and reduced renal excretion. Shock index = 128 / 85 ≈ 1.5 — severe shock. Treatment — rapid infusion therapy of adequate volume, analgesia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 68-year-old woman has had a fever for 3 days (urinary tract infection). Her condition suddenly worsened: temperature 39.5 °C, BP 80/40, pulse 125 beats/min, respiratory rate 28, the skin at first warm and flushed, later cold and mottled. Scanty urine. Blood: leukocytes 22 × 10^9^/l, lactate raised, platelets decreased, creatinine raised. BP did not rise even after infusion.
cases.ask: What condition is this? Explain the pathogenesis. What are the “warm” and “cold” phases related to? What is the cause of the thrombocytopenia and the rise in lactate?
cases.answer: Septic shock (urosepsis). Endotoxin of gram-negative bacteria activates macrophages and endothelium — inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) are released; they activate inducible NO synthase — excess NO causes marked vasodilation (distributive shock, no response to infusion). The initial “warm” (hyperdynamic) phase — the peripheral vessels are dilated and cardiac output is compensatorily increased; then, because of myocardial depression and plasma leakage from the capillaries, it passes into the “cold” (hypodynamic) phase — peripheral vasoconstriction, mottled skin. Endothelial damage and activation of the clotting system — DIC (platelets are consumed). Tissue hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction — anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acidosis. Oliguria and raised creatinine — shock kidney; tachypnea — a response to acidosis and early shock lung: multiple organ failure is developing.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In winter a 7-year-old child fell into a frozen lake and was pulled out of the water after 20 minutes. No breathing or cardiac activity, pupils dilated, body temperature 28 °C. Resuscitation restored cardiac activity; over the following days cerebral edema and impaired lung and kidney function were observed, with gradual recovery.
cases.ask: Why was resuscitation successful even after 20 minutes? What condition are the post-recovery disturbances related to, and what is their mechanism?
cases.answer: At normal temperature clinical death lasts 4–6 minutes, but hypothermia (28 °C) sharply reduces the metabolism and oxygen demand of the tissues, especially the brain neurons; in children tissue resistance to hypoxia is higher, and the death was sudden (there was no prolonged agony, and energy reserves were preserved) — this is why clinical death was prolonged and resuscitation was successful. The later disturbances are post-resuscitation disease: reperfusion injury when blood flow is restored (reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, entry of Ca2+ into cells), posthypoxic cerebral edema, lung injury due to aspiration and hypoxia (respiratory distress), renal ischemia — multiple organ failure. Such patients need prolonged observation in the intensive care unit.
